Action Sports.overview: Action Sports covers skateboarding and snowboarding safety, equipment maintenance, park/slope etiquette, fundamental and intermediate maneuvers, and outdoor stewardship.

requirements.topic_heading: Hazards, Safety Gear & First Aid in Action Sports
requirements.lead_text: Do the following:
requirements.req_text: Do the following: (a) Explain to your counselor the most likely hazards you may encounter while participating in action sports (skateboarding or snowboarding) and what you should do to anticipate, help prevent, mitigate, and respond to these hazards. (b) Review prevention, symptoms, and first-aid treatment for hypothermia, frostbite, dehydration, sunburn, heat exhaustion, heatstroke, blisters, sprains, strains, fractures, head/concussion injuries, and spinal injuries. (c) Show your helmet, wrist guards, knee/elbow pads, boots, and bindings, and explain how to inspect and fit them properly.

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: Before dropping into a concrete skatepark bowl on a skateboard or riding a BMX track, how should you verify that your helmet and protective pads meet Action Sports safety standards?
quiz_item.question: Before dropping into a concrete skatepark bowl on a skateboard or riding a BMX track, how should you verify that your helmet and protective pads meet Action Sports safety standards?
options: A. Wear a lightweight road-cycling helmet tilted back on the forehead and skip wrist guards so your hands can grip the coping.
B. Fit a CPSC or ASTM F1492 certified skate or BMX helmet level across the brow with a snug chin strap, paired with knee pads, elbow pads, and wrist guards.
C. Use an unpadded hard-shell construction hat and wrap elastic athletic tape around your ankles and wrists.
D. Loosen the helmet chin strap by three finger-widths so it can slide off easily during a fall and wear only shin guards.

quiz_item.correct_answer: B. Fit a CPSC or ASTM F1492 certified skate or BMX helmet level across the brow with a snug chin strap, paired with knee pads, elbow pads, and wrist guards.

requirements.lead_text: Do the following:
requirements.req_text: Do the following: (a) Explain four features of the free enterprise system in the United States. Describe the difference between freedom and license. Tell how the Scout Oath and Scout Law apply to business and free enterprise. (b) Describe the Industrial Revolution and tell about the major developments that marked the start of the modern industrial era in the United States. Discuss three people who had a great influence on business or industry in the United States and describe what each did. (c) Identify and describe to your counselor the five primary areas of business. (d) Explain the history of labor unions in the United States and the importance of labor unions and employers working together. Identify two major labor unions currently in existence. (e) Discuss with your counselor how business impacts the local, national, and global economy.

Free Enterprise System Features Principle 2: They organized associations that promoted industrialization (p. 19).

Free Enterprise System Features Principle 3: Although more than three-fourths of the working population in the United States was involved in agriculture at the time, the Industrial Revolution spread (p. 19).

Free Enterprise System Features Principle 4: By the end of the century, the United States became the world leader in manufacturing and spurred what is known as the Second Industrial Revolution (p. 19).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Free Enterprise System Features): The United States continues to be one of the world's largest producers of goods (p. 19).
Step 2 (Free Enterprise System Features): The result of globalization is a world economy in which the borders between countries have blurred (p. 19).
Step 3 (Free Enterprise System Features): Technology, such as the internet, has helped make global corporations and m arkets possible (p. 19).
Step 4 (Free Enterprise System Features): Globalization has grown rapidly since the 1970s, but it has been an economic trend since the end of World War II in 1945 (p. 19).

quiz_item.question: Which combination accurately describes the four foundational features of the American free enterprise system covered in Requirement 1?
options: A. Centralized government price controls, guaranteed corporate profits, mandatory union membership, and fixed production quotas.
B. Public ownership of factories, elimination of market competition, state-allocated consumer goods, and interest-free national banking.
C. Private ownership of property, freedom of enterprise and choice, the profit motive, and open market competition regulated by supply and demand.
D. Barter-only trade networks, monopolistic industry trusts, mercantilist export tariffs, and lifetime employment contracts.
choices: A. Centralized government price controls, guaranteed corporate profits, mandatory union membership, and fixed production quotas.
B. Public ownership of factories, elimination of market competition, state-allocated consumer goods, and interest-free national banking.
C. Private ownership of property, freedom of enterprise and choice, the profit motive, and open market competition regulated by supply and demand.
D. Barter-only trade networks, monopolistic industry trusts, mercantilist export tariffs, and lifetime employment contracts.
quiz_item.correct_answer: C. Private ownership of property, freedom of enterprise and choice, the profit motive, and open market competition regulated by supply and demand.

step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Business Financial Statements): Financial statements for businesses usually include income statements, balance sheets, statements of retained earnings, and statements of cash flows (p. 48).
Step 2 (Business Financial Statements): Financial statements are often audited by government agencies, accountants, firms, and other entities to ensure accuracy and for tax (p. 48).
Step 3 (Business Financial Statements): The three main financial statements are the balance sheet, income statement, and cash flow statement (p. 48).
Step 4 (Business Financial Statements): The balance sheet provides an overview of assets, liabilities, and shareholders' equity as a snapshot in time (p. 48).

patrol_quiz_bank.question: Which combination accurately describes the four foundational features of the American free enterprise system covered in Requirement 1?
options: A. Centralized government price controls, guaranteed corporate profits, mandatory union membership, and fixed production quotas.
B. Public ownership of factories, elimination of market competition, state-allocated consumer goods, and interest-free national banking.
C. Private ownership of property, freedom of enterprise and choice, the profit motive, and open market competition regulated by supply and demand.
D. Barter-only trade networks, monopolistic industry trusts, mercantilist export tariffs, and lifetime employment contracts.
choices: A. Centralized government price controls, guaranteed corporate profits, mandatory union membership, and fixed production quotas.
B. Public ownership of factories, elimination of market competition, state-allocated consumer goods, and interest-free national banking.
C. Private ownership of property, freedom of enterprise and choice, the profit motive, and open market competition regulated by supply and demand.
D. Barter-only trade networks, monopolistic industry trusts, mercantilist export tariffs, and lifetime employment contracts.
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: C. Private ownership of property, freedom of enterprise and choice, the profit motive, and open market competition regulated by supply and demand.
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (C): The U.S. free enterprise system rests on private property rights, freedom of choice for producers and consumers, the incentive of profit, and competition driven by supply and demand.

intro_notes: NOTE: Choose THREE groups that have different racial, cultural, national, or ethnic backgrounds, one of which comes from your own background. Use these groups to meet requirements 1, 2, and 3.
NOTE: The official merit badge pamphlets are now free and downloadable HERE or can be purchased at the Scout Shop.

requirements.lead_text: Do TWO of the following, choosing a different group for each:
requirements.req_text: Do TWO of the following, choosing a different group for each: (a) Go to a festival, celebration, or other event identified with one of the groups. Report on what you see and learn. (b) Go to a place of worship, school, or other institution identified with one of the groups. Report on what you see and learn. (c) Talk with a person from one of the groups about the heritage and traditions of the group. Report on what you learn. (d) Learn a song, dance, poem, or story that is traditional to one group, and teach it to a group of your friends. (e) Go to a library or museum to see a program or exhibit featuring one group's traditions. Report on what you see and learn.

quiz_item.question: When comparing three different cultural groups in the United States for Requirement 1, what is the primary goal of examining their traditions, customs, and historical contributions?
options: A. To understand how diverse cultural backgrounds shape American society, build mutual respect, and recognize shared human values alongside distinct heritages.
B. To rank cultural groups by the century they arrived in North America and determine which group should set uniform national customs.
C. To prove that regional differences in language, food, and holidays have completely disappeared in modern metropolitan areas.
D. To replace local cultural celebrations with a single standardized set of civic traditions across all states.
choices: A. To understand how diverse cultural backgrounds shape American society, build mutual respect, and recognize shared human values alongside distinct heritages.
B. To rank cultural groups by the century they arrived in North America and determine which group should set uniform national customs.
C. To prove that regional differences in language, food, and holidays have completely disappeared in modern metropolitan areas.
D. To replace local cultural celebrations with a single standardized set of civic traditions across all states.
quiz_item.correct_answer: A. To understand how diverse cultural backgrounds shape American society, build mutual respect, and recognize shared human values alongside distinct heritages.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (A): American Cultures Requirement 1 emphasizes exploring how distinct cultural groups contribute to the nation, helping Scouts overcome stereotypes and appreciate both diversity and shared civic life.

pamphlet_excerpts: About Some Differences: Old family photographs offer glimpses of the past and may provide significant clues about your own cultural background (p. 40).
About Some Differences Principle 2: Many Americans can trace their origins back to several countries (p. 40).

About Some Differences Principle 3: It's common for an American to have a multicultural heritage, that is, to keep family traditions or customs that have been passed down from several cultures (p. 40).
About Some Differences Principle 4: Some families know agreat deal about their history and preserve their heritage in daily life (p. 40).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (About Some Differences): Other families know very little about their backgrounds (p. 40).
Step 2 (About Some Differences): Your family may enjoy learning with you as you explore the culture of your ancestors (p. 40).
Step 3 (About Some Differences): It is not necessary to research your family's background before you talk with them, but it is very important to do so before you talk (p. 40).
Step 4 (About Some Differences): When you think you have found enough information in books and (with permission) on the internet, you are ready for the next step: preparing (p. 40).

quiz_item.question: According to the Declaration of Independence discussed in Requirement 1, from where do legitimate governments derive their just powers, and what unalienable rights are named?
options: A. From hereditary monarchs and parliamentary charters, guaranteeing property ownership, military protection, and tax exemption.
B. From the federal judiciary and state legislatures, guaranteeing trial by jury, interstate commerce, and municipal voting.
C. From colonial trade treaties and martial law, guaranteeing public education, national banking, and frontier land grants.
D. From the consent of the governed, instituted to secure the unalienable rights of life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness.
choices: A. From hereditary monarchs and parliamentary charters, guaranteeing property ownership, military protection, and tax exemption.
B. From the federal judiciary and state legislatures, guaranteeing trial by jury, interstate commerce, and municipal voting.
C. From colonial trade treaties and martial law, guaranteeing public education, national banking, and frontier land grants.
D. From the consent of the governed, instituted to secure the unalienable rights of life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness.
quiz_item.correct_answer: D. From the consent of the governed, instituted to secure the unalienable rights of life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (D): The Declaration of Independence states that all people are endowed with unalienable rights including life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness, and that governments derive their just powers from the consent of the governed.

requirements.lead_text: Do TWO of the following:
requirements.req_text: Do TWO of the following: (a) Select two individuals from American history, one a political leader (a president, senator, etc.) and the other a private citizen (a writer, religious leader, etc.). Find out about each person's accomplishments and compare the contributions each has made to America's heritage. (b) With your counselor's approval, choose an organization that has promoted some type of positive change in American society. Find out why the organization believed this change was necessary and how it helped to accomplish the change. Discuss how this organization is related to events or situations from America's past. (c) With your counselor's approval, interview two veterans of the U. S. military. Find out what their experiences were like. Ask the veterans what they believe they accomplished. (d) With your counselor's approval, interview three people in your community of different ages and occupations. Ask these people what America means to them, what they think is special about this country, and what American traditions they feel are important to preserve.

Share what you find with your counselor.

requirements.lead_text: Do TWO of the following:
requirements.req_text: Do TWO of the following: (a) Explain the National Register of Historic Places and how a property becomes eligible for listing in the National Register of Historic Places. Make a map of your local area, marking the points of historical interest. Tell about any National Register properties in your area. Share the map with your counselor, and describe the historical points you have indicated. (b) Research an event of historical importance that took place in or near your area. If possible, visit the place. Tell your counselor about the event and how it affected local history. Describe how the area looked then and what it now looks like. (c) Find out when, why, and how your town or neighborhood started, and what ethnic, national, or racial groups played a part. Find out how the area has changed over the past 50 years and try to explain why. (d) Take an active part in a program about an event or person in American history. Report to your counselor about the program, the part you took, and the subject. (e) Visit a historic trail or walk in your area. After your visit, share with your counselor what you have learned. Discuss the importance of this location and explain why you think it might qualify for National Register listing.

National Register of Historic Places Principle 2: Do TWO of The Following Principle 2: There are very specific criteria for a property to be listed (p. 40).

National Register of Historic Places Principle 4: Do TWO of The Following Principle 4: Once you have found what National Register properties arein your area, plot them on a map (p. 40).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (National Register of Historic Places): Step 1 (Do TWO of The Following): Your map does not have to be exact, but it should identify major streets, highways, and natural resources such as lakes and rivers (p. 40).
Step 2 (National Register of Historic Places): Step 2 (Do TWO of The Following): Your local library, chamber of commerce, or realty office might be able to provide you with amap of your town (p. 40).

Step 3 (National Register of Historic Places): Step 3 (Do TWO of The Following): Your city's website also may have a link to a map you can print out; just plug in the town and state name in your browser to begin the search (p. 40).

Step 4 (National Register of Historic Places): Step 4 (Do TWO of The Following): With more than 77,000 listings, there is a good chance aproperty in your town is listed on the National Register (p. 40).

requirements.lead_text: Do ONE of the following:
requirements.req_text: Do ONE of the following: (a) Watch two motion pictures (with the approval and permission of your counselor and parent or guardian) that are set in some period of American history. Describe to your counselor how accurate each film is with regard to the historical events depicted and also with regard to the way the characters are portrayed. (b) Read a biography (with your counselor's approval) of someone who has made a contribution to America's heritage. Tell some things you admire about this individual and some things you do not admire. Explain why you think this person has made a positive or a negative contribution to America's heritage. (c) Listen to recordings of popular songs from various periods of American history. Share five of these songs with your counselor, and describe how each song reflects the way people felt about the period in which it was popular. If a recording is not available, have a copy of the lyrics available.

Step 3 (Watch two motion pictures): For instance, many American Indians were portrayed as villains in "spaghetti" Westerns, popular, low-budget films (p. 48).
Step 4 (Watch two motion pictures): This may have been because of prejudice on the part of movie makers, or simply to show the white characters as more heroic (p. 48).

pamphlet_excerpts: Careers & Professional Pathways: The great thing about careers in American heritage is that the reis a position out there for just about anyone (p. 33).

Careers & Professional Pathways Principle 2: Employers are looking for people who can think independently, communicate well, have good research skills, and can analyze situations to relate them (p. 33).
Careers & Professional Pathways Principle 3: Studying American heritage gives you these skills and makes you a sought-after candidate (p. 33).
Careers & Professional Pathways Principle 4: Most people who want to work in American heritage major in history in college (p. 33).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Careers & Professional Pathways): Some positions require a master'sor doctorate degree, especially if you want to teach (p. 33).
Step 2 (Careers & Professional Pathways): You also might consider being a museum curator, national park ranger, historic preservation officer, or archivist (p. 33).
Step 3 (Careers & Professional Pathways): These fields require knowledge of a specific part of history (p. 33).
Step 4 (Careers & Professional Pathways): They also need to be able to find information, which requires research skills (p. 33).

pamphlet_excerpts: Different American Indian cultural areas: Pueblos were made of different types of materials (p. 7).
Different American Indian cultural areas Principle 2: The Hopi and the Zuñi used stones that were mortared together and surfaced with plaster (p. 7).
Different American Indian cultural areas Principle 3: Rio Grande Indians constructed their homes from adobe bricks of sun-dried earth mixed with straw (p. 7).
Different American Indian cultural areas Principle 4: They stretched log beams across the roofs and covered them with poles, brush, and plaster (p. 7).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Different American Indian cultural areas): Sometimes the beams projected beyond the walls and were used as pegs to hang food for drying (p. 7).
Step 2 (Different American Indian cultural areas): The women owned the apartments and all of the furnishings (p. 7).
Step 3 (Different American Indian cultural areas): In the central plaza of the village, the people dug kivas, underground chambers where men conducted sacred rituals (p. 7).
Step 4 (Different American Indian cultural areas): Men also used the kivas as clubhouses, and women usually were not allowed to enter (p. 7).

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: Why did American Indian nations across regions such as the Pacific Northwest, the Great Plains, and the Desert Southwest develop markedly different housing, diets, and clothing prior to European contact?
quiz_item.question: Why did American Indian nations across regions such as the Pacific Northwest, the Great Plains, and the Desert Southwest develop markedly different housing, diets, and clothing prior to European contact?
options: A. All tribes followed a single continental council that assigned different crafts and housing styles to each region by lottery.
B. Each Indigenous nation adapted its technology, shelter, foodways, and social organization to the specific geography, climate, and natural resources of its homeland.
C. Tribes in every region relied exclusively on imported European iron tools and domesticated horses for thousands of years before 1492.
D. Differences in shelter and diet were caused solely by proximity to Spanish missions established along the Atlantic seaboard.
choices: A. All tribes followed a single continental council that assigned different crafts and housing styles to each region by lottery.
B. Each Indigenous nation adapted its technology, shelter, foodways, and social organization to the specific geography, climate, and natural resources of its homeland.
C. Tribes in every region relied exclusively on imported European iron tools and domesticated horses for thousands of years before 1492.
D. Differences in shelter and diet were caused solely by proximity to Spanish missions established along the Atlantic seaboard.
quiz_item.correct_answer: B. Each Indigenous nation adapted its technology, shelter, foodways, and social organization to the specific geography, climate, and natural resources of its homeland.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (B): American Indian cultures developed distinct lifeways (such as cedar plank houses in the Pacific Northwest, bison hide tipis on the Plains, and adobe pueblos in the Southwest) adapted directly to local ecosystems and resources.

pamphlet_excerpts: American Indian Tribe: An American Indian tribe, group: Using dugout canoes, Plateau tribes traveled and traded widely along the Columbia and Fraser river systems (p. 57).
American Indian Tribe Principle 2: An American Indian tribe, group Principle 2: From the west came sea otter pelts and ornamental shells (p. 57).
American Indian Tribe Principle 3: An American Indian tribe, group Principle 3: Deer skins, hemp for basket making, and bitter root were brought from the interior (p. 57).

American Indian Tribe Principle 4: An American Indian tribe, group Principle 4: All sorts of goods changed hands: dried salmon, candle fish oil, baskets, carvings, even the canoes in which the traders carried their wares (p. 57).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (American Indian Tribe): Step 1 (An American Indian tribe, group): When horses came to the Plateau in the early 18th c entury, tribes like the Yakima, Nez Perce, and Cayusebecame expert horse raise rs and traders (p. 57).
Step 2 (American Indian Tribe): Step 2 (An American Indian tribe, group): The Plateau Indians had a complex system of beliefs and ceremonies (p. 57).

Step 3 (American Indian Tribe): Step 3 (An American Indian tribe, group): Everyone sought visits from guardian spirits, and when someone felt they were about to be healed by their guardian spirit, there was a ceremony (p. 57).
Step 4 (American Indian Tribe): Step 4 (An American Indian tribe, group): Shamans had visions and appeared to the people in the guise of grizzly bears (p. 57).

pamphlet_excerpts: Learn Common Terms in An: Learn 10 Common Terms: Indians are relearning lost traditions and languages and reviving their arts and crafts, their songs, dances, and stories (p. 17).

Learn Common Terms in An Principle 2: Learn 10 Common Terms Principle 2: Many have chosen not to disappear into America's "melting pot." Indians are reclaiming control over what happens to them (p. 17).
Learn Common Terms in An Principle 3: Learn 10 Common Terms Principle 3: They want to decide for themselves how they will live in the modern world (p. 17).

Learn Common Terms in An Principle 4: Learn 10 Common Terms Principle 4: The question is, how can they keep cultural roots alive and protect and preserve tribal identities, yet still be a part of modern society (p. 17).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Learn Common Terms in An): Step 1 (Learn 10 Common Terms): There is no easy answer, and no one knows what the future holds (p. 17).
Step 2 (Learn Common Terms in An): Step 2 (Learn 10 Common Terms): They may have been renowned leaders, peacemakers, or lawmakers (p. 17).
Step 3 (Learn Common Terms in An): Step 3 (Learn 10 Common Terms): Some, like Pocahontas, Sacajawea, Hahyonhwatha (known as "Hiawatha"), and Tecumseh, lived centuries ago (p. 17).

Step 4 (Learn Common Terms in An): Step 4 (Learn 10 Common Terms): Others, like Geronimo, Ira Hayes, Ben Night horse Campbell, Ada Deer, and Wilma Mankiller, are people of the 20th and 21st centuries (p. 17).

pamphlet_excerpts: Life Might Have Been: Describe How Life: This pamphlet will help you take that important first step in your journey of discovery (p. 9).
Life Might Have Been Principle 2: Describe How Life Principle 2: Use the information here as a starting point to learn more about American Indians and American heritage (p. 9).
Life Might Have Been Principle 3: Describe How Life Principle 3: You might want to focus on only one tribe to fulfill all of the merit badge requirements (p. 9).
Life Might Have Been Principle 4: Describe How Life Principle 4: You might want to learn more about Indian life in general before Europeans came, as well as after they arrived (p. 9).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Life Might Have Been): Step 1 (Describe How Life): You might also investigate how Indians live and work today and carry on their ancient traditions (p. 9).
Step 2 (Life Might Have Been): Step 2 (Describe How Life): Ask your school or public librarian for books and other materials about different Indian groups (p. 9).
Step 3 (Life Might Have Been): Step 3 (Describe How Life): If you have anatural history museum in your area, ask the curator or person in charge for information (p. 9).
Step 4 (Life Might Have Been): Step 4 (Describe How Life): See if your town or city has an American Indian center, oran Indian tribal council or similar governing group (p. 9).

options: A. All tribes followed a single continental council that assigned different crafts and housing styles to each region by lottery.
B. Each Indigenous nation adapted its technology, shelter, foodways, and social organization to the specific geography, climate, and natural resources of its homeland.
C. Tribes in every region relied exclusively on imported European iron tools and domesticated horses for thousands of years before 1492.
D. Differences in shelter and diet were caused solely by proximity to Spanish missions established along the Atlantic seaboard.
choices: A. All tribes followed a single continental council that assigned different crafts and housing styles to each region by lottery.
B. Each Indigenous nation adapted its technology, shelter, foodways, and social organization to the specific geography, climate, and natural resources of its homeland.

quiz_item.question: During a troop discussion on workplace rights for Requirement 1, a Scout asks why nineteenth and early twentieth century workers organized labor unions. Which explanation is historically accurate?
options: A. Workers organized primarily to abolish hourly wages in favor of unpaid agricultural apprenticeships and longer seven-day factory schedules.
B. Labor unions were created by railroad corporations to set nationwide retail prices and eliminate interstate freight tariffs.
C. Workers joined together to bargain collectively for safer working conditions, an eight-hour workday, fair living wages, and laws ending exploitative child labor.
D. Early unions were formed by federal courts to ban strikes and require employees to purchase their own heavy factory machinery.
choices: A. Workers organized primarily to abolish hourly wages in favor of unpaid agricultural apprenticeships and longer seven-day factory schedules.
B. Labor unions were created by railroad corporations to set nationwide retail prices and eliminate interstate freight tariffs.
C. Workers joined together to bargain collectively for safer working conditions, an eight-hour workday, fair living wages, and laws ending exploitative child labor.
D. Early unions were formed by federal courts to ban strikes and require employees to purchase their own heavy factory machinery.
quiz_item.correct_answer: C. Workers joined together to bargain collectively for safer working conditions, an eight-hour workday, fair living wages, and laws ending exploitative child labor.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (C): The American labor movement arose so workers could use collective bargaining to address workplace hazards, excessive hours, low pay, and child labor.

Step 3 (Union and Employer Organization Visit): The Labor Movement in the 20th Century Labor leaders promoted the ideas of union solidarity (a spirit of unity based on common interests) (p. 16).
Step 4 (Union and Employer Organization Visit): However, deep-rooted prejudice and fear often exerted a stronger influence on union members than idealism (p. 16).

pamphlet_excerpts: Labor Union Structure and Federation: Craft unions provide training to their members based on the model of medieval craft guilds (p. 19).
Labor Union Structure and Federation Principle 2: A trainee begins as an apprentice, learning a trade at a union sponsored school and acting as an assistant on the job (p. 19).

Labor Union Structure and Federation Principle 3: After successfully completing a training period of four or more years, the apprentice becomes a fully qualified skilled worker, or journey worker (p. 19).
Labor Union Structure and Federation Principle 4: The labor force serves two distinct parts of the nation'seconomy: the private sector and the public sector (p. 19).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Labor Union Structure and Federation): The private sector refers to the aspects of the economy that are under the control of individuals and privately owned businesses (p. 19).
Step 2 (Labor Union Structure and Federation): The public sector is under the control of the federal, state, or local governments (p. 19).
Step 3 (Labor Union Structure and Federation): Another way to analyze the workforce is in terms of unorganized versus organized labor (p. 19).
Step 4 (Labor Union Structure and Federation): In unorganized labor situations, the individual employee addresses problems one-on-one with his or her supervisor and the managerial chain (p. 19).

pamphlet_excerpts: American Labor History Timeline: Us and Them: The Struggles Between Labor and Management (p. 16).
American Labor History Timeline Principle 2: Big business fought union efforts to have any influence in the workplace (p. 16).
American Labor History Timeline Principle 3: Management used the courts, private armies, and federal troops to put down labor activity (p. 16).
American Labor History Timeline Principle 4: Employers contracted with prisons to hire convicts as strike breakers (p. 16).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (American Labor History Timeline): Additionally, employers hired new immigrants, African Americans, and Latinos to break strikes, often causing racial unrest (p. 16).
Step 2 (American Labor History Timeline): Trade unionism grew in fits and starts in response to the success or failure of strikes, boom-and-bust business cycles, and union militancy (p. 16).
Step 3 (American Labor History Timeline): The Labor Movement in the 20th Century Labor leaders promoted the ideas of union solidarity (a spirit of unity based on common interests) (p. 16).
Step 4 (American Labor History Timeline): However, deep-rooted prejudice and fear often exerted a stronger influence on union members than idealism (p. 16).

pamphlet_excerpts: Globalization and Workforce Impacts: Us and Them: The Struggles Between Labor and Management (p. 12).
Globalization and Workforce Impacts Principle 2: For more than 200 years, the United States participated in an international economy (p. 12).
Globalization and Workforce Impacts Principle 3: Trade took place between nations, and governments set the rules (p. 12).
Globalization and Workforce Impacts Principle 4: Commerce in the 21st century involves a global economy (p. 12).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Globalization and Workforce Impacts): Corporations, investment bankers, and traders treat the world as one big market (p. 12).
Step 2 (Globalization and Workforce Impacts): Global business is changing so rapidly that democratic governments are losing their ability to protect national interests and their labor force (p. 12).
Step 3 (Globalization and Workforce Impacts): Using computers and communications satellites, the companies send manufacturing specifications to plants around the world (p. 12).
Step 4 (Globalization and Workforce Impacts): Then they ship the parts to another country for assembly. "Made in America" doesn't mean what it once (p. 12).

pamphlet_excerpts: Collective Bargaining Negotiations: The foremost concern of a company owner (an individual or a group of investors) is to make a profit (p. 46).
Collective Bargaining Negotiations Principle 2: They make decisions about whether to continue to invest in the companies based on the profitability of those businesses (p. 46).

Collective Bargaining Negotiations Principle 3: Just as management may shut down a division in a company to cutcosts and improve profitability, the owner may sell an unprofitable company to protect (p. 46).
Collective Bargaining Negotiations Principle 4: Financial institutions, investment groups, and individuals often buy shares of stock in a company (p. 46).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Collective Bargaining Negotiations): Each share represents a piece of the company, a percentage of ownership (p. 46).
Step 2 (Collective Bargaining Negotiations): Some companies offer an employee stock-option plan that allows employees to acquire shares of company stock and receive stock distributions (p. 46).
Step 3 (Collective Bargaining Negotiations): Shareholders want a return on their investment in the company (p. 46).
Step 4 (Collective Bargaining Negotiations): Most look for a short term profit, which pressures company management to take short-term action at the expense of long-term goals (p. 46).

Step 2 (Careers in Labor Relations): A federal administrative law judge must have experience as a lawyer and pass a competitive examination administered by (p. 58).
Step 3 (Careers in Labor Relations): The judge is appointed (for life) to the bench by one of several federal agencies and then receives judicial training from an organization (p. 58).
Step 4 (Careers in Labor Relations): Many conciliators, mediators, and arbitrators have lawdegrees with a specialization in conflict management (p. 58).

requirements.lead_text: Complete ONE of the following options:
requirements.req_text: Complete ONE of the following options: (a) Option A, Beef Cattle. Do ALL of the following: (1) Visit a farm or ranch where beef cattle are produced under any of these systems: feeding market cattle for harvest, cow/calf operation (producing cattle for sale to commercial feeders), or producing purebred cattle for sale as breeding stock to others. Talk with the operator to learn how the cattle were handled, fed, weighed, and shipped. Describe what you saw and explain what you learned. If you cannot visit a cattle ranch or farm, view a video from a breed association, or research the internet (with your parent or guardian's permission) for information on beef cattle production. Tell about your findings. (2) Sketch a plan of a feedlot to include its forage and grain storage facilities, and loading chute for 30 or more fattening steers; or sketch a corral plan with cutting and loading chutes for handling 50 or more beef cows and their calves at one time. (3) Make a sketch showing the principal wholesale and retail cuts of beef. Tell about the U. S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) dual grading system of beef. Tell the basis of each grade in each system. (4) Define the following terms: bull, steer, bullock, cow, heifer, freemartin, heiferette, and calf. (b) Option B, Dairy. Do ALL of the following: (1) Tell how a cow or a goat converts forage and grain into milk. Explain the differences in feeds typically used for dairy cows versus those fed to beef cows. (2) Make a chart showing the components in cow's milk or goat's milk. Chart the amount of each component. (3) Explain the requirements for producing grade A milk. Tell how and why milk is pasteurized. (4) Tell about the kinds of equipment used for milking and the sanitation standards that must be met on dairy farms. (5) Define the following terms: bull, cow, steer, heifer, springer, buck, doe, and kid. (6) Visit a dairy farm or a milk processing plant. Describe what you saw and explain what you learned. If you cannot visit a dairy farm or processing plant, view a video from a breed or dairy association, or research the internet (with your parent or guardian's permission) for information on dairying. Tell about your findings. (c) Option C, Horse. Do ALL of the following: (1) Make a sketch of a useful saddle horse barn and exercise yard. (2) Tell about the history of the horse and the benefits it has brought to people. Using the four breeds of horses you chose in requirement 1, discuss the different special uses of each breed. (3) Define the following terms: mare, stallion, gelding, foal, colt, filly; mustang, quarter horse, draft horse, pacer, trotter; pinto, calico, palomino, roan, overo, and tobiano. (4) Visit a horse farm. Describe what you saw and explain what you learned. If you cannot visit a horse farm, view a video from a breed association, or research the internet (with your parent or guardian's permission) for information on horses. Tell about your findings. (5) Outline the proper feeding of a horse doing light work. Explain why the amount and kind of feed will change according to the kind of horse and the work it does. Describe what colic is, what can cause it, and its symptoms. (d) Option D, Sheep or Goat. Choose one and do ALL of the following based upon the choice: (1) Make a sketch of a live lamb or goat. Show the location of the various wholesale and retail cuts. (2) Discuss how wools are sorted and graded. (3) List products that can be made from the milk. (4) Based on your choice, do ONE of the following: (a) Raise a lamb or goat from weaning to market weight. Keep records of feed intake, weight gains, medication, vaccination, and mortality. Present your records to your counselor for review. (b) Visit a farm or ranch where sheep or goats are raised. Describe what you saw and explain what you learned. If you cannot visit a sheep or goat farm or ranch, view a video from a breed association, or research the internet (with your parent or guardian's permission) for information on sheep or goats. Tell about your findings. (5) Define the following terms for a sheep (wether, ewe, ram, and lamb) OR a goat (doe, nanny, kid, buck, and billy). (e) Option E, Hog. Do ALL of the following: (1) Make a sketch showing the principal wholesale and retail cuts of pork. Tell about the recommended USDA grades of pork. Tell the basis for each grade. (2) Outline in writing the proper feeding programs used from the breeding of a gilt or sow through the weaning of the litter. Discuss the feeding programs for the growth and finishing periods. (3) Do ONE of the following: (a) Raise a feeder pig from weaning to market weight. Keep records of feed intake, weight gains, medication, vaccination, and mortality. Present your records to your counselor for review. (b) Visit a farm where hogs are produced, or visit a packing plant handling hogs. Describe what you saw and explain what you learned. If you cannot visit a hog production unit or packing plant, view a video from a packer or processor, or research the internet (with your parent or guardian's permission) for information on hogs. Tell about your findings. (4) Define the following terms: gilt, sow, barrow, and boar. (f) Option F, Avian. Do ALL of the following: (1) Make a sketch of a layer house or broiler house showing nests, roosts, feeders, waterers, and means of ventilation. Explain how insulation, ventilation, temperature controls, automatic lights, and other environmental controls are used to protect birds from heat, cold, and bad weather. Explain the importance of light for egg production. (2) Explain why overcrowding is dangerous for poultry flocks. (3) Tell about the grading of eggs. Describe the classes of chicken meat. (4) Do ONE of the following: (a) Manage an egg-producing flock for five months. Keep records of feed purchased, eggs sold, medication, vaccination, and mortality. Present your records to your counselor for review. (b) Raise five chickens from hatching. Keep records of feed intake, weight gains, medication, vaccination, and mortality. Present your records to your counselor for review. (c) Visit a commercial avian production facility. Describe what you saw and explain what you learned. If you cannot visit a commercial facility, view a video from a poultry association, or research the internet (with your parent or guardian's permission) for information on poultry production. Tell about your findings. (5) Define the following terms: chick, pullet, hen, cockerel, cock, and capon.

sub_requirements.sub_req_text: Option B, Dairy. Do ALL of the following: (1) Tell how a cow or a goat converts forage and grain into milk. Explain the differences in feeds typically used for dairy cows versus those fed to beef cows. (2) Make a chart showing the components in cow's milk or goat's milk. Chart the amount of each component. (3) Explain the requirements for producing grade A milk. Tell how and why milk is pasteurized. (4) Tell about the kinds of equipment used for milking and the sanitation standards that must be met on dairy farms. (5) Define the following terms: bull, cow, steer, heifer, springer, buck, doe, and kid. (6) Visit a dairy farm or a milk processing plant. Describe what you saw and explain what you learned. If you cannot visit a dairy farm or processing plant, view a video from a breed or dairy association, or research the internet (with your parent or guardian's permission) for information on dairying. Tell about your findings.

(2) Tell about the history of the horse and the benefits it has brought to people. Using the four breeds of horses you chose in requirement 1, discuss the different special uses of each breed. (3) Define the following terms: mare, stallion, gelding, foal, colt, filly; mustang, quarter horse, draft horse, pacer, trotter; pinto, calico, palomino, roan, overo, and tobiano. (4) Visit a horse farm. Describe what you saw and explain what you learned. If you cannot visit a horse farm, view a video from a breed association, or research the internet (with your parent or guardian's permission) for information on horses. Tell about your findings. sub_requirements.sub_req_text: Option E, Hog. Do ALL of the following: (1) Make a sketch showing the principal wholesale and retail cuts of pork. Tell about the recommended USDA grades of pork. Tell the basis for each grade. (2) Outline in writing the proper feeding programs used from the breeding of a gilt or sow through the weaning of the litter. Discuss the feeding programs for the growth and finishing periods. (3) Do ONE of the following: (a) Raise a feeder pig from weaning to market weight. Keep records of feed intake, weight gains, medication, vaccination, and mortality. Present your records to your counselor for review. (b) Visit a farm where hogs are produced, or visit a packing plant handling hogs. Describe what you saw and explain what you learned. If you cannot visit a hog production unit or packing plant, view a video from a packer or processor, or research the internet (with your parent or guardian's permission) for information on hogs. Tell about your findings. (4) Define the following terms: gilt, sow, barrow, and boar.

sub_requirements.label: (f)
sub_requirements.text: Option F, Avian. Do ALL of the following: (1) Make a sketch of a layer house or broiler house showing nests, roosts, feeders, waterers, and means of ventilation. Explain how insulation, ventilation, temperature controls, automatic lights, and other environmental controls are used to protect birds from heat, cold, and bad weather. Explain the importance of light for egg production. (2) Explain why overcrowding is dangerous for poultry flocks. (3) Tell about the grading of eggs. Describe the classes of chicken meat. (4) Do ONE of the following: (a) Manage an egg-producing flock for five months. Keep records of feed purchased, eggs sold, medication, vaccination, and mortality. Present your records to your counselor for review. (b) Raise five chickens from hatching. Keep records of feed intake, weight gains, medication, vaccination, and mortality. Present your records to your counselor for review. (c) Visit a commercial avian production facility. Describe what you saw and explain what you learned. If you cannot visit a commercial facility, view a video from a poultry association, or research the internet (with your parent or guardian's permission) for information on poultry production. Tell about your findings. (5) Define the following terms: chick, pullet, hen, cockerel, cock, and capon.

pamphlet_excerpts: Careers & Professional Pathways: Farm and ranch managers also make the business decisions, such as securing loans to finance the purchase of livestock, feed, and equipment (p. 87).
Careers & Professional Pathways Principle 2: Those who oversee large spreads often have several employees (p. 87).
Careers & Professional Pathways Principle 3: Large farms and ranches may have dozens of full-time workers. today's agriculture often lie in offfarm positions (p. 87).

pamphlet_excerpts: General Knowledge: The history of animation is as old as the history of story telling (p. 21).
General Knowledge Principle 2: The word animate means "alive." When early humans first painted animals and hunting scenes on cave walls, they lit fires to show off their work (p. 21).
General Knowledge Principle 3: The dancing flames cast irregular light in the caves, making the images of prehistoric animals appear to be alive and moving (p. 21).
General Knowledge Principle 4: Also, from the earliest times, children worldwide have used a light source to project hand shadows onto a wall to create the shapes of animals (p. 21).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (General Knowledge): This kind of entertainment can be enjoyed by a group of friends (p. 21).
Step 2 (General Knowledge): The shared experience of creating lifelike imitation is a key part of the attraction of animation (p. 21).
Step 3 (General Knowledge): The idea of projecting shadows led to the first magic lantern shows, starting around the mid to late 1700s and lasting until the introduction (p. 21).
Step 4 (General Knowledge): A primitive projection device like a wooden box with a candle inside was fitted with a lens (p. 21).

B. Binocular parallax shifts depth perception between the left and right eyes, while keyframes are discarded background sketches.
C. Refractive dispersion slows light entering the cornea, while keyframes are every single in-between drawing made by assistant animators.
D. Persistence of vision and beta movement cause the brain to bridge rapid sequential frames into smooth motion, while keyframes define the primary start and end poses of an action.

pamphlet_excerpts: Principles of Animation: The principles of animation are a set of 12 basic ideas applied to animation to create appealing, believable results (p. 35).
Principles of Animation Principle 2: They were introduced by two of the original Disney animators, Ollie Johnston and Frank Thomas, in their book, Disney Animation: The Illusion (p. 35).
Principles of Animation Principle 3: Since that time, the principles have become standard in the animation industry (p. 35).
Principles of Animation Principle 4: Straight Ahead Action and Pose to Pose Straight-ahead action and pose to pose are the two main methods for animating (p. 35).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Principles of Animation): Using straight-ahead action, the animator draws or animates frame by frame, doing the drawings in order: 1, 2, 3, 4 (p. 35).
Step 2 (Principles of Animation): With pose-to-pose animation, in contrast, the animator draws or poses the main (key) frames of the animation before filling in the in-between (p. 35).
Step 3 (Principles of Animation): Using the pose-to-pose method, the animator might do drawing 1, then drawing 25, and then drawing 47, before going back to do the drawings (p. 35).
Step 4 (Principles of Animation): Most animators use the pose-to-pose method because it offers benefits in timing and frame composition (p. 35).

options: A. Chromatic aberration blends primary colors on the screen, while keyframes are the final audio tracks mixed after rendering.
B. Binocular parallax shifts depth perception between the left and right eyes, while keyframes are discarded background sketches.
C. Refractive dispersion slows light entering the cornea, while keyframes are every single in-between drawing made by assistant animators.
D. Persistence of vision and beta movement cause the brain to bridge rapid sequential frames into smooth motion, while keyframes define the primary start and end poses of an action.
choices: A. Chromatic aberration blends primary colors on the screen, while keyframes are the final audio tracks mixed after rendering.
B. Binocular parallax shifts depth perception between the left and right eyes, while keyframes are discarded background sketches.
C. Refractive dispersion slows light entering the cornea, while keyframes are every single in-between drawing made by assistant animators.
D. Persistence of vision and beta movement cause the brain to bridge rapid sequential frames into smooth motion, while keyframes define the primary start and end poses of an action.
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: D. Persistence of vision and beta movement cause the brain to bridge rapid sequential frames into smooth motion, while keyframes define the primary start and end poses of an action.
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (D): Animation relies on persistence of vision and perceptual motion processing across sequential frames, with lead animators setting extreme poses (keyframes) and in-between frames completing the transition.

pamphlet_excerpts: Principles of Archaeological Science: Students of archaeology study a variety of subjects, including many sciences (p. 16).

Principles of Archaeological Science Principle 2: The scientific analysis of sites and artifacts requires a knowledge of geology, paleontology, physics, chemistry, botany, zoology, and statistics (p. 16).
Principles of Archaeological Science Principle 3: Interdisciplinary programs that combine archaeology with various other fields of study are common (p. 16).
Principles of Archaeological Science Principle 4: Historical archaeologists usually major in anthropology or history (p. 16).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Principles of Archaeological Science): To work as a field archaeologist, previous experience is often required (usually obtained by spending a summer in an archaeological field) (p. 16).
Step 2 (Principles of Archaeological Science): Archaeological field schools provide the best way to learn howto properly excavate and document archaeological sites, and also to find (p. 16).
Step 3 (Principles of Archaeological Science): You can begin now to prepare for your college courseworkby taking all of the science, history, and language classes (p. 16).
Step 4 (Principles of Archaeological Science): Strong communication skills are vital to an archaeologist, so you'll need a good grounding in writing, speech, and foreign languages (p. 16).

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: How does archaeology differ from paleontology, and why is recording an artifact's exact three-dimensional context and stratigraphic layer essential before removing it from the ground?
quiz_item.question: How does archaeology differ from paleontology, and why is recording an artifact's exact three-dimensional context and stratigraphic layer essential before removing it from the ground?
options: A. Archaeology studies dinosaur fossils and igneous rock formations, and removing artifacts quickly prevents sunlight from fading their mineral crystals.
B. Archaeology studies past human cultures through material remains, and an artifact's in-situ context and stratum reveal its age, use, and association with surrounding human activity.
C. Archaeology focuses exclusively on estimating the cash auction value of ancient coins, which depends on how deep the coin was buried.
D. Archaeology is the study of living insect populations, and stratigraphy measures how fast topsoil erodes during summer rainstorms.
choices: A. Archaeology studies dinosaur fossils and igneous rock formations, and removing artifacts quickly prevents sunlight from fading their mineral crystals.
B. Archaeology studies past human cultures through material remains, and an artifact's in-situ context and stratum reveal its age, use, and association with surrounding human activity.
C. Archaeology focuses exclusively on estimating the cash auction value of ancient coins, which depends on how deep the coin was buried.
D. Archaeology is the study of living insect populations, and stratigraphy measures how fast topsoil erodes during summer rainstorms.
quiz_item.correct_answer: B. Archaeology studies past human cultures through material remains, and an artifact's in-situ context and stratum reveal its age, use, and association with surrounding human activity.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (B): Unlike paleontology (which studies fossilized prehistoric life such as dinosaurs), archaeology investigates past human societies through material culture, where provenance and stratigraphic context provide critical scientific data.

Of the archaeological process Principle 3: They may use aerial photographs and pictures taken from satellites to home in on the places they are trying to find (p. 33).
Of the archaeological process Principle 4: They talk to people living in the area, Measuring an obsidian artifact from the who often have the deepest knowledge (p. 33).

pamphlet_excerpts: Combined Total of Five Archaeological: Learn About A Combined Total: This idea of relationships between objects is important (p. 14).
Combined Total of Five Archaeological Principle 2: Learn About A Combined Total Principle 2: Think of all the little parts that go together to make asmartphone (p. 14).

Combined Total of Five Archaeological Principle 3: Learn About A Combined Total Principle 3: If you take the individual parts out of a smartphone and study each one separately, will that tell you how the phone functions (p. 14).
Combined Total of Five Archaeological Principle 4: Learn About A Combined Total Principle 4: You must look at all of the parts in place inside the phone to see how they work together (p. 14).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Combined Total of Five Archaeological): Step 1 (Learn About A Combined Total): Like a smartphone, an archaeological site is a complicated package that must be opened carefully and studied as a whole if we are to make sense (p. 14).

Step 2 (Combined Total of Five Archaeological): Step 2 (Learn About A Combined Total): A researcher who looks at only a few stone tools and afew kernels of corn might find that, by themselves, the artifacts reveal little (p. 14).

Step 3 (Combined Total of Five Archaeological): Step 3 (Learn About A Combined Total): A few kernels of corn found in a space that did not have a hearth or any other artifacts would suggest that the room was probably a storeroom (p. 14).

Step 4 (Combined Total of Five Archaeological): Step 4 (Learn About A Combined Total): Compared with an isolated find, artifacts found together at a site can provide more information about the people who lived there and everyday activities (p. 14).

step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (It is important to protect archaeological): Archaeology clubs and professional associations promote the appreciation of the past and help protect cultural resources (p. 14).
Step 2 (It is important to protect archaeological): Libraries are a rich source of information about archaeology and ancient cultures (p. 14).
Step 3 (It is important to protect archaeological): Librarians can help you find books about the science of archaeology and about the peoples and periods of the past that interest (p. 14).
Step 4 (It is important to protect archaeological): The internet also offers many opportunities for exploring the world of archaeology via computer (p. 14).

pamphlet_excerpts: Careers & Professional Pathways: Students of archaeology study a variety of subjects, including many sciences (p. 79).
Careers & Professional Pathways Principle 2: The scientific analysis of sites and artifacts requires a knowledge of geology, paleontology, physics, chemistry, botany, zoology, and statistics (p. 79).
Careers & Professional Pathways Principle 3: Interdisciplinary programs that combine archaeology with various other fields of study are common (p. 79).
Careers & Professional Pathways Principle 4: Historical archaeologists usually major in anthropology or history (p. 79).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Careers & Professional Pathways): To work as a field archaeologist, previous experience is often required (usually obtained by spending a summer in an archaeological field) (p. 79).
Step 2 (Careers & Professional Pathways): Archaeological field schools provide the best way to learn howto properly excavate and document archaeological sites, and also to find (p. 79).
Step 3 (Careers & Professional Pathways): You can begin now to prepare for your college courseworkby taking all of the science, history, and language classes (p. 79).
Step 4 (Careers & Professional Pathways): Strong communication skills are vital to an archaeologist, so you'll need a good grounding in writing, speech, and foreign languages (p. 79).

requirements.lead_text: Do ONE of the following:
requirements.req_text: Do ONE of the following: (a) With your parent or guardian's and counselor's permission, assist a qualified archaeologist for at least eight hours with a project being worked on. Projects may include surveying, site monitoring, site stabilization, surface excavation, laboratory analysis, use of digital archaeological technology, or public outreach. Describe your involvement in the project, what you learned about archaeology, and the steps of archaeological inquiry. Note: Visiting an archaeological site will require advance planning. An archaeological site during study can be a dangerous place. While there, you will need to closely follow the archaeologist's directions and comply with all the safety procedures. Be aware of the changing conditions at the site. (b) With your counselor's approval, take part in a simulated archaeological project designed by a qualified archaeologist. The project must include the use of a simulated archaeological site including artifacts and features for the site. Using the steps of archaeological inquiry, analyze the artifacts and features and document the spatial relationships of the artifacts and features at the simulated site. Explain how the environment and time can affect the interpretation of an artifact and the overall archaeological site. Tell how you would share the results of your analysis with other researchers and the public. Note: To find out how to make a simulated archaeological site, talk with a professional archaeologist, trained avocational archaeologist, museum school instructor, science teacher, advisor from a local archaeology society, or other qualified instructor.

Under the supervision of a qualified Principle 2: As you can see, archaeology has become an important science for exploring our past and preserving our heritage (p. 28).
Under the supervision of a qualified Principle 3: Visitor centers have been built at many archaeological sites where you can view artifacts and learn about the people who made and used them (p. 28).
Under the supervision of a qualified Principle 4: Museums, schools, and public buildings may also have exhibits that share with everyone the knowledge gained by studying the past (p. 28).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Under the supervision of a qualified): Archaeology clubs and professional associations promote the appreciation of the past and help protect cultural resources (p. 28).
Step 2 (Under the supervision of a qualified): Libraries are a rich source of information about archaeology and ancient cultures (p. 28).
Step 3 (Under the supervision of a qualified): Librarians can help you find books about the science of archaeology and about the peoples and periods of the past that interest (p. 28).
Step 4 (Under the supervision of a qualified): The internet also offers many opportunities for exploring the world of archaeology via computer (p. 28).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: How does archaeology differ from paleontology, and why is recording an artifact's exact three-dimensional context and stratigraphic layer essential before removing it from the ground?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: How does archaeology differ from paleontology, and why is recording an artifact's exact three-dimensional context and stratigraphic layer essential before removing it from the ground?
options: A. Archaeology studies dinosaur fossils and igneous rock formations, and removing artifacts quickly prevents sunlight from fading their mineral crystals.
B. Archaeology studies past human cultures through material remains, and an artifact's in-situ context and stratum reveal its age, use, and association with surrounding human activity.
C. Archaeology focuses exclusively on estimating the cash auction value of ancient coins, which depends on how deep the coin was buried.
D. Archaeology is the study of living insect populations, and stratigraphy measures how fast topsoil erodes during summer rainstorms.
choices: A. Archaeology studies dinosaur fossils and igneous rock formations, and removing artifacts quickly prevents sunlight from fading their mineral crystals.

C. Archaeology focuses exclusively on estimating the cash auction value of ancient coins, which depends on how deep the coin was buried.
D. Archaeology is the study of living insect populations, and stratigraphy measures how fast topsoil erodes during summer rainstorms.
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: B. Archaeology studies past human cultures through material remains, and an artifact's in-situ context and stratum reveal its age, use, and association with surrounding human activity.
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (B): Unlike paleontology (which studies fossilized prehistoric life such as dinosaurs), archaeology investigates past human societies through material culture, where provenance and stratigraphic context provide critical scientific data.

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: While shooting on the archery range, an arrow slips off your bow rest and lands on the ground 4 feet in front of the shooting line while other archers are still at full draw. What must you do?
quiz_item.question: While shooting on the archery range, an arrow slips off your bow rest and lands on the ground 4 feet in front of the shooting line while other archers are still at full draw. What must you do?
options: A. Lean forward across the shooting line and grab the arrow quickly before anyone notices.
B. Leave the arrow on the ground, never reach or step across the shooting line while the range is hot, and wait for the Range Officer's three-whistle 'Retrieve Arrows' command.
C. Signal your buddy in the next lane to kick the arrow back behind the waiting line.
D. Use the tip of your unstrung bow limbs to hook the dropped arrow shaft while adjacent archers are releasing.

quiz_item.correct_answer: B. Leave the dropped arrow untouched in front of the shooting line until the Range Officer blows three whistles to retrieve arrows.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (B): Stepping or reaching across an active shooting line puts you directly in the path of adjacent bows; any arrow forward of the line is retrieved only after all bows are racked on the 3-whistle signal.

pamphlet_excerpts: Care and Storage of As: Explain The Proper Use Care: The hunting arm guard usually is wider and longer than guards used on field and target ranges (p. 25).
Care and Storage of As Principle 2: Explain The Proper Use Care Principle 2: Protect your shooting fingers with a shooting glove or tab (p. 25).
Care and Storage of As Principle 3: Explain The Proper Use Care Principle 3: Even the lightest bow will soon make untrained fingers sensitive, eventually causing blisters (p. 25).
Care and Storage of As Principle 4: Explain The Proper Use Care Principle 4: All archers should use finger protection, no matter how tough they think their fingers (p. 25).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Care and Storage of As): Step 1 (Explain The Proper Use Care): The most experienced and skilled archers always shoot with a glove or tab (p. 25).
Step 2 (Care and Storage of As): Step 2 (Explain The Proper Use Care): Without a glove or tab, the release of your arrow, which is the most crucial motion in shooting, maybe faulty (p. 25).
Step 3 (Care and Storage of As): Step 3 (Explain The Proper Use Care): The glove type of finger protection has three fingertips connected to a wrist strap (p. 25).
Step 4 (Care and Storage of As): Step 4 (Explain The Proper Use Care): The glove should fit snugly, but not tightly, over the three shooting fingers (p. 25).

Step 3 (Archery Core Field Standard): Target archers straddle the firing line, with one foot in front of and one foot behind the line (p. 52).
Step 4 (Archery Core Field Standard): These four organizations govern archery tournaments (p. 52).

requirements.lead_text: Working under the supervision of a certified USA Archery Level 1 Instructor or a certified long-term camp staff member (i. e., a National Camping School [NCS] Range Activities Director; or a Rangemaster over age 18 who is trained by an NCS Range Activities Director or by a USA Archery Level 1 Instructor), do ONE of the following options: Note: When using a Genesis bow, apply the requirements in Option A.
requirements.req_text: Working under the supervision of a certified USA Archery Level 1 Instructor or a certified long-term camp staff member (i. e., a National Camping School [NCS] Range Activities Director; or a Rangemaster over age 18 who is trained by an NCS Range Activities Director or by a USA Archery Level 1 Instructor), do ONE of the following options: Note: When using a Genesis bow, apply the requirements in Option A. (a) Option A, Recurve Bow or Longbow. Do ALL of the following: (1) Name and point to the parts of the recurve or longbow you are shooting. (2) Explain how to properly care for and store recurve bows and longbows. (3) Demonstrate and explain USA Archery's 11 Steps of Shooting for the bow you are shooting. (4) Demonstrate the proper way to string a recurve bow or longbow. (5) Using a bow square, locate and mark with dental floss, crimp-on, or other method, the nocking point on the bowstring of the bow you are using. (6) Do ONE of the following: (a) Using a recurve bow or longbow and arrows with a finger release, shoot a single round of ONE of the following: (1) An NFAA field round of 14 targets and make a score of 60 points (2) A Scouting America field round of 14 targets and make a score of 80 points (3) A World Archery/USA Archery indoor round and make a score of 80 points (Indoor rounds may be shot outdoors if this is more convenient.) (4) An NFAA indoor round and make a score of 50 points (Indoor rounds may be shot outdoors if this is more convenient.) (b) Shooting 30 arrows in five-arrow ends at an 80-centimeter (32-inch) five-color target at 10 yards and using the 10 scoring regions, make a score of 150 points. (b) Option B, Compound Bow. Do ALL of the following: (1) Name and point to the parts of the compound bow you are shooting. (2) Explain how to properly care for and store compound bows. (3) Demonstrate and explain USA Archery's 11 Steps of Shooting for the bow you are shooting. (4) Explain why it is necessary to have the string or cable on a compound bow replaced at an archery shop. (5) Locate and mark with dental floss, crimp-on, or other method, the nocking point on the bowstring of the bow you are using. (6) Do ONE of the following: (a) Using a compound bow and arrows with a finger release, shoot a single round of ONE of the following: (1) An NFAA field round of 14 targets and make a score of 70 points (2) A Scouting America field round of 14 targets and make a score of 90 points (3) A World Archery/USA Archery indoor round and make a score of 90 points (Indoor rounds may be shot outdoors if this is more convenient.) (4) An NFAA indoor round and make a score of 60 points (Indoor rounds may be shot outdoors if this is more convenient.) (b) Shooting at an 80-centimeter (32-inch) five-color target using the 10 scoring regions, make a minimum score of 160 points. Accomplish this in the following manner: Shoot 15 arrows in five-arrow ends, at a distance of 10 yards AND Shoot 15 arrows in five-arrow ends, at a distance of 15 yards.

sub_requirements.sub_req_text: Option A, Recurve Bow or Longbow. Do ALL of the following: (1) Name and point to the parts of the recurve or longbow you are shooting. (2) Explain how to properly care for and store recurve bows and longbows. (3) Demonstrate and explain USA Archery's 11 Steps of Shooting for the bow you are shooting. (4) Demonstrate the proper way to string a recurve bow or longbow. (5) Using a bow square, locate and mark with dental floss, crimp-on, or other method, the nocking point on the bowstring of the bow you are using. (6) Do ONE of the following: (a) Using a recurve bow or longbow and arrows with a finger release, shoot a single round of ONE of the following: (1) An NFAA field round of 14 targets and make a score of 60 points (2) A Scouting America field round of 14 targets and make a score of 80 points (3) A World Archery/USA Archery indoor round and make a score of 80 points (Indoor rounds may be shot outdoors if this is more convenient.) (4) An NFAA indoor round and make a score of 50 points (Indoor rounds may be shot outdoors if this is more convenient.) (b) Shooting 30 arrows in five-arrow ends at an 80-centimeter (32-inch) five-color target at 10 yards and using the 10 scoring regions, make a score of 150 points.

sub_requirements.label: (b)
sub_requirements.text: Option B, Compound Bow. Do ALL of the following: (1) Name and point to the parts of the compound bow you are shooting. (2) Explain how to properly care for and store compound bows. (3) Demonstrate and explain USA Archery's 11 Steps of Shooting for the bow you are shooting. (4) Explain why it is necessary to have the string or cable on a compound bow replaced at an archery shop. (5) Locate and mark with dental floss, crimp-on, or other method, the nocking point on the bowstring of the bow you are using. (6) Do ONE of the following: (a) Using a compound bow and arrows with a finger release, shoot a single round of ONE of the following: (1) An NFAA field round of 14 targets and make a score of 70 points (2) A Scouting America field round of 14 targets and make a score of 90 points (3) A World Archery/USA Archery indoor round and make a score of 90 points (Indoor rounds may be shot outdoors if this is more convenient.) (4) An NFAA indoor round and make a score of 60 points (Indoor rounds may be shot outdoors if this is more convenient.) (b) Shooting at an 80-centimeter (32-inch) five-color target using the 10 scoring regions, make a minimum score of 160 points. Accomplish this in the following manner: Shoot 15 arrows in five-arrow ends, at a distance of 10 yards AND Shoot 15 arrows in five-arrow ends, at a distance of 15 yards.

sub_requirements.sub_req_text: Option B, Compound Bow. Do ALL of the following: (1) Name and point to the parts of the compound bow you are shooting. (2) Explain how to properly care for and store compound bows. (3) Demonstrate and explain USA Archery's 11 Steps of Shooting for the bow you are shooting. (4) Explain why it is necessary to have the string or cable on a compound bow replaced at an archery shop. (5) Locate and mark with dental floss, crimp-on, or other method, the nocking point on the bowstring of the bow you are using. (6) Do ONE of the following: (a) Using a compound bow and arrows with a finger release, shoot a single round of ONE of the following: (1) An NFAA field round of 14 targets and make a score of 70 points (2) A Scouting America field round of 14 targets and make a score of 90 points (3) A World Archery/USA Archery indoor round and make a score of 90 points (Indoor rounds may be shot outdoors if this is more convenient.) (4) An NFAA indoor round and make a score of 60 points (Indoor rounds may be shot outdoors if this is more convenient.) (b) Shooting at an 80-centimeter (32-inch) five-color target using the 10 scoring regions, make a minimum score of 160 points. Accomplish this in the following manner: Shoot 15 arrows in five-arrow ends, at a distance of 10 yards AND Shoot 15 arrows in five-arrow ends, at a distance of 15 yards.

patrol_quiz_bank.question: While shooting on the archery range, an arrow slips off your bow rest and lands on the ground 4 feet in front of the shooting line while other archers are still at full draw. What must you do?
options: A. Lean forward across the shooting line and grab the arrow quickly before anyone notices.
B. Leave the arrow on the ground, never reach or step across the shooting line while the range is hot, and wait for the Range Officer's three-whistle 'Retrieve Arrows' command.
C. Signal your buddy in the next lane to kick the arrow back behind the waiting line.
D. Use the tip of your unstrung bow limbs to hook the dropped arrow shaft while adjacent archers are releasing.
choices: A. Lean forward across the shooting line and grab the arrow quickly before anyone notices.
B. Leave the arrow on the ground, never reach or step across the shooting line while the range is hot, and wait for the Range Officer's three-whistle 'Retrieve Arrows' command.
C. Signal your buddy in the next lane to kick the arrow back behind the waiting line.
D. Use the tip of your unstrung bow limbs to hook the dropped arrow shaft while adjacent archers are releasing.
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: B. Leave the dropped arrow untouched in front of the shooting line until the Range Officer blows three whistles to retrieve arrows.
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (B): Stepping or reaching across an active shooting line puts you directly in the path of adjacent bows; any arrow forward of the line is retrieved only after all bows are racked on the 3-whistle signal.

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: In Architecture Requirement 1, Roman architect Vitruvius stated that every good building must satisfy three core principles (firmitas, utilitas, venustas). What do these three principles mean in modern architectural practice?
quiz_item.question: In Architecture Requirement 1, Roman architect Vitruvius stated that every good building must satisfy three core principles (firmitas, utilitas, venustas). What do these three principles mean in modern architectural practice?
options: A. Maximum height, minimal window area, and exclusive use of imported marble facades.
B. Rapid demolition capability, temporary zoning compliance, and lowest possible construction wages.
C. Structural soundness and durability (firmness), functional layout for its intended use (commodity), and aesthetic beauty and proportion (delight).
D. Subterranean foundation depth, solar roof orientation, and cast-iron interior ornamentation.
choices: A. Maximum height, minimal window area, and exclusive use of imported marble facades.
B. Rapid demolition capability, temporary zoning compliance, and lowest possible construction wages.
C. Structural soundness and durability (firmness), functional layout for its intended use (commodity), and aesthetic beauty and proportion (delight).
D. Subterranean foundation depth, solar roof orientation, and cast-iron interior ornamentation.
quiz_item.correct_answer: C. Structural soundness and durability (firmness), functional layout for its intended use (commodity), and aesthetic beauty and proportion (delight).
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (C): The Vitruvian triad defines architecture through firmness (structural integrity and durability), commodity (functional utility for occupants), and delight (visual harmony and beauty).
