requirements.lead_text: Do ONE of the following:
requirements.req_text: Do ONE of the following: (a) With your parent or guardian's and counselor's permission and approval, arrange to meet with an architect. Ask to see the scale model of a building and the drawings that a builder would use to construct this building. Discuss why the different building materials were selected. Look at the details in the drawings and the model to see how the materials and components are attached to each other during construction. (b) With your parent or guardian's and counselor's permission and approval, arrange to meet with an architect at a construction site. Ask the architect to bring drawings that the builder uses to construct the building. While at the site, discuss why the different building materials being used were selected. Discuss how the different building materials and components are attached to each other during construction. Note: To visit a construction site will require advance planning. You will need permission from a parent or guardian, counselor, the architect, and the construction site manager. A construction site is a very dangerous place. While there, you will need to closely follow the site manager's directions and comply with all the safety procedures, including wearing a hard hat, protective eyewear, and proper footwear. Be aware of the changing conditions at the site, and stay with the architect or site manager. (c) Interview someone who might be your client (such as a prospective homeowner or business owner) if you were an architect. Find out what your client's requirements would be for designing a new home or business building. Write a short program including a list of requirements for the project, the functions of the building and site, how the functions relate to one another, and the goals of the project.

patrol_quiz_bank.question: In Architecture Requirement 1, Roman architect Vitruvius stated that every good building must satisfy three core principles (firmitas, utilitas, venustas). What do these three principles mean in modern architectural practice?
options: A. Maximum height, minimal window area, and exclusive use of imported marble facades.
B. Rapid demolition capability, temporary zoning compliance, and lowest possible construction wages.
C. Structural soundness and durability (firmness), functional layout for its intended use (commodity), and aesthetic beauty and proportion (delight).
D. Subterranean foundation depth, solar roof orientation, and cast-iron interior ornamentation.
choices: A. Maximum height, minimal window area, and exclusive use of imported marble facades.
B. Rapid demolition capability, temporary zoning compliance, and lowest possible construction wages.
C. Structural soundness and durability (firmness), functional layout for its intended use (commodity), and aesthetic beauty and proportion (delight).
D. Subterranean foundation depth, solar roof orientation, and cast-iron interior ornamentation.
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: C. Structural soundness and durability (firmness), functional layout for its intended use (commodity), and aesthetic beauty and proportion (delight).
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (C): The Vitruvian triad defines architecture through firmness (structural integrity and durability), commodity (functional utility for occupants), and delight (visual harmony and beauty).

pamphlet_excerpts: Discuss Forms Humankind Means: Your counselor: The question of what "art" is has occupied the minds of philosophers and critics ever since humankind began to think and argue (p. 8).

Discuss Forms Humankind Means Principle 2: Your counselor Principle 2: The term has been applied to many forms of visual media, especially to the fine arts, drawing, painting, sculpture, and print making (p. 8).
Discuss Forms Humankind Means Principle 3: Your counselor Principle 3: But it also includes architecture, industrial design, fashion design, pottery, and weaving (p. 8).

Discuss Forms Humankind Means Principle 4: Your counselor Principle 4: The difference is that fine arts are concerned only with beauty and expression and the others, though the art may be beautiful, focus first on function (p. 8).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Discuss Forms Humankind Means): Step 1 (Your counselor): This merit badge pamphlet concentrates on two-dimensional art, specifically drawing and painting in various media (p. 8).
Step 2 (Discuss Forms Humankind Means): Step 2 (Your counselor): One requirement introduces you to design applications in the fields of graphic arts and industrial design (p. 8).
Step 3 (Discuss Forms Humankind Means): Step 3 (Your counselor): After you learn about art history and design principles, you will understand how these fields relate to fine art (p. 8).
Step 4 (Discuss Forms Humankind Means): Step 4 (Your counselor): Since prehistoric people first made cave paintings, artists have tried to portray reality (p. 8).

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: When discussing the elements and principles of design in Art Requirement 1, how does an artist use complementary colors and value contrast to establish a clear focal point in a composition?
quiz_item.question: When discussing the elements and principles of design in Art Requirement 1, how does an artist use complementary colors and value contrast to establish a clear focal point in a composition?
options: A. By placing colors directly opposite each other on the color wheel (such as blue and orange) and pairing bright highlights against dark shadows to draw the viewer's eye to the center of interest.
B. By mixing every pigment on the palette into a uniform neutral gray so no single area of the canvas stands out.
C. By using only a single pencil line weight across the entire paper and avoiding any shading or color variation.
D. By painting the focal subject the exact same hue and brightness as the background border to camouflage the main figure.
choices: A. By placing colors directly opposite each other on the color wheel (such as blue and orange) and pairing bright highlights against dark shadows to draw the viewer's eye to the center of interest.
B. By mixing every pigment on the palette into a uniform neutral gray so no single area of the canvas stands out.
C. By using only a single pencil line weight across the entire paper and avoiding any shading or color variation.
D. By painting the focal subject the exact same hue and brightness as the background border to camouflage the main figure.
quiz_item.correct_answer: A. By placing colors directly opposite each other on the color wheel (such as blue and orange) and pairing bright highlights against dark shadows to draw the viewer's eye to the center of interest.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (A): Complementary hues (opposites on the color wheel) and strong value contrast (light against dark) create visual emphasis that directs the viewer's attention to the composition's focal point.

pamphlet_excerpts: Elements of Art and Design Balance Balance is the visual stability of the composition (p. 16).
Elements of Art and Design Principle 2: If a work of art has visual balance, then the viewer feels that the elements have been arranged just right (p. 16).
Elements of Art and Design Principle 3: If there is an imbalance, then the viewer feels something's wrong, that the elements need to be rearranged (p. 16).
Elements of Art and Design Principle 4: A formal balance occurs when similar elements are placed on each side of the central axis (a drawn or imaginary line through the center of the work) (p. 16).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Elements of Art and Design): The different elements of art, line, value, shape, space, color, and texture, all influence the visual weight of a composition (p. 16).
Step 2 (Elements of Art and Design): For example, a small area of bright color can balance a larger area of dull color (p. 16).
Step 3 (Elements of Art and Design): Elements of Art and Design Elements of Art and Design When you create art, you are expressing your ideas, your feelings, or your beliefs (p. 16).
Step 4 (Elements of Art and Design): If you intend to share your art with other people, you need to know how to organize your design so that they will understand what your art is telling (p. 16).

pamphlet_excerpts: Principles of Design: Six Principles of Design: These principles are guidelines, not rules, to help you express yourself artistically (p. 23).

Principles of Design Principle 2: Six Principles of Design Principle 2: Understanding these principles also will help you to appreciate how other artists try to communicate through their work (p. 23).
Principles of Design Principle 3: Six Principles of Design Principle 3: The six principles of design are rhythm, balance, proportion, variety, emphasis, and unity (p. 23).
Principles of Design Principle 4: Six Principles of Design Principle 4: Rhythm indicates movement by the repetition of a certain artelement or combination of elements (p. 23).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Principles of Design): Step 1 (Six Principles of Design): The repeated element, a shape or line, for example, is called a motif (p. 23).
Step 2 (Principles of Design): Step 2 (Six Principles of Design): The artist uses the repetition of a motif to lead the viewer's eye around the work of art (p. 23).
Step 3 (Principles of Design): Step 3 (Six Principles of Design): Random rhythm happens when a motif is repeated in no apparent order, with irregulars pacing between one motif and the next (p. 23).
Step 4 (Principles of Design): Step 4 (Six Principles of Design): Regular rhythm occurs when identical motifs with identical spacing between them are repeated (p. 23).

step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Render a subject of your choice): Paint is formed when a pigment is mixed with a binding medium (p. 39).
Step 2 (Render a subject of your choice): Pigment is finely ground, colored powder that comes from natural sources like minerals and plants or from chemicals (p. 39).
Step 3 (Render a subject of your choice): Binding medium is a liquid substance that holds pigment particles together and attaches them to a surface (p. 39).
Step 4 (Render a subject of your choice): This substance is also called a vehicle because it "carries" the pigment (p. 39).

pamphlet_excerpts: Careers & Professional Pathways: An artist who makes art for personal pleasure does not have toget training (p. 61).
Careers & Professional Pathways Principle 2: But if you want a career in the visual arts, you will need some formal lessons (p. 61).
Careers & Professional Pathways Principle 3: Colleges and universities offer four- or five-year programs that lead to the bachelor of fine arts and master of fine arts degrees (p. 61).
Careers & Professional Pathways Principle 4: In addition to the core courses common to all major areas of study, these programs include art history and studioart classes (p. 61).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Careers & Professional Pathways): A portfolio is a collection of samples of the artist'sbest work (p. 61).
Step 2 (Careers & Professional Pathways): Many art and design schools expect to see a portfolio and evaluate the student's talent and quality of work before they decide whether to accept him (p. 61).
Step 3 (Careers & Professional Pathways): Every year, various schools host a "portfolio day" so young artists can review their portfolios with representatives from many differentart (p. 61).
Step 4 (Careers & Professional Pathways): Independent schools of art and design offer two-year programs that lead to an associate of art or bachelor of fine arts degree (p. 61).

C. By using only a single pencil line weight across the entire paper and avoiding any shading or color variation.
D. By painting the focal subject the exact same hue and brightness as the background border to camouflage the main figure.

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: When evaluating how a machine learning model makes predictions in Artificial Intelligence Requirement 1, why can an AI system produce biased or inaccurate outputs even when its software code has no syntax errors?
quiz_item.question: When evaluating how a machine learning model makes predictions in Artificial Intelligence Requirement 1, why can an AI system produce biased or inaccurate outputs even when its software code has no syntax errors?
options: A. Because machine learning algorithms physically wear out their silicon transistors after processing more than a thousand queries.
B. Because AI models never use training data and instead generate answers using purely random voltage fluctuations.
C. Because computer processors automatically rewrite their own operating systems to ignore human instructions after compilation.

D. Because machine learning models learn statistical patterns from their training data, so unrepresentative, incomplete, or historically skewed data will cause the model to reproduce those biases and errors.
choices: A. Because machine learning algorithms physically wear out their silicon transistors after processing more than a thousand queries.
B. Because AI models never use training data and instead generate answers using purely random voltage fluctuations.
C. Because computer processors automatically rewrite their own operating systems to ignore human instructions after compilation.

D. Because machine learning models learn statistical patterns from their training data, so unrepresentative, incomplete, or historically skewed data will cause the model to reproduce those biases and errors.
quiz_item.correct_answer: D. Because machine learning models learn statistical patterns from their training data, so unrepresentative, incomplete, or historically skewed data will cause the model to reproduce those biases and errors.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (D): AI and machine learning systems infer patterns directly from training datasets; if the training data contains gaps or historical biases, the resulting model outputs will reflect those flaws, requiring human verification.

requirements.lead_text: Practical Application. Do ONE of the following:
requirements.req_text: Practical Application. Do ONE of the following: (a) With your counselor's approval, choose an artificial intelligence project based on your personal interest or a community need. Develop a plan outlining the project's objectives, data requirements, and potential ethical considerations. Implement the project utilizing appropriate artificial intelligence tools, languages, or platforms. Share your project with your counselor. Discuss the steps you followed to create the project and your experience during the process. (b) With your counselor's approval, design a short lesson plan on AI and teach it to your patrol or a group of Scouts. The lesson should include an AI-generated age-appropriate explanation of AI, examples of how AI is used in both everyday life as well as in the workplace, and an interactive demonstration of how Scouts could utilize AI to assist them with a school assignment, Scouting activity, or rank advancement. Share information on the development process and teaching experience with your counselor.

requirements.lead_text: Career Exploration. Do ONE of the following:
requirements.req_text: Career Exploration. Do ONE of the following: (a) Identify three career opportunities that would use skills and knowledge in artificial intelligence or automation. Pick one and research the training, education, certification requirements, experience, and expenses associated with entering the field. Research the prospects for employment, starting salary, advancement opportunities, and career goals associated with this career. Discuss what you learned with your counselor and whether you might be interested in this career. (b) Interview an artificial intelligence or automation professional. Learn about their day-to-day work, the challenges they face, and their vision for the future of artificial intelligence or automation. Inquire about training, education, certification requirements, experience, and expenses associated with entering the field. Share what you learned with your counselor.

patrol_quiz_bank.question: When evaluating how a machine learning model makes predictions in Artificial Intelligence Requirement 1, why can an AI system produce biased or inaccurate outputs even when its software code has no syntax errors?
options: A. Because machine learning algorithms physically wear out their silicon transistors after processing more than a thousand queries.
B. Because AI models never use training data and instead generate answers using purely random voltage fluctuations.
C. Because computer processors automatically rewrite their own operating systems to ignore human instructions after compilation.

D. Because machine learning models learn statistical patterns from their training data, so unrepresentative, incomplete, or historically skewed data will cause the model to reproduce those biases and errors.
choices: A. Because machine learning algorithms physically wear out their silicon transistors after processing more than a thousand queries.
B. Because AI models never use training data and instead generate answers using purely random voltage fluctuations.
C. Because computer processors automatically rewrite their own operating systems to ignore human instructions after compilation.

D. Because machine learning models learn statistical patterns from their training data, so unrepresentative, incomplete, or historically skewed data will cause the model to reproduce those biases and errors.
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: D. Because machine learning models learn statistical patterns from their training data, so unrepresentative, incomplete, or historically skewed data will cause the model to reproduce those biases and errors.

Step 3 (Hazards, First Aid & Safety): In cold weather, wear layers to keep in the heat (p. 11).
Step 4 (Hazards, First Aid & Safety): Bring along a woolen cap, scarf, gloves, extra socks, and a coat (p. 11).

options: A. View the Sun directly through binoculars while wearing polarized sunglasses, and use a bright white LED lantern at night to read star charts.

B. Never look at the Sun through any telescope, binoculars, or camera without a certified front-aperture solar filter or indirect pinhole projection, and use a dim red flashlight at night to preserve dark adaptation.
C. Thread a dark glass eyepiece filter onto the back of a large reflector telescope to view sunspots, and shine a green laser pointer into the eyes of observers to line up constellations.
D. Wipe morning dew off telescope objective lenses with a dry paper towel and warm frozen eyepieces over an open camp stove flame.

pamphlet_excerpts: Light Pollution and Sky Observation: Light pollution is, very simply, too much artificial light concentrated in urban areas (areas around cities) (p. 24).
Light Pollution and Sky Observation Principle 2: The glare of streetlights, outdoor signs, parking-lot lights, dusk-to-dawn security lights, and outdoor fixtures around private homes creates (p. 24).
Light Pollution and Sky Observation Principle 3: Turbulent air can ruin views of the Moon, planets, and faint nebulae (p. 24).
Light Pollution and Sky Observation Principle 4: Wind less nights are better for studying the Moon and planets (p. 24).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Light Pollution and Sky Observation): Other conditions that can affect observing are clouds, high or low humidity, and air pollution such as dust and chemicals (p. 24).
Step 2 (Light Pollution and Sky Observation): Faint stars may be visible only on clear, dark nights (p. 24).
Step 3 (Light Pollution and Sky Observation): If light pollution interferes with your star gazing, trythese tricks (p. 24).
Step 4 (Light Pollution and Sky Observation): This will help prevent light from streetlights, passing cars, and the glowing sky itself from ruining your night vision (p. 24).

pamphlet_excerpts: Aid of Diagrams or Real: Repeated bumping, shaking, and dropping can cause the lenses to break or become misaligned. Keep your equipment clean (p. 62).
Aid of Diagrams or Real Principle 2: Keep lenses free from dirt, debris, fingerprints, and moisture (p. 62).
Aid of Diagrams or Real Principle 3: Use a cloth (such as a microfiber cloth) and cleaner made especially for lenses (p. 62).
Aid of Diagrams or Real Principle 4: Apply cleaner very sparingly to the cloth and never directly to the lenses. Keep dust from buildingup on lenses (p. 62).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Aid of Diagrams or Real): Aside from normal cleaning, you may use a very soft brush (such as camel's hair), or compressed air if you take some precautions (p. 62).
Step 2 (Aid of Diagrams or Real): You want to avoid any contact with the lenses and any liquid (p. 62).
Step 3 (Aid of Diagrams or Real): Always hold the can upright and never tilted or directly overhead while spraying (p. 62).
Step 4 (Aid of Diagrams or Real): Use a few short (a second or two) bursts of air; stop immediately if the can starts to feel cold (p. 62).

pamphlet_excerpts: Visible Planets: List The Names: Venus also appears only in the early evening or early morning sky, but it is much easier to see than Mercury (p. 35).
Visible Planets Principle 2: List The Names Principle 2: Sometimes called the morning or the evening star, diamond white and brilliant Venus is the brightest planet as seen from the Earth (p. 35).
Visible Planets Principle 3: List The Names Principle 3: If Venus is in the evening sky, you can't miss (p. 35).

Visible Planets Principle 4: List The Names Principle 4: Because different parts of their sunlit areas are visible from Earth at different times, Mercury and Venus have phases similar to the Moon's (p. 35).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Visible Planets): Step 1 (List The Names): At different times, they appear full, gibbous (three-quarters full), half-full (like a first-quarter or last quarter moon), as a crescent (p. 35).
Step 2 (Visible Planets): Step 2 (List The Names): When Mercury or Venus is on the same side of the Sun as Earth, the planet's unlit side faces Earth (p. 35).
Step 3 (Visible Planets): Step 3 (List The Names): As the planet moves around the Sun away from Earth, its sunlit side becomes visible as a thin crescent and grows gradually as the planet (p. 35).
Step 4 (Visible Planets): Step 4 (List The Names): When Mercury or Venus is near the other side of the Sun, we can see almost all of its sunlit face, the full phase (p. 35).

Composition of the Sun, its relationship Principle 3: Sometimes it is rare to seesights like meteor showers or dramatic eclipses (p. 9).
Composition of the Sun, its relationship Principle 4: In learning about astronomy, you will study how activities in space affect your own planet (p. 9).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Composition of the Sun, its relationship): Your daily schedule, daytime and nighttime, is dictated by Earth's rotation (p. 9).
Step 2 (Composition of the Sun, its relationship): Earth's orbit around the Sun takes a year and gives us the changing seasons (p. 9).
Step 3 (Composition of the Sun, its relationship): The Sun's energy affects the weather, and the gravitational pull between Earth and the Moon creates and controls ocean tides (p. 9).
Step 4 (Composition of the Sun, its relationship): It wasn't until 2011 that NASA's Kepler spacecraft discovered two Earth-sized planets beyond the solar system (p. 9).

requirements.lead_text: With your counselor's approval and guidance, do ONE of the following:
requirements.req_text: With your counselor's approval and guidance, do ONE of the following: (a) Visit a planetarium or astronomical observatory. Submit a written report, a scrapbook, OR a video presentation afterward to your counselor that includes the following information: activities occurring there, exhibits and displays you saw, telescopes and other instruments being used, and celestial objects you observed. (b) Plan and participate in an observation session that includes using binoculars or a telescope and includes at least 10 celestial objects beyond those observed in requirement 4. These might be lunar features, Messier objects, additional constellations or planets, or artificial satellites including the International Space Station. List the celestial objects you want to observe and find each in a star chart, guidebook or by using an app. Prepare a log or notebook. Discuss with your counselor what you hope to observe prior to your observation session. Review your log or notebook with your counselor afterward. (c) Plan and host a star party for your Scout troop or other group such as your class at school. Use binoculars or a telescope to show and explain celestial objects to the group. (d) Help an astronomy club in your community hold a star party that is open to the public. (e) Personally take a series of photographs or digital images of the movement of the Moon, a planet, an asteroid, meteor, or a comet. In your visual display, label each image and include the date and time it was taken. Show all positions on a star chart or map. Show your display at school or at a troop meeting. Explain the changes you observed. (f) With your parent or guardian's and counselor's approval, use online observing opportunities such as SkyNet to observe planets, comets, galaxies, and/or the sun. Describe your experience to your counselor.

pamphlet_excerpts: Guidance Do ONE: Your Counselor's Approval and Guidance: A spectrometer separates light coming from an object into apattern of colored lines, much like a rainbow, called a spectrum (p. 64).
Guidance Do ONE Principle 2: Your Counselor's Approval and Guidance Principle 2: Each element, such as hydrogen, oxygen, or carbon, gives offor absorbs particular colors of light (p. 64).
Guidance Do ONE Principle 3: Your Counselor's Approval and Guidance Principle 3: So the unique color pattern can be used to identify the elements that make up the object (p. 64).
Guidance Do ONE Principle 4: Your Counselor's Approval and Guidance Principle 4: The colors can be shifted slightly if the object is moving toward or away from the Earth (p. 64).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Guidance Do ONE): Step 1 (Your Counselor's Approval and Guidance): Thus, a spectrum can also be used to measure the speed with which objects are approaching or receding from us (p. 64).

Step 2 (Guidance Do ONE): Step 2 (Your Counselor's Approval and Guidance): Astronomical photography allows you to keep a record of your observations of the sky and to share your experiences with friends and family (p. 64).

Step 3 (Guidance Do ONE): Step 3 (Your Counselor's Approval and Guidance): Modern digital cameras are very sensitive to light, and objects appear brighter and clearer in photographs than through a telescope or binoculars (p. 64).

Step 4 (Guidance Do ONE): Step 4 (Your Counselor's Approval and Guidance): In addition, you can adjust and process digital images to bring out even more details and colors that you cannot see with the eye (p. 64).

requirements.req_text: Do ONE of the following: (a) Identify three career opportunities that would use skills and knowledge in astronomy. Pick one and research the training, education, certification requirements, experience, and expenses associated with entering the field. Research the prospects for employment, starting salary, advancement opportunities and career goals associated with this career. Discuss what you learned with your counselor and share what short-term and long-term goals you might have if you pursued this.

patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: B. Never look at the Sun through any telescope, binoculars, or camera without a certified front-aperture solar filter or indirect pinhole projection, and use a dim red flashlight at night to preserve dark adaptation.
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (B): Looking at the Sun through unfiltered optics concentrates solar energy onto the retina and causes instant, permanent blindness; certified front-aperture solar filters or indirect projection are required, and red light preserves night vision.

pamphlet_excerpts: Hazards, First Aid & Safety: Like anyone else, athletes can get injured or sustain an illness (such as a heat-related sickness) (p. 57).
Hazards, First Aid & Safety Principle 2: Proper training and conditioning will help keep you healthy (p. 57).

step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Hazards, First Aid & Safety): Muscular athletes might consider basketball, football, or soccer (p. 57).
Step 2 (Hazards, First Aid & Safety): In weightlifting competitions, for example, athletes compete against others in their own weight class (p. 57).
Step 3 (Hazards, First Aid & Safety): Take responsibility and precautions for minimizing risk and avoiding injury by following the information in the "Ready, Set, Go" chapter (p. 57).
Step 4 (Hazards, First Aid & Safety): If you are injured, you should not try to play through the pain (p. 57).

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: During a warm afternoon track practice for the 1,500-meter run, a Scout stops sweating, becomes confused and unsteady, and has hot, flushed skin. What is your patrol's immediate first-aid action?
quiz_item.question: During a warm afternoon track practice for the 1,500-meter run, a Scout stops sweating, becomes confused and unsteady, and has hot, flushed skin. What is your patrol's immediate first-aid action?
options: A. Have the Scout jog two slow cool-down laps around the track while sipping a sports drink.

B. Recognize life-threatening heatstroke: call 911 immediately, move the Scout into shade, remove excess layers, and rapidly cool the body with cold water or ice packs at the neck, armpits, and groin.
C. Wrap the Scout in a warm fleece blanket to prevent chills and wait 30 minutes before notifying the counselor.
D. Give the confused Scout salt tablets and hot tea while keeping their track warm-up jacket zipped.

pamphlet_excerpts: Pre-Participation Physical & Health Check: Calcium is found in dairy products such as milk, cheese, and yogurt, and foods such as nuts, beans, broccoli, and canned salmon (p. 7).
Pre-Participation Physical & Health Check Principle 2: Making sure you have at least four servings of calcium daily will help ensure that your bones stay strong throughout your life (p. 7).

Pre-Participation Physical & Health Check Principle 3: If you do not get enough calcium in your diet while you are young, you could be at risk for the bone-thinning disease called osteoporosis (p. 7).
Pre-Participation Physical & Health Check Principle 4: Failing to fuel and refuel your body with good foods can lead to fatigue and injury; you will also be more likely to getsick (p. 7).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Pre-Participation Physical & Health Check): Develop good eating habits now so that they will become second nature to you throughout your lifetime (p. 7).
Step 2 (Pre-Participation Physical & Health Check): For more information about nutrition and physical fitness, read the Cooking and Personal Fitness merit badge pamphlets (p. 7).
Step 3 (Pre-Participation Physical & Health Check): To be a strong, healthy performer in athletics and in life, avoid tobacco, alcohol, and other harmful substances (p. 7).
Step 4 (Pre-Participation Physical & Health Check): Smoking makes you cough and wheeze, and it interferes with proper lung growth and lung function (p. 7).

requirements.lead_text: Select an athletic activity that interests you, then do the following:
requirements.req_text: Select an athletic activity that interests you, then do the following: (a) With guidance from your counselor, establish a personal training program suited to the activity you have chosen. Follow this training program for three months. (b) Use a chart or other tracking method to monitor your progress during this time. (c) Explain to your counselor the equipment necessary to participate in this activity and the appropriate clothing for the activity and the time of year. pamphlet_excerpts: Careers and Professional Pathways: Regardless if they are considered amateur or professional, athletes should uphold high standards (p. 21).
Careers and Professional Pathways Principle 2: They The Olympic Games once featured the world's best amateurs (p. 21).
Careers and Professional Pathways Principle 3: When the modern Games began in 1896, only amateurs were allowed to compete (p. 21).
Careers and Professional Pathways Principle 4: However, the rules changed in 1986 and professionals competed for the first time at the 1988 Olympic Games (p. 21).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Careers and Professional Pathways): Each Olympic sports group now has the authority to determine whether professionals can compete in its particular event (p. 21).
Step 2 (Careers and Professional Pathways): When participating in athletics, you should practice good sportsmanship (p. 21).
Step 3 (Careers and Professional Pathways): This includes treating opponents, teammates, coaches, officials, and spectators with respect (p. 21).
Step 4 (Careers and Professional Pathways): Athletes should shake hands and congratulate opponents after participating inan event, whether or not they have won (p. 21).

requirements.req_text: Complete the activities in FOUR of the following options and show improvement over a three-month period: (a) Option A, Sprinting. Do ALL of the following: (1) 100-meter dash (2) 200-meter dash (b) Option B, Long-Distance Running. Do ALL of the following: (1) 3k run (2) 5k run (c) Option C, Long Jump OR High Jump. Do ALL of the following: (1) Running long jump OR running high jump (best of three tries) (2) Standing long jump OR standing high jump (best of three tries) (d) Option D, Swimming. Do ALL of the following: (1) 100-meter swim (2) 200-meter swim (e) Option E, Pull-Ups AND Push-Ups. Do ALL of the following: (1) Pull-ups in two minutes (2) Push-ups in two minutes (f) Option F, Baseball Throw. Do ALL of the following: (1) Baseball throw for accuracy, 10 throws at a target (distance to be determined by age): ages 11 to 12, 20 feet; ages 13 to 15, 30 feet; ages 16 to 17, 40 feet (2) Baseball throw for distance, five throws (total distance) (g) Option G, Basketball Shooting. Do ALL of the following: (1) Basketball shot for accuracy, 10 free-throw shots (2) Basketball throw for skill and agility, the following shots: (a) Left-side layup (b) Right-side layup (c) Left side of hoop, along the key line (d) Right side of hoop, along the key line (e) Where key line and free-throw line meet, left side (f) Where key line and free-throw line meet, left side (g) Top of the key (h) Another spot along the three-point line (h) Option H, Football Kick OR Soccer Kick. Do ALL of the following: (1) Goals from the 10-yard line, eight kicks (2) Football kick or soccer kick for distance, five kicks (total distance) (i) Option I, Weight Training. Do ALL of the following: (1) Chest/bench press, two sets of 15 repetitions each (2) Leg curls, two sets of 15 repetitions each

pamphlet_excerpts: Careers & Professional Pathways: Choose an activity that matches your body type and abilities (p. 21).
Careers & Professional Pathways Principle 2: During the year, you might want to participate in a variety of athletic activities so that you gain overall fitness (p. 21).
Careers & Professional Pathways Principle 3: This also can help you determine which athletic endeavor you like the best (p. 21).
Careers & Professional Pathways Principle 4: Participating in an athletic activity means taking the time to learn the rules and proper training methods (p. 21).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Careers & Professional Pathways): Your coach can help you learn about the official rules and regulations of the activity you choose and can make sure that you have the right equipment (p. 21).
Step 2 (Careers & Professional Pathways): Ask your merit badge counselor or coach for help in learning the rules and regulations for the athletic activities you pursue (p. 21).
Step 3 (Careers & Professional Pathways): Use charts to monitor your progress for three months in four of the groups listed in requirement 5 (p. 21).
Step 4 (Careers & Professional Pathways): You may want to practice and train throughout the week and then test yourself each Saturday (p. 21).

intro_notes: Scouts BSA Test Lab Pilot Badge (Valid through 2026-12-31). The Auctioneering Badge is a dynamic blend of public speaking and salesmanship that offers Scouts the opportunity to develop essential communication and persuasion skills. Scouts will learn about the history of auctioneering, develop presentation techniques, and build rapport with an audience. They’ll engage in mock auctions to practice creating demand and closing deals while also learning how to handle challenges and uphold ethical standards. This badge fosters confidence and critical thinking skills that are powerful tools for personal growth, leadership roles, and future success.

NOTE: Any registered adult Scouting America volunteer may serve as the counselor/reviewer for a Test Lab badge. Upon completion of all requirements and the official Scouting America Test Lab survey, Scouts receive an official Certificate of Completion that converts to Merit Badge credit if the badge graduates to permanent status.

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: During a live charity auction, a bidder raises their hand to place a $100 bid, and simultaneously a collaborator in the crowd places a fake 'shill' bid solely to artificially drive up the price without intending to buy. Under the National Auctioneers Association Code of Ethics, how must the auctioneer handle shill bidding?
quiz_item.question: During a live charity auction, a bidder raises their hand to place a $100 bid, and simultaneously a collaborator in the crowd places a fake 'shill' bid solely to artificially drive up the price without intending to buy. Under the National Auctioneers Association Code of Ethics, how must the auctioneer handle shill bidding?
options: A. Encourage secret shill bidders in the audience so the seller gets a higher commission.
B. Strictly prohibit fake or shill bidding, disclose whether an item is Absolute or Reserve before bidding opens, and recognize only bona fide transparent bids.
C. Change the auction terms from Absolute to Reserve after the gavel falls.
D. Invent phantom bids from the podium after the reserve price has already been met.
choices: A. Encourage secret shill bidders in the audience so the seller gets a higher commission.
B. Strictly prohibit fake or shill bidding, disclose whether an item is Absolute or Reserve before bidding opens, and recognize only bona fide transparent bids.
C. Change the auction terms from Absolute to Reserve after the gavel falls.
D. Invent phantom bids from the podium after the reserve price has already been met.
quiz_item.correct_answer: B. Strictly prohibit fake or shill bidding, disclose whether an item is Absolute or Reserve before bidding opens, and recognize only bona fide transparent bids.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (B): Auctioneering ethics and state licensing laws require complete transparency in bid calling; undisclosed shill bidding is fraudulent and destroys buyer trust.

requirements.req_text: With permission from your parents or Guardian, contact a professional auctioneer and record an interview with the auctioneer that lasts approximately 5 to 10 minutes. Do one of the following: (A) Shadow that auctioneer for a day and discuss with your counselor what you learned about auctioneering and being an auctioneer. (B) Attend a live auction of any type. (C) View an online auction until the sale is concluded and discuss it with your counselor.

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: During a live charity auction, a bidder raises their hand to place a $100 bid, and simultaneously a collaborator in the crowd places a fake 'shill' bid solely to artificially drive up the price without intending to buy. Under the National Auctioneers Association Code of Ethics, how must the auctioneer handle shill bidding?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: During a live charity auction, a bidder raises their hand to place a $100 bid, and simultaneously a collaborator in the crowd places a fake 'shill' bid solely to artificially drive up the price without intending to buy. Under the National Auctioneers Association Code of Ethics, how must the auctioneer handle shill bidding?
options: A. Encourage secret shill bidders in the audience so the seller gets a higher commission.
B. Strictly prohibit fake or shill bidding, disclose whether an item is Absolute or Reserve before bidding opens, and recognize only bona fide transparent bids.
C. Change the auction terms from Absolute to Reserve after the gavel falls.
D. Invent phantom bids from the podium after the reserve price has already been met.
choices: A. Encourage secret shill bidders in the audience so the seller gets a higher commission.
B. Strictly prohibit fake or shill bidding, disclose whether an item is Absolute or Reserve before bidding opens, and recognize only bona fide transparent bids.
C. Change the auction terms from Absolute to Reserve after the gavel falls.
D. Invent phantom bids from the podium after the reserve price has already been met.
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: B. Strictly prohibit fake or shill bidding, disclose whether an item is Absolute or Reserve before bidding opens, and recognize only bona fide transparent bids.
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (B): Auctioneering ethics and state licensing laws require complete transparency in bid calling; undisclosed shill bidding is fraudulent and destroys buyer trust.
patrol_quiz_bank.pamphlet_page_ref: Auctioneering Test Lab Resource Guide, pp. 4-9

requirements.lead_text: Safety and Registration. Do the following:
requirements.req_text: Safety and Registration. Do the following: (a) Explain to your counselor the hazards you are most likely to encounter during automotive maintenance activities, and what you should do to anticipate, help prevent, mitigate, or lessen these hazards. (b) Discuss with your counselor the safety equipment, tools, and clothing used while checking or repairing a motor vehicle. Use this equipment, tools, and/or clothing (when needed or called for) in meeting the requirements for this merit badge. (c) Explain the different ways motor vehicles are powered. (d) Explain the safety considerations when performing maintenance on a vehicle equipped with a high-voltage electrical system. (e) Review the maintenance chart in the vehicle owner's manual. Explain the requirements and time limits. (f) Explain the purpose, importance, and limitations of safety belts and passive restraints. (g) Find out the requirements for your state's emissions and safety inspections (as applicable), including how often a vehicle needs to be inspected. (h) Explain the importance of registering a vehicle and find out the annual registration fee for renewing your family car's registration.

step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Hazards, First Aid & Safety): Air bags are required on all new passenger vehicles sold in the United States (p. 20).
Step 2 (Hazards, First Aid & Safety): If a front-end crash occurs, sensors in the air bags notice that the car has suddenly slowed down or even stopped (a process called deceleration) (p. 20).
Step 3 (Hazards, First Aid & Safety): This triggers a chemical reaction that fills the air bags with gas (p. 20).
Step 4 (Hazards, First Aid & Safety): In less than 1/20 of a second, the air bags balloon out, cushioning the driver and passenger (p. 20).

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: You are preparing to crawl beneath a vehicle to inspect the exhaust and suspension for Automotive Maintenance Requirement 1. Which safety procedure is strictly required before anyone goes under the car?
quiz_item.question: You are preparing to crawl beneath a vehicle to inspect the exhaust and suspension for Automotive Maintenance Requirement 1. Which safety procedure is strictly required before anyone goes under the car?
options: A. Raise one corner of the bumper with the emergency scissor jack from the trunk, leave the transmission in neutral, and crawl underneath immediately.
B. Keep the engine running inside a closed garage to warm the fluids while supporting the frame on hollow concrete cinder blocks.

C. Park on a firm level surface, set the parking brake, chock the wheels, lift the vehicle at manufacturer-specified jack points, and lower it onto rated mechanical jack stands before going underneath.
D. Stack wooden two-by-fours on top of a hydraulic floor jack saddle and rely on the hydraulic cylinder pressure alone to hold the vehicle up.
choices: A. Raise one corner of the bumper with the emergency scissor jack from the trunk, leave the transmission in neutral, and crawl underneath immediately.
B. Keep the engine running inside a closed garage to warm the fluids while supporting the frame on hollow concrete cinder blocks.

C. Park on a firm level surface, set the parking brake, chock the wheels, lift the vehicle at manufacturer-specified jack points, and lower it onto rated mechanical jack stands before going underneath.
D. Stack wooden two-by-fours on top of a hydraulic floor jack saddle and rely on the hydraulic cylinder pressure alone to hold the vehicle up.
quiz_item.correct_answer: C. Park on a firm level surface, set the parking brake, chock the wheels, lift the vehicle at manufacturer-specified jack points, and lower it onto rated mechanical jack stands before going underneath.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (C): Hydraulic jacks can fail or leak pressure without warning; a vehicle must always be supported on properly rated mechanical jack stands on level ground with wheels chocked before anyone works beneath it.

requirements.lead_text: General Maintenance. Do the following:
requirements.req_text: General Maintenance. Do the following: (a) Demonstrate how to check the following: (1) Brake fluid (2) Engine oil (3) Coolant (4) Power steering fluid (5) Windshield washer fluid (6) Transmission fluid (7) Battery fluid (if possible) and condition of the battery terminals (b) Locate the fuse boxes; determine the type and size of fuses. Demonstrate the proper replacement of burned-out fuses. (c) Demonstrate how to check the condition and tension of belts and hoses. (d) Check the vehicle for proper operation of its lights, including the interior overhead lights, instrument lights, warning lights, and exterior bulbs. (e) Locate and check the air filter(s).

pamphlet_excerpts: General Maintenance: Belts and hoses that need to be replaced might feel brittle or mushy when you pinch them; they also might show cracks (p. 16).
General Maintenance Principle 2: To accurately check the tension of belts, you must use abelt tension gauge (p. 16).
General Maintenance Principle 3: However, you can get a rough idea of tension by depressing the belt in the middle of its longest straight section (p. 16).
General Maintenance Principle 4: Modern serpentine belts donot show obvious wear; use amanufacturerapproved wear gauge to determineif replacement is needed (p. 16).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (General Maintenance): While keeping the engine and other internal systems is vital in extending the life of a car, don't forget to maintain the car'soutside (p. 16).
Step 2 (General Maintenance): Most older-model cars were painted with a clear-coat finish that protects the metal or fiberglass car body and provides an attractive shine (p. 16).
Step 3 (General Maintenance): Clear-coat colors also are easily matched if one panel of the car must be replaced after an accident (p. 16).
Step 4 (General Maintenance): If you use a commercialcar wash product, follow the instructions on the bottle and be sure to use plenty of water to rinse the car completely (p. 16).

pamphlet_excerpts: Automotive Maintenance Core Field Standard: An electric vehicle (EV) works differently than a traditional gasoline car (p. 30).

Automotive Maintenance Core Field Standard Principle 2: Instead of using an internal combustion engine that runs on gasoline, an EV uses an electric motor powered by electricity stored in a large battery (p. 30).
Automotive Maintenance Core Field Standard Principle 3: EVs have a big battery pack, usually located under the floor or in the back of the car (p. 30).
Automotive Maintenance Core Field Standard Principle 4: This battery stores electricity, much like how your phone stores power (p. 30).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Automotive Maintenance Core Field Standard): The battery is charged by plugging it into a charging station or a wall outlet. 2 (p. 30).
Step 2 (Automotive Maintenance Core Field Standard): The electric motor in an EV is like the engine in a regular car, but it runs on electricity (p. 30).
Step 3 (Automotive Maintenance Core Field Standard): When you step on the accelerator pedal, the electric motor receives electricity from the battery and uses it to generate motion (p. 30).
Step 4 (Automotive Maintenance Core Field Standard): The controller manages the flow of electricity from the battery to the electric motor (p. 30).

pamphlet_excerpts: Cooling System: Manufacturers generally recommend an equal mixture of water and ethylene-glycol antifreeze (p. 60).
Cooling System Principle 2: This coolant mixture offers good cooling during the summer and protects the engine down to about 35 degrees below zero Fahrenheit in the winter (p. 60).
Cooling System Principle 3: When you use this type of coolant, you should not add water (p. 60).
Cooling System Principle 4: Coolant should be checked regularly and replaced about every 30,000 miles or two years, or up to five years in some newer vehicles (p. 60).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Cooling System): The system also might need to be flushed if there is too much dirt and rust in the coolant (p. 60).
Step 2 (Cooling System): To check the car's coolant in most new cars, you need only to check the coolant level on the plastic coolant reservoir and, if necessary, add coolant (p. 60).
Step 3 (Cooling System): If your car does not have one of these reservoirs, you will need to remove the radiator cap to check the fluid, but only if the engine is cool (p. 60).
Step 4 (Cooling System): To remove the cap, wrap a cloth around the cap and slowly loosen it to the first stop (p. 60).

pamphlet_excerpts: Ignition and Electrical Systems: A voltage regulator controls the amount of recharging (p. 69).
Ignition and Electrical Systems Principle 2: The lighting system includes the interior overhead lights, instrument lights, headlights, taillights, turn signals, warning lights, hazard lights (p. 69).
Ignition and Electrical Systems Principle 3: When you open a car door, plunger-type switches close a circuit to the interior lights and make them (p. 69).
Ignition and Electrical Systems Principle 4: When you apply the brakes, a switch under the pedal closes a circuit to the brake light bulbs so they light (p. 69).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Ignition and Electrical Systems): Wires connect the battery to many other accessories, including the sound system, heating and cooling systems, and (if the car has them) power (p. 69).
Step 2 (Ignition and Electrical Systems): In some cases (such as the sound system and the heating and cooling systems), you must also turn the ignitions witch on to close the circuit (p. 69).
Step 3 (Ignition and Electrical Systems): A solenoid is a coil of wire that wraps around a metal core (p. 69).
Step 4 (Ignition and Electrical Systems): Electricity magnetizes the coil and makes the core move, opening or closing an electrical circuit (p. 69).

pamphlet_excerpts: Drive Train: You may have seen this idea at work on a bicycle (p. 33).
Drive Train Principle 2: If your chain is on a small chain ring in the front and a large sprocket in the back, it will help you climb a very steep hill (p. 33).
Drive Train Principle 3: If it is on a large chain ring and a small sprocket, it will help you pedal along a flat road at high speed (p. 33).
Drive Train Principle 4: A key difference between a car transmission and a bicycle gear set is that on a bicycle, you can use any chain ring with any sprocket (p. 33).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Drive Train): On a car, however, the gears on the input shaft (coming from the engine) and the output shaft (going toward the wheels) are always connected in pairs (p. 33).
Step 2 (Drive Train): Each time you shift gears, the transmission tells a different pair of gears to send power to the wheels (p. 33).
Step 3 (Drive Train): There are two basic types of transmissions: manual and automatic (p. 33).
Step 4 (Drive Train): With a manual transmission, just before shifting gears, the driver must push a pedal down to release the clutch (p. 33).

pamphlet_excerpts: Brake System: Check the owner'smanual to learn how to turn on the lights for your particular vehicle (p. 46).
Brake System Principle 2: Light bulbs in a car burn out just like the ones at home, and you must replace them (p. 46).
Brake System Principle 3: You should check all the lights on your vehicle from time to time to make sure they work properly (p. 46).
Brake System Principle 4: Turn on the headlights, which will simultaneously light the instrument lights and taillights (p. 46).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Brake System): Engage the high beams on the headlights and make sure that both headlights' high beams work (p. 46).
Step 2 (Brake System): Have a friend step on the brake pedal while you check to see that the brake lights work (p. 46).
Step 3 (Brake System): Have your friend start the engine, apply the brakes, and shift into reverse while you check the backup lights (p. 46).
Step 4 (Brake System): Return the carto park and turn off then engine, then turn on the hazard light switch and turn indicator (p. 46).

requirements.lead_text: Do TWO of the following:
requirements.req_text: Do TWO of the following: (a) Determine the value of three different vehicles you are interested in purchasing. One must be new and one must be used; the third vehicle can be new or used. For each vehicle, find out the requirements and cost of automobile insurance to include basic liability and options for collision, comprehensive, towing, and rental car. Using the three vehicles you chose and with your counselor's assistance, complete the operation/maintenance chart provided in the Automotive Maintenance merit badge pamphlet. Use this information to determine the operating cost per mile for each vehicle, and discuss what you learn with your counselor. (b) Choose a car cleaner and wax product for a vehicle you want to clean. Explain clear-coat paint and the precautions necessary for care. Clean the vehicle, both inside and out, and wax the exterior. Use a vinyl and rubber protectant (on vinyl tops, rubber door seals, sidewalls, etc.) and explain the importance of this protectant. (c) Locate the manufacturer's jack. Use the jack to demonstrate how to engage the jack correctly on the vehicle, then change a tire correctly. (d) Perform an oil filter and oil change on a vehicle. Explain how to properly dispose of the used oil and filter.

options: A. Raise one corner of the bumper with the emergency scissor jack from the trunk, leave the transmission in neutral, and crawl underneath immediately.
B. Keep the engine running inside a closed garage to warm the fluids while supporting the frame on hollow concrete cinder blocks.

C. Park on a firm level surface, set the parking brake, chock the wheels, lift the vehicle at manufacturer-specified jack points, and lower it onto rated mechanical jack stands before going underneath.
D. Stack wooden two-by-fours on top of a hydraulic floor jack saddle and rely on the hydraulic cylinder pressure alone to hold the vehicle up.

requirements.topic_heading: Aviation Basics and Mechanics of Flight
requirements.lead_text: Aviation Basics and Mechanics of Flight. Do the following:
requirements.req_text: Aviation Basics and Mechanics of Flight. Do the following: (a) Define "aircraft." Describe three kinds of aircraft today, and their typical uses. (b) Provide a brief overview of the evolution of flight, and discuss three notable times in history important to aviation. (c) Explain the difference between a fixed wing and a rotary wing aircraft, and the benefits of each. (d) Explain the operation of piston, turbine, and jet engines. (e) Using a model aircraft, describe the four forces that act on an aircraft in flight. (f) Explain how an airfoil generates lift, specifically noting Bernoulli's principle. (g) Identify and describe the aerodynamic control surfaces on the aircraft of your choice, and explain how they operate to control its attitude and direction of flight. (h) Explain the purposes and functions of the various instruments found in a typical single-engine aircraft: attitude indicator, heading indicator, altimeter, airspeed indicator, turn and bank indicator, vertical speed indicator, compass, navigation, communication, and engine performance indicators.

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: In Aviation Requirement 1, how do the four aerodynamic forces act on an airplane in steady, level, unaccelerated flight, and how does the wing generate lift?
quiz_item.question: In Aviation Requirement 1, how do the four aerodynamic forces act on an airplane in steady, level, unaccelerated flight, and how does the wing generate lift?
options: A. Lift equals weight and thrust equals drag; the airfoil's camber and angle of attack accelerate airflow over the upper surface to lower static pressure (Bernoulli's principle) while deflecting air downward (Newton's third law).
B. Thrust must be four times greater than weight while drag equals lift; the wing generates lift solely from hot exhaust gases blowing across the ailerons.
C. Weight exceeds lift by twenty percent to keep the aircraft stable, and lift is produced by spinning the propeller in reverse at cruising altitude.
D. Drag propels the aircraft forward while lift pushes the nose down, relying on atmospheric vacuum above the fuselage.
choices: A. Lift equals weight and thrust equals drag; the airfoil's camber and angle of attack accelerate airflow over the upper surface to lower static pressure (Bernoulli's principle) while deflecting air downward (Newton's third law).
B. Thrust must be four times greater than weight while drag equals lift; the wing generates lift solely from hot exhaust gases blowing across the ailerons.
C. Weight exceeds lift by twenty percent to keep the aircraft stable, and lift is produced by spinning the propeller in reverse at cruising altitude.
D. Drag propels the aircraft forward while lift pushes the nose down, relying on atmospheric vacuum above the fuselage.
quiz_item.correct_answer: A. Lift equals weight and thrust equals drag; the airfoil's camber and angle of attack accelerate airflow over the upper surface to lower static pressure (Bernoulli's principle) while deflecting air downward (Newton's third law).
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (A): In steady, level flight, opposing forces are balanced (lift equals weight, thrust equals drag), and wings generate lift through pressure differentials described by Bernoulli's principle combined with downward airflow deflection under Newton's third law.

requirements.lead_text: Flight Operations. Do TWO of the following:
requirements.req_text: Flight Operations. Do TWO of the following: (a) Using a flight simulator software package, set a course and fly the headings you have established with a successful take-off and landing. (b) Under supervision, perform a preflight inspection of an aircraft. (c) Observe and/or participate in an aircraft maintenance activity. Describe the maintenance schedule and requirements for an aircraft of your choice. (d) Obtain and learn how to read an aeronautical chart. Measure a true course on the chart; correct it for magnetic variation, compass deviation, and wind drift to determine a navigational heading for an aircraft. (e) With your parent or guardian's permission, take a discovery flight in an aircraft. Record the date, place, type of aircraft, and duration of flight. Report on your impressions of the flight.

pamphlet_excerpts: Flight Operations: Technicians can calculate closely just how much the deviation will be for any airplane (p. 50).
Flight Operations Principle 2: In every aircraft, you will find a deviation card mounted near the compass that tells us how to correct the magnetic course for deviation (p. 50).
Flight Operations Principle 3: Remember, the magnetic course from Indianapolis International (IND) to Crawfordsville Airport (CFJ) is 300 degrees (p. 50).
Flight Operations Principle 4: Our deviation card tells us that for a magnetic course of 300 degrees, we should steer a course of 301 degrees (p. 50).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Flight Operations): In other words the compass deviation in our airplane at this course is 1 degree higher than the magnetic course (p. 50).
Step 2 (Flight Operations): We can now proceed to steer at 301 degrees, confident that we will soon see the Crawfordsville Airport (p. 50).
Step 3 (Flight Operations): For requirement 2(e), you learned that your airs peed indicators hows how fast you are passing through the air, not over the ground (p. 50).
Step 4 (Flight Operations): If you are flying into a 25-knot headwind, you are actually traveling over the ground at 25 knots less than your airs peed (p. 50).

requirements.lead_text: Airport Operations. Do ONE of the following:
requirements.req_text: Airport Operations. Do ONE of the following: (a) Visit an airport. After the visit, report on how the facilities are used, how runways are numbered, and how runways are determined to be "active." (b) Visit a Federal Aviation Administration facility: Airport Traffic Control Tower (ATCT), Terminal Radar Approach Control (TRACON), Air Route Traffic Control Center (ARTCC), or Flight Standards District Office (FSDO). Report on the operation and your impressions of the facility. (c) Visit a military aviation facility. Learn how that facility supports defense and/or civilian activities. Report on the operation and your impressions of the facility. (d) Visit an aviation museum or attend an air show. Report on your impressions of the museum or show, and what you learned from the experience.

pamphlet_excerpts: Airport Operations: Providing weather and information services for all pilots is the primary responsibility of the flight service station (p. 73).
Airport Operations Principle 2: As its name suggests, a control tower is an elevated structure from which airport controllers operate (p. 73).
Airport Operations Principle 3: The people in the control tower have four primary responsibilities (p. 73).
Airport Operations Principle 4: The actual TRACON facility might not be located in the control tower or even on the airport site (p. 73).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Airport Operations): When you visit a terminal radar control facility, expect to enter a darkened room lit only by the glow of radar screens (p. 73).
Step 2 (Airport Operations): Controllers skillfully observe and maneuver the "blips" that appear on their screens; each blip represents an aircraft (p. 73).
Step 3 (Airport Operations): If you have ever played a computer or video game, you have some idea of the intense nature of this responsibility (p. 73).
Step 4 (Airport Operations): Most of the facilities mentioned welcome visitors, and you can find their phone numbers in your phone book (p. 73).

requirements.lead_text: Personal & Professional Aviation Opportunities. Do the following:
requirements.req_text: Personal & Professional Aviation Opportunities. Do the following: (a) Explain the following: the student pilot, the recreational pilot, the remote pilot, and the private pilot certificates. (b) Describe the benefits of the instrument rating. (c) Explain the following: the commercial pilot certificate, the airline transport pilot certificate, and certified flight instructor (CFI). (d) Identify an Aviation Exploring Post and/or Civil Air Patrol facility in your area. Learn about their activities and membership requirements. (e) Identify three career opportunities that would use skills and knowledge in aviation. Pick one and research the training, education, certification requirements, experience, and expenses associated with entering the field. Research the prospects for employment, starting salary, advancement opportunities, and career goals associated with this career. Discuss what you learned with your counselor and whether you might be interested in this career.

pamphlet_excerpts: Personal & Professional Aviation Opportunities: The recreational pilot certificate has some important restrictions (p. 57).

Personal & Professional Aviation Opportunities Principle 2: Most importantly, the pilot can fly only during daylight hours and in airspace where he or she does not need to communicate with airtraffic control (p. 57).
Personal & Professional Aviation Opportunities Principle 3: Of all the certificates and ratings, the recreational pilot certificate is the easiest to obtain (p. 57).
Personal & Professional Aviation Opportunities Principle 4: It requires 30 hours of flight instruction (three hours of which must be solo flight time) (p. 57).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Personal & Professional Aviation Opportunities): The recreational pilot may earn additional privileges (p. 57).

Step 2 (Personal & Professional Aviation Opportunities): The FAA created the sport pilot's license in 2004 to help lower the barriers of entry-level aviation by making flying more affordable and accessible (p. 57).
Step 3 (Personal & Professional Aviation Opportunities): If you are an enthusiast of light-sport aircraft (LSA), consider a sport pilot certificateif you want to fly one (p. 57).

Step 4 (Personal & Professional Aviation Opportunities): Like the recreational pilot certificate, this certificate will allow the pilot to carry only one passenger at up to 10,000 feet above sea (p. 57).

patrol_quiz_bank.question: In Aviation Requirement 1, how do the four aerodynamic forces act on an airplane in steady, level, unaccelerated flight, and how does the wing generate lift?
options: A. Lift equals weight and thrust equals drag; the airfoil's camber and angle of attack accelerate airflow over the upper surface to lower static pressure (Bernoulli's principle) while deflecting air downward (Newton's third law).
B. Thrust must be four times greater than weight while drag equals lift; the wing generates lift solely from hot exhaust gases blowing across the ailerons.
C. Weight exceeds lift by twenty percent to keep the aircraft stable, and lift is produced by spinning the propeller in reverse at cruising altitude.
D. Drag propels the aircraft forward while lift pushes the nose down, relying on atmospheric vacuum above the fuselage.
choices: A. Lift equals weight and thrust equals drag; the airfoil's camber and angle of attack accelerate airflow over the upper surface to lower static pressure (Bernoulli's principle) while deflecting air downward (Newton's third law).

patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: A. Lift equals weight and thrust equals drag; the airfoil's camber and angle of attack accelerate airflow over the upper surface to lower static pressure (Bernoulli's principle) while deflecting air downward (Newton's third law).
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (A): In steady, level flight, opposing forces are balanced (lift equals weight, thrust equals drag), and wings generate lift through pressure differentials described by Bernoulli's principle combined with downward airflow deflection under Newton's third law.

pamphlet_excerpts: Winter Sports Safety, First Aid & Hazards: There are two types of venomous snakes in the United States (p. 22).
Winter Sports Safety, First Aid & Hazards Principle 2: Pit vipers (rattlesnakes, copperheads, and cottonmouths) have triangular heads with pit marks on both sides of the head (p. 22).
Winter Sports Safety, First Aid & Hazards Principle 3: Coral snakes have black snouts and bands of red and yellow separated by bands of black (p. 22).
Winter Sports Safety, First Aid & Hazards Principle 4: Coral snakes inject powerful venom that works on the victim's nervous system; pit-viper venom affects the circulatory system (p. 22).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Winter Sports Safety, First Aid & Hazards): A hiking stick does double duty when you walk through places where snakes might lurk (p. 22).
Step 2 (Winter Sports Safety, First Aid & Hazards): Walk slowly and use the stick to poke amongst ones and brush ahead (p. 22).
Step 3 (Winter Sports Safety, First Aid & Hazards): Watch where you put your hands as you collect firewood or climb over rocks and logs (p. 22).
Step 4 (Winter Sports Safety, First Aid & Hazards): The bite of a nonvenomous snake causes only minor puncture wounds (p. 22).

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: Three miles into a steep backpacking trek, a Scout feels a warm, rubbing 'hot spot' on their heel before any skin has blistered. According to Backpacking Requirement 1, what should the crew do?
quiz_item.question: Three miles into a steep backpacking trek, a Scout feels a warm, rubbing 'hot spot' on their heel before any skin has blistered. According to Backpacking Requirement 1, what should the crew do?
options: A. Hike faster for the next five miles until reaching camp so the foot becomes numb to the friction.
B. Pour untreated stream water into the boot to cool the heel and tighten the bootlaces as hard as possible.
C. Cut a hole in the hiking sock over the heel and apply antibiotic ointment directly to the wet wool.
D. Stop immediately, remove the boot and sock to let the foot dry, and apply moleskin or adhesive athletic tape over the hot spot before a fluid blister forms.

pamphlet_excerpts: 10 Scout Basic Essentials: How much your pack weighs depends on the length of the adventure you have planned, the amount of food and equipment you must carry, and your personal (p. 53).
10 Scout Basic Essentials Principle 2: For comfort on the trail, a pack containing everything you need for a safe trek should tip the scale at no more than 25 percent of your body's weight (p. 53).
10 Scout Basic Essentials Principle 3: If your pack weighs more, here are some tips for lightening your pack without compromising your health or safety. 1 (p. 53).
10 Scout Basic Essentials Principle 4: Do a shakedown before every trip to "shake out" everything you won't need. 2 (p. 53).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (10 Scout Basic Essentials): Divide group gear so that each person carries a fair share. 3 (p. 53).
Step 2 (10 Scout Basic Essentials): Gradually replace your heavy equipment and clothing with lighter items (p. 53).
Step 3 (10 Scout Basic Essentials): Choose lightweight hiking boots over stiff, heavy footwear. 5 (p. 53).
Step 4 (10 Scout Basic Essentials): Prepare one-pot meals featuring pasta, powdered sauce mixes, and other ingredients that are dry, easy to pack, and not very heavy. 6 (p. 53).

pamphlet_excerpts: Leave No Trace & Outdoor Ethics: Extending courtesy to other outdoor visitors is a natural habit of backpackers (p. 61).
Leave No Trace & Outdoor Ethics Principle 2: If you carry amobile telephone for emergency communication, turn it off and stow it in your pack until you need (p. 61).
Leave No Trace & Outdoor Ethics Principle 3: Appreciate the company of those you meet on the trail and at campsites near yours, but respect their desire for quiet and solitude (p. 61).
Leave No Trace & Outdoor Ethics Principle 4: If you encounter horseback riders or pack animals, stop and ask the lead rider (p. 61).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Leave No Trace & Outdoor Ethics): The lead rider will probably ask you to step a fewpaces downhill from the trail and stand quietly while the animals pass (p. 61).
Step 2 (Leave No Trace & Outdoor Ethics): If you encounter other hikers or backpackers going uphill when you are going downhill, give them the right of-way (p. 61).
Step 3 (Leave No Trace & Outdoor Ethics): Step aside on a rock or a log to minimize your impact (p. 61).
Step 4 (Leave No Trace & Outdoor Ethics): If possible, camp away from trails and other visitors (p. 61).

Step 4 (That you can read topographic maps): If you find you can't determine your position, the best thing to do is stop walking (p. 74).

pamphlet_excerpts: Properly Prepare for and Deal: Getting injured while out on the trail is one of the biggest risks for which you need to be prepared (p. 16).
Properly Prepare for and Deal Principle 2: Fortunately, many trail injuries, scrapes, bruises, blisters, and sunburn, usually are not very troublesome (p. 16).
Properly Prepare for and Deal Principle 3: Soap, water, bandages, and other items in your first-aid kit will take care of the majority of medical problems you may encounter (p. 16).
Properly Prepare for and Deal Principle 4: However, the danger of a more serious injury is magnified by your distance from emergency response (p. 16).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Properly Prepare for and Deal): Miles up a trail, you must rely on your own resources and those of your companions (p. 16).
Step 2 (Properly Prepare for and Deal): Know how to prevent, recognize, and treat the health hazards that may arise during a backpacking trip (p. 16).
Step 3 (Properly Prepare for and Deal): The brief discussions that follow are intended only to alert you to the dangers (p. 16).
Step 4 (Properly Prepare for and Deal): Consult a first-aid manual for complete information (p. 16).

pamphlet_excerpts: Leave No Trace & Outdoor Ethics: Extending courtesy to other outdoor visitors is a natural habit of backpackers (p. 61).
Leave No Trace & Outdoor Ethics Principle 2: If you carry amobile telephone for emergency communication, turn it off and stow it in your pack until you need (p. 61).
Leave No Trace & Outdoor Ethics Principle 3: Appreciate the company of those you meet on the trail and at campsites near yours, but respect their desire for quiet and solitude (p. 61).
Leave No Trace & Outdoor Ethics Principle 4: If you encounter horseback riders or pack animals, stop and ask the lead rider (p. 61).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Leave No Trace & Outdoor Ethics): The lead rider will probably ask you to step a fewpaces downhill from the trail and stand quietly while the animals pass (p. 61).
Step 2 (Leave No Trace & Outdoor Ethics): If you encounter other hikers or backpackers going uphill when you are going downhill, give them the right of-way (p. 61).
Step 3 (Leave No Trace & Outdoor Ethics): Step aside on a rock or a log to minimize your impact (p. 61).
Step 4 (Leave No Trace & Outdoor Ethics): If possible, camp away from trails and other visitors (p. 61).

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: When weaving a reed or wood-splint basket for Basketry Requirement 1, why must you soak the reed beforehand, and how should you handle cutting tools and awls?
quiz_item.question: When weaving a reed or wood-splint basket for Basketry Requirement 1, why must you soak the reed beforehand, and how should you handle cutting tools and awls?
options: A. Soaking reed in boiling wax makes it brittle enough to snap by hand, and you should pull a pocketknife blade toward your chest for leverage.
B. Soaking dry reed in warm water makes the plant fibers pliable so they bend without cracking or splintering into your fingers, and you must always cut or push awls away from your body and hands.
C. Soaking reed in mineral spirits dissolves the bark, and you should hold the basket between your bare knees while stabbing downward with a sharp awl.
D. Reed should never touch water before weaving, and spokes should be trimmed by biting them or snapping them against a metal table edge.

pamphlet_excerpts: Baskets Plaited Coiled Ribbed: Your counselor that you are able: The following are common weaves used in this pamphlet (p. 11).

Baskets Plaited Coiled Ribbed Principle 2: Your counselor that you are able Principle 2: Sometimes called over-under weave, the plain weave is done with rigid stakes or spokes, and weavers that wrap around the stakes in an over-one (p. 11).
Baskets Plaited Coiled Ribbed Principle 3: Your counselor that you are able Principle 3: Spokes and stakes usually are more rigid and thicker reed than weavers (p. 11).
Baskets Plaited Coiled Ribbed Principle 4: Your counselor that you are able Principle 4: Continuous weave looks much the same as plain weave, but it is woven with a different technique (p. 11).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Baskets Plaited Coiled Ribbed): Step 1 (Your counselor that you are able): This weave is created over an odd number of stakes (p. 11).

Step 2 (Baskets Plaited Coiled Ribbed): Step 2 (Your counselor that you are able): It is not done one row at a time, but continuously from beginning to end, with additional weavers added when more length is needed (p. 11).

Step 3 (Baskets Plaited Coiled Ribbed): Step 3 (Your counselor that you are able): This method of weaving involves the weaver passing over two or more stakes and under two or more stakes at a time (p. 11).

Step 4 (Baskets Plaited Coiled Ribbed): Step 4 (Your counselor that you are able): This weave, sometimes called pairing, involves two weavers, each alternately twisting over and under consecutive spokes (p. 11).

patrol_quiz_bank.question: When weaving a reed or wood-splint basket for Basketry Requirement 1, why must you soak the reed beforehand, and how should you handle cutting tools and awls?
options: A. Soaking reed in boiling wax makes it brittle enough to snap by hand, and you should pull a pocketknife blade toward your chest for leverage.
B. Soaking dry reed in warm water makes the plant fibers pliable so they bend without cracking or splintering into your fingers, and you must always cut or push awls away from your body and hands.
C. Soaking reed in mineral spirits dissolves the bark, and you should hold the basket between your bare knees while stabbing downward with a sharp awl.
D. Reed should never touch water before weaving, and spokes should be trimmed by biting them or snapping them against a metal table edge.

pamphlet_excerpts: Need for Bird Study: Birds lend life, color, and music to the outdoors, and they are an important part of the ecosystems that keep this planet healthy (p. 10).
Need for Bird Study Principle 2: Because they are sensitive to changes in the environment, birds are valuable indicators of trouble, including pollution and habitat loss (p. 10).
Need for Bird Study Principle 3: It was the near-disappearance of bald eagles, peregrine falcons, and brown pelicans decades ago that alerted people to the dangers of many (p. 10).
Need for Bird Study Principle 4: Major, rapid declines in the number of songbirds have shown that we must preserve large areas for wildlife habitat (p. 10).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Need for Bird Study): Each species is lumped with its closest relatives to form a genus, usually on the basis of physical characteristics like the shapes of certain bones (p. 10).
Step 2 (Need for Bird Study): Closely related genera (the plural of "genus") are grouped together to form a family (p. 10).
Step 3 (Need for Bird Study): Most field guides are arranged in this taxonomic order (p. 10).
Step 4 (Need for Bird Study): Because related birds often act and look somewhat the same, knowing these relationships can help you identify a new, puzzling species (p. 10).
