pamphlet_excerpts: International law and how it differs: Amnesty International is a worldwide movement dedicated to protecting human rights as set out in the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (p. 64).
International law and how it differs Principle 2: Its members campaign to abolish the death penalty, torture, and degrading punishment (p. 64).

International law and how it differs Principle 3: They advocate prompt and fair trials for all political prisoners, and try to ensure that abusers are brought to justice in accordance with international (p. 64).
International law and how it differs Principle 4: Amnesty International cooperates with other international agencies and organizations, such as the United Nations, to further shared goals (p. 64).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (International law and how it differs): Each year it publishes global reports on the state of human rights in most nations of the world, including the United States (p. 64).
Step 2 (International law and how it differs): Despite winning the Nobel Peace Prize in 1977, Amnesty International is considered by many to be acontroversial organization (p. 64).

Step 3 (International law and how it differs): In more than 60 countries around the world, CARE provides food, disaster aid, health care training, self-help development programs, and economic (p. 64).
Step 4 (International law and how it differs): As an independent organization, CARE partners with other humanitarian groups and builds relationships with governments to influence policy (p. 64).

pamphlet_excerpts: A government is represented abroad: These official representatives are organized into delegations (p. 85).
A government is represented abroad Principle 2: The larger, more permanent delegations are called missions (p. 85).
A government is represented abroad Principle 3: The U. S. Mission to the North Atlantic Treaty Organization isan example of a permanent mission (p. 85).
A government is represented abroad Principle 4: A passport is an official document issued to a citizen by agovernment affirming the individual's nationality (p. 85).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (A government is represented abroad): A visa is a permit to enter another country and must be issued by the country one wishes to enter (p. 85).
Step 2 (A government is represented abroad): It is a special seal stamped on a valid passport that indicates an official of that country has approved the visit (p. 85).
Step 3 (A government is represented abroad): Prior to leaving, the traveler should apply for avisa, if required by that particular country, at the appropriate foreign embassy or nearest (p. 85).

Step 4 (A government is represented abroad): An alien (foreign national) wishing to enter the United States must apply for a visa outside the United States at embassies and consulates worldwide (p. 85).

requirements.lead_text: Do TWO of the following (with your parent or guardian's permission) and share with your counselor what you have learned:
requirements.req_text: Do TWO of the following (with your parent or guardian's permission) and share with your counselor what you have learned: (a) Visit the website of the U. S. State Department. Learn more about an issue you find interesting that is discussed on this website. (b) Visit the website of an international news organization or foreign government, OR examine a foreign newspaper available at your local library, bookstore, or newsstand. Find a news story about a human right realized in the United States that is not recognized in another country. (c) Visit with a student or Scout from another country and discuss the typical values, holidays, ethnic foods, and traditions practiced or enjoyed there. (d) Attend or participate in a World Organization of the Scouting Movement (WOSM) event such as the World Scout Jamboree, World Scout Moot, World Scout Congress, Jamboree Over The Air, or Jamboree Over The Internet. Attendance at a national or regional Jamboree sponsored by a WOSM-National Scout Organization is also allowed. (e) Participate in or attend an international event in your area, such as an ethnic festival, concert, or play.

pamphlet_excerpts: Hazards, First Aid & Safety: Dehydration, caused by lack of water in the body, can occur in cold or warm weather, anytime a person is sweating profusely and/or not drinking enough (p. 28).
Hazards, First Aid & Safety Principle 2: Avoid dehydration by drinking plenty of fluids and eating enough throughout the day to keep your body well-balanced (p. 28).
Hazards, First Aid & Safety Principle 3: If you become weary or develop a headache or body aches, or if you become confused, rest in the shade and sip water until the symptoms subside (p. 28).
Hazards, First Aid & Safety Principle 4: If the freezing continues, the area will stiffen and become grayish-white in color (p. 28).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Hazards, First Aid & Safety): To treat the victim, thaw the affected area only if there is no risk of refreezing (p. 28).
Step 2 (Hazards, First Aid & Safety): Put cold fingers under the armpit and the warm palm of your hand on frostbitten nose, ears, or cheeks (p. 28).
Step 3 (Hazards, First Aid & Safety): In a shelter, if possible, put cold feet on a companion's bare belly, or immerse the affected area in lukewarm water, no warmer than 108 degrees (p. 28).
Step 4 (Hazards, First Aid & Safety): If blisters develop, apply a large sterile dressing (p. 28).

Step 3 (Yourself Properly Dressed for Belaying): Step 3 (Present yourself properly dressed for belaying): Dispose of webbing that shows any sign of damage or that has an unknown history (p. 49).

Step 4 (Yourself Properly Dressed for Belaying): Step 4 (Present yourself properly dressed for belaying): Take time to store equipment correctly so that it will last longer and be in good shape the next time you want to use (p. 49).

pamphlet_excerpts: Climbing Core Field Standard: Whenever you are climbing, rappelling, or belaying on rock faces, wear a helmet that has been specifically designed for climbing (p. 42).
Climbing Core Field Standard Principle 2: A helmet will protect your head against stones and debris falling from above, and may prevent injuries if you collide with a rock face during a fall (p. 42).
Climbing Core Field Standard Principle 3: A chin strap helps keep aclimber's helmet from falling off or shifting (p. 42).
Climbing Core Field Standard Principle 4: The helmets, hardware, and ropes used for climbing, rappelling, and belaying have been developed over more than 150 years of mountaineering (p. 42).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Climbing Core Field Standard): The UIAA (Union Internationale des Associations d'Alpinisme) is a group of mountain-travel experts who set standards and testing procedures (p. 42).
Step 2 (Climbing Core Field Standard): The CE (Conformité Européenne, which translates to European Community) maintains similar standards for excellence (p. 42).
Step 3 (Climbing Core Field Standard): All ropes, harnesses, helmets, and hardware used by Scouts for climbing, rappelling, and belaying must be specifically designed for climbing (p. 42).
Step 4 (Climbing Core Field Standard): Wear a properly fitted helmet when climbing above shoulder height whether you are on a rock face, tower, or artificial wall (p. 42).

Digital stopwatch, 100-foot measuring tape, and heart-rate/recovery log sheet.
Discipline-specific protective headgear (ASTM/Snell helmet) and properly fitted footwear.
Hydration water bottle (1L minimum), electrolyte pack, and pre-activity warm-up mat.

pamphlet_excerpts: Climbing Core Field Standard: For tying together the ends of two ropes, the most reliable knot is the double fisherman's knot (p. 53).
Climbing Core Field Standard Principle 2: It can also be used to secure the ends of a piece of cord to form a runner (p. 53).
Climbing Core Field Standard Principle 3: Half of a double fisherman's knot (also known as a barrel knot) can be used as a stopper knot at the end of a rope (p. 53).
Climbing Core Field Standard Principle 4: Lay about 2 feet of the ends of two ropes alongside one another, ends opposite (p. 53).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Climbing Core Field Standard): Loosely loop one rope end twice around the other, then thread the end of that rope through the loops (p. 53).
Step 2 (Climbing Core Field Standard): Carefully tighten the two parts of the knot, then slide them (p. 53).
Step 3 (Climbing Core Field Standard): If they don't fit together neatly, the knot is incorrectly tied (p. 53).
Step 4 (Climbing Core Field Standard): The knot is commonly tied with accessory cord by a climber to ascend a rope or to secure abelay system in order to release the be layer (p. 53).

pamphlet_excerpts: Harness, Helmet and Gloves: Using a harness that fits properly helps make climbing and rappelling safer, more comfortable, and fun (p. 57).
Harness, Helmet and Gloves Principle 2: Commercially made climbing harnesses usually require only that you put your legs through leg loops and then secure the waists trap with a buckle (p. 57).
Harness, Helmet and Gloves Principle 3: The leg loops of some harnesses can be adjusted; you should just be able to slip two fingers between the loop and your thigh (p. 57).

Harness, Helmet and Gloves Principle 4: If the harnesses available to you are not adjustable, you will need to choose one that fits your body snugly but not tight enough to restrict circulation (p. 57).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Harness, Helmet and Gloves): A 30-foot length of nylon tubular webbing can be wrapped around your body and tied in special ways to form a reliable tied harness for climbing (p. 57).
Step 2 (Harness, Helmet and Gloves): Each tied harness must be tied exactly right every time to ensure your safety (p. 57).
Step 3 (Harness, Helmet and Gloves): There-fore, you must learn how to tie a seat harness from a qualified instructor (p. 57).
Step 4 (Harness, Helmet and Gloves): Once you have mastered tying one of these types of seat harnesses, you can use the following descriptions as reminders of the correct methods (p. 57).

Belaying Belaying Climbers Rappellers Principle 2: Belaying Principle 2: Anyone involved in Scouting America rappelling activities must be belayed (p. 60).
Belaying Belaying Climbers Rappellers Principle 3: Belaying Principle 3: Make the knot big enough that it cannot slip through arappel device, and work out any slack (p. 60).
Belaying Belaying Climbers Rappellers Principle 4: Belaying Principle 4: Exchange verbal signals with your be layer, then back up to the edge of the cliff (p. 60).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Belaying Belaying Climbers Rappellers): Step 1 (Belaying): Keep your feet flat against the wall's face and your weight on your heels (p. 60).
Step 2 (Belaying Belaying Climbers Rappellers): Step 2 (Belaying): Walk down the wall backward, letting the rope slide slowly through your hands and the rappel device (p. 60).
Step 3 (Belaying Belaying Climbers Rappellers): Step 3 (Belaying): Avoid lunging or lurching movements that might put stress on the anchor system (p. 60).
Step 4 (Belaying Belaying Climbers Rappellers): Step 4 (Belaying): To stop, bend the rope behind your body so that no more rope slips through your brake hand (p. 60).

pamphlet_excerpts: Climbing Directly Belay Rope: Climbing: Verbal Signals for Climbers and Be layers Verbal signals allow a climber and a be layer to communicate and work together as a team even if they cannot (p. 65).
Climbing Directly Belay Rope Principle 2: Climbing Principle 2: Get in the habit of using verbal signals every time you are climbing or belaying (p. 65).

Climbing Directly Belay Rope Principle 3: Climbing Principle 3: Arrange the rope so that your stronger hand (usually your right hand if you are right-handed) will be the brake hand, the hand closest to the free end (p. 65).
Climbing Directly Belay Rope Principle 4: Climbing Principle 4: Exchange verbal signals (see the boxed text later in this chapter) with a climber (p. 65).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Climbing Directly Belay Rope): Step 1 (Climbing): As the climber ascends, pull through the belay device any slack that forms in the rope, and let the loose rope pile up next to your feet (p. 65).
Step 2 (Climbing Directly Belay Rope): Step 2 (Climbing): While holding the rope firmly with your brake hand, slide your guide hand out along the rope (p. 65).
Step 3 (Climbing Directly Belay Rope): Step 3 (Climbing): Keeping slack in the rope to a minimum will limit the length of a fall if the climber slips (p. 65).
Step 4 (Climbing Directly Belay Rope): Step 4 (Climbing): Running the rope through a belay device allows a be layer to stop a fall easily, just by moving the belay rope to one side (p. 65).

pamphlet_excerpts: Ways to store rope, hardware: Whenever you are climbing, rappelling, or belaying on rock faces, wear a helmet that has been specifically designed for climbing (p. 42).
Ways to store rope, hardware Principle 2: A helmet will protect your head against stones and debris falling from above, and may prevent injuries if you collide with a rock face during a fall (p. 42).
Ways to store rope, hardware Principle 3: A chin strap helps keep aclimber's helmet from falling off or shifting (p. 42).
Ways to store rope, hardware Principle 4: The helmets, hardware, and ropes used for climbing, rappelling, and belaying have been developed over more than 150 years of mountaineering (p. 42).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Ways to store rope, hardware): The UIAA (Union Internationale des Associations d'Alpinisme) is a group of mountain-travel experts who set standards and testing procedures (p. 42).
Step 2 (Ways to store rope, hardware): The CE (Conformité Européenne, which translates to European Community) maintains similar standards for excellence (p. 42).

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: When examining and storing collectible coins for Coin Collecting Requirement 1, how should you hold a coin to preserve its numismatic grade, and what do the mint marks 'P', 'D', 'S', and 'W' indicate?
quiz_item.question: When examining and storing collectible coins for Coin Collecting Requirement 1, how should you hold a coin to preserve its numismatic grade, and what do the mint marks 'P', 'D', 'S', and 'W' indicate?
options: A. Pinch the flat obverse and reverse faces firmly between bare thumbs and scrub tarnished coins with baking soda paste; the letters indicate purity grades of platinum, diamond, silver, and tungsten.
B. Hold coins with serrated steel pliers and store them loose in PVC vinyl pouches; the letters indicate the four quarters of the fiscal year.

C. Hold a coin only by its outer rim/edge over a soft pad so skin oils do not etch the flat surfaces, and recognize 'P', 'D', 'S', and 'W' as the U.S. Mint facilities in Philadelphia, Denver, San Francisco, and West Point.
D. Polish every coin with steel wool to make it shine before gluing it into a cardboard album; the letters indicate the last initial of the President.

pamphlet_excerpts: Different Ways to Store: Three Different Ways to Store: A modern gold ingot Before people used coins in exchange for goods, they traded with hand-fashioned gold and silver pieces called ingots (p. 21).
Different Ways to Store Principle 2: Three Different Ways to Store Principle 2: These varied in size and shape as well as in value (p. 21).
Different Ways to Store Principle 3: Three Different Ways to Store Principle 3: At every transaction, the merchant or trader had to weigh each ingot and verify that the metal was genuine (p. 21).
Different Ways to Store Principle 4: Three Different Ways to Store Principle 4: Later, ingots were stamped with aseal that verified the weight, contents, and purity of the metal (p. 21).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Different Ways to Store): Step 1 (Three Different Ways to Store): People realized that itwas much easier to do business with stamped ingots (p. 21).
Step 2 (Different Ways to Store): Step 2 (Three Different Ways to Store): The most famous of these first coins are from the Greek kingdom of Lydia (located in modern-day western Turkey) (p. 21).

Step 3 (Different Ways to Store): Step 3 (Three Different Ways to Store): They are made of electrum (a natural alloy of gold and silver) and carry a stamped lion'shead on the obverse and crude markings on the reverse (p. 21).

Step 4 (Different Ways to Store): Step 4 (Three Different Ways to Store): Coins made of electrum did not always contain equal portions of gold and silver, so the value among coins differed even if the weights were equal (p. 21).

requirements.req_text: Do the following and explain to your counselor the design features, designer name, designer initials, and where to find them for each item: (a) Collect a one-cent coin from the year group: 1959-2008 (that is, dated between 1959 and 2008) and a one-cent coin from the year group 2010-present. (b) Collect two five-cent coins, one from each of these year groups: 1959-2003 and 2006-present. Explain how and why the five-cent coins issued in 2004-2005 were different from either of the other two year groups. (c) Collect a ten-cent coin from 1965-present. (d) Collect a twenty-five-cent coin from 1965-1998, two examples from the 50-State Quarter®/territories Program 1999-2009, two designs from the America the Beautiful® program 2010-2021 and two designs from the American Women Quarter® program (2022-2024). Explain the purpose of each of those programs. (e) Collect a half dollar coin from 1965-present. (f) Collect a dollar coin from each of the following design groups: Susan B. Anthony (1979-1981, 1999); Sacagawea (2000-2008); and U. S. Presidents (2007-2016, 2020).

pamphlet_excerpts: Counselor The People Depicted: For your counselor the people depicted: Colonial notes were printed in sheets of eight or 16 designs and then numbered and signed by hand, usually by two or three, and sometimes as many (p. 25).

Counselor The People Depicted Principle 2: For your counselor the people depicted Principle 2: Several members of the Continental Congress and others who signed the Declaration of Independence inked their names onto the paper money (p. 25).
Counselor The People Depicted Principle 3: For your counselor the people depicted Principle 3: Many of these notes paid interest and could be exchanged or redeemed for their current value (p. 25).
Counselor The People Depicted Principle 4: For your counselor the people depicted Principle 4: Large circular holes punched into the notes were just one of the ways to show redemption (p. 25).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Counselor The People Depicted): Step 1 (For your counselor the people depicted): These cancelled notes were saved by the states but were released to collectors as curios many years ago (p. 25).
Step 2 (Counselor The People Depicted): Step 2 (For your counselor the people depicted): They account for many of the examples available to collectors today (p. 25).

Step 3 (Counselor The People Depicted): Step 3 (For your counselor the people depicted): To finance the American Revolution, the Continental Congress authorized the issue of paper money in the form of certificates (p. 25).

Step 4 (Counselor The People Depicted): Step 4 (For your counselor the people depicted): These "Continentals" had no backing in silver or gold, although it was understood that the bearer was entitled to acertain amount of gold (p. 25).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: When examining and storing collectible coins for Coin Collecting Requirement 1, how should you hold a coin to preserve its numismatic grade, and what do the mint marks 'P', 'D', 'S', and 'W' indicate?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: When examining and storing collectible coins for Coin Collecting Requirement 1, how should you hold a coin to preserve its numismatic grade, and what do the mint marks 'P', 'D', 'S', and 'W' indicate?
options: A. Pinch the flat obverse and reverse faces firmly between bare thumbs and scrub tarnished coins with baking soda paste; the letters indicate purity grades of platinum, diamond, silver, and tungsten.
B. Hold coins with serrated steel pliers and store them loose in PVC vinyl pouches; the letters indicate the four quarters of the fiscal year.

C. Hold a coin only by its outer rim/edge over a soft pad so skin oils do not etch the flat surfaces, and recognize 'P', 'D', 'S', and 'W' as the U.S. Mint facilities in Philadelphia, Denver, San Francisco, and West Point.
D. Polish every coin with steel wool to make it shine before gluing it into a cardboard album; the letters indicate the last initial of the President.

intro_notes: NOTE: Stamp and coin collecting are excluded from eligibility for this merit badge. Scouts must remember to follow the Leave No Trace Seven Principles and the Outdoor Code while on field trips and when collecting specimens. Make sure you have permission of the land manager prior to taking any samples for your collection. Collecting is prohibited in most National and State Parks. Pictures or sketches may suffice for a collection and limit impacted disturbances.
NOTE: The official merit badge pamphlets are now free and downloadable HERE or can be purchased at the Scout Shop.

pamphlet_excerpts: Growth and Development: Many well-to-do people collected fine art, musical instruments, ancient coins, and rare books (p. 8).
Growth and Development Principle 2: But with the Industrial Revolution in the early 1800s came mass production (p. 8).
Growth and Development Principle 3: Suddenly the new consumer society could afford to buy all kinds of goods (p. 8).
Growth and Development Principle 4: A collection is Don't Lose Your Marbles things, but a Marbles have been found in strange places, including ancient Egyptian tombs (p. 8).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Growth and Development): However, most collectible marbles have been produced within the last 160 years (p. 8).

Step 3 (Knowledge of Preserving and Displaying): Step 3 (Your knowledge of preserving and displaying): When you acquire an item for your collection, give it a number (p. 11).

Step 4 (Knowledge of Preserving and Displaying): Step 4 (Your knowledge of preserving and displaying): It is best to keep comic books and sports cards in their protective jackets or inboxes because handling them will decrease their value (p. 11).

pamphlet_excerpts: Knowledge of Collecting and Investing: Your knowledge of collecting and investing: For more information on identifying rocks, see the Geology merit badge pamphlet (p. 15).

Knowledge of Collecting and Investing Principle 2: Your knowledge of collecting and investing Principle 2: In your own notebook, record the specimen's number and name, date you collected the rock, description of the collection site, and other relevant data (p. 15).
Knowledge of Collecting and Investing Principle 3: Your knowledge of collecting and investing Principle 3: If you bought the rock, note the seller'sname, purchase price, and purchase date (p. 15).

Knowledge of Collecting and Investing Principle 4: Your knowledge of collecting and investing Principle 4: Determining the value of a nonprecious rock or mineral collection can be difficult because there are no price guides available as there are for other kinds (p. 15).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Knowledge of Collecting and Investing): Step 1 (Your knowledge of collecting and investing): Often the price of common rocks such as granite or limestone is quoted perpound (p. 15).

Step 2 (Knowledge of Collecting and Investing): Step 2 (Your knowledge of collecting and investing): To get a general idea of the value of your rocks, go to rock and mineral shows or to rock shops to find out what people are charging for similar (p. 15).

Step 3 (Knowledge of Collecting and Investing): Step 3 (Your knowledge of collecting and investing): Dealers and other collectors might be interested in buying some of your rocks if you have a rare one found only in a remote part of the world (p. 15).

Step 4 (Knowledge of Collecting and Investing): Step 4 (Your knowledge of collecting and investing): Perhaps you have some unique crystals that are special for their clarity, shape, and color (p. 15).

requirements.req_text: Do the following: (a) Discuss with your counselor at least 10 terms commonly used to describe your collection and be prepared to discuss the definition of each. (b) Show your counselor any two groups from your collection. Explain how you organized your collection and why you chose that method. Note: If your collection is too large to transport and your counselor is unable to view your collection directly, photographs should be available to share. (c) Explain the monetary value of your collection and where you learned about those values. (d) Explain how your collection is graded for value, physical defects, size, and age. Show the various classifications or ratings used in your collection. (e) List the national, state, or local association(s) related to or associated with your collection. (f) Explain to your counselor the purpose of and reason for the identification number (if applicable), series, brand name (if any), and any other special identification marks.

requirements.lead_text: Do ONE of the following:
requirements.req_text: Do ONE of the following: (a) For one day, keep a log in which you describe your communication activities. Keep track of the time and different ways you spend communicating, such as talking person-to-person, listening to teachers, listening to the radio or podcasts, watching television, using social media, reading books and other print media, and using any electronic communication device. Discuss with your counselor what your log reveals about the importance of communication in your life. Think of ways to improve your communication skills. (b) For three days, keep a journal of your listening experiences. Identify one example of each of the following, and discuss with your counselor when you have listened to each: obtain information, be persuaded, appreciate or enjoy something, and understand someone's feelings. (c) In a small-group setting, meet with other Scouts or with friends. Have them share personal stories about significant events in their lives that affected them in some way. Take note of how each Scout participates in the group discussion and how effectively each Scout communicates their story. Report what you have learned to your counselor about the differences you observed in effective communication. (d) List as many ways as you can think of to communicate with others (face-to-face, by telephone, letter, email, text messages, social media, and so on). For each type of communication, discuss with your counselor an instance when that method might not be appropriate or effective.

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: During an interpersonal conversation or troop leadership council meeting for Communication Requirement 1, which behavior demonstrates effective active listening?
quiz_item.question: During an interpersonal conversation or troop leadership council meeting for Communication Requirement 1, which behavior demonstrates effective active listening?
options: A. Interrupting the speaker mid-sentence to offer your own story while checking text messages on your phone.
B. Crossing your arms, looking at the floor, and formulating a rebuttal before the other person finishes speaking.
C. Repeating the exact same loud slogan louder each time an audience member asks a clarifying question.

D. Maintaining appropriate eye contact and open posture, avoiding distractions, waiting until the speaker finishes, and paraphrasing or asking clarifying questions to confirm you understood their message.
choices: A. Interrupting the speaker mid-sentence to offer your own story while checking text messages on your phone.
B. Crossing your arms, looking at the floor, and formulating a rebuttal before the other person finishes speaking.
C. Repeating the exact same loud slogan louder each time an audience member asks a clarifying question.

D. Maintaining appropriate eye contact and open posture, avoiding distractions, waiting until the speaker finishes, and paraphrasing or asking clarifying questions to confirm you understood their message.
quiz_item.correct_answer: D. Maintaining appropriate eye contact and open posture, avoiding distractions, waiting until the speaker finishes, and paraphrasing or asking clarifying questions to confirm you understood their message.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (D): Active listening involves attentiveness to both verbal content and nonverbal cues, withholding premature judgment, and paraphrasing key points to verify accurate understanding.

requirements.lead_text: Do ONE of the following:
requirements.req_text: Do ONE of the following: (a) Write to the editor of a magazine or your local newspaper to express your opinion or share information on any subject you choose. Send your message by fax, email, or regular mail. (b) Create a webpage or blog of special interest to you (for instance, your troop or crew, a hobby, or a sport). Include at least three articles or entries and one photograph or illustration, and one link to some other webpage or blog that would be helpful to someone who visits the webpage or blog you have created. Note: It is not necessary to post your webpage or blog to the internet, but if you decide to do so, you must first share it with your parent or guardian and counselor and get their permission. (c) Use desktop publishing to produce a newsletter, brochure, flyer, or other printed material for your troop or crew, class at school, or other group. Include at least one article and one photograph or illustration.

requirements.req_text: Do the following: (a) Explain to your counselor the most likely hazards you may encounter while working with composite materials and what you should do to anticipate, mitigate, prevent, and respond to these hazards. Describe the appropriate safety gear and clothing that should be used when working with composite materials. (b) Explain the precautions that must be taken when handling, storing, and disposing of resins, reinforcements, and other materials used in composites. Include in your discussion the importance of health, safety, and environmental responsibility and awareness. (c) Describe what a safety data sheet (SDS) is and tell why it is used.

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: Before mixing two-part epoxy or polyester resin with fiberglass or carbon fiber reinforcement for Composite Materials Requirement 1, what safety precautions are mandatory?
quiz_item.question: Before mixing two-part epoxy or polyester resin with fiberglass or carbon fiber reinforcement for Composite Materials Requirement 1, what safety precautions are mandatory?
options: A. Mix large batches of resin and catalyst in a tall, narrow plastic cup inside an unventilated closet and handle cut glass fibers with bare hands.

B. Read the Safety Data Sheets (SDS) for all resins and hardeners, work in a well-ventilated area, wear chemical-resistant nitrile gloves, safety goggles, long sleeves, and an appropriate dust mask/respirator, and mix small batches in shallow containers to prevent runaway exothermic heat.
C. Heat the hardener catalyst over an open flame to speed up curing and blow fiberglass sanding dust across the room with compressed air.
D. Wash uncured epoxy resin off bare skin using acetone or lacquer thinner so the solvent carries the chemicals deeper into your pores.

C. Heat the hardener catalyst over an open flame to speed up curing and blow fiberglass sanding dust across the room with compressed air.
D. Wash uncured epoxy resin off bare skin using acetone or lacquer thinner so the solvent carries the chemicals deeper into your pores.
quiz_item.correct_answer: B. Read the Safety Data Sheets (SDS) for all resins and hardeners, work in a well-ventilated area, wear chemical-resistant nitrile gloves, safety goggles, long sleeves, and an appropriate dust mask/respirator, and mix small batches in shallow containers to prevent runaway exothermic heat.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (B): Composite fibers cause skin and respiratory irritation and curing resins generate exothermic heat and fumes; SDS review, ventilation, gloves, eye protection, respiratory protection, and shallow mixing cups prevent chemical burns and overheating.

pamphlet_excerpts: Composite materials: The new composites industry developed further during World War (p. 19).
Composite materials Principle 2: The U. S. Air Force and Navy made good use of these properties of composites in many aircraft and watercraft (p. 19).
Composite materials Principle 3: After the war, the use of composites grew quickly (p. 19).
Composite materials Principle 4: Boats, trucks, sports cars, storage tanks, pipes, and ducts, almost anything imaginable, we rebuilt using composites (p. 19).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Composite materials Preparation): Inspect the works pace, reference materials, and safety controls required for Composite Materials Requirement 2 (p. 14).
Step 2 (Composite materials Execution): Apply the official Composite Materials pamphlet method for Composite materials while recording observations in your Scout Workbook (p. 14).
Step 3 (Composite materials Buddy Check): Cross-check your Composite materials technique, measurements, and results with a patrol buddy using the EDGE method (p. 14).
Step 4 (Composite materials Verification): Review your completed Composite materials evidence and demonstrate proficiency during your counselor conference (p. 14).

step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Composite materials are made): This includes toys, plastic containers of all types, and hundreds of common items we use every day (p. 31).
Step 2 (Composite materials are made): Common thermoset resins include polyester, vinyl ester, and epoxy (p. 31).
Step 3 (Composite materials are made): Polyester resins are the most commonly used because they are low in cost and are suitable for many products (p. 31).
Step 4 (Composite materials are made): Epoxy resin is tough, nonconductive, resistant to chemicals, and dimension ally stable (p. 31).

pamphlet_excerpts: Composite Materials to Complete Two: Use composite materials to complete: In large composites projects, several pieces of fiberglass reinforcement might be necessary to cover the surface (p. 60).

Composite Materials to Complete Two Principle 2: Use composite materials to complete Principle 2: When you join pieces of fiberglass reinforcement to form a seam, overlap the pieces by 1 to 3 inches (p. 60).
Composite Materials to Complete Two Principle 3: Use composite materials to complete Principle 3: This ensures that the structural properties of the laminate are not weakened (p. 60).

Composite Materials to Complete Two Principle 4: Use composite materials to complete Principle 4: If you use more than one layer of reinforcement, be sure to stagger or space out the overlaps to avoid thick buildups that also can create weak areas (p. 60).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Composite Materials to Complete Two): Step 1 (Use composite materials to complete): When you saturate the fiberglass reinforcement with resin, air can be trapped in the laminate, creating voids (p. 60).

Step 2 (Composite Materials to Complete Two): Step 2 (Use composite materials to complete): Air voids are simply bubbles, which when trapped in the cured laminate can cause problems ranging from poor appearance to structural failure (p. 60).

Step 3 (Composite Materials to Complete Two): Step 3 (Use composite materials to complete): To remove air bubbles, use a squeegee or a paint roller to push the saturated glass reinforcement evenly down to the mold surface, squeezing air (p. 60).
Step 4 (Composite Materials to Complete Two): Step 4 (Use composite materials to complete): Temperature is important in properly curing resins (p. 60).

requirements.req_text: Do ONE of the following: (a) Explore careers related to the Composite Materials merit badge. Research one career to learn about the training and education needed, costs, job prospects, salary, job duties, and career advancement. Your research methods may include, with your parent or guardian's permission, an internet or library search, an interview with a professional in the field, or a visit to a location where people in this career work. Discuss with your counselor both your findings and what about this profession might make it an interesting career. (b) Explore how you could use knowledge and skills from the Composite Materials merit badge to pursue a hobby or interest. Research any training needed, expenses, and organizations that promote or support it. Discuss with your counselor what short-term and long-term goals you might have if you pursued this.

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: Before mixing two-part epoxy or polyester resin with fiberglass or carbon fiber reinforcement for Composite Materials Requirement 1, what safety precautions are mandatory?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: Before mixing two-part epoxy or polyester resin with fiberglass or carbon fiber reinforcement for Composite Materials Requirement 1, what safety precautions are mandatory?
options: A. Mix large batches of resin and catalyst in a tall, narrow plastic cup inside an unventilated closet and handle cut glass fibers with bare hands.

B. Read the Safety Data Sheets (SDS) for all resins and hardeners, work in a well-ventilated area, wear chemical-resistant nitrile gloves, safety goggles, long sleeves, and an appropriate dust mask/respirator, and mix small batches in shallow containers to prevent runaway exothermic heat.
C. Heat the hardener catalyst over an open flame to speed up curing and blow fiberglass sanding dust across the room with compressed air.
D. Wash uncured epoxy resin off bare skin using acetone or lacquer thinner so the solvent carries the chemicals deeper into your pores.

intro_notes: NOTE: Repeating Meals or Menus: The meals prepared for Cooking merit badge requirements 4, 5, and 6 will count only toward this merit badge and may not be used for rank advancement or any other merit badge. Meals prepared for rank advancement or other merit badges may not be counted toward the Cooking merit badge. Menus used for meals in requirements 4, 5, and 6 must not be repeated. Outdoor Cooking: Where local regulations do not allow you to build a fire, the counselor may adjust the requirement to meet the law. The meals in requirements 5 and 6 may be prepared for different trips and need not be prepared consecutively. Scouts working on this badge in summer camp should take into consideration foods that can be obtained at the camp commissary.

NOTE: Check out the Digital Resource Guide for the Cooking merit badge HERE for information and helpful resources to engage your learning and assist you along on your merit badge journey! The official merit badge pamphlets are now free and downloadable HERE or can be purchased at the Scout Shop.

requirements.lead_text: Health and safety. Do the following:
requirements.req_text: Health and safety. Do the following: (a) Explain to your counselor the most likely hazards you may encounter while participating in cooking activities and what you should do to anticipate, help prevent, mitigate, and respond to these hazards. (b) Show that you know first aid for and how to prevent injuries or illnesses that could occur while preparing meals and eating, including burns and scalds, cuts, choking, and allergic reactions. (c) Describe how meat, fish, chicken, eggs, dairy products, and fresh vegetables should be stored, transported, and properly prepared for cooking. Explain how to prevent cross-contamination. (d) Discuss with your counselor food allergies, food intolerance, and food-related illnesses and diseases. Explain why someone who handles or prepares food needs to be aware of these concerns. (e) Discuss with your counselor why reading food labels is important. Explain how to identify common allergens such as peanuts, tree nuts, milk, eggs, wheat, soy, and shellfish.

Hazards, First Aid & Safety Principle 2: All good cooks should be prepared to take action should an injury occur (p. 64).

Step 3 (Hazards, First Aid & Safety): Staying safe while handling food and equipment should be a Scout's top priority (p. 64).
Step 4 (Hazards, First Aid & Safety): Failure to follow safe-food handling procedures could result in food borne illness, which is preventable and happens when a person eats (p. 64).

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: While preparing chicken fajitas at camp, a Scout uses a plastic cutting board and chef's knife to slice raw chicken breast, and then reaches for fresh bell peppers and tortillas to slice for a cold side salad. What food-safety step is required first?
quiz_item.question: While preparing chicken fajitas at camp, a Scout uses a plastic cutting board and chef's knife to slice raw chicken breast, and then reaches for fresh bell peppers and tortillas to slice for a cold side salad. What food-safety step is required first?
options: A. Wipe the knife blade on a dry camp towel and slice the raw vegetables on the same board.

B. Prevent cross-contamination by using a separate cutting board for produce, or washing, rinsing, and sanitizing the board, knife, and hands thoroughly with hot soapy water and sanitizer solution before touching ready-to-eat food.
C. Leave the raw chicken sitting in the sun at 75°F for 4 hours before cooking.
D. Rinse the cutting board briefly in cold creek water without soap or sanitizer.
choices: A. Wipe the knife blade on a dry camp towel and slice the raw vegetables on the same board.

quiz_item.correct_answer: B. Prevent cross-contamination by using a separate cutting board for produce, or washing, rinsing, and sanitizing the board, knife, and hands thoroughly with hot soapy water and sanitizer solution before touching ready-to-eat food.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (B): Raw poultry carries Salmonella and Campylobacter; transferring raw juices to ready-to-eat produce causes acute foodborne illness unless surfaces are sanitized and perishables stay out of the 40°F-140°F danger zone.

step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Cooking Basics): One of the camp cook's best friends is double-layered, heavyweight aluminum foil (p. 24).
Step 2 (Cooking Basics): It is great for cooking food in coals, and for creating simple, disposable pots and pans (p. 24).
Step 3 (Cooking Basics): Lighter-weight foils will not provide enough protection against punctures and extreme heat and the possibility of burnt food (p. 24).
Step 4 (Cooking Basics): Coals can be placed on the heavy lid of a Dutch oven to increase the temperature inside the pot (p. 24).

requirements.lead_text: Cooking at Home. Do the following: Note: The meals for requirement 4 may be prepared on different days, and they need not be prepared consecutively. The requirement calls for Scouts to plan, prepare, and serve one breakfast, one lunch, and one dinner to at least one adult; those served need not be the same for all meals.
requirements.req_text: Cooking at Home. Do the following: Note: The meals for requirement 4 may be prepared on different days, and they need not be prepared consecutively. The requirement calls for Scouts to plan, prepare, and serve one breakfast, one lunch, and one dinner to at least one adult; those served need not be the same for all meals. (a) Using the MyPlate food guide or the current USDA nutrition model, plan menus for three full days of meals (three breakfasts, three lunches, and three dinners) plus one dessert. Your menus should include enough to feed yourself and at least one adult, keeping in mind any special needs (such as food allergies) and how you keep your foods safe and free from cross-contamination. List the equipment and utensils needed to prepare and serve these meals. (b) Find recipes for each meal. Create a shopping list for your meals showing the amount of food needed to prepare for the number of people you will serve. Determine the cost for each meal. (c) Share and discuss your meal plan and shopping list with your counselor. (d) Using at least five of the 10 cooking methods from requirement 3, prepare and serve yourself and at least one adult (parent, family member, guardian, or other responsible adult) one breakfast, one lunch, one dinner, and one dessert from the meals you planned. (e) Time your cooking to have each meal ready to serve at the proper time. Have an adult verify the preparation of the meal to your counselor. (f) After each meal, ask a person you served to evaluate the meal on presentation and taste, then evaluate your own meal. Discuss what you learned with your counselor, including any adjustments that could have improved or enhanced your meals. Tell how planning and preparation help ensure a successful meal.

requirements.lead_text: Camp Cooking. Do the following:
requirements.req_text: Camp Cooking. Do the following: (a) Using the MyPlate food guide or the current USDA nutrition model, plan a menu that includes four meals, one snack, and one dessert for your patrol (or a similar size group of up to eight youth, including you) on a camping trip. These four meals must include two breakfasts, one lunch, and one dinner. Additionally, you must plan one snack and one dessert. Your menus should include enough food for each person, keeping in mind any special needs (such as food allergies) and how you keep your foods safe and free from cross-contamination. List the equipment and utensils needed to prepare and serve these meals. (b) Find or create recipes for the four meals, the snack, and the dessert you have planned. Adjust menu items in the recipes for the number to be served. Create a shopping list and budget to determine the per-person cost. (c) Share and discuss your menu plans and shopping list with your counselor. (d) In the outdoors, using your menu plans and recipes for this requirement, cook two of the four meals you planned using either a camp stove OR backpacking stove. Use a skillet OR a Dutch oven over campfire coals for the third meal, and cook the fourth meal in a foil pack OR on a skewer. Serve all of these meals to your patrol or a group of youth. (e) In the outdoors, using your menu plans and recipes for this requirement, prepare one snack and one dessert. Serve both of these to your patrol or a group of youth. (f) After each meal, have those you served evaluate the meal on presentation and taste, and then evaluate your own meal. Discuss what you learned with your counselor, including any adjustments that could have improved or enhanced your meals. Tell how planning and preparation help ensure successful outdoor cooking. (g) Lead the clean-up of equipment, utensils, and the cooking site thoroughly after each meal. Properly store or dispose of unused ingredients, leftover food, dishwater and garbage. (h) Discuss how you followed the Leave No Trace Seven Principles and the Outdoor Code when preparing your meals.

step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Camp Cooking): Everything needed for meals must be carried, soall excess weight must be eliminated (p. 21).
Step 2 (Camp Cooking): This calls for planning simpler, lighter meals that require no refrigeration, heavy equipment, or utensils (p. 21).
Step 3 (Camp Cooking): No-trace camp cooking means whatever you take to camp must be brought home, including litter, cans, and leftover food (p. 21).
Step 4 (Camp Cooking): Do not throw trash into water sources or bury it in the woods, and make sure the campsite isin better shape than you found (p. 21).

requirements.lead_text: Trail and Backpacking Meals. Do the following:
requirements.req_text: Trail and Backpacking Meals. Do the following: (a) Using the MyPlate food guide or the current USDA nutrition model, plan a day of meals for trail hiking or backpacking that includes one breakfast, one lunch, one dinner, and one snack. These meals must consider weight, not require refrigeration and are to be consumed by three to five people (including you). List the equipment and utensils needed to prepare and serve these meals. (b) Create a shopping list for your meals, showing the amount of food needed to prepare and serve each meal, and the cost for each meal. (c) Share and discuss your menu and shopping list with your counselor. Your plan must include how to repackage foods for your hike or backpacking trip to eliminate as much bulk, weight, and garbage as possible. (d) While on a trail hike or backpacking trip, prepare and serve two meals and a snack from the menu planned for this requirement. At least one of those meals must be cooked over a fire, or an approved trail stove (with proper supervision). (e) After each meal, have those you served evaluate the meal on presentation and taste, then evaluate your own meal. Discuss what you learned with your counselor, including any adjustments that could have improved or enhanced your meals. Tell how planning and preparation help ensure successful trail hiking or backpacking meals. (f) Explain to your counselor how you should divide the food and cooking supplies among the patrol in order to share the load. Discuss how to properly clean the cooking area and store your food to protect it from animals.

Step 3 (Careers & Professional Pathways): These people would have training in the agricultural, butchering, or other related fields (p. 79).
Step 4 (Careers & Professional Pathways): A variety of merit badges currently available can provide you additional information about some of these specialty careers (p. 79).

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: In Crime Prevention Requirement 1, how does Crime Prevention Through Environmental Design (CPTED) reduce neighborhood property crime without relying on vigilante action?
quiz_item.question: In Crime Prevention Requirement 1, how does Crime Prevention Through Environmental Design (CPTED) reduce neighborhood property crime without relying on vigilante action?
options: A. By encouraging youths to patrol dark alleys alone at midnight and confront suspicious strangers directly.
B. By planting dense, eight-foot hedges directly over front windows and turning off all exterior porch and street lighting.

C. By trimming overgrown shrubs around doors and windows to create clear sightlines (natural surveillance), installing motion-activated exterior lighting, securing deadbolts, and organizing a Neighborhood Watch that promptly reports suspicious activity to police.
D. By leaving garage doors open during the day and hiding spare house keys under the front doormat for convenience.
choices: A. By encouraging youths to patrol dark alleys alone at midnight and confront suspicious strangers directly.
B. By planting dense, eight-foot hedges directly over front windows and turning off all exterior porch and street lighting.

C. By trimming overgrown shrubs around doors and windows to create clear sightlines (natural surveillance), installing motion-activated exterior lighting, securing deadbolts, and organizing a Neighborhood Watch that promptly reports suspicious activity to police.
D. By leaving garage doors open during the day and hiding spare house keys under the front doormat for convenience.
quiz_item.correct_answer: C. By trimming overgrown shrubs around doors and windows to create clear sightlines (natural surveillance), installing motion-activated exterior lighting, securing deadbolts, and organizing a Neighborhood Watch that promptly reports suspicious activity to police.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (C): CPTED deters burglars by increasing visibility (clear sightlines and lighting), reinforcing physical access controls (deadbolts and window locks), and pairing safe design with observation-only Neighborhood Watch reporting to law enforcement.

requirements.req_text: Crime in Your Community, State, and Nation. Do the following: (a) With your parent or guardian's permission and the approval of your counselor, research local, state, or national news coverage of three crimes of different types. Research how common these types of crimes are in your state or in the United States. (b) Record notes on which law enforcement agencies and courts were involved in the pursuit of justice for the victims and the accused person, why you think these crimes were committed, and what could be done to prevent similar crimes. Review your research with your counselor.

pamphlet_excerpts: Crime in Your Community, State: Telephone trees can help neighbors quickly reach each other with emergency information (p. 18).
Crime in Your Community, State Principle 2: Neighborhoods are divided into small, workable areas, by streets or along natural boundaries (p. 18).
Crime in Your Community, State Principle 3: Each neighborhood group prepares a chart that has the names and phone numbers of all members (p. 18).
Crime in Your Community, State Principle 4: Each group chooses a block captain or other person for the police or sheriff's office to contact with important information (p. 18).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Crime in Your Community, State): Every person on the telephone tree knows which neighbor or neighbors to call when there is emergency information or other communications to pass (p. 18).
Step 2 (Crime in Your Community, State): Owners of emergency radio scanners can play a vital role as additional eyes and ears for the local enforcement agencies and Neighborhood Watch (p. 18).
Step 3 (Crime in Your Community, State): Because scanner owners receive information immediately, they can instantly warn members of their crime prevention group about emergencies in (p. 18).
Step 4 (Crime in Your Community, State): Your group could organize a project to remove trash, abandoned autos, and other unsightly nuisances from your neighborhood (p. 18).

requirements.lead_text: Home and Neighborhood Crime Prevention. Do the following:
requirements.req_text: Home and Neighborhood Crime Prevention. Do the following: (a) Discuss the following with your counselor: (1) How participation in activities of families, churches, sports teams, and clubs prevents crime (2) How designs of houses, neighborhoods, public buildings, stores, streets, and parks prevent crime (b) Conduct a security survey of a home, a neighborhood, a park, or a camp building with adult supervision and following youth protection guidelines using a security checklist in the Crime Prevention merit badge pamphlet or one approved by your counselor. (c) Use information from your survey for requirement 4(b) and the EDGE method to develop a lesson about how a family or Scouts can protect themselves from crime. Review your teaching plan with your counselor, then present your lesson to your family or to Scouts.

pamphlet_excerpts: Home and Neighborhood Crime Prevention: Government statistics show that burglaries have declined over the past several years (p. 24).
Home and Neighborhood Crime Prevention Principle 2: However, it is estimated that one in six homes is burglarized every year (p. 24).
Home and Neighborhood Crime Prevention Principle 3: Most burglaries are committed by beginners, and the typical burglar is a male teenager who lives either in or near the neighborhood (p. 24).
Home and Neighborhood Crime Prevention Principle 4: Burglaries most often occur between 10 a. m. and 3 p. m. because those are the hours when families usually are away from home (p. 24).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Home and Neighborhood Crime Prevention): Check your house to see how easy or difficult it would beto break (p. 24).
Step 2 (Home and Neighborhood Crime Prevention): Especially check the windows, garage doors, and front and back doors (p. 24).
Step 3 (Home and Neighborhood Crime Prevention): Burglars usually enter a home through windows and doors (p. 24).
Step 4 (Home and Neighborhood Crime Prevention): A burglar wants to break in quickly to avoid being seen (p. 24).

Step 3 (Reporting Crime): Do not open email or files you receive from people or businesses you do not know or trust (p. 8).
Step 4 (Reporting Crime): If you get something suspicious, put it in the trash just as you would any other electronic junk mail, which is known as spam (p. 8).

pamphlet_excerpts: Peers and Crime: Among the growing crime concerns in many neighborhoods are gangs, gang violence, and the use and trafficking of drugs (p. 18).
Peers and Crime Principle 2: To support their interests, gangs often commit violent offenses, cause serious injuries, and use lethal weapons (p. 18).
Peers and Crime Principle 3: Gangs can make neighborhoods unsafe and increase security costs for businesses in those areas (p. 18).
Peers and Crime Principle 4: Other costs to citizens could be the devaluation of their property because of living in an undesirable neighborhood (p. 18).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Peers and Crime): The National Youth Gang Center estimates that there are more than 650,000 members in more than 25,000 gangs in the United States (p. 18).
Step 2 (Peers and Crime): Nevertheless, gangs pose a serious threat and are responsible for much of the nation's crime (p. 18).
Step 3 (Peers and Crime): Not only do fellow gang members make quitting tough for them, sometimes even dangerous, but by then these youths have established a reputation (p. 18).
Step 4 (Peers and Crime): Such astigma can be difficult (but not impossible) to shake. or peer-group pressure (p. 18).

pamphlet_excerpts: Online Crime: Millions of crimes are reported to law enforcement agencies every year and these acts affect you and your family either directly or indirectly (p. 7).
Online Crime Principle 2: Crime is the violation of a law, a duty, or a moral principle (p. 7).
Online Crime Principle 3: Those arrested by law enforcement officers for committing crimes face prosecution and punishment (p. 7).
Online Crime Principle 4: In this pamphlet, you will learn about the different types of crimes and steps that you, and your family and neighbors, can take to help prevent (p. 7).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Online Crime): In addition to being possible victims of crime, your family and other citizens carry the financial burden of criminal acts (p. 7).
Step 2 (Online Crime): Citizens must pay, usually through higher taxes, for additionallaw enforcement officers, increased court costs, and more prisons and jails (p. 7).
Step 3 (Online Crime): Because retail stores must recoup their losses from theft and robbery, consumers also pay more for goods when owners raise prices to cover (p. 7).
Step 4 (Online Crime): Citizens also pay a price when companies and governments are victimized by less obvious criminal acts, such as theft by employees (p. 7).

B. By planting dense, eight-foot hedges directly over front windows and turning off all exterior porch and street lighting.

D. By leaving garage doors open during the day and hiding spare house keys under the front doormat for convenience.

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: In Cybersecurity Requirement 1, how do the three pillars of the CIA Triad (Confidentiality, Integrity, and Availability) protect an organization's information systems?
quiz_item.question: In Cybersecurity Requirement 1, how do the three pillars of the CIA Triad (Confidentiality, Integrity, and Availability) protect an organization's information systems?
options: A. Confidentiality prevents unauthorized disclosure of sensitive data (via encryption and access controls), Integrity ensures data is not secretly altered or tampered with (via cryptographic hashes), and Availability ensures authorized users can reliably access systems when needed (via backups and DDoS mitigation).
B. Confidentiality means keeping software bugs secret from programmers, Integrity means never updating operating systems, and Availability means posting all employee passwords on a public webpage.
C. The CIA Triad requires sharing a single administrator password across all staff members so nobody is ever locked out of the network.
D. Confidentiality deletes all files after twenty-four hours, Integrity blocks antivirus scanners, and Availability disables multi-factor authentication.
choices: A. Confidentiality prevents unauthorized disclosure of sensitive data (via encryption and access controls), Integrity ensures data is not secretly altered or tampered with (via cryptographic hashes), and Availability ensures authorized users can reliably access systems when needed (via backups and DDoS mitigation).
B. Confidentiality means keeping software bugs secret from programmers, Integrity means never updating operating systems, and Availability means posting all employee passwords on a public webpage.
C. The CIA Triad requires sharing a single administrator password across all staff members so nobody is ever locked out of the network.
D. Confidentiality deletes all files after twenty-four hours, Integrity blocks antivirus scanners, and Availability disables multi-factor authentication.
quiz_item.correct_answer: A. Confidentiality prevents unauthorized disclosure of sensitive data (via encryption and access controls), Integrity ensures data is not secretly altered or tampered with (via cryptographic hashes), and Availability ensures authorized users can reliably access systems when needed (via backups and DDoS mitigation).
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (A): The CIA Triad is the core model of information security: Confidentiality protects privacy, Integrity guards accuracy and trustworthiness against tampering, and Availability keeps systems operational for legitimate users.

requirements.lead_text: Ethics. Do the following:
requirements.req_text: Ethics. Do the following: (a) Relate three points of the Scout law to things people do on the internet or with computers, phones, and other connected electronic devices. (b) Discuss with your counselor examples of ethical and unethical behavior in cyberspace. Include how to act responsibly when you encounter situations such as: coming across an unattended or unlocked computer or mobile device; observing someone type their password or seeing it written down near a computer; or discovering a website that is not properly secured. Explain why these situations require good judgment, and how the Scout Law and personal values should guide your actions.

requirements.lead_text: Cyber Threats, Vulnerabilities, and Attacks. Do the following and discuss each with your counselor:
requirements.req_text: Cyber Threats, Vulnerabilities, and Attacks. Do the following and discuss each with your counselor: (a) Define the terms vulnerability, threat, and exploit, and give an example of each that might apply to a website or software product you use. (b) Pick one type of malware (such as virus, worm, Trojan, backdoor, spyware, or ransomware) and find out how it works. Explain what it does and the harm it can cause. (c) Identify two risks of using public Wi-Fi and describe how to reduce or avoid those risks. (d) Describe what spoofing and phishing are, and how to recognize a message or website that might be trying to trick you. Explain what steps you should take to protect yourself and others if you come across one. (e) Current Events. Do ONE of the following: (1) Read an article or a news report about a recent cybersecurity incident, such as a data breach or malware infection. Explain how the incident happened (to the best of your ability based on the information available) and what the consequences are or might be to the victim. (2) With your parent or guardian's permission, watch a movie or read a book in which cybersecurity plays a significant role. Discuss how cybersecurity topics were depicted and how realistic you think it was. (f) Create a list of what is part of your cyber attack surface including all the ways someone could try to access your personal information or devices, such as online accounts, apps, or home networks.

requirements.lead_text: Cyber Defenses. Do the following:
requirements.req_text: Cyber Defenses. Do the following: (a) Describe three technologies that are used to defend a computer or network, such as access controls, antivirus software, firewall, intrusion detection/prevention systems, and Virtual Private Network. (b) Installing updates. Do the following: (1) Explain to your counselor the importance of installing the latest updates on your computer, why they are needed, and what kinds of problems they can prevent. (2) Demonstrate to your counselor how to check for, download, and install the latest updates for your computer or mobile device, or another computer you have permission to use. (If you are unable to do this on your computer, you may use an online guide with screenshots to demonstrate this.) Show your counselor how to verify that your computer or mobile device is up-to-date. (c) System security. With your parent or guardian's permission, do THREE of the following using a computer or mobile device, and discuss with your counselor: (1) Describe what makes a good password and why. Set or change an account password to one that is "strong." (2) Describe multi-factor authentication (MFA) and how it can be used to improve security. Demonstrate how to use an authenticator app or other MFA function. (3) Install and set up a password manager. Demonstrate how it works to your counselor. (4) Run a virus scan. Show the results to your counselor. (5) Using a command line or other built-in tool, see what programs or processes are running on your computer. Discuss with your counselor what you see and what surprises you. (6) Use a command line interface to view your computer's open network connections. Discuss the results with your counselor. (7) Demonstrate how to back up your data from a mobile device to a local computer or the cloud. (8) Research best practices for protecting a home computer or network, and make a checklist of FIVE things you and your family can do to stay secure. (9) Identify one or more other vulnerabilities on your home computer or network or another computer or network you have permission to use and discuss with your counselor. With permission from the system owner, take the necessary actions to fix it.

sub_requirements.label: (c)
sub_requirements.text: System security. With your parent or guardian's permission, do THREE of the following using a computer or mobile device, and discuss with your counselor: (1) Describe what makes a good password and why. Set or change an account password to one that is "strong." (2) Describe multi-factor authentication (MFA) and how it can be used to improve security. Demonstrate how to use an authenticator app or other MFA function. (3) Install and set up a password manager. Demonstrate how it works to your counselor. (4) Run a virus scan. Show the results to your counselor. (5) Using a command line or other built-in tool, see what programs or processes are running on your computer. Discuss with your counselor what you see and what surprises you. (6) Use a command line interface to view your computer's open network connections. Discuss the results with your counselor. (7) Demonstrate how to back up your data from a mobile device to a local computer or the cloud. (8) Research best practices for protecting a home computer or network, and make a checklist of FIVE things you and your family can do to stay secure. (9) Identify one or more other vulnerabilities on your home computer or network or another computer or network you have permission to use and discuss with your counselor. With permission from the system owner, take the necessary actions to fix.

sub_requirements.sub_req_text: System security. With your parent or guardian's permission, do THREE of the following using a computer or mobile device, and discuss with your counselor: (1) Describe what makes a good password and why. Set or change an account password to one that is "strong." (2) Describe multi-factor authentication (MFA) and how it can be used to improve security. Demonstrate how to use an authenticator app or other MFA function. (3) Install and set up a password manager. Demonstrate how it works to your counselor. (4) Run a virus scan. Show the results to your counselor. (5) Using a command line or other built-in tool, see what programs or processes are running on your computer. Discuss with your counselor what you see and what surprises you. (6) Use a command line interface to view your computer's open network connections. Discuss the results with your counselor. (7) Demonstrate how to back up your data from a mobile device to a local computer or the cloud. (8) Research best practices for protecting a home computer or network, and make a checklist of FIVE things you and your family can do to stay secure. (9) Identify one or more other vulnerabilities on your home computer or network or another computer or network you have permission to use and discuss with your counselor. With permission from the system owner, take the necessary actions to fix.

requirements.lead_text: Cryptography. Do the following:
requirements.req_text: Cryptography. Do the following: (a) Research and explain to your counselor three situations where encryption is used in cybersecurity. For each situation, describe what kind of encryption is used and why it is important. (b) Show how you can know if your connection to a website is encrypted. (c) Do ONE of the following: (1) Create your own encryption code, such as a substitution cipher or code book, and demonstrate using it to encrypt and decrypt a message. Describe the strengths and weaknesses of your code. (2) Download and set up an app (from an official app store) that uses end-to-end encryption. Explain to your counselor what this means, how it works, and why it is more secure than other forms of communication (e. g. SMS). (3) Use a hashing tool (for example, using SHA or MD5) to create a checksum for a file, document, or piece of text. Have a fellow Scout or your counselor make a change to it, then recreate the checksum and compare the new checksum to the original as a demonstration of file integrity checking. (4) Create your own PGP (pretty good privacy) email key. Share your public key with others (and your counselor). Also, get their public keys and add them to your computer's key ring. Send a message that has been digitally encrypted.

sub_requirements.sub_req_text: Do ONE of the following: (1) Create your own encryption code, such as a substitution cipher or code book, and demonstrate using it to encrypt and decrypt a message. Describe the strengths and weaknesses of your code. (2) Download and set up an app (from an official app store) that uses end-to-end encryption. Explain to your counselor what this means, how it works, and why it is more secure than other forms of communication (e. g. SMS). (3) Use a hashing tool (for example, using SHA or MD5) to create a checksum for a file, document, or piece of text. Have a fellow Scout or your counselor make a change to it, then recreate the checksum and compare the new checksum to the original as a demonstration of file integrity checking. (4) Create your own PGP (pretty good privacy) email key. Share your public key with others (and your counselor). Also, get their public keys and add them to your computer's key ring. Send a message that has been digitally encrypted.

patrol_quiz_bank.question: In Cybersecurity Requirement 1, how do the three pillars of the CIA Triad (Confidentiality, Integrity, and Availability) protect an organization's information systems?
options: A. Confidentiality prevents unauthorized disclosure of sensitive data (via encryption and access controls), Integrity ensures data is not secretly altered or tampered with (via cryptographic hashes), and Availability ensures authorized users can reliably access systems when needed (via backups and DDoS mitigation).
B. Confidentiality means keeping software bugs secret from programmers, Integrity means never updating operating systems, and Availability means posting all employee passwords on a public webpage.
C. The CIA Triad requires sharing a single administrator password across all staff members so nobody is ever locked out of the network.
D. Confidentiality deletes all files after twenty-four hours, Integrity blocks antivirus scanners, and Availability disables multi-factor authentication.
choices: A. Confidentiality prevents unauthorized disclosure of sensitive data (via encryption and access controls), Integrity ensures data is not secretly altered or tampered with (via cryptographic hashes), and Availability ensures authorized users can reliably access systems when needed (via backups and DDoS mitigation).
B. Confidentiality means keeping software bugs secret from programmers, Integrity means never updating operating systems, and Availability means posting all employee passwords on a public webpage.
C. The CIA Triad requires sharing a single administrator password across all staff members so nobody is ever locked out of the network.
D. Confidentiality deletes all files after twenty-four hours, Integrity blocks antivirus scanners, and Availability disables multi-factor authentication.
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: A. Confidentiality prevents unauthorized disclosure of sensitive data (via encryption and access controls), Integrity ensures data is not secretly altered or tampered with (via cryptographic hashes), and Availability ensures authorized users can reliably access systems when needed (via backups and DDoS mitigation).
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (A): The CIA Triad is the core model of information security: Confidentiality protects privacy, Integrity guards accuracy and trustworthiness against tampering, and Availability keeps systems operational for legitimate users.

requirements.lead_text: Do the following:
requirements.req_text: Do the following: (a) Explain to your counselor the most likely hazards you may encounter while participating in cycling activities and what you should do to anticipate, help prevent, mitigate, and respond to these hazards. Explain to your counselor how to ride predictably, be conspicuous, think ahead, and ride ready. (b) Show that you know first aid for injuries or illnesses that could occur while cycling, including cuts, scratches, concussions, blisters, sunburn, heat exhaustion, heatstroke, hypothermia, frostbite, dehydration, insect stings, tick bites, and snakebite. Explain to your counselor why you should be able to identify the poisonous plants and poisonous animals that are found in your area.

pamphlet_excerpts: Hazards, First Aid & Safety: Wash cuts, scratches, and scrapes with soap and water (p. 86).
Hazards, First Aid & Safety Principle 2: Cover larger wounds with a sterile gauzepad or a clean cloth folded into a pad (p. 86).
Hazards, First Aid & Safety Principle 3: Sunburn can cause lasting skin damage and the potential for skin cancer (p. 86).
Hazards, First Aid & Safety Principle 4: Cover up to prevent sunburn, and use plenty of sunscreen with a sun protection factor (SPF) of at least 15 (p. 86).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Hazards, First Aid & Safety): To ease the pain of a mild sunburn, apply cool, wet cloths to the affected area (p. 86).
Step 2 (Hazards, First Aid & Safety): A soothing lotion containing chamomile or aloe vera may provide relief (p. 86).
Step 3 (Hazards, First Aid & Safety): A concussion is a brain injury, caused by a blow to the head or by a sudden change in motion of the head, in which the brain bounces rapidly back (p. 86).
Step 4 (Hazards, First Aid & Safety): Aperson does not need to be knocked out to have a concussion (p. 86).

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: Before departing on a 25-mile troop road ride, you check a Scout's helmet and notice the front rim sits high on the forehead (4 fingers above the eyebrows) and the side straps form a loose loop below the chin. How must the helmet be adjusted?
quiz_item.question: Before departing on a 25-mile troop road ride, you check a Scout's helmet and notice the front rim sits high on the forehead (4 fingers above the eyebrows) and the side straps form a loose loop below the chin. How must the helmet be adjusted?
options: A. Tilt the helmet back further so the Scout can see traffic lights more easily.

B. Apply the 2-V-1 helmet fit rule: level the rim 1 to 2 finger-widths above the eyebrows, adjust side sliders to form a snug 'V' right under each ear, and tighten the chin buckle until only 1 finger fits underneath.
C. Wear a thick winter beanie underneath the loose straps without tightening the retention dial.
D. Unbuckle the chin strap during uphill climbs and refasten it only on downhill segments.
choices: A. Tilt the helmet back further so the Scout can see traffic lights more easily.

B. Apply the 2-V-1 helmet fit rule: level the rim 1 to 2 finger-widths above the eyebrows, adjust side sliders to form a snug 'V' right under each ear, and tighten the chin buckle until only 1 finger fits underneath.
C. Wear a thick winter beanie underneath the loose straps without tightening the retention dial.
D. Unbuckle the chin strap during uphill climbs and refasten it only on downhill segments.

quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (B): A helmet tilted back exposes the frontal skull in a forward crash; the BSA Cycling Pamphlet's 2-V-1 fit check keeps the helmet level and secure during impact.

pamphlet_excerpts: State & Local Bicycle Traffic Laws: However, you should not delay faster drivers unnecessarily (p. 57).
State & Local Bicycle Traffic Laws Principle 2: If you are going the same speed as other vehicles, pull into line with them (p. 57).
State & Local Bicycle Traffic Laws Principle 3: Don't ride too close to the vehicle you are passing (p. 57).
State & Local Bicycle Traffic Laws Principle 4: After you pass, return to the right lane as soon asis convenient (p. 57).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (State & Local Bicycle Traffic Laws): An intersection is any point, including a driveway, where the paths of two vehicles can cross (p. 57).
Step 2 (State & Local Bicycle Traffic Laws): There are ways to get through an intersection as easily and safely as possible (p. 57).
Step 3 (State & Local Bicycle Traffic Laws): First, always move to the lane position that will allow you to ride through most efficiently (p. 57).

pamphlet_excerpts: Bicycle Safety Inspection & Maintenance: The Scouting America Bike Safety Guidelines are designed to make bicycle riding safer and more enjoyable for you and others (p. 54).
Bicycle Safety Inspection & Maintenance Principle 2: Review these guidelines with your merit badge counselor (p. 54).
Bicycle Safety Inspection & Maintenance Principle 3: As with all Scouting activities, these principles should be applied in your cycling event (p. 54).
Bicycle Safety Inspection & Maintenance Principle 4: Bicycle helmets can reduce head injuries by 85 percent, according to the NHTSA (p. 54).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Bicycle Safety Inspection & Maintenance): Make sure you can stand over the top tube of your bicycle (p. 54).
Step 2 (Bicycle Safety Inspection & Maintenance): Assure that tires are fully inflated and brakes are working properly (p. 54).
Step 3 (Bicycle Safety Inspection & Maintenance): Wear clothing that makes you more visible, such as bright neon or fluorescent colors (p. 54).
Step 4 (Bicycle Safety Inspection & Maintenance): Be on the lookout for hazards, such as potholes, broken glass, gravel, puddles, leaves, animals, or anything that could cause you to crash (p. 54).
