pamphlet_excerpts: Basic bicycle handling skills: To mount the bicycle, engage the brakes to prevent the bike from rolling (p. 53).
Basic bicycle handling skills Principle 2: Swing either leg up and over the bike and straddle the top tube (p. 53).
Basic bicycle handling skills Principle 3: Use your foot to turn the crank backward until it reaches the 10 o'clock position (p. 53).
Basic bicycle handling skills Principle 4: As your body moves up and the bike moves forward, the saddle will move (p. 53).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Basic bicycle handling skills): When the opposite pedal reaches the 12 o'clock position, make a second pedal stroke (p. 53).
Step 2 (Basic bicycle handling skills): To dismount, place the left pedal straight down and stand on it like a step (p. 53).
Step 3 (Basic bicycle handling skills): As the bike is about to come to a stop, lean alittle to the right and put your right foot on the ground (p. 53).
Step 4 (Basic bicycle handling skills): As soon as you can, position the left pedal to the 10 o'clock position in preparation for starting again (p. 53).

requirements.lead_text: Using the Scouting America buddy system, complete all of the requirements for ONE of the following options: Road Biking OR Trail or Mixed Surface Biking. Resource: The Buddy System in Scouting: Why No Scout Should Go It Alone (website)
requirements.req_text: Using the Scouting America buddy system, complete all of the requirements for ONE of the following options: Road Biking OR Trail or Mixed Surface Biking. Resource: The Buddy System in Scouting: Why No Scout Should Go It Alone (website) (a) Option A, Road Biking. Do ALL of the following: (1) Take a road safety test with your counselor and demonstrate the following: (a) On an urban street with light traffic, properly execute a left turn from the center of the street; also demonstrate an alternate left-turn technique used during periods of heavy traffic. (b) Properly execute a right turn. (c) Demonstrate appropriate actions at a right-turn-only lane when you are continuing straight. (d) Show proper curbside and road-edge riding. Show how to ride safely along a row of parked cars. (e) Cross railroad tracks properly. (2) Avoiding main highways, take two rides of 10 miles each, two rides of 15 miles each, and two rides of 25 miles each. You must make a report of the rides taken. List dates for the routes traveled, and interesting things seen on the ride. (3) After completing requirement (2) for the road biking option, do ONE of the following: (a) Lay out on a road map a 50-mile trip. Stay away from main highways. Using your map, make this ride in eight hours or less. (b) Participate in an organized bike tour of at least 50 miles. Make this ride in eight hours or less. Afterward, use the tour's cue sheet to make a map of the ride. (b) Option B, Trail or Mixed Surface Biking. Do ALL of the following: Note: These requirements may be completed using a mountain bike or other properly equipped, manually-powered cycle such as a gravel bike, tandem bike, hand-powered bike, recumbent bike, adult tricycle, or adaptive cycle. If a tandem bike is used, the Scout must actively power the cycle in concert with the other rider. (1) Demonstrate the following mountain bike handling skills to your counselor: (a) Neutral position, ready position, bike body separation (side to side, and forward and back), and body positioning for cornering (b) Show shifting skills as applicable to climbs and obstacles. (c) Show proper technique for riding up and down hills, including when you would ride seated, crouched, or standing. (2) Take a trail safety test with your counselor and demonstrate the following: (a) Show proper trail etiquette to hikers and other cyclists, including when to yield the right-of-way. Resource: Bike Trail Etiquette (video) (b) Demonstrate how to correctly cross an obstacle by either going over the obstacle on your bike or dismounting your bike and crossing over or around the obstacle. (c) Cross rocks, gravel, and roots properly (3) Describe the rules of trail riding, including how to know when a trail is unsuitable for riding. (4) On mountain biking or multi-use trails approved by your counselor, take two rides of 2 miles each, two rides of 5 miles each, and two rides of 8 miles each. You must make a report of the rides taken. List dates for the routes traveled, and interesting things seen. (5) After fulfilling the previous requirement, lay out on a trail map a 22-mile trip. You may include multiple trail systems, if needed. Stay away from main highways. Using your map, complete this ride in one day.

sub_requirements.sub_req_text: Option A, Road Biking. Do ALL of the following: (1) Take a road safety test with your counselor and demonstrate the following: (a) On an urban street with light traffic, properly execute a left turn from the center of the street; also demonstrate an alternate left-turn technique used during periods of heavy traffic. (b) Properly execute a right turn. (c) Demonstrate appropriate actions at a right-turn-only lane when you are continuing straight. (d) Show proper curbside and road-edge riding. Show how to ride safely along a row of parked cars. (e) Cross railroad tracks properly. (2) Avoiding main highways, take two rides of 10 miles each, two rides of 15 miles each, and two rides of 25 miles each. You must make a report of the rides taken. List dates for the routes traveled, and interesting things seen on the ride. (3) After completing requirement (2) for the road biking option, do ONE of the following: (a) Lay out on a road map a 50-mile trip. Stay away from main highways. Using your map, make this ride in eight hours or less. (b) Participate in an organized bike tour of at least 50 miles. Make this ride in eight hours or less. Afterward, use the tour's cue sheet to make a map of the ride.

pamphlet_excerpts: Option A Road Biking: Cycling Specialized Field Options: Road Biking / Trail or Mixed Surface Biking Principle 4: Pushyour bike into the turn, keep your head up and look at your exitpoint, one finger on each brake lever (p. 80).

sub_requirements.label: (b)
sub_requirements.text: Option B, Trail or Mixed Surface Biking. Do ALL of the following: Note: These requirements may be completed using a mountain bike or other properly equipped, manually-powered cycle such as a gravel bike, tandem bike, hand-powered bike, recumbent bike, adult tricycle, or adaptive cycle. If a tandem bike is used, the Scout must actively power the cycle in concert with the other rider. (1) Demonstrate the following mountain bike handling skills to your counselor: (a) Neutral position, ready position, bike body separation (side to side, and forward and back), and body positioning for cornering (b) Show shifting skills as applicable to climbs and obstacles. (c) Show proper technique for riding up and down hills, including when you would ride seated, crouched, or standing. (2) Take a trail safety test with your counselor and demonstrate the following: (a) Show proper trail etiquette to hikers and other cyclists, including when to yield the right-of-way. Resource: Bike Trail Etiquette (video) (b) Demonstrate how to correctly cross an obstacle by either going over the obstacle on your bike or dismounting your bike and crossing over or around the obstacle. (c) Cross rocks, gravel, and roots properly (3) Describe the rules of trail riding, including how to know when a trail is unsuitable for riding. (4) On mountain biking or multi-use trails approved by your counselor, take two rides of 2 miles each, two rides of 5 miles each, and two rides of 8 miles each. You must make a report of the rides taken. List dates for the routes traveled, and interesting things seen. (5) After fulfilling the previous requirement, lay out on a trail map a 22-mile trip. You may include multiple trail systems, if needed. Stay away from main highways. Using your map, complete this ride in one day.

sub_requirements.sub_req_text: Option B, Trail or Mixed Surface Biking. Do ALL of the following: Note: These requirements may be completed using a mountain bike or other properly equipped, manually-powered cycle such as a gravel bike, tandem bike, hand-powered bike, recumbent bike, adult tricycle, or adaptive cycle. If a tandem bike is used, the Scout must actively power the cycle in concert with the other rider. (1) Demonstrate the following mountain bike handling skills to your counselor: (a) Neutral position, ready position, bike body separation (side to side, and forward and back), and body positioning for cornering (b) Show shifting skills as applicable to climbs and obstacles. (c) Show proper technique for riding up and down hills, including when you would ride seated, crouched, or standing. (2) Take a trail safety test with your counselor and demonstrate the following: (a) Show proper trail etiquette to hikers and other cyclists, including when to yield the right-of-way. Resource: Bike Trail Etiquette (video) (b) Demonstrate how to correctly cross an obstacle by either going over the obstacle on your bike or dismounting your bike and crossing over or around the obstacle. (c) Cross rocks, gravel, and roots properly (3) Describe the rules of trail riding, including how to know when a trail is unsuitable for riding. (4) On mountain biking or multi-use trails approved by your counselor, take two rides of 2 miles each, two rides of 5 miles each, and two rides of 8 miles each. You must make a report of the rides taken. List dates for the routes traveled, and interesting things seen. (5) After fulfilling the previous requirement, lay out on a trail map a 22-mile trip. You may include multiple trail systems, if needed. Stay away from main highways. Using your map, complete this ride in one day.

Road Biking / Trail or Mixed Surface Biking Principle 2: Practice this skill on a relatively flat space with some markers (cones, half tennis balls, or rocks and sticks) and mark out a 90-degree turn (p. 80).
Road Biking / Trail or Mixed Surface Biking Principle 3: Practice riding through the turns several times, increasing your speed, off the saddle and with level pedals (p. 80).
Road Biking / Trail or Mixed Surface Biking Principle 4: Push your bike into the turn, keep your head up and look at your exit point, one finger on each brake lever (p. 80).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Road Biking / Trail or Mixed Surface Biking): On steep climbs a rider may choose one of three positions: seated, crouched, or standing (p. 80).
Step 2 (Road Biking / Trail or Mixed Surface Biking): In the seated position, the rider'sshoulders move forward and the rider may move forward on the saddle (p. 80).
Step 3 (Road Biking / Trail or Mixed Surface Biking): As the terrain becomes steeper, a rider may need to move into a crouched position similar to a ready position (p. 80).
Step 4 (Road Biking / Trail or Mixed Surface Biking): This position provides more power, bike/body separation, and better traction control (p. 80).

intro_notes: Scouts BSA Test Lab Pilot Badge (Valid through 2026-11-01). Dancing is a fun and exciting way to express yourself, stay active, and connect with others. Every style of dance—from hip hop and ballet to cultural and partner dances—has its own rhythm, history, and story to tell. In the Dance Test Lab Badge, you’ll learn how to move safely, warm up properly, and understand what makes every dance unique. You’ll explore different styles of dance, learn about famous dancers, and even perform your own routine. Whether you’re new to dancing or already love it, this badge will help you build confidence, creativity, and coordination while having a great time moving to the beat.

NOTE: Any registered adult Scouting America volunteer may serve as the counselor/reviewer for a Test Lab badge. Upon completion of all requirements and the official Scouting America Test Lab survey, Scouts receive an official Certificate of Completion that converts to Merit Badge credit if the badge graduates to permanent status.

requirements.lead_text: Preventing Injury. Do the following:
requirements.req_text: Preventing Injury. Do the following: (a) Explain to your counselor how you can prevent injuries while participating in dancing activities and what you should do to anticipate, help prevent, mitigate, and respond to these hazards. Explain what you need to take into consideration before trying potentially dangerous moves including but not limited to jumps, flips, and lifts. (b) Explain to your counselor how to appropriately warm-up prior to dancing activities to protect joints and prevent injury. Demonstrate three dance warm-ups. (c) Show that you know first aid for injuries that could occur while dancing, including cuts, scratches, abrasions, concussions, blisters, sprains, stress fractures, tendonitis, and back injuries. (d) Explain the importance of wearing the right clothing and gear for dance, including appropriate footwear.

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: Before starting an energetic 45-minute rehearsal involving jumps, turns, and partner lifts on a studio floor, a dancer notices a wet water spill near the center of the floor and skips warm-ups to save time. What two safety steps must happen before dancing begins?
quiz_item.question: Before starting an energetic 45-minute rehearsal involving jumps, turns, and partner lifts on a studio floor, a dancer notices a wet water spill near the center of the floor and skips warm-ups to save time. What two safety steps must happen before dancing begins?
options: A. Dance around the wet spot at full speed and stretch only after rehearsal ends.
B. Dry and inspect the studio floor for slip and trip hazards first, wear proper footwear, and complete a progressive cardiovascular warm-up and dynamic mobility routine.
C. Practice high-impact jumps immediately on cold muscles to warm up faster.
D. Sprinkle talcum powder over the wet puddle and attempt overhead partner lifts without a spotter.
choices: A. Dance around the wet spot at full speed and stretch only after rehearsal ends.
B. Dry and inspect the studio floor for slip and trip hazards first, wear proper footwear, and complete a progressive cardiovascular warm-up and dynamic mobility routine.
C. Practice high-impact jumps immediately on cold muscles to warm up faster.
D. Sprinkle talcum powder over the wet puddle and attempt overhead partner lifts without a spotter.
quiz_item.correct_answer: B. Dry and inspect the studio floor for slip and trip hazards first, wear proper footwear, and complete a progressive cardiovascular warm-up and dynamic mobility routine.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (B): Dynamic warm-ups increase muscle elasticity and joint synovial fluid, while a clean, dry sprung floor prevents ankle sprains and falls.

Step 2 (Styles of Dance Execution): Apply the official Dance pamphlet method for Styles of Dance while recording observations in your Scout Workbook (p. 18).
Step 3 (Styles of Dance Buddy Check): Cross-check your Styles of Dance technique, measurements, and results with a patrol buddy using the EDGE method (p. 18).
Step 4 (Styles of Dance Verification): Review your completed Styles of Dance evidence and demonstrate proficiency during your counselor conference (p. 18).

requirements.lead_text: Research. Research TWO of the types of dance you learned about in requirement 3 by doing the following for EACH type of dance you chose:
requirements.req_text: Research. Research TWO of the types of dance you learned about in requirement 3 by doing the following for EACH type of dance you chose: (a) Give a brief history, including its origin, how it came to be in the United States if it originated elsewhere, and where in the world/country it is most often performed. (b) Name/describe different variations of this style of dancing, if any. (c) Name some specific types of dance steps/moves particular to this type of dance. Does this dance tell a story through movement? If so, please describe. (d) Include information on at least one person who became well-known performing, teaching, or choreographing this type of dance. (e) Note if anyone with a physical disability (such a person with hearing or sight impairment or a person who uses a wheelchair) could participate in this type of dancing. What accommodations would that person need to participate? (f) Locate and share a place near you/in your state where you could watch or participate in this type of dance as a part of a performance, competition, or class. Find out when and where this is offered and what the cost would be to watch or participate. (g) Watch a performance of this type of dance and discuss with your counselor. (While viewing an in-person performance is preferable, a recorded performance may also be permitted.)

requirements.lead_text: Learn and Perform a Dance. Do the following:
requirements.req_text: Learn and Perform a Dance. Do the following: (a) Learn a dance. Use at least THREE types of warm-ups prior to your routine to prepare different muscle groups for the exercise. The dance may be solo, group, or partner dance and can use a memorized choreographed routine or an improvised dance. It should be a minimum of 2 minutes long or several shorter dances that add up to at least 2 minutes. The dance should demonstrate at least three different dance moves/steps and should contain music with Scout-appropriate lyrics, if applicable. (b) Perform the dance for your counselor or submit a video of your performance to your counselor. Describe to your counselor what precautions you took to avoid injury before and during your performance. Name or describe the 3 different dance moves that you learned, the 3 different warm-ups you chose, and the 5 Elements of Dance in your routine.

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: Before starting an energetic 45-minute rehearsal involving jumps, turns, and partner lifts on a studio floor, a dancer notices a wet water spill near the center of the floor and skips warm-ups to save time. What two safety steps must happen before dancing begins?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: Before starting an energetic 45-minute rehearsal involving jumps, turns, and partner lifts on a studio floor, a dancer notices a wet water spill near the center of the floor and skips warm-ups to save time. What two safety steps must happen before dancing begins?
options: A. Dance around the wet spot at full speed and stretch only after rehearsal ends.
B. Dry and inspect the studio floor for slip and trip hazards first, wear proper footwear, and complete a progressive cardiovascular warm-up and dynamic mobility routine.
C. Practice high-impact jumps immediately on cold muscles to warm up faster.
D. Sprinkle talcum powder over the wet puddle and attempt overhead partner lifts without a spotter.
choices: A. Dance around the wet spot at full speed and stretch only after rehearsal ends.
B. Dry and inspect the studio floor for slip and trip hazards first, wear proper footwear, and complete a progressive cardiovascular warm-up and dynamic mobility routine.
C. Practice high-impact jumps immediately on cold muscles to warm up faster.
D. Sprinkle talcum powder over the wet puddle and attempt overhead partner lifts without a spotter.
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: B. Dry and inspect the studio floor for slip and trip hazards first, wear proper footwear, and complete a progressive cardiovascular warm-up and dynamic mobility routine.
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (B): Dynamic warm-ups increase muscle elasticity and joint synovial fluid, while a clean, dry sprung floor prevents ankle sprains and falls.
patrol_quiz_bank.pamphlet_page_ref: Dance Test Lab Resource Guide, pp. 4-9

pamphlet_excerpts: Using X-ray films or images: Support for the Tooth The supportive tissues of the tooth are called theperiodontium, which includes the periodontal ligament, the alveolar bone (p. 14).
Using X-ray films or images Principle 2: The cementum, periodontal ligament, andalveolar bone connect the teeth to the jaws (p. 14).
Using X-ray films or images Principle 3: When one of these is damaged or missing, the tooth will loosen and eventually fall (p. 14).
Using X-ray films or images Principle 4: The supportive tissues actually get stronger from vigorous use (p. 14).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Using X-ray films or images): This strong, fiber like tissue anchors the root to the bone and cushions the surrounding bone against the shock of chewing and biting (p. 14).
Step 2 (Using X-ray films or images): When extracting a tooth, the dentist cuts the periodontal ligament that connects the tooth to the bone (p. 14).
Step 3 (Using X-ray films or images): The bony part of the upper and lower jaws that surrounds and supports the roots of the teeth and the gums is called the alveolar bone (p. 14).
Step 4 (Using X-ray films or images): Alveolar means "hollow." The alveolar bone has hollow places, or sockets, that house the roots of the teeth (p. 14).

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: In Dentistry Requirement 1, how do the four main tissues of a human tooth (enamel, dentin, pulp, and cementum) function, and how does dental plaque cause a cavity (caries)?
quiz_item.question: In Dentistry Requirement 1, how do the four main tissues of a human tooth (enamel, dentin, pulp, and cementum) function, and how does dental plaque cause a cavity (caries)?
options: A. Pulp forms the hard outer biting shell while enamel is the soft nerve center; cavities occur when cold water cracks the cementum on the crown.
B. Dentin covers the outside of the root while enamel lines the jawbone; cavities are caused by brushing with fluoridated toothpaste.
C. Cementum is the translucent biting edge of incisors while enamel contains blood vessels; plaque protects the tooth from dietary sugars.

D. Enamel is the hard mineralized outer crown layer, dentin is the underlying porous layer, pulp houses nerves and blood vessels, and cementum anchors the root to the periodontal ligament; bacteria in plaque biofilm ferment sugars into acids that demineralize enamel.

quiz_item.correct_answer: D. Enamel is the hard mineralized outer crown layer, dentin is the underlying porous layer, pulp houses nerves and blood vessels, and cementum anchors the root to the periodontal ligament; bacteria in plaque biofilm ferment sugars into acids that demineralize enamel.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (D): Enamel protects the crown over dentin and the central neurovascular pulp while cementum covers the root; cariogenic bacteria in plaque metabolize dietary carbohydrates into acids that dissolve tooth enamel unless removed by brushing, flossing, and fluoride protection.

pamphlet_excerpts: Dentistry Core Field Standard: Healthy people produce about 6 cups of saliva a day (p. 33).
Dentistry Core Field Standard Principle 2: When and how often you eat may affect your dental health more than what and how much you eat (p. 33).
Dentistry Core Field Standard Principle 3: You don't have to give up sugar to protect your teeth (p. 33).
Dentistry Core Field Standard Principle 4: If you eat sweet foods and drinks only at mealtimes and faithfully brush and floss your teeth afterward, you can usually avoid tooth decay (p. 33).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Dentistry Core Field Standard): The extra saliva produced to digest a meal will help wash away or neutralize acids, but eating sugary foods between meals will keep the acid level (p. 33).
Step 2 (Dentistry Core Field Standard): If you must snack, choose foods that are low in sugar content: peanuts, popcorn, pretzels, olives, eggs, meats, milk, and plain yogurt (p. 33).
Step 3 (Dentistry Core Field Standard): Snacking before bedtime is harmful because of the reduced production of saliva during sleep (p. 33).
Step 4 (Dentistry Core Field Standard): The plaque remains undisturbed on the teeth for hours (p. 33).

requirements.req_text: Do TWO of the following: (a) Make a model tooth out of soap, clay, paper-mâché, or wax. Using a string and a large hand brush, show your troop or a school class proper tooth-brushing and flossing procedures. (b) Make a poster on the prevention of dental disease. Show the importance of good oral health. (c) Collect at least five advertisements for different toothpastes. List the claims that each one makes. Tell about the accuracy of the advertisements. (d) Write a feature story for your school newspaper on the proper care of teeth and gums. Include in your story how the use of tobacco products can negatively affect a person's oral health. (e) Make drawings and write about the progress of dental decay. Describe the types of dental filling and treatments a dentist can use to repair dental decay problems.

pamphlet_excerpts: Careers & Professional Pathways: They work directly with dentists and orthodontists and have little patient contact (p. 56).
Careers & Professional Pathways Principle 2: Education and Cost of Training The basic training for dentists is four years of dental school after graduation from college (p. 56).

Careers & Professional Pathways Principle 3: Upon successful completion of dental school requirements, the graduate is awarded a doctor of dental surgery (D. D. S.) or a doctor of dental medicine (p. 56).
Careers & Professional Pathways Principle 4: To practice, he or she must pass both a written national board and a state or regional examination (p. 56).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Careers & Professional Pathways): After passing the boards, the dental school graduate may apply to the state board of dentistry for a license to practice general dentistry (p. 56).
Step 2 (Careers & Professional Pathways): The sponsoring institution may decide whether the dentist must pay for his or her advanced training, or whether he or she should receive a stipend (p. 56).
Step 3 (Careers & Professional Pathways): It is common practice to offer paid residency programs in hospitals in the areas of pediatric dentistry, oral surgery, and general dentistry (p. 56).
Step 4 (Careers & Professional Pathways): Postgraduate training in dental schools for the other specialties usually require tuition (p. 56).

pamphlet_excerpts: Historical Origins and Evolution: This program, which was not available for mainframe computers, helped start a trend of companies installing personal computers in the workplace (p. 23).
Historical Origins and Evolution Principle 2: Two years later, IBM introduced its PC (or personal computer) based on the Intel 8088 microprocessor (p. 23).
Historical Origins and Evolution Principle 3: The PC ran it sown version of Visi Calc as well as other software programs, including a word processor (p. 23).
Historical Origins and Evolution Principle 4: The original IBM PC cost $3,000 when it debuted in 1981, around $7,500 in 2012, adjusted for inflation (p. 23).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Historical Origins and Evolution): Today's desktop computers, thousands of times more powerful, can be purchased for only a fewhundred dollars (p. 23).
Step 2 (Historical Origins and Evolution): Microsoft later created a similar operating system, MS-DOS, for use on computers made by many different companies (p. 23).
Step 3 (Historical Origins and Evolution): The IBM PC and other computers using the MS-DOS platform dominated the business and home computer markets, helping make Microsoft one (p. 23).
Step 4 (Historical Origins and Evolution): Apple's Macintosh® computer also had great influence on the industry (p. 23).

pamphlet_excerpts: Text Sound and Pictures Are: Explain to Your Counselor How: The U. S. military used first-generation digital computers like this ENIAC to calculate trajectories of artillery shells and to help build weapons (p. 22).

Text Sound and Pictures Are Principle 2: Explain to Your Counselor How Principle 2: The military used these first-generation digital computers to calculate weapon trajectories and help build atomic bombs (p. 22).

Text Sound and Pictures Are Principle 3: Explain to Your Counselor How Principle 3: Each of these computers weighed tons, filled an entire room, and consumed enough electricity to light up a small town (p. 22).

Text Sound and Pictures Are Principle 4: Explain to Your Counselor How Principle 4: They also required thousands of vacuum tubes, which tended to overheat and burn out, needing to be replaced often (p. 22).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Text Sound and Pictures Are): Step 1 (Explain to Your Counselor How): The first commercially built computer was Mauchly's and Eckert's UNIVAC (p. 22).

Step 2 (Text Sound and Pictures Are): Step 2 (Explain to Your Counselor How): It was designed to be a general-purpose, or "universal," computer that would serve scientists, business people, and engineers alike (p. 22).

Step 3 (Text Sound and Pictures Are): Step 3 (Explain to Your Counselor How): The UNIVAC was a stored-program computer, meaning the program didn't have to be fed into the computer as it was running (p. 22).

Step 4 (Text Sound and Pictures Are): Step 4 (Explain to Your Counselor How): Another innovation in the UNIVAC was its ability to take input from data on magnetic tape, rather than from punched cards (p. 22).

pamphlet_excerpts: A program or software application: This applies not only to your home computer but also to any device that can be connected to the internet such as cell phones (p. 49).
A program or software application Principle 2: Such programs, often attached to some useful software, "spy" on you, tracking your movements on the web (p. 49).
A program or software application Principle 3: Spyware can also install secret programs on your computer (p. 49).
A program or software application Principle 4: Database manager (DBM) programs are used for organizing, storing, and keeping track of a set of information called a database (p. 49).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (A program or software application): The data are organized in lines called records, with each record consisting of a number of fields (p. 49).
Step 2 (A program or software application): For each new record, the same set of fields is stored, with different contents in each field (p. 49).
Step 3 (A program or software application): A troop attendance database could be set up with a record for each Scout in the troop (p. 49).
Step 4 (A program or software application): Each record would consist of fields for the Scout's name, patrol, rank, troop meeting attendance, campout attendance, and other events (p. 49).

requirements.lead_text: Do THREE of the following. For each project you complete, copy the files to a backup device and share the finished projects with your counselor.
requirements.req_text: Do THREE of the following. For each project you complete, copy the files to a backup device and share the finished projects with your counselor. (a) Using a spreadsheet or database program, develop a food budget for a patrol weekend campout OR create a troop roster that includes the name, rank, patrol, and telephone number of each Scout. Show your counselor that you can sort the roster by each of the following categories: rank, patrol, and alphabetically by name. (b) Using a word processor, write a draft letter inviting the parents or guardians of your troop's Scouts to a troop event. Resource: Word Processing Tutorial (video) (c) Using a graphics program, design and draw a campsite plan for your troop OR create a flyer for an upcoming troop event, incorporating text and some type of visual such as a photograph or an illustration. (d) Using a presentation software program, develop a report about a topic approved by your counselor. For your presentation, create at least five slides, with each one incorporating text and some type of visual such as a photograph or an illustration. (e) Using a digital device, take a picture of a troop activity. Send or transfer this image to a device where it can be shared with your counselor. (f) Make a digital recording of your voice, transfer the file to a different device, and have your counselor play back the recording. (g) Create a blog and use it as an online journal of your Scouting activities, including group discussions and meetings, campouts, and other events. Include at least five entries and two photographs or illustrations. Share your blog with your counselor. You need not post the blog to the internet; however, if you choose to go live with your blog, you must first share it with your parent or guardian AND counselor AND get their approval. (h) Create a webpage for your troop, patrol, school, or place of worship. Include at least three articles and two photographs or illustrations. Include at least one link to a website of interest to your audience. You need not post the page to the internet; however, if you decide to do so, you must first share the webpage with your parent or guardian AND counselor AND get their approval.

Research one career to learn about the training and education needed, costs, job prospects, salary, job duties, and career advancement. Discuss with your counselor both your findings and what about this profession might make it an interesting career. (b) Explore how you could use knowledge and skills from the Digital Technology merit badge to pursue a hobby or interest. Research any training needed, expenses, and organizations that promote or support it. Discuss with your counselor what short-term and long-term goals you might have if you pursued this.

Research one career to learn about the training and education needed, costs, job prospects, salary, job duties, and career advancement. Your research methods may include, with your parent or guardian's permission, an internet or library search, an interview with a professional in the field, or a visit to a location where people in this career work. Discuss with your counselor both your findings and what about this profession might make it an interesting career.

pamphlet_excerpts: Person-First Language: Many people with disabilities want to emphasize what they are able to do rather than emphasize their disabilities (p. 9).
Person-First Language Principle 2: Remember that people with disabilities are people first (p. 9).
Person-First Language Principle 3: Each person gets to decide how he or she should be described (p. 9).
Person-First Language Principle 4: You should use person-first language when talking about people who are not personal acquaintances or about people with disabilities as agroup (p. 9).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Person-First Language): When you make a new friend or talk about an individual, show a person-first attitude by calling the individual what he orshe wants to be called (p. 9).
Step 2 (Person-First Language): Many people with disabilities see their condition as part ofwho they are, just like their gender, hair or eye color, or ethnicity (p. 9).
Step 3 (Person-First Language): Writing and talking with person-first language is a good habit to get into because it is the proper form for most situations (p. 9).
Step 4 (Person-First Language): Don't call someone an epileptic when you mean to say the person has epilepsy (p. 9).

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: In Disabilities Awareness Requirement 1, what is the respectful standard when communicating with or referring to a person with a disability, and why is it important to recognize invisible disabilities?
quiz_item.question: In Disabilities Awareness Requirement 1, what is the respectful standard when communicating with or referring to a person with a disability, and why is it important to recognize invisible disabilities?
options: A. Speak only to the person's companion or interpreter in a loud voice, and assume anyone who does not use a wheelchair has no disability.
B. Push a person's wheelchair or grab a blind person's white cane without asking so you can move them through doorways faster.

C. Speak directly to the individual using respectful people-first or preferred language, ask before offering physical assistance, and recognize that many disabilities (such as autism, epilepsy, diabetes, hearing loss, or learning differences) are not immediately visible.
D. Avoid inviting Scouts with physical or sensory disabilities on campouts so the troop does not have to adjust trail plans.

pamphlet_excerpts: Agency That Works With People: Visit an agency that works: If a career in audiology interests you, you should begin early to get the background needed (p. 19).
Agency That Works With People Principle 2: Visit an agency that works Principle 2: In school, take biology, physical science, language, and physical education classes (p. 19).
Agency That Works With People Principle 3: Visit an agency that works Principle 3: Get an after-schooljob or volunteer with an agency or organization that serves people who have disabilities (p. 19).
Agency That Works With People Principle 4: Visit an agency that works Principle 4: Audiologists are trained to detect and diagnose hearing problems (p. 19).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Agency That Works With People): Step 1 (Visit an agency that works): An audiologist uses an instrument called anaudiometer to test a person's hearing (p. 19).
Step 2 (Agency That Works With People): Step 2 (Visit an agency that works): An audiologist also may give behavioral tests to find out how a person reacts to various sounds and vibrations (p. 19).
Step 3 (Agency That Works With People): Step 3 (Visit an agency that works): Most audiologists have at least a master's degree and many have a doctorate degree (p. 19).
Step 4 (Agency That Works With People): Step 4 (Visit an agency that works): College programs in audiology include courses in hearing, speech, and language (p. 19).

requirements.lead_text: Do TWO of the following:
requirements.req_text: Do TWO of the following: (a) Talk with a Scout who has a disability and learn about the Scout's experiences taking part in Scouting activities and earning different merit badges. Discuss what you have learned with your counselor. (b) Talk with an individual who has a disability and learn about this person's experiences and the activities in which this person likes to participate. Discuss what you have learned with your counselor. (c) Learn how people with disabilities take part in a particular adaptive sport or recreational activity. Discuss what you have learned with your counselor. (d) Learn about independent living aids such as service animals, canes, and augmentative communication devices such as captioned telephones and videophones. Discuss with your counselor how people use such aids. (e) Plan or participate in an activity that helps others understand what a person with a visible or invisible disability experiences. Discuss what you have learned with your counselor.

requirements.lead_text: Do ONE of the following options:
requirements.req_text: Do ONE of the following options: (a) Option A, Access. Visit TWO of the following locations and take notes about the accessibility to people with disabilities. In your notes, give examples of five things that could be done to improve upon the site and five things about the site that make it friendly to people with disabilities. Discuss your observations with your counselor. (1) Your school (2) Your place of worship (3) A Scouting event or campsite (4) A public exhibit or attraction (such as a theater, museum, or park) (b) Option B, Accommodation. Visit TWO of the following locations and take notes while observing features and methods that are used to accommodate people with invisible disabilities. While there, ask staff members to explain any accommodation features that may not be obvious. Note anything you think could be done to better accommodate people who have invisible disabilities. Discuss your observations with your counselor. (1) Your school (2) Your place of worship (3) A Scouting event or campsite (4) A public exhibit or attraction (such as a theater, museum, or park)

pamphlet_excerpts: Access / Accommodation: An accommodation is just a different way of doing things that is tailored to the individual needs of a person with a disability (p. 36).
Access / Accommodation Principle 2: Most schools are accommodating students with disabilities to make learning better (p. 36).
Access / Accommodation Principle 3: Accommodations also happen in workplaces to make work easier and in public attractions to make experiences more enjoyable (p. 36).
Access / Accommodation Principle 4: For requirement 4b, you are to identify accommodations that already exist at certain places and suggest better accommodations (p. 36).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Access / Accommodation): You will need to talk with staff members at the locations or facilities to help you understand the accommodations, because they often are not obvious (p. 36).
Step 2 (Access / Accommodation): Next time you are in a public place, look at how accessible (usable) the location is for people with disabilities (p. 36).
Step 3 (Access / Accommodation): Some of the accessibility projects suggested in this pamphlet might be done as service projects for achieving the ranks of Star, Life, or Eagle (p. 36).
Step 4 (Access / Accommodation): Ifyou wish to do aproject for rank advancement, check with your Scoutmaster to be sure your undertaking meets the standards for leadership service (p. 36).

requirements.lead_text: Explain what advocacy is. Do ONE of the following:
requirements.req_text: Explain what advocacy is. Do ONE of the following: (a) Present a counselor-approved disabilities awareness program to a Cub Scout pack or other group. During your presentation, explain and use person-first language. (b) Find out about disabilities awareness education programs in your school or school system, or contact a disability advocacy agency. Volunteer with a program or agency for eight hours. (c) Using resources such as disability advocacy agencies, government agencies, the internet (with your parent or guardian's permission), and news magazines, learn about myths and misconceptions that influence the general public's understanding of people with disabilities. List 10 myths and misconceptions about people with disabilities and learn the facts about each myth. Share your list with your counselor, then use it to make a presentation to a Cub Scout pack or other group.

pamphlet_excerpts: Disability Advocacy and Self-Determination: We are all hurt by mistaken ideas and misunderstandings about people with disabilities and what they can and cannotdo (p. 19).
Disability Advocacy and Self-Determination Principle 2: Learn the facts so you can share the correct information with others (p. 19).
Disability Advocacy and Self-Determination Principle 3: Fact: Having a disability is not the same as being sick (p. 19).
Disability Advocacy and Self-Determination Principle 4: Many people with disabilities are in excellent physical condition, healthy, athletic, and strong (p. 19).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Disability Advocacy and Self-Determination): Some people who have disabilities also have illnesses, just as some nondisabled people are ill (p. 19).
Step 2 (Disability Advocacy and Self-Determination): Myth: A person with a disability has a poor quality of life or lives a life totally different from people without disabilities (p. 19).
Step 3 (Disability Advocacy and Self-Determination): Fact: Overall, people with disabilities live like anyone else (p. 19).
Step 4 (Disability Advocacy and Self-Determination): The attitude that a disability ruins a person's life can be more disabling than the disability itself (p. 19).

pamphlet_excerpts: Commitment to your counselor describing: Advocacy, Attitudes, and Awareness Advocacy means supporting, promoting, encouraging, or defending something (p. 44).
Commitment to your counselor describing Principle 2: To be an advocate for people with disabilities means you support and encourage positive attitudes about people with disabilities (p. 44).

Commitment to your counselor describing Principle 3: It can also mean that you are brave enough to challenge false and unfair beliefs or call to account those who mistreat people with disabilities (p. 44).
Commitment to your counselor describing Principle 4: You help strip away the labels so that people can see each other as individuals (p. 44).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Commitment to your counselor describing): You help build bridges of understanding and respect among all people, regardless of their abilities (p. 44).
Step 2 (Commitment to your counselor describing): In completing the requirements for the Disabilities Awareness merit badge, you have learned things that you can now teach to others (p. 44).

Step 3 (Commitment to your counselor describing): Use what you have learned to put together a disabilities awareness program that you present (with your counselor's approval) to a Cub Scout pack (p. 44).
Step 4 (Commitment to your counselor describing): Teach the group about person-first language and demonstrate its importance while giving your presentation (p. 44).

pamphlet_excerpts: Careers & Professional Pathways: Whatever activities you enjoy, you can be sure there are many people, with and without disabilities, who like doing the same things (p. 19).
Careers & Professional Pathways Principle 2: Maybe you belong to a club for people who share your interest, such as an astronomy club or a collectors' group (p. 19).
Careers & Professional Pathways Principle 3: You might have a friend from the club who has a disability (p. 19).
Careers & Professional Pathways Principle 4: Talk with your friend about his or her experiences (p. 19).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Careers & Professional Pathways): Find out what adaptations or adjustments, if any, your friend has made or used to take part in favorite activities or do everyday tasks (p. 19).
Step 2 (Careers & Professional Pathways): Talk with a Scout who has a disability and learn about the Scout's experiences in Scouting (p. 19).
Step 3 (Careers & Professional Pathways): Have any badges presented especially difficult or unsolvable problems (p. 19).
Step 4 (Careers & Professional Pathways): Find out about any adaptive gear or techniques the Scout may have used to achieve Scouting goals (p. 19).

options: A. Speak only to the person's companion or interpreter in a loud voice, and assume anyone who does not use a wheelchair has no disability.

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: When observing an unfamiliar dog in Dog Care Requirement 1, which combination of canine body language signals indicates the dog is fearful, stressed, or defensive and should not be crowded?
quiz_item.question: When observing an unfamiliar dog in Dog Care Requirement 1, which combination of canine body language signals indicates the dog is fearful, stressed, or defensive and should not be crowded?
options: A. Ears pinned flat back, tail tucked tightly between the legs, stiff posture, raised hackles, whale eye (showing the whites of the eyes), lip licking, or a low growl.
B. A loose, wiggly body posture with a play bow (front elbows on the ground, hindquarters raised) and a relaxed, open mouth.
C. Sitting calmly at the handler's side with soft eyes, neutral ear position, and gentle tail wagging at mid-level.
D. Rolling onto its side in a quiet home living room to fall asleep after eating dinner.
choices: A. Ears pinned flat back, tail tucked tightly between the legs, stiff posture, raised hackles, whale eye (showing the whites of the eyes), lip licking, or a low growl.

quiz_item.correct_answer: A. Ears pinned flat back, tail tucked tightly between the legs, stiff posture, raised hackles, whale eye (showing the whites of the eyes), lip licking, or a low growl.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (A): Stiff muscles, pinned ears, tucked tail, showing the whites of the eyes ('whale eye'), yawning/lip-licking under tension, and growling are clear canine warning signs of fear or defensiveness.

Step 3 (House-training Obedience Training and Socialization): Step 3 (Explain The Importance of House-training): The first step in training your dog is house-training, or getting your dog to urinate and defecate outside (p. 35).

Step 4 (House-training Obedience Training and Socialization): Step 4 (Explain The Importance of House-training): Puppies generally need to go to the bathroom after they eat, when they wake up from a nap, and after playing hard (p. 35).

Correct Way to Obedience Train Principle 2: Gradually, over a short period, increase your control until your dog is completely comfortable being on the leash (p. 37).
Correct Way to Obedience Train Principle 3: Multiple, short periods of training are most effective (p. 37).
Correct Way to Obedience Train Principle 4: Four or five sessions a day, five to 10 minutes each, works well for puppies (p. 37).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Correct Way to Obedience Train): Older dogs can tolerate sessions of up to 20 minutes long (p. 37).
Step 2 (Correct Way to Obedience Train): The American Kennel Club's Canine Good Citizen® certification program rewards dogs that have good manners at home and in the community (p. 37).
Step 3 (Correct Way to Obedience Train): The program stresses responsible pet ownership and basic good manners for dogs (p. 37).
Step 4 (Correct Way to Obedience Train): It's important for every dog to know these five basic commands (p. 37).

step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Discuss The Proper Vaccination Schedule): Step 1 (Discuss The Proper Vaccination Schedule): If you think your dog is sick, take a closer look (p. 55).

Step 2 (Discuss The Proper Vaccination Schedule): Step 2 (Discuss The Proper Vaccination Schedule): You can a check a dog's pulse on the inside of the hind leg, high on the inner thigh near where the leg meets the belly (p. 55).
Step 3 (Discuss The Proper Vaccination Schedule): Step 3 (Discuss The Proper Vaccination Schedule): Normal pulse rates vary among different types of dogs (p. 55).
Step 4 (Discuss The Proper Vaccination Schedule): Step 4 (Discuss The Proper Vaccination Schedule): Smaller breeds and toy breeds can have heart rates that exceed 120 beats per minute (p. 55).

pamphlet_excerpts: Precautions to take in handling: Keeping Your Dog Healthy. heartwormsociety. org Heart worm disease can affect dogs in every state (p. 57).
Precautions to take in handling Principle 2: In adult dogs most intestinal parasites are picked up from the stool of an infected dog (except tapeworms, which are spread by fleas) (p. 57).

Precautions to take in handling Principle 3: Because this can easily happen when dogs are sniffing around outside, adult dogs should also have a stool check a couple of times a year to screen (p. 57).
Precautions to take in handling Principle 4: Remember, most internal parasites are not visible to the nakedeye, so don't assume they are not a problem just because you don't see them (p. 57).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Precautions to take in handling): Dogs can get heart worms through the bite of a mosquito that carries the parasite (p. 57).
Step 2 (Precautions to take in handling): A dog might be infected for a longtime before you know about it because it takes awhile for the worms to cause damage to the dog's heart (p. 57).
Step 3 (Precautions to take in handling): Symptoms ofheartworms could include sluggishness and coughing (p. 57).
Step 4 (Precautions to take in handling): These can progress to heart failure, which can cause death (p. 57).

Veterinary Hospital or An Animal Principle 3: Visit a veterinary hospital Principle 3: The next important ancestor, called Cynodictis was the first to have doglikecharacteristics, such as a shortened fifth toe, 42 teeth, and longer legs (p. 9).
Veterinary Hospital or An Animal Principle 4: Visit a veterinary hospital Principle 4: Then came a descendent of Cynodictis, called Tomarctus, which resembled today's dogs even (p. 9).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Veterinary Hospital or An Animal): Step 1 (Visit a veterinary hospital): This animal had short, erect ears, long legs and tail, and adewclaw that had developed from the shortened fifth toe (p. 9).
Step 2 (Veterinary Hospital or An Animal): Step 2 (Visit a veterinary hospital): Also, Tomarctus probably behaved much like today's dogs (p. 9).
Step 3 (Veterinary Hospital or An Animal): Step 3 (Visit a veterinary hospital): All breeds of dogs and wolves evolved from Tomarctus (p. 9).
Step 4 (Veterinary Hospital or An Animal): Step 4 (Visit a veterinary hospital): Scientists group them in a family called Canidae (p. 9).

quiz_item.question: In Drafting Requirement 1, how does third-angle orthographic projection represent a three-dimensional object on a flat drawing sheet, and how are object lines distinguished from hidden lines?
options: A. It shows only a single artistic watercolor painting of the building with no measurements, using dotted lines for all outer walls.
B. It places the right-side view above the top view and uses thick wavy freehand lines for invisible interior cavities.
C. It stretches all vertical edges at a forty-five degree angle without a scale ratio and draws centerlines with solid heavy ink.

D. It aligns the front, top, and right-side views at 90-degree projection angles to show exact scaled dimensions, using thick solid lines for visible edges and medium dashed lines for hidden internal features.
choices: A. It shows only a single artistic watercolor painting of the building with no measurements, using dotted lines for all outer walls.
B. It places the right-side view above the top view and uses thick wavy freehand lines for invisible interior cavities.
C. It stretches all vertical edges at a forty-five degree angle without a scale ratio and draws centerlines with solid heavy ink.

D. It aligns the front, top, and right-side views at 90-degree projection angles to show exact scaled dimensions, using thick solid lines for visible edges and medium dashed lines for hidden internal features.
quiz_item.correct_answer: D. It aligns the front, top, and right-side views at 90-degree projection angles to show exact scaled dimensions, using thick solid lines for visible edges and medium dashed lines for hidden internal features.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (D): Orthographic projection aligns multiple 2D views (typically front, top, and right side) to convey exact geometry to scale, using a standardized alphabet of lines where visible edges are thick solid lines and hidden edges are dashed.

requirements.lead_text: Using the formatted sheet of paper you prepared for your manual project, produce a pencil drawing as it would be used for manufacturing. Fill in all title block information. The manual drawing may be any one of the following drawing types:
requirements.req_text: Using the formatted sheet of paper you prepared for your manual project, produce a pencil drawing as it would be used for manufacturing. Fill in all title block information. The manual drawing may be any one of the following drawing types: (a) Architectural: Make a scale drawing of an architectural project. The architectural drawing may be a floor plan; electrical, plumbing, or mechanical service plan; elevation plan; or landscaping plan. Use an architect's scale and show dimensions to communicate the actual size of features. Include any important sectional drawings, notes, and considerations necessary for construction. Properly print a bill of materials for at least three of the raw materials or components in the project. (b) Mechanical: Make a scale drawing of some mechanical device or interesting object. The mechanical drawing may be of the orthographic (third-angle) or isometric style. Use an engineer's scale and show dimensions to communicate the actual size of features. Include any important sectional drawings, notes, and manufacturing considerations. Properly print a bill of materials for at least three of the raw materials or components in the assembly. (c) Electrical: Draw a simple schematic of a radio or electronic circuit. Properly print a bill of materials including all of the major electrical components used in the circuit. Use standard drawing symbols to represent the electronic components.

requirements.lead_text: Produce a computer-aided design (CAD) drawing as it would be used in manufacturing. Fill in all title block information. The CAD drawing may be any one of the following drawing types:
requirements.req_text: Produce a computer-aided design (CAD) drawing as it would be used in manufacturing. Fill in all title block information. The CAD drawing may be any one of the following drawing types: (a) Architectural: Make a scale drawing of an architectural project. The architectural drawing may be a floor plan; electrical, plumbing, or mechanical service plan; elevation plan; or landscaping plan. Use an architect's scale and show dimensions to communicate the actual size of features. Include any important sectional drawings, notes, and considerations necessary for construction. (b) Mechanical: Make a scale drawing of some mechanical device or interesting object. The mechanical drawing may be of the orthographic (third-angle) or isometric style. Use an engineer's scale and show dimensions to communicate the actual size of features. Include any important sectional drawings, notes, and manufacturing considerations. (c) Electrical: Draw a simple schematic of a radio or electronic circuit. Properly print a bill of materials including all of the major electrical components used in the circuit. Use standard drawing symbols to represent the electronic components.

step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (CAD vs. Manual Drafting Workflow): On a computer, it is as easy as typing on a keyboard (p. 15).
Step 2 (CAD vs. Manual Drafting Workflow): Computers can depict lines and features using units of millionths of an inch or even smaller (p. 15).
Step 3 (CAD vs. Manual Drafting Workflow): With computers, accuracy is easier to achieve, for example, computers allow the dr after to quickly draw multiple lines to the exact same length (p. 15).
Step 4 (CAD vs. Manual Drafting Workflow): Manual drawing may be accurate enough for many designs, but many others, such as tiny electronic circuits, demand much greater accuracy than (p. 15).

requirements.lead_text: Do ONE of the following:
requirements.req_text: Do ONE of the following: (a) Visit a facility or industry workplace where drafting is part of the business. Ask to see an example of the work that is done there, the different drafting facilities, and the tools used. (1) Find out how much of the drafting done there is manual and how much is done using CAD. If CAD is used, find out what software is used and how and why it was chosen. (2) Ask about the drafting services provided. Ask who uses the designs produced in the drafting area and how those designs are used. Discuss how the professionals who perform drafting cooperate with other individuals in the drafting area and other areas of the business. (3) Ask how important the role of drafting is to producing the end product or service that this business supplies. Find out how drafting contributes to the company's end product or service. (b) Using resources you find on your own such as at the library and on the internet (with your parent or guardian's permission), learn more about the drafting trade and discuss the following with your counselor. (1) The drafting tools used in the past, why and how they were used. Explain which tools are still used today and how their use has changed with the advent of new tools. Discuss which tools are being made obsolete by newer tools in the industry. (2) Tell what media types were used in the past and how drawings were used, stored, and reproduced. Tell how the advent of CAD has changed the media used, and discuss how these changes affect the storage or reproduction of drawings. (3) Discuss whether the types of media have changed such that there are new uses the drawings, or other outputs, produced by designers. Briefly discuss how new media types are used in the industry today.

requirements.lead_text: Demonstrate that you know how to respond to electrical emergencies by doing the following:
requirements.req_text: Demonstrate that you know how to respond to electrical emergencies by doing the following: (a) Explain how to turn off power for a particular circuit and the whole house in the event of an emergency. (b) Demonstrate how to rescue a person touching a live wire in the home. (c) Describe how to safely get out of a car in an accident if you suspect a utility wire is on the car. (d) Show how to render first aid to a person who is unconscious from an apparent electrical shock. (e) Show how to treat an electrical burn. (f) Explain what to do in the event of an electrical fire. (g) Explain what to do if caught out in the open during an electrical storm.

pamphlet_excerpts: That you know how to respond: Place a victim who is unconscious but who is breathing normally in a recovery position (p. 46).
That you know how to respond Principle 2: This will prevent the person from choking on saliva, blood (from a bitten tongue), or vomit, and will help keep the airway open (p. 46).
That you know how to respond Principle 3: Continue to monitor the person's breathing until medical help arrives (p. 46).
That you know how to respond Principle 4: However, do not move a person with suspected spinal injury unless it is absolutely necessary (p. 46).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (That you know how to respond): Recovery position for a person who may have a spinal injury (p. 46).
Step 2 (That you know how to respond): Electric current comes into your home on overhead or underground wires (p. 46).
Step 3 (That you know how to respond): From your electrical meter, heavy, well-insulated wires run to a main distribution center or breaker box, where the main disconnect switch (p. 46).
Step 4 (That you know how to respond): If necessary, you can use that switch to shut off all electric current in your house (p. 46).

C. Throw a bucket of tap water over the extension cord to cool the sparks and extinguish the electrical arc.
D. Use a metal pry bar to lift the live copper wire off the person's hand while standing on a damp garage floor.

pamphlet_excerpts: Constructing a Working Electromagnet: This experiment shows that a wire carrying a current is surrounded by an invisible magnetic field, or force, and it illustrates how closely electricity (p. 18).
Constructing a Working Electromagnet Principle 2: Step 1, Wrap a length of insulated (plastic-coated) wire about 20 times around a cardboard tube (p. 18).
Constructing a Working Electromagnet Principle 3: Step 3, Slide a small compass into the middle of the cardboard tube (p. 18).
Constructing a Working Electromagnet Principle 4: Step 4, Swivel the paper clip against and away from one thumbtack to switch the electric circuit (p. 18).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Constructing a Working Electromagnet): Watch what happens to the compass needle as you open and close the circuit (p. 18).
Step 2 (Constructing a Working Electromagnet): When you close the circuit, the electric current produces magnetism in the coil of wire (p. 18).
Step 3 (Constructing a Working Electromagnet): The magnetism all around the wire makes the compass needle swing (p. 18).
Step 4 (Constructing a Working Electromagnet): When the circuit is broken (you open the paper-clip switch), no magnetism is produced so the needle again points north (p. 18).

Step 4 (Simple drawing): When the circuit is broken (you open the paper-clip switch), no magnetism is produced so the needle again points north (p. 18).

pamphlet_excerpts: Overloading An Electric Circuit Means: Define what overloading an electric circuit: Electric current comes into your home on overhead or underground wires (p. 46).

Overloading An Electric Circuit Means Principle 2: Define what overloading an electric circuit Principle 2: From your electrical meter, heavy, well-insulated wires run to a main distribution center or breaker box, where the main disconnect switch is located (p. 46).

Overloading An Electric Circuit Means Principle 3: Define what overloading an electric circuit Principle 3: If necessary, you can use that switch to shut off all electric current in your house (p. 46).

Overloading An Electric Circuit Means Principle 4: Define what overloading an electric circuit Principle 4: The fuse box or circuit breaker panel is typically located in a utility room, in an electric room, in a mechanical room, or near the main power feed (p. 46).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Overloading An Electric Circuit Means): Step 1 (Define what overloading an electric circuit): Fuses and circuit breakers act as guards: They prevent currents that are toostrong from traveling into your home's branch circuits (p. 46).

Step 2 (Overloading An Electric Circuit Means): Step 2 (Define what overloading an electric circuit): If the transfer of electricity becomes greater than a fuse is designed to handle, the metal element inside the fuse melts and the fuse blows (p. 46).
Step 3 (Overloading An Electric Circuit Means): Step 3 (Define what overloading an electric circuit): A circuit breaker automatically opens and "trips" the circuit (p. 46).

Step 4 (Overloading An Electric Circuit Means): Step 4 (Define what overloading an electric circuit): Every time you switch on another light or appliance, more current travels through that branch circuit (p. 46).

pamphlet_excerpts: Floor plan wiring diagram: Electric current comes into your home on overhead or underground wires (p. 46).
Floor plan wiring diagram Principle 2: From your electrical meter, heavy, well-insulated wires run to a main distribution center or breaker box, where the main disconnect switch is located (p. 46).
Floor plan wiring diagram Principle 3: If necessary, you can use that switch to shut off all electric current in your house (p. 46).
Floor plan wiring diagram Principle 4: The fuse box or circuit breaker panel is typically located in a utility room, in an electric room, in a mechanical room, or near the main power feed (p. 46).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Floor plan wiring diagram): Fuses and circuit breakers act as guards: They prevent currents that are toostrong from traveling into your home's branch circuits (p. 46).
Step 2 (Floor plan wiring diagram): If the transfer of electricity becomes greater than a fuse is designed to handle, the metal element inside the fuse melts and the fuse blows (p. 46).
Step 3 (Floor plan wiring diagram): A circuit breaker automatically opens and "trips" the circuit (p. 46).
Step 4 (Floor plan wiring diagram): Every time you switch on another light or appliance, more current travels through that branch circuit (p. 46).

requirements.lead_text: Do TWO of the following:
requirements.req_text: Do TWO of the following: (a) Connect a buzzer, bell, or light with a battery. Have a key or switch in the line. (b) Make and run a simple electric motor (from a kit is acceptable, if approved by your counselor ahead of time). (c) Build a simple rheostat. Show that it works. (d) Build a single-pole, double-throw switch. Show that it works. (e) Explain how 3-way switch wiring works in a lighting circuit. (f) Connect two lights together in a series circuit along with a battery and a switch. Then connect the same circuit in parallel. Discuss the differences in the two circuits.

pamphlet_excerpts: Careers & Professional Pathways: The electrical industry has several general areas with many types of careers available in each area (p. 73).
Careers & Professional Pathways Principle 2: These areas include manufacturing, construction, merchandising, operating, servicing or maintaining, and engineering electrical parts, equipment (p. 73).
Careers & Professional Pathways Principle 3: Some positions require a college degree, while a degree from a vocational school is adequate for other careers (p. 73).
Careers & Professional Pathways Principle 4: Some companies allow on-the-job training, but almost all require at least a high school diploma (p. 73).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Careers & Professional Pathways): In electricity manufacturing (electrical generating stations, transmission, and distribution substation systems) positions are available (p. 73).
Step 2 (Careers & Professional Pathways): Occupations include assemblers, that is, the people who help build electrical equipment and/or systems (p. 73).
Step 3 (Careers & Professional Pathways): A high school education is needed as well as mechanical aptitude (p. 73).
Step 4 (Careers & Professional Pathways): Merchandising, or sales, is another field for those interested in electricity (p. 73).

D. Use a metal pry bar to lift the live copper wire off the person's hand while standing on a damp garage floor.

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: When soldering electronic components onto a printed circuit board for Electronics Requirement 1, which safety practices protect your eyes, lungs, and static-sensitive integrated circuits?
quiz_item.question: When soldering electronic components onto a printed circuit board for Electronics Requirement 1, which safety practices protect your eyes, lungs, and static-sensitive integrated circuits?
options: A. Hold extra solder wire in your mouth while working, lean directly over the rising flux smoke, and rest the hot iron on the workbench mat.
B. Wear wool sweaters to build up static charge, flick excess molten solder off the tip with your wrist, and touch capacitor terminals immediately after unplugging a power supply.

C. Wear ANSI safety glasses to guard against solder splashes, use lead-free rosin-core solder in a well-ventilated area (avoiding flux fumes), return the iron to its heat-resistant stand, wear a grounded ESD wrist strap for static-sensitive chips, and wash hands after working.
D. Dip the hot soldering iron tip into a cup of cold water between joints and test whether the tip is hot by touching it with a fingertip.

pamphlet_excerpts: Careers & Professional Pathways: The electronics industry has several general areas with many types of careers available in each area (p. 10).
Careers & Professional Pathways Principle 2: These areas include manufacturing, merchandising, operating, servicing or maintaining, and engineering electronic parts and equipment (p. 10).
Careers & Professional Pathways Principle 3: Some positions require a college degree, while a degree from a vocational school is adequate for other careers (p. 10).
Careers & Professional Pathways Principle 4: Some companies allow on-the-job training, but almost all require at least a high school diploma (p. 10).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Careers & Professional Pathways): In electronics manufacturing, most positions are in factories (p. 10).
Step 2 (Careers & Professional Pathways): Occupations include assemblers, that is, the people who help build electronic equipment (p. 10).
Step 3 (Careers & Professional Pathways): Ahigh school education is needed as well as mechanical aptitude (p. 10).
Step 4 (Careers & Professional Pathways): Merchandising, or sales, is another field for those interested in electronics (p. 10).

requirements.lead_text: Emergency Situations. Do the following:
requirements.req_text: Emergency Situations. Do the following: (a) Discuss with your counselor the aspects of emergency preparedness and include in your discussion the kinds of questions that are important to ask yourself as you consider each of these: prevention, protection, mitigation, response, and recovery. pamphlet_excerpts: Emergency Situations: About 100 nuclear power plants currently operate in the United States (p. 22).
Emergency Situations Principle 2: While there have been few nuclear accidents at these plants, an earthquake and tsunami in March 2011 triggered aserious accident at a nuclear power plant (p. 22).
Emergency Situations Principle 3: A 12-mile exclusion zone around the plant displaced 78,000 people (p. 22).
Emergency Situations Principle 4: During an emergency at a nuclear facility, radiation can be released that is dangerous to people near the plant (p. 22).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Emergency Situations): State and local governments have preparedness plans for areas in a 10-mile radius and 50-mile radius from all nuclear power plants (p. 22).
Step 2 (Emergency Situations): You can get emergency information from the power company that operates the plant or from the local Office of Emergency Management (p. 22).
Step 3 (Emergency Situations): You and your family should have and be familiar with this information (p. 22).
Step 4 (Emergency Situations): The worst nuclear emergency in the United States happened in 1979 at the Three Mile Island nuclear power plant in Pennsylvania (p. 22).

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: In Emergency Preparedness Requirement 1, emergency management is organized around five mission areas: Prevention, Protection, Mitigation, Response, and Recovery. Which action is an example of Mitigation before a disaster strikes?
quiz_item.question: In Emergency Preparedness Requirement 1, emergency management is organized around five mission areas: Prevention, Protection, Mitigation, Response, and Recovery. Which action is an example of Mitigation before a disaster strikes?
options: A. Strapping a home water heater to wall studs in an earthquake zone, elevating utilities above flood level, or clearing defensible brush space around a home to reduce future disaster damage.
B. Dispatching search-and-rescue helicopters during the peak of a hurricane to pull stranded residents from rooftops.
C. Applying for long-term federal rebuilding loans six months after a tornado destroys a town business district.
D. Waiting until a wildfire evacuation order is issued to start looking for flashlights, water bottles, and family phone numbers.
choices: A. Strapping a home water heater to wall studs in an earthquake zone, elevating utilities above flood level, or clearing defensible brush space around a home to reduce future disaster damage.
B. Dispatching search-and-rescue helicopters during the peak of a hurricane to pull stranded residents from rooftops.
C. Applying for long-term federal rebuilding loans six months after a tornado destroys a town business district.
D. Waiting until a wildfire evacuation order is issued to start looking for flashlights, water bottles, and family phone numbers.
quiz_item.correct_answer: A. Strapping a home water heater to wall studs in an earthquake zone, elevating utilities above flood level, or clearing defensible brush space around a home to reduce future disaster damage.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (A): Mitigation consists of sustained actions taken before an emergency (such as seismic bracing, flood elevation, and fuel reduction) that eliminate or reduce the long-term risk and severity of loss of life and property.

requirements.lead_text: Planning for Family Emergencies. Do the following:
requirements.req_text: Planning for Family Emergencies. Do the following: (a) At a family meeting, discuss the situations on the chart you created for requirement 1(b) and make emergency plans for sheltering-in-place and for evacuation of your home. Discuss your family meeting and plans with your counselor. (b) Develop and practice a plan of escape for your family in case of fire in your home. Draw a floor plan with escape routes and a map with a safe meeting place. Discuss your family's home escape plan with your counselor. (c) Using a checklist in the Emergency Preparedness merit badge pamphlet or one approved by your counselor, prepare or inspect a family disaster kit for sheltering-in-place and for evacuation of your home. Review the needs and uses of the items in a kit with your counselor.

requirements.req_text: Preventing Accidents and Emergencies. Do ONE of the following: (a) Using a home safety checklist included in the Emergency Preparedness merit badge pamphlet or one approved by your counselor, inspect a home (or a similar building near where you live or at a camp) for safety hazards with the help of an adult. Present your completed checklist to and discuss your findings with your counselor. (b) Develop emergency prevention plans for five family activities outside the home, as approved by your counselor. (Examples are taking a picnic to a park, seeing a movie, attending a worship service, an outing at a beach, traveling to visit a relative, or attending a ball game or concert.) Each plan should include an analysis of possible hazards, proposals to prevent, protect from, mitigate, respond to, and recover from emergencies, and the reasons for the actions that you propose.

Step 3 (Preventing Accidents and Emergencies): You can respond by knowing what actions you will take ahead of time (p. 19).

pamphlet_excerpts: Dangerous Situations: As much as possible, be prepared before trouble strikes in public (p. 71).
Dangerous Situations Principle 2: For instance, get into the habit of looking for exits in any public building you enter (p. 71).
Dangerous Situations Principle 3: Be aware that in some situations, the best thing to do is to keep yourself safe and possibly leave the scene (p. 71).
Dangerous Situations Principle 4: During an emergency, you may help save lives by using your knowledge of first aid and of situations that might be dangerous (p. 71).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Dangerous Situations): Earning the Lifesaving merit badge, for instance, will prepare youto react safely and effectively in the event of water emergencies (p. 71).
Step 2 (Dangerous Situations): Electrical appliances usually are safe, but eventually wires fray, plugs break, and parts loosen (p. 71).
Step 3 (Dangerous Situations): Furthermore, circuits in your home might be overloaded with too many extension cords and appliances (p. 71).
Step 4 (Dangerous Situations): It is extremely dangerous to touch a "live" wire, that is, a wire that has electrical current running (p. 71).

pamphlet_excerpts: Signaling for Help: You can also "talk" to a pilot with body signals (p. 40).
Signaling for Help Principle 2: Learn the 11 standard body signals illustrated in this chapter (p. 40).
Signaling for Help Principle 3: A pilot says "yes" by dipping the nose of the plane (p. 40).
Signaling for Help Principle 4: Zigzagging, or fishtailing, the plane means "no." If your message has been understood, the pilot will rock the plane from side to side or flash green (p. 40).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Signaling for Help): If your message has not been understood, the pilot will make a complete right-hand circle or flash red lights (p. 40).
Step 2 (Signaling for Help): In places where people get lost frequently, such as in mountainous or wilderness areas, volunteer search-and-rescue teams have formed to meet the need (p. 40).
Step 3 (Signaling for Help): Searchers in helicopters and on horseback, as well as trained dogs, all try to find lost people (p. 40).
Step 4 (Signaling for Help): In some places, Scouts and Venturers have specialized search-and-rescue activities and participate actively in operations (p. 40).

Moving an Injured Person Principle 3: When moving an injured person, no matter what method you are using, make sure you rest enough so that you do not become asecond casualty (p. 55).
Moving an Injured Person Principle 4: If just you and a buddy are doing the transporting, stop every 30 to 60 minutes and rest 5 to 10 minutes (p. 55).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Moving an Injured Person): How often you stop will depend on how much the victim weighs and how rugged the terrain (p. 55).
Step 2 (Moving an Injured Person): Two first-aiders can transport a conscious person with the four-handed seat (p. 55).
Step 3 (Moving an Injured Person): Use this carry only if the victim is conscious and can hold (p. 55).
Step 4 (Moving an Injured Person): Both bearers should grab their own right wrist with the left hand (p. 55).
