requirements.lead_text: Emergency Service. Do the following:
requirements.req_text: Emergency Service. Do the following: (a) Discuss with your counselor the duties that a Scout troop should be prepared to do, the training they need, and the safety precautions they should take for the following emergency services: (1) Crowd and traffic control (2) Messenger service during an incident (3) Collection and distribution services (4) Group feeding, shelter, and sanitation (b) Prepare a written plan for mobilizing your troop when needed to do emergency service. If your troop already has a mobilization plan, present the plan to your counselor and tell your part in making the plan work. (c) Using a checklist in the Emergency Preparedness merit badge pamphlet or one approved by your counselor, prepare or inspect a personal emergency service pack for a mobilization call. Explain the needs and uses of the contents to your counselor. (d) Take part in an emergency service project, either a real one or a practice exercise, with a Scouting troop or a community agency or at Scout camp or at a school. Review what you learned and practiced with your counselor.

pamphlet_excerpts: Emergency Service: It is important to coordinate efforts with local officials who will know what supplies are most needed (p. 82).
Emergency Service Principle 2: During and after some disasters, such as floods and tornadoes, many people may be without food and clothing (p. 82).
Emergency Service Principle 3: Scout troops working under the direction of their leaders and local officials can help collect needed items and get them to a central distribution (p. 82).
Emergency Service Principle 4: Usually, officials will setup collection and distribution points at places such as places of worship, fire stations, schools, and other public (p. 82).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Emergency Service): If your troop has developed a master map of your community, you will know where food stores (p. 82).
Step 2 (Emergency Service): Scouts also can distribute leaflets or instructions for the Red Cross, the local emergency management agency, or other local authorities (p. 82).
Step 3 (Emergency Service): Many Scouting units already know about and have experience collecting and distributing food through their work in the Scouting for Food (p. 82).
Step 4 (Emergency Service): Scout troops in the past have helped police and fire departments and emergency management officials handle crowd and traffic control (p. 82).

pamphlet_excerpts: First Aid Merit Badge: One of the first requirements for this merit badge is to earn the First Aid merit badge (p. 15).
First Aid Merit Badge Principle 2: You need to be able to recognize what is wrong with a person and then react to the emergency with the correct treatment until medical help arrives (p. 15).
First Aid Merit Badge Principle 3: You should know first aid so well that you would be able to react to any situation immediately (p. 15).
First Aid Merit Badge Principle 4: What would you do in these situations? You are eating pizza with some friends (p. 15).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (First Aid Merit Badge): Suddenly, your friend's little sister darts in and grabs some pizza (p. 15).
Step 2 (First Aid Merit Badge): Asshe runs away giggling and eating, she trips and starts choking (p. 15).
Step 3 (First Aid Merit Badge): She turns blue and stops breathing. You are camping out with your patrol (p. 15).
Step 4 (First Aid Merit Badge): During some free time, you offer to take a new patrol member on a hike around the lake (p. 15).

requirements.lead_text: Careers. Do ONE of the following:
requirements.req_text: Careers. Do ONE of the following: (a) Interview an emergency services coordinator or a civil servant about their work in disaster management. Learn about how they chose this career and about their duties. Discuss what you learned with your counselor and whether you might be interested in this career. (b) Identify three career opportunities that would use skills and knowledge in emergency services. Pick one and research the training, education, certification requirements, experience, and expenses associated with entering the field. Research the prospects for employment, starting salary, advancement opportunities, and career goals associated with this career. Discuss what you learned with your counselor and whether you might be interested in this career. (c) Identify how you might use the skills and knowledge in the field of emergency preparedness to pursue a personal hobby and/or healthy lifestyle. Research the additional training required, expenses, and affiliation with organizations that would help you maximize the enjoyment and benefit you might gain from it. Discuss what you learned with your counselor and share what short-term and long-term goals you might have if you pursued this.

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: In Emergency Preparedness Requirement 1, emergency management is organized around five mission areas: Prevention, Protection, Mitigation, Response, and Recovery. Which action is an example of Mitigation before a disaster strikes?

options: A. Strapping a home water heater to wall studs in an earthquake zone, elevating utilities above flood level, or clearing defensible brush space around a home to reduce future disaster damage.
B. Dispatching search-and-rescue helicopters during the peak of a hurricane to pull stranded residents from rooftops.
C. Applying for long-term federal rebuilding loans six months after a tornado destroys a town business district.
D. Waiting until a wildfire evacuation order is issued to start looking for flashlights, water bottles, and family phone numbers.

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: According to the First and Second Laws of Thermodynamics covered in Energy Requirement 1, what happens when chemical energy in coal or natural gas is converted into electrical energy at a power plant?
quiz_item.question: According to the First and Second Laws of Thermodynamics covered in Energy Requirement 1, what happens when chemical energy in coal or natural gas is converted into electrical energy at a power plant?
options: A. Total energy increases by thirty percent during combustion, and 100 percent of the heat is converted into usable electricity with zero waste.
B. Energy is completely destroyed inside the steam turbine, violating conservation of energy whenever the generator spins.
C. Entropy decreases in the surrounding atmosphere as waste heat spontaneously flows from the cold river back into the hot boiler.

D. Total energy is conserved (First Law), but during every energy conversion some high-grade energy degrades into lower-grade waste heat dispersed to the surroundings, increasing total entropy (Second Law).
choices: A. Total energy increases by thirty percent during combustion, and 100 percent of the heat is converted into usable electricity with zero waste.
B. Energy is completely destroyed inside the steam turbine, violating conservation of energy whenever the generator spins.
C. Entropy decreases in the surrounding atmosphere as waste heat spontaneously flows from the cold river back into the hot boiler.

D. Total energy is conserved (First Law), but during every energy conversion some high-grade energy degrades into lower-grade waste heat dispersed to the surroundings, increasing total entropy (Second Law).
quiz_item.correct_answer: D. Total energy is conserved (First Law), but during every energy conversion some high-grade energy degrades into lower-grade waste heat dispersed to the surroundings, increasing total entropy (Second Law).
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (D): The First Law of Thermodynamics states that energy cannot be created or destroyed, only converted in form; the Second Law states that every real conversion loses some usable energy as waste heat, increasing entropy.

requirements.req_text: Conduct an energy audit of your home. Keep a 14-day log that records what you and your family did to reduce energy use. Include the following in your report and, after the 14-day period, discuss what you have learned with your counselor. (a) List the types of energy used in your home such as electricity, wood, oil, liquid petroleum, and natural gas, and tell how each is delivered and measured, and the current cost; OR record the transportation fuel used, miles driven, miles per gallon, and trips using your family car or another vehicle. (b) Describe ways you and your family can use energy resources more wisely. In preparing your discussion, consider the energy required for the things you do and use on a daily basis (cooking, showering, using lights, driving, watching TV, using the computer). Explain what is meant by sustainable energy sources. Explain how you can change your energy use through reuse and recycling.

patrol_quiz_bank.question: According to the First and Second Laws of Thermodynamics covered in Energy Requirement 1, what happens when chemical energy in coal or natural gas is converted into electrical energy at a power plant?
options: A. Total energy increases by thirty percent during combustion, and 100 percent of the heat is converted into usable electricity with zero waste.
B. Energy is completely destroyed inside the steam turbine, violating conservation of energy whenever the generator spins.
C. Entropy decreases in the surrounding atmosphere as waste heat spontaneously flows from the cold river back into the hot boiler.

D. Total energy is conserved (First Law), but during every energy conversion some high-grade energy degrades into lower-grade waste heat dispersed to the surroundings, increasing total entropy (Second Law).
choices: A. Total energy increases by thirty percent during combustion, and 100 percent of the heat is converted into usable electricity with zero waste.
B. Energy is completely destroyed inside the steam turbine, violating conservation of energy whenever the generator spins.
C. Entropy decreases in the surrounding atmosphere as waste heat spontaneously flows from the cold river back into the hot boiler.

D. Total energy is conserved (First Law), but during every energy conversion some high-grade energy degrades into lower-grade waste heat dispersed to the surroundings, increasing total entropy (Second Law).
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: D. Total energy is conserved (First Law), but during every energy conversion some high-grade energy degrades into lower-grade waste heat dispersed to the surroundings, increasing total entropy (Second Law).
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (D): The First Law of Thermodynamics states that energy cannot be created or destroyed, only converted in form; the Second Law states that every real conversion loses some usable energy as waste heat, increasing entropy.

C. Because reverse engineering means copying only the exterior paint color of a product while ignoring how its internal gears and circuits operate.
D. Because the engineering design process eliminates the need for mathematics, physics, or safety standards.

Step 3 (Types of Engineers): Step 3 (Work of Six Types): The goal of analysis is to understand the object's behavior without the time and expense of building and testing physical models (p. 38).
Step 4 (Types of Engineers): Step 4 (Work of Six Types): Computer-aided engineering tools are used for simulation and analysis (p. 38).

Engineer Discuss Work This Principle 2: Visit with an engineer Principle 2: The design engineer uses new and existing ideas to solve a new problem or to solve an old problem in a new way (p. 38).

Engineer Discuss Work This Principle 3: Visit with an engineer Principle 3: These engineers find solutions that work according to the project's requirements, stay within the budget, and are easy and safe to use (p. 38).
Engineer Discuss Work This Principle 4: Visit with an engineer Principle 4: The solutions must be doable, long-lasting, practical to maintain or repair, and environmentally safe (p. 38).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Engineer Discuss Work This): Step 1 (Visit with an engineer): The analytical engineer is mainly responsible for creating mathematical models of physical problems (p. 38).

Step 2 (Engineer Discuss Work This): Step 2 (Visit with an engineer): Analysis is the process of using the methods and tools of mathematics to simulate (mimic) how a physical object will behave in response (p. 38).

Step 3 (Engineer Discuss Work This): Step 3 (Visit with an engineer): The goal of analysis is to understand the object's behavior without the time and expense of building and testing physical models (p. 38).
Step 4 (Engineer Discuss Work This): Step 4 (Visit with an engineer): Computer-aided engineering tools are used for simulation and analysis (p. 38).

requirements.lead_text: Do TWO of the following:
requirements.req_text: Do TWO of the following: (a) Transforming Motion. Using common materials or a construction set, make a simple model that will demonstrate motion. Explain how the model uses basic mechanical elements like levers and inclined planes to demonstrate motion. Describe an example where this mechanism is used in a real product. (b) Using Electricity. Make a list of 10 electrical appliances in your home. Find out approximately how much electricity each uses in one month. Learn how to find out the amount and cost of electricity used in your home during periods of light and heavy use. List five ways to conserve electricity. (c) Understanding Electronics. Using an electronic device such as a smartphone or tablet computer, find out how sound, video, text or images travel from one location to another. Explain how the device was designed for ease of use, function, and durability. (d) Using Materials. Do experiments to show the differences in strength and heat conductivity in wood, metal, and plastic. Discuss with your counselor what you have learned. (e) Converting Energy. Do an experiment to show how mechanical, heat, chemical, solar, and/or electrical energy may be converted from one or more types of energy to another. Explain your results. Describe to your counselor what energy is and how energy is converted and used in your surroundings. (f) Moving People. Find out the different ways people in your community get to work. Make a study of traffic flow (number of vehicles and relative speed) in both heavy and light traffic periods. Discuss with your counselor what might be improved to make it easier for people in your community to get where they need to go. (g) Building an Engineering Project. Enter a project in a science or engineering fair or similar competition. (This requirement may be met by participation on an engineering competition project team.) Discuss with your counselor what your project demonstrates, the kinds of questions visitors to the fair asked you, and how well you were able to answer their questions.

step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (In your own words, define entrepreneur ship): Entrepreneurs contribute to nearly every aspect of society (p. 17).

C. An entrepreneur identifies an unmet customer need or market opportunity, organizes resources to create a compelling value proposition, and assumes calculated financial and operational risk to build a venture.
D. An entrepreneur works only in non-profit municipal departments that do not sell goods or services to customers.

requirements.lead_text: Create a written business plan for your idea that includes all of the following:
requirements.req_text: Create a written business plan for your idea that includes all of the following: (a) Product or Service (1) Describe the product or service to be offered. (2) Identify goals for your business. (3) Explain how you can make enough of the product or perform the service to meet your goals. (4) Identify and describe the potential liability risks for your product or service. (5) Determine what type of license, if any, you might need in order to sell or make your product or service. (b) Market Analysis (1) Identify the types of people who would buy your product or service. (2) Identify your business's competitors, and describe their strengths and weaknesses. (3) Describe what makes your product or service unique. (c) Financial (1) Determine how much money you will need to start your business, and identify how you will obtain the money. (2) Determine the cost of offering your product or service and the price you will charge in order to make a profit. (3) Describe what will happen with the money you make from the sales of your product or service. (d) Personnel (1) Determine what parts of the business you will handle yourself, and describe your qualifications. (2) Determine whether you will need additional help to operate your business. If you will need help, describe the responsibilities and qualifications needed for the personnel who will fill each role. (e) Promotion and Marketing (1) Describe the methods you will use to promote your business to potential customers. (2) Explain how you will utilize the internet and social media to increase awareness of your product or service. (3) Design a promotional flyer or poster for your product or service.

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: When designing an ecological experiment for Environmental Science Requirement 1, how do biotic factors differ from abiotic factors, and what is the purpose of a control group?
quiz_item.question: When designing an ecological experiment for Environmental Science Requirement 1, how do biotic factors differ from abiotic factors, and what is the purpose of a control group?
options: A. Biotic factors are living components (plants, animals, fungi, bacteria) and abiotic factors are nonliving physical/chemical conditions (sunlight, temperature, soil pH, dissolved oxygen); the control group is kept at baseline conditions so you can isolate the effect of the single independent variable being tested.
B. Biotic factors are rocks and rainfall while abiotic factors are predators and pollinators; the control group has every variable changed at once.
C. Biotic and abiotic factors are identical synonyms for air pollution, and a scientific experiment never compares treated samples against untreated baselines.
D. Abiotic factors refer only to synthetic plastics, and the control group is discarded before recording any measurements.

Step 4 (Environmental Science Core Field Standard): If you have a camera (one that takes photographs quietly!), you may take photographs (p. 68).

requirements.req_text: Air Pollution. Then, compare two modes of transportation (e. g., gasoline-powered vs. electric vehicles, gasoline-powered car vs. bicycle, etc.). pamphlet_excerpts: Air Pollution: Meanwhile, new technologies must be developed to lessen our reliance on fossil fuels (p. 41).
Air Pollution Principle 2: The Clean Air Act of 1970 created federal air pollution regulations that each state must enforce (p. 41).
Air Pollution Principle 3: Since this enactment, the United States has significantly lowered the levels of six major air pollutants including sulfur dioxides, nitrogen oxides (p. 41).
Air Pollution Principle 4: There are several ways that the nitrogen oxides, sulfurdioxides, and particulates that power plants and industries release into the air have been lowered (p. 41).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Air Pollution): Some plants burn coal that has a lower sulfur content (p. 41).
Step 2 (Air Pollution): Others remove the sulfur from coal or convert coal to a liquid or gas before it is burned (p. 41).
Step 3 (Air Pollution): A third way to reduce greenhouse gas emissions is to use alternative sources of power, such as wind, water, or solar energy (p. 41).
Step 4 (Air Pollution): An added benefit of using alternative energy sources is that they can produce electricity without producing thermal pollution (p. 41).

pamphlet_excerpts: Water Pollution: Farmers can keep fertilizer out of runoff by using only small amounts at a time or by switching to farming practices that require less fertilizer (p. 45).
Water Pollution Principle 2: They can cut their use of pesticides or switch to biological controls (p. 45).
Water Pollution Principle 3: There have been improvements in water quality in the United States thanks to the Clean Water Act (p. 45).

requirements.lead_text: Land Pollution. Do ONE of the following and discuss with your counselor:
requirements.req_text: Land Pollution. Do ONE of the following and discuss with your counselor: (a) In an area (yard, park, golf course, farm, etc.) approved by your counselor, make a list of the pesticides, herbicides, and fertilizers used and how often they are applied. Identify the benefits of their use and the environmental impact, including effects on non-target species (including humans), what happens if the chemicals infiltrate into the groundwater, and what happens to any runoff of the chemicals. (b) Learn about the erosion process and identify an example of where erosion occurs. Determine where the eroded material ends up and how erosion can be minimized. (c) Learn about a land pollution incident that led to a site being listed on Environmental Protection Agency's Superfund National Priority List. Identify what caused the incident, what the effects were on the environment, what remediation has been done, and the current condition of the site.

requirements.lead_text: Rare, Threatened, or Endangered Species. Do ONE of the following and discuss with your counselor:
requirements.req_text: Rare, Threatened, or Endangered Species. Do ONE of the following and discuss with your counselor: (a) Do research on one endangered species found in your state. Learn about its natural habitat, why it is endangered, what is being done to preserve it, and how many individual species are left in the wild. Prepare a 100-word report about the species and include a drawing or photo. Present your report to your patrol or troop. (b) Do research on one species that was endangered or threatened but that has now recovered. Learn about how the species recovered, and what its new status is. Prepare a 100-word report on the species and include a drawing or photo. Present your report to your patrol or troop. (c) With your parent or guardian and counselor's approval, work with a natural resource professional to identify a completed project that has been designed to improve the habitat for a threatened or endangered species in your area. Visit the site and report on what you saw to your patrol or troop.

requirements.lead_text: Pollution Prevention, Resource Recovery, and Conservation. Do ONE of the following and discuss with your counselor:
requirements.req_text: Pollution Prevention, Resource Recovery, and Conservation. Do ONE of the following and discuss with your counselor: (a) Determine five ways to conserve resources or use resources more efficiently in your home, school, or camp. Practice at least two of these methods for at least one week. (b) Explain Resource Recovery and why it is important to reduce pollution. Collect samples or take photos of 10 items that can demonstrate the principle of Reduce, Reuse, Recycle. Explain your collection, how these materials are currently handled, and potential improvements. (c) Identify five items in your household that will become hazardous waste. Explain how they should be properly stored, what special care is needed for disposal, and proper disposal options available in your area.

patrol_quiz_bank.question: When designing an ecological experiment for Environmental Science Requirement 1, how do biotic factors differ from abiotic factors, and what is the purpose of a control group?
options: A. Biotic factors are living components (plants, animals, fungi, bacteria) and abiotic factors are nonliving physical/chemical conditions (sunlight, temperature, soil pH, dissolved oxygen); the control group is kept at baseline conditions so you can isolate the effect of the single independent variable being tested.
B. Biotic factors are rocks and rainfall while abiotic factors are predators and pollinators; the control group has every variable changed at once.
C. Biotic and abiotic factors are identical synonyms for air pollution, and a scientific experiment never compares treated samples against untreated baselines.
D. Abiotic factors refer only to synthetic plastics, and the control group is discarded before recording any measurements.

step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (General Knowledge): Many adventures may be quite exhilarating but are not exploration (p. 13).

Step 3 (General Knowledge): Taking a sailing trip in the Caribbean, hiking in the mountains, or joining a guided tour of ancient ruins is exciting, but it is not exploration (p. 13).
Step 4 (General Knowledge): However, if you took a sailing trip to the Caribbean to study reef ecology or you hiked in the mountains to survey wildlife (p. 13).

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: In Exploration Requirement 1, what distinguishes purposeful scientific exploration from casual sightseeing or recreational adventure tourism?
quiz_item.question: In Exploration Requirement 1, what distinguishes purposeful scientific exploration from casual sightseeing or recreational adventure tourism?
options: A. Exploration requires traveling without maps, first aid kits, or communication gear so every hazard comes as a surprise.
B. Sightseeing involves peer-reviewed field journals, whereas scientific exploration prohibits taking photographs, measurements, or specimen notes.
C. Exploration only occurs in outer space or on unmapped polar ice caps and cannot be conducted in local caves, watersheds, or forests.

D. Purposeful exploration defines clear scientific or geographic objectives before departure, manages field risks systematically, and documents observations, measurements, and discoveries to expand shared human knowledge.
choices: A. Exploration requires traveling without maps, first aid kits, or communication gear so every hazard comes as a surprise.
B. Sightseeing involves peer-reviewed field journals, whereas scientific exploration prohibits taking photographs, measurements, or specimen notes.
C. Exploration only occurs in outer space or on unmapped polar ice caps and cannot be conducted in local caves, watersheds, or forests.

D. Purposeful exploration defines clear scientific or geographic objectives before departure, manages field risks systematically, and documents observations, measurements, and discoveries to expand shared human knowledge.
quiz_item.correct_answer: D. Purposeful exploration defines clear scientific or geographic objectives before departure, manages field risks systematically, and documents observations, measurements, and discoveries to expand shared human knowledge.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (D): The Exploration Merit Badge emphasizes that true exploration combines thorough expedition planning and risk management with systematic observation, data logging, and reporting findings back to the broader community.

pamphlet_excerpts: History of Exploration: This is a key requirement and an important responsibility (p. 18).
History of Exploration Principle 2: Consider what skills are necessary for your endeavor and determine who can provide the expertise needed (p. 18).
History of Exploration Principle 3: The skills that each individual brings to the team will help you determine how many expedition members (p. 18).
History of Exploration Principle 4: Limit the group size by seeking out people with multiple skills (p. 18).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (History of Exploration): Team behavior and chemistry are important considerations (p. 18).
Step 2 (History of Exploration): If a brilliant scientist on your team lacks the social skills to getalong with others, you might reevaluate that person's role to avoid friction (p. 18).
Step 3 (History of Exploration): Everyone at some time or another has been on a team that was not functional (p. 18).
Step 4 (History of Exploration): Poor behavior might be only an annoyance in your normal environment, but it becomes a critical issue and more difficult to deal with in the field (p. 18).

pamphlet_excerpts: Importance of Exploration: While not all of us want to jump in a kayak and paddle the length of the Amazon, the evidence suggests that humans move around more than any other mammal (p. 18).
Importance of Exploration Principle 2: Scientists are researching the human genome (completeset of genes) to see if there is a genetic basis for this urge in our species (p. 18).
Importance of Exploration Principle 3: This research in itself is exploration, and it is being done in a laboratory (p. 18).
Importance of Exploration Principle 4: This gene controls a chemical messenger within our brains known as dopamine, which is important for learning (p. 18).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Importance of Exploration): Studies have shown this variation of the dopamine gene to be strongly related to curiosity and restlessness (p. 18).
Step 2 (Importance of Exploration): About 20 percent of all people have this gene variation, which makes them more likely to explore new places, ideas, foods, and other new things (p. 18).
Step 3 (Importance of Exploration): These people tend to seek movement, change, and adventure (p. 18).
Step 4 (Importance of Exploration): This genetic variation has been strongly linked to human migration, and it occurs frequently in nomads, people who move around a lot (p. 18).

requirements.lead_text: Expedition Planning. Discuss with your counselor each of the following steps for conducting a successful exploration activity. Explain the need for each step.
requirements.req_text: Expedition Planning. Discuss with your counselor each of the following steps for conducting a successful exploration activity. Explain the need for each step. (a) Identify the objectives (establish goals). (b) Plan the mission. Create an expedition agenda or schedule. List potential documents or permits needed. (c) Budget and plan for adequate financial resources. Estimate costs for travel, equipment, accommodations, meals, permits or licenses, and other expedition expenses. (d) Determine equipment and supplies required for personal and mission needs for the length of the expedition. (e) Determine communication and transportation needs. Plan how to keep in contact with your base or the outside world, and determine how you will communicate with each other on-site. (f) Establish safety and first-aid procedures (including planning for medical evacuation). Identify the hazards that explorers could encounter on the expedition and establish procedures to prevent or avoid those hazards. (g) Determine team selection. Identify who is essential for the expedition to be successful and what skills are required by the expedition leader. (h) Establish detailed recordkeeping (documentation) procedures. Plan the interpretation and sharing of information at the conclusion of the expedition.

pamphlet_excerpts: Expedition Planning: Make safety a priority in preparing for an expedition (p. 54).
Expedition Planning Principle 2: One early decision you must make is whether you will have a trained medic on the trip (p. 54).
Expedition Planning Principle 3: If so, as the leader you should work with this person to screen participants for medical conditions that could cause trouble later (p. 54).
Expedition Planning Principle 4: Require all potential members of the expedition to be open about their medical needs (p. 54).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Expedition Planning): Remember that if someone is injured or becomes illon the road, they may need to be evacuated and the trip might be cut short or delayed (p. 54).
Step 2 (Expedition Planning): This clearance should also confirm that the participant has had all appropriate vaccinations (p. 54).
Step 3 (Expedition Planning): If your activity will be strenuous or stressful, a waiver of liability for each participant is advisable (p. 54).
Step 4 (Expedition Planning): Few people have medical evacuation coverage included in their health insurance, so it is vital that each expedition member obtains an insurance policy (p. 54).

requirements.lead_text: Prepare for an Expedition. With your parent or guardian's permission and counselor's approval, prepare for an actual expedition to an area you have not previously explored; the place may be nearby or far away. Do the following:
requirements.req_text: Prepare for an Expedition. With your parent or guardian's permission and counselor's approval, prepare for an actual expedition to an area you have not previously explored; the place may be nearby or far away. Do the following: (a) Make your preparations under the supervision of a trained expedition leader, expedition planner, or other qualified adult experienced in exploration (such as a school science teacher, museum representative, or qualified instructor). (b) Use the steps listed in requirement 6 to guide your preparations. List the items of equipment and supplies you will need. Discuss with your counselor why you chose each item and how it will be of value on the expedition. Determine who should go on the expedition. (c) Conduct a pre-expedition check, covering the steps in requirement 6, and share the results with your counselor. With your counselor, walk through the Scouting America SAFE Checklist for your expedition. Ensure that all foreseeable hazards for your expedition are adequately addressed.

Expedition Permission Actual Expedition Principle 2: Prepare for an Expedition Principle 2: Field knowledge of all applicable BSA standards and a commitment to implement and follow BSApolicies and procedures are essential parts of the supervisor's (p. 63).

Expedition Permission Actual Expedition Principle 3: Prepare for an Expedition Principle 3: For youth participants in any potentially strenuous activity, the supervisor should receive a complete health history from a health-care professional (p. 63).

Expedition Permission Actual Expedition Principle 4: Prepare for an Expedition Principle 4: Adult participants and youth involved in higher-risk activity (e. g., scuba) may require professional evaluation in addition to the health history (p. 63).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Expedition Permission Actual Expedition): Step 1 (Prepare for an Expedition): The supervisor should adjust all supervision, discipline, and protection to anticipate potential risks associated with individual health conditions (p. 63).
Step 2 (Expedition Permission Actual Expedition): Step 2 (Prepare for an Expedition): Neither youth nor adults should participate in activities for which they are unfit (p. 63).
Step 3 (Expedition Permission Actual Expedition): Step 3 (Prepare for an Expedition): To do so would place both the individual and others at risk. 3 (p. 63).

Step 4 (Expedition Permission Actual Expedition): Step 4 (Prepare for an Expedition): A key part of the supervisor's responsibility is to know the area or course for the activity and to determine that it is well-suited and free (p. 63).

requirements.lead_text: Go on an Expedition. Complete the following:
requirements.req_text: Go on an Expedition. Complete the following: (a) With your parent or guardian's permission and under the supervision of your counselor or a counselor-approved qualified person, use the planning steps you learned in requirement 6 and the preparations you completed in requirement 7 to personally undertake an actual expedition to an area you have not previously explored. (b) Discuss with your counselor about the vital role of outdoor ethics in exploration, explaining how they promote responsible and mindful adventuring. Explain how you applied the Outdoor Code, Leave No Trace, and Tread Lightly! principles during your expedition. (c) After you return, compile a report on the results of your expedition and how you accomplished your objective(s). Include a statement of the objectives, note your findings and observations, include photos, note any discoveries, report any problems or adverse events, and have a conclusion (whether you reached your objective or not). The post-expedition report must be at least one page and no more than three; one page can be photos, graphs, or figures.

Go on an Expedition Principle 2: Explorers may be on land, in a cave, below or above water, or in space (p. 67).
Go on an Expedition Principle 3: Wherever they may be, they share the positive environmental ethic that helps keep our waters, mountains, air, and other locales enjoyable for generations (p. 67).
Go on an Expedition Principle 4: Consider your group's size, age, and skill level (p. 67).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Go on an Expedition): Gather information (geography, weather, regulations) about the place you will be visiting, and allow enough time to get there. 2 (p. 67).
Step 2 (Go on an Expedition): Follow and use established trails and campsites. 3 (p. 67).
Step 3 (Go on an Expedition): Packout all leftover food and trash, this may include human waste, toilet paper, and hygiene products (p. 67).
Step 4 (Go on an Expedition): Examine cultural or historic structures, artifacts, rocks, plants, and other natural objects, but leave them alone. 5 (p. 67).

requirements.lead_text: Career Opportunities. Do ONE of the following:
requirements.req_text: Career Opportunities. Do ONE of the following: (a) Explore careers related to this merit badge. Research one career to learn about the training and education needed, costs, job prospects, salary, job duties, and career advancement. Your research methods may include, with your parent or guardian's permission, an internet or library search, an interview with a professional in the field, or a visit to a location where people in this career work. Discuss with your counselor both your findings and what about this profession might make it an interesting career. (b) Explore how you could use knowledge and skills from this merit badge to pursue a hobby. Research any training needed, expenses, and organizations that promote or support it. Discuss with your counselor what short-term and long-term goals you might have if you pursued this.

Step 3 (Careers & Professional Pathways): For youth participants in any potentially strenuous activity, the supervisor should receive a complete health history from a health-care professional (p. 31).
Step 4 (Careers & Professional Pathways): Adult participants and youth involved in higher-risk activity (e. g., scuba) may require professional evaluation in addition to the health (p. 31).

D. Purposeful exploration defines clear scientific or geographic objectives before departure, manages field risks systematically, and documents observations, measurements, and discoveries to expand shared human knowledge.

pamphlet_excerpts: Outline on What A Family: Prepare an outline: The family is the basic unit of society and is important to both individuals and communities (p. 9).
Outline on What A Family Principle 2: Prepare an outline Principle 2: The world in which we live is rapidly changing, making today's society much more complex than ever (p. 9).

Outline on What A Family Principle 3: Prepare an outline Principle 3: As you earn this merit badge, you will realize why it is important to know more about family life and how to strengthen our families (p. 9).

Outline on What A Family Principle 4: Prepare an outline Principle 4: Families are the small groups in which we learn our first and most important lessons about how to live and be happy in the larger society (p. 9).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Outline on What A Family): Step 1 (Prepare an outline): Strong families are the foundation of strong communities (p. 9).
Step 2 (Outline on What A Family): Step 2 (Prepare an outline): You know that a strong foundation is needed to construct a sturdy building (p. 9).

Step 3 (Outline on What A Family): Step 3 (Prepare an outline): Think of society as the building, the family as the foundation of that building, and individuals and the community as pieces of building material (p. 9).
Step 4 (Outline on What A Family): Step 4 (Prepare an outline): All the parts are important and none can be left out, but it all starts with a strong foundation (p. 9).

D. Because communities function best when families refuse to discuss budgets, schedules, or household duties together.

requirements.lead_text: Do the following: Note: Some of the issues surrounding requirement 6 for the family meeting could be considered of a personal nature. Use discretion when reviewing this requirement with the Scout. Discussion of each of these subjects will very likely carry over to more than one family meeting.
requirements.req_text: Do the following: Note: Some of the issues surrounding requirement 6 for the family meeting could be considered of a personal nature. Use discretion when reviewing this requirement with the Scout. Discussion of each of these subjects will very likely carry over to more than one family meeting. (a) Discuss with your counselor how to plan and carry out a family meeting. (b) Prepare a meeting agenda that includes the following topics, review it with your parent or guardian, and then carry out one or more family meetings: (1) How living the principles of the Scout Oath and Scout Law contributes to your family life (2) The greatest dangers and addictions facing youth in today's society (examples include mental health challenges, use of tobacco products, alcohol, or drugs and other items such as debts, social media, etc.) (3) Discuss with a parent or guardian how bodily changes can affect the choices you make as you physically and mentally mature. (4) Personal and family finances (5) A crisis situation within your family and whom you can turn to for support during these situations. (6) The effect of technology on your family (7) Good etiquette and manners

sub_requirements.sub_req_text: Prepare a meeting agenda that includes the following topics, review it with your parent or guardian, and then carry out one or more family meetings: (1) How living the principles of the Scout Oath and Scout Law contributes to your family life (2) The greatest dangers and addictions facing youth in today's society (examples include mental health challenges, use of tobacco products, alcohol, or drugs and other items such as debts, social media, etc.) (3) Discuss with a parent or guardian how bodily changes can affect the choices you make as you physically and mentally mature. (4) Personal and family finances (5) A crisis situation within your family and whom you can turn to for support during these situations. (6) The effect of technology on your family (7) Good etiquette and manners.

requirements.lead_text: Do the following:
requirements.req_text: Do the following: (a) Discuss with your counselor the safety equipment, tools, and clothing used while checking or repairing farm equipment. Use this equipment, tools, and/or clothing (when needed or called for) in meeting the requirements for this merit badge. (b) Draw a plan showing a well-equipped farm shop. Point out the shop's mandatory safety devices and features. (c) Find all the universal warning and safety symbols on a piece of equipment and explain what they mean. (d) Describe what a safety data sheet (SDS) is and tell why it is used. Obtain the SDS for any engine coolant, oil, grease, fuel, hydraulic or transmission fluid, or other flammable or hazardous materials you use in meeting the requirements for this merit badge.

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: While inspecting a tractor and rotary mower attachment for Farm Mechanics Requirement 1, which safety rules apply to the Power Take-Off (PTO) shaft, Rollover Protective Structure (ROPS), and hydraulic lines?
quiz_item.question: While inspecting a tractor and rotary mower attachment for Farm Mechanics Requirement 1, which safety rules apply to the Power Take-Off (PTO) shaft, Rollover Protective Structure (ROPS), and hydraulic lines?
options: A. Remove the plastic PTO master shield for easier greasing, step across the spinning shaft while the engine is at full throttle, and leave the seatbelt unbuckled with a ROPS frame.
B. Search for pinhole leaks in high-pressure hydraulic hoses by running your bare fingertips along the pressurized hose while a helper works the control lever.

C. Keep all PTO master shields and driveline guards securely in place, disengage the PTO, shut off the engine, and pocket the ignition key before servicing implements, wear the seatbelt whenever ROPS is installed, and use a piece of cardboard or wood (never bare skin) to check for pinhole hydraulic leaks.
D. Prop up a raised front-end loader bucket with a hollow brick and crawl underneath without installing cylinder safety stops.

pamphlet_excerpts: Short History of Fingerprinting: Give A Short History: Galton was able to scientifically prove what Herschel and Faulds already suspected: that fingerprints are permanent and unique to each individual (p. 13).
Short History of Fingerprinting Principle 2: Give A Short History Principle 2: According to Galton's calculations, the odds of two individual fingerprints being the same were 1 in 64 billion (p. 13).

Short History of Fingerprinting Principle 3: Give A Short History Principle 3: In 1891, Juan Vucetich, an Argentine police official, began the first fingerprint files based on Galton pattern types (p. 13).
Short History of Fingerprinting Principle 4: Give A Short History Principle 4: In 1892, Vucetich made the first criminal fingerprint identification (p. 13).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Short History of Fingerprinting): Step 1 (Give A Short History): The classification system was based on Galton's observations, as revised by Sir Edward Richard Henry (p. 13).

Step 2 (Short History of Fingerprinting): Step 2 (Give A Short History): In 1903, the New York State prison system became the first agency in the United States to regularly use fingerprints to identify criminals (p. 13).
Step 3 (Short History of Fingerprinting): Step 3 (Give A Short History): The Leavenworth bureau became the first to operate on more than a local basis (p. 13).

Step 4 (Short History of Fingerprinting): Step 4 (Give A Short History): It gradually began to offer a free fingerprint exchange service among a growing list of participating lawenforcement officers (p. 13).

quiz_item.question: In Fingerprinting Requirement 1, why are friction ridge skin patterns useful for lifelong personal identification, and what are the three primary fingerprint pattern families classified by Sir Francis Galton and Sir Edward Henry?
options: A. Friction ridge arrangements are unique to each individual (even identical twins) and remain unchanged in pattern from before birth until decomposition; the three main pattern families are loops, whorls, and arches.
B. Fingerprints change completely every seven years as a person ages; the three main pattern families are squares, triangles, and spirals.
C. Only the thumb has friction ridges while the other four fingers are smooth; patterns are classified by skin temperature and ink color.
D. Identical twins share identical fingerprints on all ten digits; the three pattern families are epidermal, dermal, and subcutaneous.
choices: A. Friction ridge arrangements are unique to each individual (even identical twins) and remain unchanged in pattern from before birth until decomposition; the three main pattern families are loops, whorls, and arches.
B. Fingerprints change completely every seven years as a person ages; the three main pattern families are squares, triangles, and spirals.
C. Only the thumb has friction ridges while the other four fingers are smooth; patterns are classified by skin temperature and ink color.
D. Identical twins share identical fingerprints on all ten digits; the three pattern families are epidermal, dermal, and subcutaneous.
quiz_item.correct_answer: A. Friction ridge arrangements are unique to each individual (even identical twins) and remain unchanged in pattern from before birth until decomposition; the three main pattern families are loops, whorls, and arches.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (A): Formed in the fetal dermal papillae, friction ridge patterns are both unique to every person and permanent throughout life, categorized into loops (about 60-65%), whorls (30-35%), and arches (5%).

Step 3 (Automated Fingerprint Identification Systems AFIS): Step 3 (Explain The Difference): They can confirm identity for access to medical records and bank accounts and for proper use of travel documents (p. 35).

Step 4 (Automated Fingerprint Identification Systems AFIS): Step 4 (Explain The Difference): Using computers, thousands of comparisons per second can be made and it is no longer necessary to limit searches to only as mall portion of the entire (p. 35).

pamphlet_excerpts: Counselor You Can Identify: Your counselor you can identify: Fingerprints are classified into three basic types, loops, arches, and whorls, based on the patterns made by the ridges that cover the skin (p. 18).
Counselor You Can Identify Principle 2: Your counselor you can identify Principle 2: Learning to recognize these general patterns and their subcategories is not hard (p. 18).

Counselor You Can Identify Principle 3: Your counselor you can identify Principle 3: Study the examples shown in this pamphlet, then complete the worksheet found on page 38 to show your counselor you can identify the three basic types (p. 18).
Counselor You Can Identify Principle 4: Your counselor you can identify Principle 4: Also identify the pattern types of your own fingerprints (p. 18).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Counselor You Can Identify): Step 1 (Your counselor you can identify): In the loop pattern, the ridges begin on one side of the finger, curve or turn back sharply, and end on the same side (p. 18).
Step 2 (Counselor You Can Identify): Step 2 (Your counselor you can identify): The loop may slope or "lean" toward either the thumb or the little finger (p. 18).

Step 3 (Counselor You Can Identify): Step 3 (Your counselor you can identify): If you can identify the two bones in your forearm, the radius and ulna, then you can remember the two subcategoriesof loops (p. 18).

Step 4 (Counselor You Can Identify): Step 4 (Your counselor you can identify): The ridges of a radial loop begin and end on the same side of the hand as the thumb (or the radius, the bone that is on the inside of the arm) (p. 18).

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: In Fire Safety Requirement 1, what are the four elements of the fire tetrahedron, and what is the correct procedure if you are inside a bedroom and the home smoke alarm sounds at night?
quiz_item.question: In Fire Safety Requirement 1, what are the four elements of the fire tetrahedron, and what is the correct procedure if you are inside a bedroom and the home smoke alarm sounds at night?
options: A. Nitrogen, carbon dioxide, water vapor, and ash; stand up straight to breathe the warm air near the ceiling and hide inside a bedroom closet.
B. Wood, paper, gasoline, and electricity; open all windows wide to feed fresh breeze to the hallway before gathering your toys and electronics.
C. Smoke, flame, sparks, and soot; run back inside the burning house after escaping to retrieve family photo albums.

D. Fuel, heat, an oxidizing agent (oxygen), and an uninhibited chemical chain reaction; stay low beneath toxic smoke, feel closed doors with the back of your hand before opening, use your secondary window escape if the door is hot, and meet at your family's outside meeting place.
choices: A. Nitrogen, carbon dioxide, water vapor, and ash; stand up straight to breathe the warm air near the ceiling and hide inside a bedroom closet.
B. Wood, paper, gasoline, and electricity; open all windows wide to feed fresh breeze to the hallway before gathering your toys and electronics.

quiz_item.correct_answer: D. Fuel, heat, an oxidizing agent (oxygen), and an uninhibited chemical chain reaction; stay low beneath toxic smoke, feel closed doors with the back of your hand before opening, use your secondary window escape if the door is hot, and meet at your family's outside meeting place.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (D): Extinguishing a fire requires removing fuel, heat, oxygen, or the chemical chain reaction (the fire tetrahedron); during a home fire, smoke inhalation is the primary killer, so occupants must crawl low, check doors for heat, exit immediately, and never re-enter.

requirements.lead_text: Fire Safety at Home. Do the following:
requirements.req_text: Fire Safety at Home. Do the following: (a) Describe how to prevent the frequent causes of home fires, including unattended cooking, electricity, smoking, clothes dryers, and rechargeable batteries. (b) Describe how to prevent frequent causes of seasonal and holiday-related home fires, including fires related to home heating, holiday trees, candles, and fireworks. (c) Demonstrate how to safely light and extinguish a candle. Discuss with your counselor, then with your family, how to safely use candles. (d) Using the Home Fire Safety Checklist in the Fire Safety merit badge pamphlet or one approved by your counselor, and with the help of an adult, inspect a home (or a similar building near where you live or at a camp) for fire safety hazards. Present your completed checklist to your counselor and discuss your findings. (e) Determine if, and what types of, smoke and CO alarms are required in homes in your community. List what types of smoke and CO alarms your home has, their locations, and their expiration dates. (f) Demonstrate maintenance of smoke and CO alarms to your counselor and review plans to replace expired alarms. (g) Develop a home fire-escape plan and a fire-drill schedule with your family, draw a floor plan of your home with exits marked and a map showing your family meeting point, and conduct a home fire drill. (h) Explain what to do and what not to do if you smell natural gas and if you smell smoke. (i) Explain how you would report a fire to have the fire department respond.

requirements.lead_text: Fire Safety at Camp. Do the following:
requirements.req_text: Fire Safety at Camp. Do the following: (a) Explain how the Leave No Trace Seven Principles and the Outdoor Code apply to camping fires. (b) Demonstrate lighting a match safely, the proper way to extinguish it, and to dispose of it. Explain the similarities and differences between safety matches and strike-anywhere matches. (c) Explain and demonstrate making sparks with flint and steel or with a ferro rod and catching a spark to create a flame. Extinguish the flame safely using one of the principles of the fire tetrahedron. (d) Demonstrate the safe way to start a charcoal fire. (e) Describe three common campsite fire lays. Collect, prepare, and set up tinder, kindling, and fuel for a campfire following the Leave No Trace Seven Principles and the Outdoor Code. Ignite your fire lay and safely extinguish your fire. (f) Demonstrate using a camp stove. (g) Explain how to set up and keep a campsite safe from fire. (h) Develop a lesson plan to teach a fire safety skill or topic, such as lighting a candle or a match or a charcoal fire or a lantern or a camp stove or using flint and steel or setting up a fire lay. Review your lesson plan with your counselor. Teach your skill or topic to one or more Scouts using the EDGE method.

requirements.req_text: Careers. Do ONE of the following: (a) Visit a fire station in-person. Identify the various types of fire service vehicles. From the firefighters you meet during your visit, learn about the fire prevention activities in your community and about their careers. Discuss with your counselor what you learned during your tour and interviews. (b) Identify three career opportunities that would use skills and knowledge in the field of fire safety. Pick one and research the training, education, certification requirements, experience, and expenses associated with entering the field. Research the prospects for employment, starting salary, advancement opportunities and career goals associated with this career. Discuss what you learned with your counselor and whether you might be interested in this career.

patrol_quiz_bank.question: In Fire Safety Requirement 1, what are the four elements of the fire tetrahedron, and what is the correct procedure if you are inside a bedroom and the home smoke alarm sounds at night?
options: A. Nitrogen, carbon dioxide, water vapor, and ash; stand up straight to breathe the warm air near the ceiling and hide inside a bedroom closet.
B. Wood, paper, gasoline, and electricity; open all windows wide to feed fresh breeze to the hallway before gathering your toys and electronics.
C. Smoke, flame, sparks, and soot; run back inside the burning house after escaping to retrieve family photo albums.

D. Fuel, heat, an oxidizing agent (oxygen), and an uninhibited chemical chain reaction; stay low beneath toxic smoke, feel closed doors with the back of your hand before opening, use your secondary window escape if the door is hot, and meet at your family's outside meeting place.

B. Wood, paper, gasoline, and electricity; open all windows wide to feed fresh breeze to the hallway before gathering your toys and electronics.

requirements.lead_text: Handling a First Aid Emergency. Do the following:
requirements.req_text: Handling a First Aid Emergency. Do the following: (a) Explain the steps necessary to assess and handle a first aid emergency, including a safety evaluation of the scene. (b) Tell how you would obtain emergency medical assistance from your home and from a remote location on a wilderness camping trip. (c) Demonstrate the precautions you must take to reduce the risk of transmitting an infection between you and the victim while administering first aid, including the safe disposal of used first aid supplies. (d) Demonstrate evaluation of and management of a patient's airway and breathing. (e) Demonstrate a thorough examination of an accident victim. (f) Discuss why shock is an emergency. (g) Define the term triage and describe examples of triage situations that you may encounter.

Handling a First Aid Emergency Principle 2: To do this, get the help of others in your group and lift the victim in the same position as found (p. 19).
Handling a First Aid Emergency Principle 3: Remember: Do not move the victim unless you absolutely have to for safety reasons (p. 19).
Handling a First Aid Emergency Principle 4: It is impossible to know for sure if the victim has any diseases (p. 19).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Handling a First Aid Emergency): You should consider all body fluids to be infectious (p. 19).
Step 2 (Handling a First Aid Emergency): Wear nonlatex gloves and, if you might be splashed by blood, vomit, or other body fluids, also wear a protective mask and eye shield (p. 19).
Step 3 (Handling a First Aid Emergency): Your sunglasses, rain gear, and bandana or neckerchief (over your mouth and nose) would work if nothing else is available (p. 19).
Step 4 (Handling a First Aid Emergency): Provide Urgent Treatment If the person is Breathing and bleeding, these are your immediate concerns when treating the victim of an accident (p. 19).

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: During a woodland trail hike, your patrol discovers an adult hiker lying at the base of a wet rock ledge with bright red blood spurting from a lower-leg wound and a downed power line 25 feet uphill. What is your patrol's immediate first-aid sequence?
quiz_item.question: During a woodland trail hike, your patrol discovers an adult hiker lying at the base of a wet rock ledge with bright red blood spurting from a lower-leg wound and a downed power line 25 feet uphill. What is your patrol's immediate first-aid sequence?
options: A. Sprint straight to the victim without gloves to apply a tourniquet before checking the overhead wire.

B. Stop and size up scene safety first (confirm the downed wire does not endanger the approach zone), put on nitrile gloves for Universal Precautions, direct a buddy to call 911 with GPS coordinates, and apply firm direct pressure with a sterile gauze dressing to control arterial bleeding.
C. Have two Scouts carry the hiker 100 yards down the rocky trail before checking airway, breathing, or severe bleeding.
D. Pour cold stream water onto the open arterial wound and elevate both legs 18 inches before checking scene hazards.

quiz_item.correct_answer: B. Stop and size up scene safety first (confirm the downed wire does not endanger the approach zone), put on nitrile gloves for Universal Precautions, direct a buddy to call 911 with GPS coordinates, and apply firm direct pressure with a sterile gauze dressing to control arterial bleeding.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (B): Under the First Aid Merit Badge Pamphlet emergency action sequence (Check-Call-Care), rescuers must first verify scene safety so they do not become a second victim, apply Universal Precautions (BSI barriers), summon EMS immediately, and treat life-threatening conditions (airway, breathing, severe bleeding) before minor injuries.

requirements.lead_text: Preparing for First Aid Emergencies. Do the following:
requirements.req_text: Preparing for First Aid Emergencies. Do the following: (a) Obtain a copy of the Scout Annual Health and Medical Record and discuss the importance of the form including information on immunizations, allergies, medications, health history, and medical examinations to providing first aid at Scouting events. (b) Using checklists provided in the First Aid merit badge pamphlet or ones approved by your counselor, do the following: (1) Assemble a personal first-aid kit for hiking and backpacking. Demonstrate the proper use of each item in your first-aid kit to your counselor. (2) With your counselor, inspect a unit, home, vehicle, or camp first-aid kit and discuss your findings.

pamphlet_excerpts: Preparing for First Aid Emergencies: Life-Threatening Emergencies with the person at all times (p. 93).
Preparing for First Aid Emergencies Principle 2: Having it back at camp does no good when it is needed on the trail (p. 93).
Preparing for First Aid Emergencies Principle 3: Step 1, Call 911 or your local emergency-response number (p. 93).
Preparing for First Aid Emergencies Principle 4: Step 2, Check the victim for a medical ID bracelet, necklace, or information card (p. 93).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Preparing for First Aid Emergencies): Ask if the person is carrying a prescribed emergency medical kit (p. 93).
Step 2 (Preparing for First Aid Emergencies): You might be able to assist the person under certain circumstances AND if you are trained and allowed to assist by state or local regulations (p. 93).
Step 3 (Preparing for First Aid Emergencies): If so, follow the kit instructions exactly and assist the person by locating the medication kit and handing it to him (p. 93).
Step 4 (Preparing for First Aid Emergencies): It is best that the individual administers the medication (p. 93).

requirements.lead_text: Wounds with No External Bleeding. Describe the symptoms and signs of, show first aid for, and explain prevention of these wounds:
requirements.req_text: Wounds with No External Bleeding. Describe the symptoms and signs of, show first aid for, and explain prevention of these wounds: (a) Closed wounds, such as a bruise (contusion) or a hematoma (b) Superficial, partial thickness, and full thickness thermal (heat) burns or scalds (c) Chemical burns (d) Electrical burns (e) Sunburn (f) Snow blindness (g) Immersion foot, frostnip, frostbite, and ice burns (h) Abrasions, such as chafing and rope burns (i) Blisters on the hands, feet, buttocks, and shoulders (j) Puncture wounds from splinters, rope splinters, nails, and fish hooks (k) Rash from poisonous plants (l) Bug bites of chiggers, ticks, mosquitoes, and biting gnats (m) Bee stings (n) Bites of spiders (o) Sting of a scorpion (p) Bite of a pet or wild mammal or human (q) Bite of a venomous snake

pamphlet_excerpts: Wounds with No External Bleeding: The bites of mosquitoes, chiggers, and nosee-ums are irritating but not usually dangerous (p. 14).
Wounds with No External Bleeding Principle 2: More troublesome are ticks, some spiders, and some ants (p. 14).
Wounds with No External Bleeding Principle 3: To avoid getting bitten by ticks, wear long pants and along-sleeved shirt whenever you are in tick infested woodlands and fields (p. 14).
Wounds with No External Bleeding Principle 4: Button your collar and tuck your pant cuffs into your boots or socks (p. 14).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Wounds with No External Bleeding): Inspect yourself daily, especially the hairy parts of your body, and immediately remove any ticks you find (p. 14).
Step 2 (Wounds with No External Bleeding): Ticks bury their heads beneath the skin of their victims (p. 14).
Step 3 (Wounds with No External Bleeding): To remove a tick, with gloved hands, grasp it with tweezers close to the skin and gently pull until it comes loose (p. 14).
Step 4 (Wounds with No External Bleeding): Don't squeeze, twist, or jerk the tick, as doing so could leave its mouth parts still buried in the skin (p. 14).

pamphlet_excerpts: Bleeding Wounds: Cuts and Scrapes (Abrasions) Cuts may be caused by knives, razors, or broken glass (p. 37).
Bleeding Wounds Principle 2: An abrasion is a wound that occurs as a result of the outer layers of the skin being rubbed or scraped (p. 37).
Bleeding Wounds Principle 3: Abrasions may happen when the skin is scraped against a hard surface, for example, when a bicyclist falls onto the pavement (p. 37).
Bleeding Wounds Principle 4: Sometimes dirt and gravel get ground into the abrasion, which increases the likelihood of infection (p. 37).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Bleeding Wounds): To protect yourself from cuts and scrapes, dress appropriately for the activity, for instance, jeans, boots, gloves, longsleeved shirt (p. 37).
Step 2 (Bleeding Wounds): A few simple precautions can help you avoid the pain of the treatment and healing process (p. 37).
Step 3 (Bleeding Wounds): Treat a minor cut or scrape by flushing the area with clean water for at least five minutes, or until all foreign matter appears to be washed away (p. 37).
Step 4 (Bleeding Wounds): Remember to protect yourself withnonlatex gloves and other precautions as needed, as well asby washing your hands before and after treating (p. 37).

pamphlet_excerpts: Breathing Emergencies: If you suspect that frostbite extends below skin level, removewet clothing and wrap the injured area in a dry blanket (p. 61).
Breathing Emergencies Principle 2: Get the victim under the care of a physician as soon as possible (p. 61).
Breathing Emergencies Principle 3: Rewarm the area only if there is no chance of refreezing (p. 61).
Breathing Emergencies Principle 4: To treat frostnip, move the victim into a tent or building, then warm the injured area (p. 61).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Breathing Emergencies): If an ear or cheek is frozen, remove a glove and warm the injury with the palm of your hand (p. 61).
Step 2 (Breathing Emergencies): Slip a frost nipped hand under your clothing and tuck it beneath an armpit (p. 61).
Step 3 (Breathing Emergencies): Treat frost nipped toes by putting the victim's bare feet against the warm skin of your belly (p. 61).
Step 4 (Breathing Emergencies): The human body is 70 percent water, which is essential to maintain our body temperature (p. 61).

pamphlet_excerpts: Loss of Consciousness: Taking too many drugs or drinking too much alcohol can make aperson lose consciousness (p. 63).
Loss of Consciousness Principle 2: Never give an unconscious person anything to drink, throw water on the face, or offer stimulants such as smelling salts (p. 63).
Loss of Consciousness Principle 3: Do not shake or slap the person in an effort to wake him orher (p. 63).
Loss of Consciousness Principle 4: A loss of consciousness for more than two minutes is a serious medical condition (p. 63).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Loss of Consciousness): An unconscious person might have been hit in the head or had a heart attack or stroke (p. 63).
Step 2 (Loss of Consciousness): People with diabetes can lose consciousness from either very high or very low blood sugar (p. 63).
Step 3 (Loss of Consciousness): Look for an emergency medical ID bracelet or necklace or an information card that identifies health problems such as diabetes (p. 63).
Step 4 (Loss of Consciousness): Whenever a person is unconscious for more than a minute or two, call 911 or your local emergency-response number for medical assistance (p. 63).

pamphlet_excerpts: Heart Attack: Cold- and Heat-Related Conditions and Injuries Cold- and Heat-Related Conditions and Injuries The human body works best if it has a constant temperature (p. 59).
Heart Attack Principle 2: A person who is exposed to cold environmental conditions and loses body heat faster than it can be generated will be in grave danger (p. 59).
Heart Attack Principle 3: The person's body temperature may become too low to support life (p. 59).
Heart Attack Principle 4: Likewise, a person whose body has overheated and cannot cool itself sufficiently may die if fast emergency medical care cannot be found (p. 59).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Heart Attack): These temperature related emergencies require fast, lifesaving first aid (p. 59).
Step 2 (Heart Attack): Hypothermia occurs when a person's body is losing more heat than it can generate (p. 59).
Step 3 (Heart Attack): It is a danger for anyone who is not dressed warmly enough, although exposure to cold is seldom the only cause (p. 59).
Step 4 (Heart Attack): Dehydration is a common contributing factor to hypothermia (p. 59).

pamphlet_excerpts: Muscle and Bone Injuries: A fall, a violent blow, a collision, a twisting injury, all can cause a fracture (a broken bone) or a dislocation (p. 45).
Muscle and Bone Injuries Principle 2: Open fractures can occur when the sharp bone ends penetrate the skin or when an object goes through the skin from the outside and breaks the bone (p. 45).
Muscle and Bone Injuries Principle 3: Most of the time a victim will have just one injury that isnot life threatening (p. 45).
Muscle and Bone Injuries Principle 4: After checking to rule out and treat the "hurry cases," do a quick, but complete, assessment of the entire body, paying special attention for signs (p. 45).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Muscle and Bone Injuries): Begin treatment only after determining the number and location of the injuries (p. 45).
Step 2 (Muscle and Bone Injuries): A "yes" answer suggests that the person might have a fracture (p. 45).
Step 3 (Muscle and Bone Injuries): Many people believe if they can move the part, the bone isnot broken (p. 45).
Step 4 (Muscle and Bone Injuries): Although they might be reluctant to doso, many people can voluntarily move a fractured part (p. 45).

pamphlet_excerpts: Head and Spine Injuries: Place the forearm in a sling with the hand raised higher than the elbow, then tie the upperarm against the side of the body with awide cravat bandage (p. 41).
Head and Spine Injuries Principle 2: Placing the splinted arm in a sling with the hand slightly raised will also immobilize the elbow joint (p. 41).
Head and Spine Injuries Principle 3: The backbone (spinal column) is made up of small bones called vertebrae that surround and protect the spinal cord (p. 41).
Head and Spine Injuries Principle 4: If avertebra is broken or dislocated, the spinal cord may be injured (p. 41).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Head and Spine Injuries): Fractures of the neck and back are extremely dangerous, because movement might further damage the spinal cord and cause permanent paralysis or even (p. 41).
Step 2 (Head and Spine Injuries): Whenever someone has fallen, been involved in an automobile accident, or suffered a blow to the head, assume there is an injury to the neck (p. 41).
Step 3 (Head and Spine Injuries): The victim may or may not be suffering from pain, paralysis, cuts and bruises, or swelling (p. 41).
Step 4 (Head and Spine Injuries): The injured area may be deformed or abnormally shaped, or there maybe no symptoms at all (p. 41).

pamphlet_excerpts: Moving a Patient: When a person must be moved for some distance or his or her injuries are serious, you should carry the person on a stretcher (p. 15).
Moving a Patient Principle 2: When available, use a litter or rescue basket made especially for transporting injured persons (p. 15).
Moving a Patient Principle 3: Make a stretcherout of two poles (longer than the victim is tall), for example, strong branches, tool handles, oars, orthe poles from a wall tent (p. 15).
Moving a Patient Principle 4: Secure two Scout shirts (insideout, with all the buttons buttoned) over the poles to form astretcher (p. 15).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Moving a Patient): If possible, overlap the bottoms of the shirts to form a more secure bedding (p. 15).
Step 2 (Moving a Patient): Explain the steps (procedures) in cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) (p. 15).
Step 3 (Moving a Patient): One way to stay healthy and safe both at home and when you are in the out-of-doors is to recognize that there is an element of risk in many activities (p. 15).
Step 4 (Moving a Patient): By being aware of risk and adjusting your behavior to manage it, you will also bein a stronger position to provide assistance (p. 15).

pamphlet_excerpts: Heat- and Cold-Related Conditions: Cold- and Heat-Related Conditions and Injuries Heatstroke Heatstroke, much more serious than heat exhaustion, can lead to death if not treated immediately (p. 59).
Heat- and Cold-Related Conditions Principle 2: Left untreated, heat exhaustion can develop into heatstroke (p. 59).
Heat- and Cold-Related Conditions Principle 3: In heatstroke, the body's cooling system begins to fail and the person's core temperature rises to life-threatening levels (above 105 degrees) (p. 59).
Heat- and Cold-Related Conditions Principle 4: One type of heatstroke develops in young, healthy people from dehydration and over exertion in hot weather, especially in high humidity (p. 59).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Heat- and Cold-Related Conditions): The first sign of true heat stroke is often collapse (p. 59).
Step 2 (Heat- and Cold-Related Conditions): On a hot day, if someone collapses without warning, you must consider heatstroke (p. 59).
Step 3 (Heat- and Cold-Related Conditions): The other type of heatstroke usually happens in elderly people when the weather is very hot, especially with high humidity (p. 59).
Step 4 (Heat- and Cold-Related Conditions): The signals are similar to exercise-related heatstroke except that the skin is hot and dry because there is no sweating (p. 59).

pamphlet_excerpts: Mental Health Conditions: How to Handle an Emergency How to Handle an Emergency Even the best plans can fall apart (p. 17).
Mental Health Conditions Principle 2: Most of the time first aid is relatively simple because you are dealing with a single injury or illness (p. 17).
Mental Health Conditions Principle 3: You must, however, be prepared to handle more complex situations (p. 17).
Mental Health Conditions Principle 4: You might be the first to arrive or the most qualified, thus the person who is most able to take charge (p. 17).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Mental Health Conditions): Good Samaritan laws protect anyone making a good-faith effort to help the victim of an injury or illness (p. 17).
Step 2 (Mental Health Conditions): Whenever you are confronted with a first-aidemergency, use your skills to the best of your ability and training (p. 17).
Step 3 (Mental Health Conditions): No one expects you to have the knowledge of a physician (p. 17).
Step 4 (Mental Health Conditions): However, Scouting's history is filled with stories of Scouts who used their training to help others, sometimes even saving lives. 1 (p. 17).

pamphlet_excerpts: Miscellaneous Conditions: Cold- and Heat-Related Conditions and Injuries Heatstroke Heatstroke, much more serious than heat exhaustion, can lead to death if not treated immediately (p. 63).
Miscellaneous Conditions Principle 2: Left untreated, heat exhaustion can develop into heatstroke (p. 63).
Miscellaneous Conditions Principle 3: In heatstroke, the body's cooling system begins to fail and the person's core temperature rises to life-threatening levels (above 105 degrees) (p. 63).
Miscellaneous Conditions Principle 4: One type of heatstroke develops in young, healthy people from dehydration and over exertion in hot weather, especially in high humidity (p. 63).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Miscellaneous Conditions): The first sign of true heat stroke is often collapse (p. 63).
Step 2 (Miscellaneous Conditions): On a hot day, if someone collapses without warning, you must consider heatstroke (p. 63).
Step 3 (Miscellaneous Conditions): The other type of heatstroke usually happens in elderly people when the weather is very hot, especially with high humidity (p. 63).
Step 4 (Miscellaneous Conditions): The signals are similar to exercise-related heatstroke except that the skin is hot and dry because there is no sweating (p. 63).

pamphlet_excerpts: Teach a first-aid skill or topic: Moving an Ill or Injured Person The decision to move an accident victim should be made carefully (p. 29).

Teach a first-aid skill or topic Principle 2: In many cases, there will be emergency medical crews, fire department personnel, or others with special equipment and training who will transport (p. 29).

Teach a first-aid skill or topic Principle 3: If, however, someone is in danger from fire, smoke, water, electrical hazards, poisonous gases, exposure, or other immediate danger, you must move (p. 29).
Teach a first-aid skill or topic Principle 4: You might also need to move an injured person in order to give that person proper care, or reach another victim (p. 29).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Teach a first-aid skill or topic): Move the person only as far as is necessary, and do not endanger yourself (p. 29).
Step 2 (Teach a first-aid skill or topic): Sometimes you will find that a victim's injuries are minor enough that the person can move with some assistance (p. 29).
Step 3 (Teach a first-aid skill or topic): Before attempting to move someone, make sure the person is not suffering from any of the following conditions (p. 29).
Step 4 (Teach a first-aid skill or topic): When time is critical, you might need to decide between moving the person to a place where they can get care or waiting for help to come (p. 29).
