requirements.lead_text: Do ONE of the following:
requirements.req_text: Do ONE of the following: (a) Visit an emergency medical station house or training center in person. From the medical first responders that you meet during your visit, learn about how they serve their community and about their careers. Discuss with your counselor what you learned during your tour and interviews. (b) Interview an emergency medical services professional about their work. Learn about how they chose this career and about their duties. Discuss what you learned with your counselor and whether you might be interested in this career. (c) Identify three career opportunities that would use skills and knowledge in emergency medical services. Pick one and research the training, education, certification requirements, experience, and expenses associated with entering the field. Research the prospects for employment, starting salary, advancement opportunities, and career goals associated with this career. Discuss what you learned with your counselor and whether you might be interested in this career. (d) Identify how you might use the skills and knowledge in the field of emergency medical services to pursue a personal hobby and/or healthy lifestyle. Research the additional training required, expenses, and affiliation with organizations that would help you maximize the enjoyment and benefit you might gain from it. Discuss what you learned with your counselor and share what short-term and long-term goals you might have if you pursued this.

pamphlet_excerpts: First Aid Careers and Pathways: Visit an emergency medical station house: Moving an Ill or Injured Person The decision to move an accident victim should be made carefully (p. 25).

First Aid Careers and Pathways Principle 2: Visit an emergency medical station house Principle 2: In many cases, there will be emergency medical crews, fire department personnel, or others with special equipment and training who will transport (p. 25).

First Aid Careers and Pathways Principle 3: Visit an emergency medical station house Principle 3: If, however, someone is in danger from fire, smoke, water, electrical hazards, poisonous gases, exposure, or other immediate danger, you must move (p. 25).

First Aid Careers and Pathways Principle 4: Visit an emergency medical station house Principle 4: You might also need to move an injured person in order to give that person proper care, or reach another victim (p. 25).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (First Aid Careers and Pathways): Step 1 (Visit an emergency medical station house): Move the person only as far as is necessary, and do not endanger yourself (p. 25).

Step 2 (First Aid Careers and Pathways): Step 2 (Visit an emergency medical station house): Sometimes you will find that a victim's injuries are minor enough that the person can move with some assistance (p. 25).

Step 3 (First Aid Careers and Pathways): Step 3 (Visit an emergency medical station house): Before attempting to move someone, make sure the person is not suffering from any of the following conditions (p. 25).

Step 4 (First Aid Careers and Pathways): Step 4 (Visit an emergency medical station house): When time is critical, you might need to decide between moving the person to a place where they can get care or waiting for help to come (p. 25).

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: In Fish and Wildlife Management Requirement 1, what does 'carrying capacity' mean for a wildlife habitat, and how do regulated hunting and fishing seasons support conservation?
quiz_item.question: In Fish and Wildlife Management Requirement 1, what does 'carrying capacity' mean for a wildlife habitat, and how do regulated hunting and fishing seasons support conservation?
options: A. Carrying capacity is the maximum weight of fish a single angler can carry in a creel, and wildlife agencies ban all habitat restoration.

B. Carrying capacity is the maximum population of a given species that a habitat's food, water, cover, and space can sustainably support year-round without degrading the ecosystem; science-based harvest limits and excise taxes on sporting gear (Pittman-Robertson and Dingell-Johnson Acts) fund habitat conservation and prevent overpopulation starvation.
C. Carrying capacity measures the number of paved roads inside a national park, and wildlife management relies on introducing invasive species to replace native predators.
D. Carrying capacity never changes between summer and winter, so removing all predators permanently guarantees unlimited herd health.
choices: A. Carrying capacity is the maximum weight of fish a single angler can carry in a creel, and wildlife agencies ban all habitat restoration.

B. Carrying capacity is the maximum population of a given species that a habitat's food, water, cover, and space can sustainably support year-round without degrading the ecosystem; science-based harvest limits and excise taxes on sporting gear (Pittman-Robertson and Dingell-Johnson Acts) fund habitat conservation and prevent overpopulation starvation.

Carrying capacity is the maximum population of a given species that a habitat's food, water, cover, and space can sustainably support year-round without degrading the ecosystem; science-based harvest limits and excise taxes on sporting gear (Pittman-Robertson and Dingell-Johnson Acts) fund habitat conservation and prevent overpopulation starvation.

requirements.lead_text: Do ONE of the following:
requirements.req_text: Do ONE of the following: (a) Observe and record 25 species of wildlife. Your list may include mammals, birds, reptiles, amphibians, and fish. Write down when and where each animal was seen. (b) List the wildlife species in your state that are classified as endangered, threatened, exotic, non-native, game species, furbearers, or migratory game birds. Discuss with your counselor management practices in place or being developed for at least three of these species. (c) Start a scrapbook of North American fish and wildlife. Insert markers to divide the book into separate parts for mammals, birds, reptiles, amphibians, and fish. Collect articles on such subjects as life histories, habitat, behavior, and feeding habits on all of the five categories and place them in your notebook accordingly. Articles and pictures may be taken from newspapers or science, nature, and outdoor magazines, or from other sources including the internet (with your parent or guardian's permission). Enter at least five articles on mammals, five on birds, five on reptiles, five on amphibians, and five on fish. Put each animal on a separate sheet in alphabetical order. Include pictures whenever possible.

requirements.lead_text: Do ONE of the following:
requirements.req_text: Do ONE of the following: (a) Determine the age of five species of fish from scale samples or identify various age classes of one species in a lake and report the results. (b) Conduct a creel census on a small lake to estimate catch per unit effort and report the results to your counselor. (c) Examine the stomach contents of three fish and record the findings. It is not necessary to catch any fish for this option. (d) Make a freshwater aquarium. Include at least four species of native plants and four species of animal life, such as whirligig beetles, freshwater shrimp, tadpoles, water snails, and golden shiners. After 60 days of observation, discuss with your counselor the life cycles, food chains, and management needs you have recognized. Before completing this requirement, check local laws on releasing these organisms back into the wild, and follow your counselor's direction in disposing of these organisms humanely and safely.

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: In Fish and Wildlife Management Requirement 1, what does 'carrying capacity' mean for a wildlife habitat, and how do regulated hunting and fishing seasons support conservation?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: In Fish and Wildlife Management Requirement 1, what does 'carrying capacity' mean for a wildlife habitat, and how do regulated hunting and fishing seasons support conservation?
options: A. Carrying capacity is the maximum weight of fish a single angler can carry in a creel, and wildlife agencies ban all habitat restoration.

B. Carrying capacity is the maximum population of a given species that a habitat's food, water, cover, and space can sustainably support year-round without degrading the ecosystem; science-based harvest limits and excise taxes on sporting gear (Pittman-Robertson and Dingell-Johnson Acts) fund habitat conservation and prevent overpopulation starvation.
C. Carrying capacity measures the number of paved roads inside a national park, and wildlife management relies on introducing invasive species to replace native predators.
D. Carrying capacity never changes between summer and winter, so removing all predators permanently guarantees unlimited herd health.

requirements.lead_text: Do the following:
requirements.req_text: Do the following: (a) Explain to your counselor the most likely hazards you may encounter while participating in fishing activities, and what you should do to anticipate, help prevent, mitigate, and respond to these hazards. (b) Discuss the prevention of and treatment for the following health concerns that could occur while fishing: cuts and scratches, puncture wounds, insect bites, hypothermia, dehydration, heat exhaustion, heatstroke, and sunburn. (c) Explain how to remove a barbed hook that is lodged in someone's arm. (d) Name and explain five safety practices you should always follow while fishing.

pamphlet_excerpts: Hazards, First Aid & Safety: If you or someone in your group shows signs of a heat reaction, get to acool, shady place (p. 15).
Hazards, First Aid & Safety Principle 2: Have the person lie down with the feet, head, and shoulders slightly raised, and remove excess clothing (p. 15).

Hazards, First Aid & Safety Principle 3: Cool the victim any way you can (cover the person with cool, wet towels, or sponge the person with cool water; fan the person; place the victim in a stream) (p. 15).
Hazards, First Aid & Safety Principle 4: If you do not see a rapid recovery, seek medical attention right away (p. 15).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Hazards, First Aid & Safety): Most sunburns are first-degree burns, but prolonged exposure to the sun can cause blistering, a second-degree burn (p. 15).
Step 2 (Hazards, First Aid & Safety): Sunburn is easy to prevent by applying plenty of sunscreen and clothing with a sun protection factor (SPF) rating of at least 30 (p. 15).
Step 3 (Hazards, First Aid & Safety): Reapply if you are sweating and after you have been in water (p. 15).
Step 4 (Hazards, First Aid & Safety): A broad-brimmed hat, long-sleeved shirt, and long pants provide even more protection (p. 15).

quiz_item.question: While fishing from a dock for Fishing Requirement 1, a barbless hook embeds past the bend into a companion's forearm (nowhere near the eye or major arteries), or a barbed hook catches in the skin. What safe practices prevent and treat hook injuries?
options: A. Cast sidearm in a crowded group without looking behind you, and yank a deeply embedded treble hook straight backward with rusty pliers.
B. Hold fish hooks between your lips while tying knots, and treat a hook near the eye by pushing it deeper with a pocketknife.

C. Always check overhead and behind you for clearance before casting, wear eye protection and a PFD near water, crimp barbs flat for easier removal, and remove a simple surface hook using the string-yank or push-through-and-clip-the-barb method (seeking medical care for deep, facial, or eye hooks).
D. Wipe pond mud into the puncture wound after pulling the hook out and skip washing the skin with soap and clean water.

pamphlet_excerpts: Differences Between Two Types: Used in swimming, particularly when a fish needs aquick thrust of speed (p. 20).
Differences Between Two Types Principle 2: Most fish have monocularvision, each eye sees separately, offering a wide field of view (p. 20).
Differences Between Two Types Principle 3: They may be equipped with teeth so that a fish can grip its prey while feeding (p. 20).
Differences Between Two Types Principle 4: Transparent protective plates growing from the skin that can be replaced if lost (p. 20).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Differences Between Two Types): The forward fin, supported by sharp spines, is used for balance (p. 20).
Step 2 (Differences Between Two Types): The spines also protect the fish from its predators (p. 20).
Step 3 (Differences Between Two Types): Tackle catalogs list rods and reels by weight and function, allowing the angler to make informed choices (p. 20).
Step 4 (Differences Between Two Types): Afixed-line pole does not have a reel, and therefore is called a "pole" instead of a "rod." Cane poles are usually made from dried bamboo (p. 20).

pamphlet_excerpts: Proper Use of Two Different: Varieties of lines of different weights, diameters, and construction are available, made for different types of fishing, fly-fishing, spin-fishing (p. 54).

Proper Use of Two Principle 2: Proper Use of Two Different Principle 2: Mono filament lines come labeled as nylon, which floats, and fluorocarbon, which sinks. allowing for different delivery of lures and baits (p. 54).

Step 3 (Essential Fishing Knots and Rigging): Double the line to make a 3- to 4-inch loop, then pass the end of the loop through the hook eye (p. 56).
Step 4 (Essential Fishing Knots and Rigging): Hold the standing part between thumb and forefinger and tie a loose overhand knot in the double line with the other hand (p. 56).

Step 3 (Catching, Identifying, and Releasing Fish): Most fish reproduce by the female laying eggs that the male fertilizes in the water (p. 9).
Step 4 (Catching, Identifying, and Releasing Fish): The females of some species might lay many thousands of eggs, while some other species lay only a fewhundred (p. 9).

pamphlet_excerpts: If regulations and health concerns permit: Keep in mind that not all fish should be filleted (p. 79).
If regulations and health concerns permit Principle 2: Removing the meat of some fish from the bones and skin makes it easier to cook and to eat (p. 79).
If regulations and health concerns permit Principle 3: Step 1, Lay the fish on its side and make a cut just behind the gills down to the backbone (p. 79).

If regulations and health concerns permit Principle 4: Step 2, Start at the cut made in step 1 and run the point of the knife alongside the backbone, down to where it starts to click along the tops of the ribs (p. 79).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (If regulations and health concerns permit): Cut alongside the ribs, working back toward the tail until the entire side of the fish is free from the ribs and backbone, but leave it attached (p. 79).
Step 2 (If regulations and health concerns permit): Step 3, Lay the side flat and hook a forefinger under the skin near the tail (p. 79).
Step 3 (If regulations and health concerns permit): Run the knife into the meat next to the skin and hold the blade against the inside of the skin at an angle of about 45 degrees (p. 79).
Step 4 (If regulations and health concerns permit): Holding the blade steady, gently lift the forefinger holding the skin and pull (p. 79).

options: A. Cast sidearm in a crowded group without looking behind you, and yank a deeply embedded treble hook straight backward with rusty pliers.
B. Hold fish hooks between your lips while tying knots, and treat a hook near the eye by pushing it deeper with a pocketknife.

D. Wipe pond mud into the puncture wound after pulling the hook out and skip washing the skin with soap and clean water.

pamphlet_excerpts: Hazards, First Aid & Safety: Even a gentle sport like fly-fishing can come with its perils (p. 77).
Hazards, First Aid & Safety Principle 2: Agood angler will be well-versed in first-aid for cuts, scratches, puncture wounds, and insect bites and stings (p. 77).
Hazards, First Aid & Safety Principle 3: Cuts and scratches are wounds, openings in the skin and tissues that can allow germs to enter the body and cause infection (p. 77).
Hazards, First Aid & Safety Principle 4: Wash minor scratches and cuts with soap and water (p. 77).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Hazards, First Aid & Safety): On camping trips, clean and rebandage small wounds daily (p. 77).
Step 2 (Hazards, First Aid & Safety): Larger cuts should be treated with direct pressure to stop bleeding, then cleaned as well as possible to limit infection (p. 77).
Step 3 (Hazards, First Aid & Safety): Cover an open wound with a sterile gauze pad or clean cloth that has been folded to make a pad (p. 77).
Step 4 (Hazards, First Aid & Safety): Hold the pad in position with tape, a cravat bandage, or other binder (p. 77).

quiz_item.question: Why does Fly-Fishing Requirement 1 emphasize wearing polarized eye protection, pinching down hook barbs, and fastening a snug wading belt over chest waders in moving water?
options: A. Polarized glasses shield the eyes from high-speed flies blown off-course by wind while cutting surface glare, barbless hooks reduce injury to both anglers and released fish, and a snug wading belt prevents chest waders from rapidly filling with heavy water if you slip in the current.
B. Wading belts are worn around the ankles to weigh your boots down in deep river channels, and polarized glasses allow you to see in total darkness at midnight.
C. Chest waders without a belt act as a life jacket that floats you upright if they fill with forty gallons of cold river water.
D. Fly-fishers cast lead sinkers weighing four ounces that require welding goggles to block ultraviolet sparks from the graphite rod.

pamphlet_excerpts: Match A Fly Rod Line: Lines vary by weight, and must be matched to the rod (p. 13).
Match A Fly Rod Line Principle 2: They come in different styles (called tapers) and colors and are designed either to float on the surface of the water or to sink to different depths (p. 13).
Match A Fly Rod Line Principle 3: Intermediate lines, for example, sink very slowly and can be fished just below the surface (p. 13).
Match A Fly Rod Line Principle 4: Heavily weighted lines sink quite rapidly and are designed to get down deep very quickly (p. 13).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Match A Fly Rod Line): Most fly-fishing is done with floating lines, which are the easiest to cast and control (p. 13).
Step 2 (Match A Fly Rod Line): But there are times and conditions when fish lie deeply in the water and are not feeding at or near the surface (p. 13).
Step 3 (Match A Fly Rod Line): A sinking line is then useful to get the fly down to them (p. 13).
Step 4 (Match A Fly Rod Line): Sinking lines usually come in drab, darker colors so that the fish cannot spot them (p. 13).

requirements.req_text: Demonstrate how to tie proper knots to prepare a fly rod for fishing: (a) Tie backing to the arbor of a fly reel spool using an arbor knot. Step 4 (Tie Proper Knots to Prepare): Attach the backing to the reel spool with an arbor knot (p. 24).

pamphlet_excerpts: Essential Fly-Fishing Knots and Leaders: Use these flies to catch trout, bass andpanfish on the water's surface (p. 38).
Essential Fly-Fishing Knots and Leaders Principle 2: Traditional trout flies that float are called dry flies (p. 38).
Essential Fly-Fishing Knots and Leaders Principle 3: They are designed to imitate the adult forms of mayflies, caddis flies, and other insects that trout and other fish feed (p. 38).
Essential Fly-Fishing Knots and Leaders Principle 4: Anglers use dry flies to catch fish that are feeding on surface-hatching insects (p. 38).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Essential Fly-Fishing Knots and Leaders): The dry flies are tied in patterns to look like the specific species of insect (p. 38).
Step 2 (Essential Fly-Fishing Knots and Leaders): This is called matching the hatch, and itis one of the most important principles in fishing (p. 38).
Step 3 (Essential Fly-Fishing Knots and Leaders): If you seefish feeding on a specific insect then you should use a fly that closely imitates this food source (p. 38).
Step 4 (Essential Fly-Fishing Knots and Leaders): In addition to shape, color and movement, the size of the fly is also important when matching the hatch (p. 38).

pamphlet_excerpts: Ability to Cast A Fly: A large plastic hoop (such as a hula hoop) makes an excellent target for practicing casting (p. 33).
Ability to Cast A Fly Principle 2: Make sure your thumb is on top of the rod's cork grip and that you have a firm hold (p. 33).
Ability to Cast A Fly Principle 3: Now, strip out 20 to 30 feet of line from the reel (p. 33).
Ability to Cast A Fly Principle 4: You might want to make a mark 30 feet from the line tip, using a waterproof marker (p. 33).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Ability to Cast A Fly): With that length of line in front of you, more or less in a straight line, start with the rod tip down near the ground orthe surface of the water (p. 33).
Step 2 (Ability to Cast A Fly): Smoothly accelerate the rod through the vertical, or 12 o'clock, position and then stop it abruptly (p. 33).
Step 3 (Ability to Cast A Fly): This loads the rod like a spring and then vigorously launches the fly line up and behind (p. 33).
Step 4 (Ability to Cast A Fly): The line will soar up and behind you in a loop that will quickly straighten (p. 33).

pamphlet_excerpts: Go to a suitable fishing location: Fly fishermen fish for many species of saltwater fish (p. 62).

Go to a suitable fishing location Principle 2: Because saltwater fish are usually much larger than their freshwater cousins, anglers casting for them require specially designed rods and lines (p. 62).

Go to a suitable fishing location Principle 3: Some of the species can be taken on a regular flyrod, but extra care must be taken to clean, rinse, and lubricate the equipment to reduce the corrosive (p. 62).
Go to a suitable fishing location Principle 4: Three species of fish that live in the shallow, subtropical waters of Florida are among the finest fly-fishing trophies (p. 62).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Go to a suitable fishing location): Tarpon are the largest of the three and can reach weights of more than 150 pounds (p. 62).
Step 2 (Go to a suitable fishing location): They are spectacular jumpers and are sometimes called "silver kings." Bone fish seldom grow to more than 10 pounds (p. 62).
Step 3 (Go to a suitable fishing location): The permit is found on some of the same flats where anglers look for tarpon and bone fish (p. 62).
Step 4 (Go to a suitable fishing location): Many expert anglers have never caught a permit and would consider their first the fish of a lifetime (p. 62).

pamphlet_excerpts: Leave No Trace & Outdoor Ethics: Principle and the Outdoor Code for your specific activity or destination (p. 88).
Leave No Trace & Outdoor Ethics Principle 2: Check with Local Land managers: Check with local land managers to be sure you are using the proper techniques (p. 88).
Leave No Trace & Outdoor Ethics Principle 3: Whether you fish for a few hours, an entire day, or plan to camp and fish, it is important to minimize your impact on the land (p. 88).
Leave No Trace & Outdoor Ethics Principle 4: In high-use areas, concentrate your activity where vegetation is already absent (p. 88).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Leave No Trace & Outdoor Ethics): Use wading gear to reduce stream and lake side impact (p. 88).
Step 2 (Leave No Trace & Outdoor Ethics): Use existing trails and select designated or existing fishing areas (p. 88).
Step 3 (Leave No Trace & Outdoor Ethics): In more remote, less-traveled areas, avoid creating newt rails that cause erosion, and avoid places where impacts are just beginning to show (p. 88).
Step 4 (Leave No Trace & Outdoor Ethics): If camping overnight, always camp at least 200 feet from shorelines (p. 88).

intro_notes: NOTE: Scouts must remember to follow the Leave No Trace Seven Principles and the Outdoor Code while on field trips and when collecting specimens. Make sure you have permission of the land manager prior to taking any samples for your collection. Collecting is prohibited in most National and State Parks. Pictures or sketches may suffice for a collection and limit impacted disturbances. NOTE: The official merit badge pamphlets are now free and downloadable HERE or can be purchased at the Scout Shop.

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: When preparing a field notebook of local trees for Forestry Requirement 1, which combination of botanical characteristics allows you to accurately identify a tree species in the field?
quiz_item.question: When preparing a field notebook of local trees for Forestry Requirement 1, which combination of botanical characteristics allows you to accurately identify a tree species in the field?
options: A. Counting the number of birds perched in the upper branches and measuring the shadow length at noon.
B. Tasting unknown berries and chewing raw inner bark from every tree along the trail.
C. Measuring only the total height of the trunk without examining the leaves, twigs, buds, or fruit.

D. Examining whether branching and leaf arrangement are opposite (such as maple, ash, dogwood) or alternate (such as oak, birch, hickory), whether leaves are simple or compound with lobed or toothed margins, along with bark texture, winter buds, and seeds/cones.
choices: A. Counting the number of birds perched in the upper branches and measuring the shadow length at noon.
B. Tasting unknown berries and chewing raw inner bark from every tree along the trail.
C. Measuring only the total height of the trunk without examining the leaves, twigs, buds, or fruit.

D. Examining whether branching and leaf arrangement are opposite (such as maple, ash, dogwood) or alternate (such as oak, birch, hickory), whether leaves are simple or compound with lobed or toothed margins, along with bark texture, winter buds, and seeds/cones.
quiz_item.correct_answer: D. Examining whether branching and leaf arrangement are opposite (such as maple, ash, dogwood) or alternate (such as oak, birch, hickory), whether leaves are simple or compound with lobed or toothed margins, along with bark texture, winter buds, and seeds/cones.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (D): Dendrology (tree identification) relies on systematic keys comparing opposite vs. alternate twig arrangement, simple vs. compound leaf structure, leaf margins, bark patterns, buds, and reproductive structures (acorns, samaras, or cones).

pamphlet_excerpts: Collect and identify wood samples: Whatever its origins, damage from certain insects, diseases, fires, and invasive species often can be reduced if the forest is healthy (p. 28).
Collect and identify wood samples Principle 2: Pieces of wood are valuable in identifying and understanding the trees from which they came (p. 28).

Collect and identify wood samples Principle 3: Appearance, color, grain, texture, weight, general feel, and sometimes even the aroma of a wood all are clues to its growing patterns, strengths (p. 28).
Collect and identify wood samples Principle 4: Each year during the spring and summer, most trees increase their diameter by adding two new layers of wood (p. 28).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Collect and identify wood samples): The layer formed by the cambium in the spring grows quickly (p. 28).
Step 2 (Collect and identify wood samples): Because the cells are large, this spring wood looks light in color (p. 28).
Step 3 (Collect and identify wood samples): Because the cells are smaller, this summer wood appears darker (p. 28).
Step 4 (Collect and identify wood samples): When a tree is cut or a core sample taken, the light and dark layers show as alternating rings of light and dark wood (p. 28).

pamphlet_excerpts: Contributions forests: Forests are among Earth's great filters for cleansing the atmosphere and replenishing it with oxygen (p. 45).
Contributions forests Principle 2: Carbon dioxide is also produced when plants and animals decay and when wood, coal, gasoline, and other carbon-based materials burn (p. 45).
Contributions forests Principle 3: Plants must absorb carbon dioxide in order to survive (p. 45).
Contributions forests Principle 4: In achemical reaction charged with sunlight, chlorophyll allows plants to combine water with carbon dioxide to produce the simple sugars plants use (p. 45).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Contributions forests): The process is called photosynthesis, making something with the aid of light (p. 45).
Step 2 (Contributions forests): A by-product of photosynthesis is the oxygen animals need for survival (p. 45).
Step 3 (Contributions forests): Plants absorbing carbon dioxide can store it, a process called sequestration, and slow its return to the atmosphere (p. 45).
Step 4 (Contributions forests): Carbon is stored in a tree's trunk and roots, and in the soil of a forest (p. 45).

pamphlet_excerpts: Forest management means: The main treatments making up silvicultural systems involve the felling of trees and the regeneration of a new forest for the future (p. 55).
Forest management means Principle 2: Systems that result in trees of approximately the same age are called even-aged systems (p. 55).
Forest management means Principle 3: Systems that result in trees of many ages are termed uneven-aged systems (p. 55).
Forest management means Principle 4: Each system includes steps to establish seedlings and actions to encourage the health and productivity of a developing stand (p. 55).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Forest management means): Some tree species grow best in an even-aged forest, while others grow best in uneven-aged stands (p. 55).
Step 2 (Forest management means): Clear-cutting is the harvesting of all trees in an area except those that are necessary to maintain water quality, fish habitat (p. 55).
Step 3 (Forest management means): The clear-cut can then be regenerated by broadcasting seeds, from sprouts, or by planting seedlings (p. 55).
Step 4 (Forest management means): The new trees will have equal access to sunlight (p. 55).

requirements.lead_text: With your parent or guardian's and counselor's approval, do ONE of the following:
requirements.req_text: With your parent or guardian's and counselor's approval, do ONE of the following: (a) Visit a managed public or private forest area with the manager or a forester who is familiar with it. Write a brief report describing the type of forest, the management objectives, and the forestry techniques used to achieve the objectives. (b) With a knowledgeable individual, visit a current or past logging operation or wood-using manufacturing plant. Write a brief report describing the following: (1) The species and size of trees harvested or used (2) The origin of the forest or stands of trees utilized (e. g., planted or natural) (3) The forest's successional stage, its future, and, if it is a past logging operation, the regeneration that is occurring, whether planted or natural (4) Where the trees are coming from (land ownership) or where they are going (type of mill or processing plant) (5) The products that are made from the trees (6) How the products are made and used (7) How waste materials from the logging operation or manufacturing plant are or were disposed of or utilized (c) Take part in a forest-fire prevention campaign in cooperation with your local fire warden, state wildfire agency, forester, or counselor. Write a brief report describing the campaign, how it will help prevent wildfires, and your part in it.

pamphlet_excerpts: Managed Public or Private Forest: Do ONE of The Following: Your merit badge counselor and parents can help you arrange a visit to a managed forest, a logging operation, or a manufacturing plant that uses wood (p. 71).
Managed Public or Private Forest Principle 2: Do ONE of The Following Principle 2: You can see for yourself how the work of forestry is carried (p. 71).

Managed Public or Private Forest Principle 3: Do ONE of The Following Principle 3: You also will have opportunities to visit with forestry professionals and learn more about their backgrounds, training, and responsibilities (p. 71).
Managed Public or Private Forest Principle 4: Do ONE of The Following Principle 4: Plan the trip well in advance so that the forestry professionals will have time to prepare for your visit (p. 71).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Managed Public or Private Forest): Step 1 (Do ONE of The Following): Get permission in advance if you want to take photographs during your visit (p. 71).

Step 2 (Managed Public or Private Forest): Step 2 (Do ONE of The Following): Do some research on the forest, logging operation, or manufacturing plant you plan to visit, and think about some of the questions you want answered (p. 71).

Step 3 (Managed Public or Private Forest): Step 3 (Do ONE of The Following): In a managed forest, for example, you can find out about the management objectives and the forestry techniques used to achieve those objectives (p. 71).

Step 4 (Managed Public or Private Forest): Step 4 (Do ONE of The Following): You might also research or ask about the species of trees grown, the silvicultural system used, or whether replanting is done with seedlings or seeds (p. 71).

pamphlet_excerpts: Consequences to forests that result: Whatever its origins, damage from certain insects, diseases, fires, and invasive species often can be reduced if the forest is healthy (p. 36).
Consequences to forests that result Principle 2: To lessen the danger of devastating fires, foresters might intentionally set fire to an area (p. 36).

Consequences to forests that result Principle 3: This prescribed burning is carefully planned, and the fire is set according to a prescription written for the conditions that exist and the objectives (p. 36).
Consequences to forests that result Principle 4: The fire exposes the soil, releases nutrients into the soil, eliminates some insects and diseases, and removes undesirable trees or brush (p. 36).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Consequences to forests that result): Wildfires are uncontrolled fires, and they can be avoided or made less severe by prescribed burning (p. 36).
Step 2 (Consequences to forests that result): The easiest fire to fight is the one that does not start (p. 36).
Step 3 (Consequences to forests that result): The Leave No Trace principle of minimizing the impact of campfires also isan important guideline for preventing fires that would pose athreat (p. 36).
Step 4 (Consequences to forests that result): In addition to following the Leave No Trace principles, use care in burning anything (p. 36).

pamphlet_excerpts: Careers & Professional Pathways: Your merit badge counselor and parents can help you arrange a visit to a managed forest, a logging operation, or a manufacturing plant that uses wood (p. 75).
Careers & Professional Pathways Principle 2: You can see for yourself how the work of forestry is carried (p. 75).
Careers & Professional Pathways Principle 3: You also will have opportunities to visit with forestry professionals and learn more about their backgrounds, training, and responsibilities (p. 75).
Careers & Professional Pathways Principle 4: Plan the trip well in advance so that the forestry professionals will have time to prepare for your visit (p. 75).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Careers & Professional Pathways): Get permission in advance if you want to take photographs during your visit (p. 75).
Step 2 (Careers & Professional Pathways): Do some research on the forest, logging operation, or manufacturing plant you plan to visit, and think about some of the questions you want answered (p. 75).
Step 3 (Careers & Professional Pathways): In a managed forest, for example, you can find out about the management objectives and the forestry techniques used to achieve those objectives (p. 75).

Step 4 (Careers & Professional Pathways): You might also research or ask about the species of trees grown, the silvicultural system used, or whether replanting is done with seedlings or seeds (p. 75).

B. Tasting unknown berries and chewing raw inner bark from every tree along the trail.

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: In Game Design Requirement 1, how do a game's core mechanics, theme, medium, and victory conditions work together, and why do designers distinguish between games of emergence and games of progression?
quiz_item.question: In Game Design Requirement 1, how do a game's core mechanics, theme, medium, and victory conditions work together, and why do designers distinguish between games of emergence and games of progression?
options: A. Core mechanics refer exclusively to the cardboard box artwork, while victory conditions are kept secret from players until the game is over.

B. Core mechanics are the rules and actions players repeat to pursue the victory condition within the game's medium and theme; games of emergence use a small set of rules that combine into vast strategic possibilities (like chess), whereas games of progression guide players through a pre-designed sequence of levels or story stages.
C. Games of emergence have no rules at all, whereas games of progression never allow a player to make choices.
D. Game balance means ensuring that the player who goes first automatically wins every match regardless of skill.

Step 3 (Terms for Game Analysis): Board games or card games may include a second, simpler set of rules for new players (p. 49).
Step 4 (Terms for Game Analysis): Balance is a description of the relative strength of different resources, mechanics, objectives, or starting states (p. 49).

Record in your game design notebook whether or not your change had the expected effect. (c) Repeat 6(b) at least two more times and record the results in your game design notebook.

pamphlet_excerpts: Blind test your game: In addition to tracking game actions, watch body language to help you understand the players' emotional state during the test (p. 82).
Blind test your game Principle 2: Blind testers should be similar to the people you imagine will be playing your game when it is finished (p. 82).
Blind test your game Principle 3: Consider asking other Scouts or Scout leaders to test your game during a troop meeting or campout (p. 82).
Blind test your game Principle 4: Otherwise, a family member and classmates or friends could be testers (p. 82).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Blind test your game): Begin a play testing session by handing the testers any rules or instruction sheets that you have written to go with the prototype components (p. 82).
Step 2 (Blind test your game): Do not give them extra instructions on how the game is played, but you can provide questions for them to think about while they play (p. 82).
Step 3 (Blind test your game): During the play test, if the players get confused by the rules or stuck, they should make up whatever rules they need for play to continue (p. 82).
Step 4 (Blind test your game): This is what would happen if someone bought a new board or card game and the rules were confusing or incomplete (p. 82).

pamphlet_excerpts: Careers and Professional Pathways: Work within the game industry is not a career everyone can pursue no matter how hard they try, but that does not mean game design cannot be incorporated (p. 23).
Careers and Professional Pathways Principle 2: Comingup with a fun, exciting, and balanced ruleset is a good skill to have in almost any career (p. 23).
Careers and Professional Pathways Principle 3: Teachers can employ game elements in the classroom to make learning a more engaging, participatory experience (p. 23).
Careers and Professional Pathways Principle 4: You can also use the psychology of rewarding tasks to get yourself to do things you would not normally want (p. 23).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Careers and Professional Pathways): If you have a game that you want to pitch to a publisher, remember these tips. Show your best, most finished, and most ofall fun game (p. 23).
Step 2 (Careers and Professional Pathways): Make sure that the testers are having a blast when they play your game (p. 23).
Step 3 (Careers and Professional Pathways): Be prepared to hand over all the game design documentation. Nondisclosure Agreements (NDAs) protect you and your game idea (p. 23).
Step 4 (Careers and Professional Pathways): It is good practice to get anyone who is looking at your game to sign an NDA (p. 23).

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: While preparing soil beds and applying fertilizers or pest controls for Gardening Requirement 1, which health and safety practices are essential?
quiz_item.question: While preparing soil beds and applying fertilizers or pest controls for Gardening Requirement 1, which health and safety practices are essential?
options: A. Leave metal garden rakes and hoes lying face-up in tall grass with the sharp tines pointing skyward so you can spot them easily.
B. Lift heavy bags of compost by bending straight over at the waist with locked knees and twisting your spine.

C. Wear work gloves, sturdy closed-toe shoes, sun protection, and updated tetanus immunization; lift heavy loads with your legs while keeping your back straight; store rakes and hoes with tines turned down or hung on racks; and strictly follow all product label directions and PPE rules when handling fertilizers or pesticides.
D. Mix double the recommended concentration of garden pesticide in an unlabeled drinking cup and spray it upwind on a gusty afternoon.

Step 3 (Honeybees Are Used in Pollinating): First, they practice what biologists call flower fidelity (p. 59).
Step 4 (Honeybees Are Used in Pollinating): That is, on a foraging trip they visit only one kind of flower so that when they transfer pollen it is to a flower that can use (p. 59).

requirements.lead_text: Do ONE of the following and record weekly observations. Discuss the results of your project with your counselor.
requirements.req_text: Do ONE of the following and record weekly observations. Discuss the results of your project with your counselor. (a) Build a compost bin and maintain it for 90 days. (b) Build a vermicompost bin (worm compost bin) and maintain it for 90 days. (c) Build a hydroponic garden containing three vegetables or herbs, or three ornamental plants. Maintain this garden through harvest or flowering, or for 90 days. (d) Build one water garden, either in a container (at least 12 by 6 inches and 6 inches deep), or in the ground as a small, decorative pond no larger than 6 by 3 feet and 24 inches deep. Maintain the water garden for 90 days. (e) Prepare a honey super for use on a hive or colony. Remove a filled honey super from the hive or colony and prepare the honey for sale. (f) Grow a garden of your own using soil from seed or plantings to harvest or for 90 days, whichever is earlier. This can be an outdoor garden or indoors using appropriate containers, and should include at least three types of plants approved by your counselor.

requirements.req_text: Do ONE of the following: (a) Identify three career opportunities that would use skills and knowledge in gardening. Pick one and research the training, education, certification requirements, experience, and expenses associated with entering the field. Research the prospects for employment, starting salary, advancement opportunities and career goals associated with this career. Discuss what you learned with your counselor and whether you might be interested in this career. (b) Identify how you might use the skills and knowledge in gardening to pursue a personal hobby and/or healthy lifestyle. Research the additional training required, expenses, and affiliation with organizations that would help you maximize the enjoyment and benefit you might gain from it. Discuss what you learned with your counselor and share what short-term and long-term goals you might have if you pursued this.

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: In Genealogy Requirement 1, what is the difference between a primary genealogical source and a secondary source when researching your family's pedigree chart?
quiz_item.question: In Genealogy Requirement 1, what is the difference between a primary genealogical source and a secondary source when researching your family's pedigree chart?
options: A. A primary source is an original record created at or near the time of the event by a direct participant or official witness (such as an original birth certificate, parish baptismal register, or contemporaneous ship manifest), whereas a secondary source is compiled later from other accounts (such as a published county history or an unsourced online family tree).
B. A primary source is any story repeated at a family reunion fifty years later, whereas a secondary source is a courthouse marriage license signed by the officiating judge.
C. A primary source refers only to relatives on your father's side, whereas a secondary source refers to relatives on your mother's side.
D. Secondary sources are always 100 percent error-free and never need to be verified against vital records or federal census schedules.

step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Careers and Professional Pathways): Everyone who belongs to this organization should be able to trace his or her ancestry to this couple (p. 19).
Step 2 (Careers and Professional Pathways): The purposes of afamily organization are to do good research into the ancestry and descendants of a couple and to record and share the information (p. 19).
Step 3 (Careers and Professional Pathways): Such an organization often publishes extensive family genealogies and newsletters that may be available in some major libraries (p. 19).
Step 4 (Careers and Professional Pathways): A surname organization is based on a surname that is associated with a specific geographical area and time period (p. 19).

pamphlet_excerpts: You Have Learned: Then you must know where to go to find accurate answers (p. 17).
You Have Learned Principle 2: If your family moved to the United States from another country, it is important to ask your parents or guardians and other relatives (p. 17).
You Have Learned Principle 3: Even if you are not formally interviewing all these people, write down or record the information they tell (p. 17).
You Have Learned Principle 4: Not all the information someone tells you is necessarily correct (p. 17).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (You Have Learned): Relationships (such as great-uncle Ralph was Grandpa Erickson's brother) are usually correct (p. 17).
Step 2 (You Have Learned): But names, places, and dates may not be accurate (p. 17).
Step 3 (You Have Learned): Double-check the information you gather against other records (p. 17).
Step 4 (You Have Learned): It can be fun to talk to them and discover what they have and to hear what they know (p. 17).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: In Genealogy Requirement 1, what is the difference between a primary genealogical source and a secondary source when researching your family's pedigree chart?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: In Genealogy Requirement 1, what is the difference between a primary genealogical source and a secondary source when researching your family's pedigree chart?
options: A. A primary source is an original record created at or near the time of the event by a direct participant or official witness (such as an original birth certificate, parish baptismal register, or contemporaneous ship manifest), whereas a secondary source is compiled later from other accounts (such as a published county history or an unsourced online family tree).
B. A primary source is any story repeated at a family reunion fifty years later, whereas a secondary source is a courthouse marriage license signed by the officiating judge.
C. A primary source refers only to relatives on your father's side, whereas a secondary source refers to relatives on your mother's side.
D. Secondary sources are always 100 percent error-free and never need to be verified against vital records or federal census schedules.

pamphlet_excerpts: Hazards, First Aid & Safety: Learn how to recognize, and avoid, the poisonous plants in your area, such as poison ivy, poison oak, and poison sumac (p. 66).
Hazards, First Aid & Safety Principle 2: If you think you have touched a poisonous plant, immediately wash the affected skin with soap and water (p. 66).
Hazards, First Aid & Safety Principle 3: Wipe with rubbing alcohol and apply a soothing skin treatment such as calamine lotion (p. 66).
Hazards, First Aid & Safety Principle 4: Prevent sunburn by limiting exposure to the sun, covering up, and wearing a broad-brimmed hat (p. 66).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Hazards, First Aid & Safety): Use a sunscreen with a sun protection factor (SPF) of at least 15 (p. 66).
Step 2 (Hazards, First Aid & Safety): Treat a painful sunburn by applying cool, wet cloths (p. 66).
Step 3 (Hazards, First Aid & Safety): Stay in the shade if possible, and cover up (long pants, long-sleeved shirt, a brimmed hat) to avoid further overexposure to the sun (p. 66).
Step 4 (Hazards, First Aid & Safety): Symptoms can include pale, clammy skin; nausea and headache; dizziness and fainting; muscle cramps; and weakness or lack of energy (p. 66).

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: While navigating off-trail with a handheld GPS receiver to locate a cache for Geocaching Requirement 1, what field safety and environmental stewardship rules apply?
quiz_item.question: While navigating off-trail with a handheld GPS receiver to locate a cache for Geocaching Requirement 1, what field safety and environmental stewardship rules apply?
options: A. Keep your eyes glued to the GPS screen while walking briskly near cliff edges, talus slopes, and busy roadways.
B. Reach bare-handed deep into dark rock crevices, hollow logs, and stone walls without looking first, and pry apart historic cemetery masonry to find micro-caches.
C. Cross fenced private ranch land with 'No Trespassing' signs whenever the GPS arrow points straight across the pasture.

D. Look up from the GPS screen whenever moving to watch your footing and surroundings, never thrust bare hands into blind crevices where snakes or spiders may shelter, respect private property and park permissions, and practice Cache In Trash Out (CITO) by packing out litter.
choices: A. Keep your eyes glued to the GPS screen while walking briskly near cliff edges, talus slopes, and busy roadways.
B. Reach bare-handed deep into dark rock crevices, hollow logs, and stone walls without looking first, and pry apart historic cemetery masonry to find micro-caches.
C. Cross fenced private ranch land with 'No Trespassing' signs whenever the GPS arrow points straight across the pasture.

D. Look up from the GPS screen whenever moving to watch your footing and surroundings, never thrust bare hands into blind crevices where snakes or spiders may shelter, respect private property and park permissions, and practice Cache In Trash Out (CITO) by packing out litter.
quiz_item.correct_answer: D. pamphlet_excerpts: Global Positioning System GPS Works: GPS technology can be used anywhere in the world 24 hours a day because the system of satellites circles Earth all the time, and some number of them (p. 11).
Global Positioning System GPS Works Principle 2: The system works in any kind of weather and does not require any setup fee or subscription charge (p. 11).
Global Positioning System GPS Works Principle 3: A GPS receiver (GPSr) calculates its position by carefully timing the signals sent by the 24 to 30 GPS satellites high above Earth (p. 11).
Global Positioning System GPS Works Principle 4: At any given time, there are usually several satellites over any given place on Earth (p. 11).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Global Positioning System GPS Works): Each satellite continually transmits data that indicates its location and the current time (p. 11).
Step 2 (Global Positioning System GPS Works): All GPS satellites transmit signals at the same instant, but the signals arrive at a GPS receiver at slightly different times (p. 11).
Step 3 (Global Positioning System GPS Works): The farther the receiver is from a satellite, the longer the signal takes to reach the receiver (p. 11).
Step 4 (Global Positioning System GPS Works): The receiver uses the arrival time of each signal to measure the distance to each satellite (p. 11).

Steps to Finding Your First Principle 4: Four Steps to Finding Principle 4: Geocachers are encouraged to seek out new places to hide caches rather than put them where others already exist (p. 42).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Steps to Finding Your First): Step 1 (Four Steps to Finding): Areas that are not suitable for geocaches include schools, government buildings, cemeteries, airports, military installations (p. 42).

Step 2 (Steps to Finding Your First): Step 2 (Four Steps to Finding): Geocaches can only be placed at Scout camps if the location is on a portion of the property that is available to the general public to seek (p. 42).
Step 3 (Steps to Finding Your First): Step 3 (Four Steps to Finding): Your cache must be in a location that is safe to get (p. 42).

Step 4 (Steps to Finding Your First): Step 4 (Four Steps to Finding): It's essential to get permission from the landowner or land manager, and to avoid placing caches anywhere the seekers might encounter danger (p. 42).

requirements.lead_text: Do ONE of the following:
requirements.req_text: Do ONE of the following: (a) If a Cache to Eagle® series exists in your council, visit at least three of the locations in the series. Describe the projects that each cache you visit highlights, and explain how the Cache to Eagle® program helps share our Scouting service with the public. (b) Create a Scouting-related Travel Bug® that promotes one of the values of Scouting. Release your Travel Bug into a public geocache and, with your parent or guardian's permission, monitor its progress at www. geocaching. com for 30 days. Keep a log, and share this with your counselor at the end of the 30-day period. (c) Set up and hide a public geocache, following the guidelines in the Geocaching merit badge pamphlet. Before doing so, share with your counselor a three-month maintenance plan for the geocache where you are personally responsible for those three months. After setting up the geocache, with your parent or guardian's permission, follow the logs online for 30 days and share them with your counselor. You must archive the geocache when you are no longer maintaining it. (d) Explain what Cache In Trash Out (CITO) means, and describe how you have practiced CITO at public geocaches or at a CITO event. Then, either create CITO containers to leave at public caches, or host a CITO event for your unit or for the public.

quiz_item.question: In Geology Requirement 1, how does James Hutton's principle of uniformitarianism ('the present is the key to the past') help geologists interpret the rock cycle?
options: A. It states that all rocks on Earth formed simultaneously during a single afternoon and have never changed since.

B. It explains that the physical, chemical, and biological geological processes observable today (such as volcanic cooling forming igneous rock, weathering and deposition forming sedimentary rock, and heat and pressure forming metamorphic rock) operated by the same natural laws throughout Earth's history.
C. It proves that sedimentary sandstone only forms deep inside the molten outer core of the planet.
D. It states that fossils found in upper rock layers are always millions of years older than undisturbed rock layers buried far beneath them.
choices: A. It states that all rocks on Earth formed simultaneously during a single afternoon and have never changed since.

B. It explains that the physical, chemical, and biological geological processes observable today (such as volcanic cooling forming igneous rock, weathering and deposition forming sedimentary rock, and heat and pressure forming metamorphic rock) operated by the same natural laws throughout Earth's history.
C. It proves that sedimentary sandstone only forms deep inside the molten outer core of the planet.
D. It states that fossils found in upper rock layers are always millions of years older than undisturbed rock layers buried far beneath them.
quiz_item.correct_answer: B. quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (B): Uniformitarianism holds that ongoing geologic processes (magma crystallization, erosion, sedimentation, lithification, and metamorphism) explain the rock structures and stratigraphic record formed over geologic time.

pamphlet_excerpts: Geologic Map of Your Area: Review a geologic map: Rock texture, or grain size, provides information about the depth at which the minerals in the magma began to cool, forming igneous rocks (p. 66).

Geologic Map of Your Area Principle 2: Review a geologic map Principle 2: As an example, if you find a fine-grainedigneous rock, you interpret the rock to be an extrusive rock that cooled at or near the surface (p. 66).
Geologic Map of Your Area Principle 3: Review a geologic map Principle 3: Coarse-grained igneous rocks are intrusive rocks that cooled over very long periods of time (p. 66).

Geologic Map of Your Area Principle 4: Review a geologic map Principle 4: These deep rocks get to the surface when tectonic (mountain-building) forces uplift the area and the material covering the intrusive rock is eroded away by wind (p. 66).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Geologic Map of Your Area): Step 1 (Review a geologic map): Another important characteristic of igneous rocks is color, which indicates the kinds of rock minerals (p. 66).
Step 2 (Geologic Map of Your Area): Step 2 (Review a geologic map): Lighter colored igneous rocks such as granite are usually formed fromsialic or silicic magmas, rich in quartz and feldspar (p. 66).

Step 3 (Geologic Map of Your Area): Step 3 (Review a geologic map): Darker colored igneous rocks such as black- or green-colored gabbrosor basalts are formed frommafic magmas, rich in iron and magnesium (p. 66).

Step 4 (Geologic Map of Your Area): Step 4 (Review a geologic map): Weathering of rocks exposed at Earth's surface yields two types of materials: solid grains and chemicals dissolved in water (p. 66).

requirements.lead_text: Do ONE of the following options:
requirements.req_text: Do ONE of the following options: (a) Option A, Surface and Sedimentary Processes. Do ALL of the following: (1) Conduct an experiment approved by your counselor that demonstrates how sediments settle from suspension in water. Explain to your counselor what the exercise shows and why it is important. (2) Using topographical maps provided by your counselor, plot the stream gradients (different elevations divided by distance) for four different stream types (straight, meandering, dendritic, trellis). Explain which ones flow fastest and why, and which ones will carry larger grains of sediment and why. (3) On a stream diagram, show areas where you will find the following features: cut bank, fill bank, point bar, medial channel bars, and lake delta. Describe the relative sediment grain size found in each feature. (4) Conduct an experiment approved by your counselor that shows how some sedimentary material carried by water may be too small for you to see without a magnifier. (5) Visit a nearby stream. Find clues that show the direction of water flow, even if the water is missing. Record your observations in a notebook, and sketch those clues you observe. Discuss your observations with your counselor. (b) Option B, Energy Resources. Do ALL of the following: (1) List the top five Earth resources used to generate electricity in the United States. (2) Discuss source rock, trap, and reservoir rock, the three components necessary for the occurrence of oil and gas underground. (3) Explain how each of the following items is used in subsurface exploration to locate oil or gas: reflection seismic, electric well logs, stratigraphic correlation, offshore platform, geologic map, subsurface structure map, subsurface isopach map, and core samples and cutting samples. (4) Using at least 20 data points provided by your counselor, create a subsurface structure map and use it to explain how subsurface geology maps are used to find oil, gas, or coal resources. (5) Do ONE of the following: (a) Make a display or presentation showing how oil and gas or coal is found, extracted, and processed. You may use maps, books, articles from periodicals, and research found on the internet (with your parent or guardian's permission). Share the display with your counselor or a small group (such as your class at school) in a five-minute presentation. (b) With your parent or guardian's and counselor's permission and assistance, arrange for a visit to an operating drilling rig. While there, talk with a geologist and ask to see what the geologist does onsite. Ask to see cutting samples taken at the site. (c) Option C, Mineral Resources. Do ALL of the following: (1) Define rock. Discuss the three classes of rocks including their origin and characteristics. (2) Define mineral. Discuss the origin of minerals and their chemical composition and identification properties, including hardness, specific gravity, color, streak, cleavage, luster, and crystal form. (3) Do ONE of the following: (a) Collect 10 different rocks or minerals. Record in a notebook where you obtained (found, bought, traded) each one. Label each specimen, identify its class and origin, determine its chemical composition, and list its physical properties. Share your collection with your counselor. (b) With your counselor's assistance, identify 15 different rocks and minerals. List the name of each specimen, tell whether it is a rock or mineral, and give the name of its class (if it is a rock) or list its identifying physical properties (if it is a mineral). (4) List three of the most common road-building materials used in your area. Explain how each material is produced and how each is used in road building. (5) Do ONE of the following: (a) With your parent or guardian's and counselor's approval, visit an active mining site, quarry, or sand and gravel pit. Tell your counselor what you learned about the resources extracted from this location and how these resources are used by society. (b) With your counselor, choose two examples of rocks and two examples of minerals. Discuss the mining of these materials and describe how each is used by society. (c) With your parent or guardian's and counselor's approval, visit the office of a civil engineer and learn how geology is used in construction. Discuss what you learned with your counselor. (d) Option D, Earth History. Do ALL of the following: (1) Create a chart showing suggested geological eras and periods. Determine which period the rocks in your region might have been formed. (2) Explain the theory of plate tectonics. Make a chart explaining, or discuss with your counselor, how the processes of plate tectonics work. Discuss how plate tectonics determines the distribution of most of the Earth's volcanoes, earthquakes, and mountain belts. (3) Explain to your counselor the processes of burial and fossilization, and discuss the concept of extinction. (4) Explain to your counselor how fossils provide information about ancient life, environment, climate, and geography. Discuss the following terms and explain how animals from each habitat obtain food: benthonic, pelagic, littoral, lacustrine, open marine, brackish, fluvial, eolian, and protected reef. (5) Collect 10 different fossil plants or animals OR (with your counselor's assistance) identify 15 different fossil plants or animals. Record in a notebook where you obtained (found, bought, traded) each one. Classify each specimen to the best of your ability, and explain how each one might have survived and obtained food. Tell what else you can learn from these fossils. (6) Do ONE of the following: (a) Visit a science museum or the geology department of a local university that has fossils on display. With your parent or guardian's and counselor's approval, before you go, make an appointment with a curator or guide who can show you how the fossils are preserved and prepared for display. (b) Visit a structure in your area that was built using fossiliferous rocks. Determine what kind of rock was used and tell your counselor the kinds of fossil evidence you found there. (c) Visit a rock outcrop that contains fossils. Determine what kind of rock contains the fossils, and tell your counselor the kinds of fossil evidence you found at the outcrop. (d) Prepare a display or presentation on your state fossil. Include an image of the fossil, the age of the fossil, and its classification. You may use maps, books, articles from periodicals, and research found on the internet (with your parent or guardian's permission). Share the display with your counselor or a small group (such as your class at school). If your state does not have a state fossil, you may select a state fossil from a neighboring state.

sub_requirements.sub_req_text: Option B, Energy Resources. Do ALL of the following: (1) List the top five Earth resources used to generate electricity in the United States. (2) Discuss source rock, trap, and reservoir rock, the three components necessary for the occurrence of oil and gas underground. (3) Explain how each of the following items is used in subsurface exploration to locate oil or gas: reflection seismic, electric well logs, stratigraphic correlation, offshore platform, geologic map, subsurface structure map, subsurface isopach map, and core samples and cutting samples. (4) Using at least 20 data points provided by your counselor, create a subsurface structure map and use it to explain how subsurface geology maps are used to find oil, gas, or coal resources. (5) Do ONE of the following: (a) Make a display or presentation showing how oil and gas or coal is found, extracted, and processed. You may use maps, books, articles from periodicals, and research found on the internet (with your parent or guardian's permission). Share the display with your counselor or a small group (such as your class at school) in a five-minute presentation. (b) With your parent or guardian's and counselor's permission and assistance, arrange for a visit to an operating drilling rig. While there, talk with a geologist and ask to see what the geologist does onsite. Ask to see cutting samples taken at the site.

sub_requirements.label: (c)
sub_requirements.text: Option C, Mineral Resources. Do ALL of the following: (1) Define rock. Discuss the three classes of rocks including their origin and characteristics. (2) Define mineral. Discuss the origin of minerals and their chemical composition and identification properties, including hardness, specific gravity, color, streak, cleavage, luster, and crystal form. (3) Do ONE of the following: (a) Collect 10 different rocks or minerals. Record in a notebook where you obtained (found, bought, traded) each one. Label each specimen, identify its class and origin, determine its chemical composition, and list its physical properties. Share your collection with your counselor. (b) With your counselor's assistance, identify 15 different rocks and minerals. List the name of each specimen, tell whether it is a rock or mineral, and give the name of its class (if it is a rock) or list its identifying physical properties (if it is a mineral). (4) List three of the most common road-building materials used in your area. Explain how each material is produced and how each is used in road building. (5) Do ONE of the following: (a) With your parent or guardian's and counselor's approval, visit an active mining site, quarry, or sand and gravel pit. Tell your counselor what you learned about the resources extracted from this location and how these resources are used by society. (b) With your counselor, choose two examples of rocks and two examples of minerals. Discuss the mining of these materials and describe how each is used by society. (c) With your parent or guardian's and counselor's approval, visit the office of a civil engineer and learn how geology is used in construction. Discuss what you learned with your counselor.

sub_requirements.sub_req_text: Option C, Mineral Resources. Do ALL of the following: (1) Define rock. Discuss the three classes of rocks including their origin and characteristics. (2) Define mineral. Discuss the origin of minerals and their chemical composition and identification properties, including hardness, specific gravity, color, streak, cleavage, luster, and crystal form. (3) Do ONE of the following: (a) Collect 10 different rocks or minerals. Record in a notebook where you obtained (found, bought, traded) each one. Label each specimen, identify its class and origin, determine its chemical composition, and list its physical properties. Share your collection with your counselor. (b) With your counselor's assistance, identify 15 different rocks and minerals. List the name of each specimen, tell whether it is a rock or mineral, and give the name of its class (if it is a rock) or list its identifying physical properties (if it is a mineral). (4) List three of the most common road-building materials used in your area. Explain how each material is produced and how each is used in road building. (5) Do ONE of the following: (a) With your parent or guardian's and counselor's approval, visit an active mining site, quarry, or sand and gravel pit. Tell your counselor what you learned about the resources extracted from this location and how these resources are used by society. (b) With your counselor, choose two examples of rocks and two examples of minerals. Discuss the mining of these materials and describe how each is used by society. (c) With your parent or guardian's and counselor's approval, visit the office of a civil engineer and learn how geology is used in construction. Discuss what you learned with your counselor.

sub_requirements.label: (d)
sub_requirements.text: Option D, Earth History. Do ALL of the following: (1) Create a chart showing suggested geological eras and periods. Determine which period the rocks in your region might have been formed. (2) Explain the theory of plate tectonics. Make a chart explaining, or discuss with your counselor, how the processes of plate tectonics work. Discuss how plate tectonics determines the distribution of most of the Earth's volcanoes, earthquakes, and mountain belts. (3) Explain to your counselor the processes of burial and fossilization, and discuss the concept of extinction. (4) Explain to your counselor how fossils provide information about ancient life, environment, climate, and geography. Discuss the following terms and explain how animals from each habitat obtain food: benthonic, pelagic, littoral, lacustrine, open marine, brackish, fluvial, eolian, and protected reef. (5) Collect 10 different fossil plants or animals OR (with your counselor's assistance) identify 15 different fossil plants or animals. Record in a notebook where you obtained (found, bought, traded) each one. Classify each specimen to the best of your ability, and explain how each one might have survived and obtained food. Tell what else you can learn from these fossils. (6) Do ONE of the following: (a) Visit a science museum or the geology department of a local university that has fossils on display. With your parent or guardian's and counselor's approval, before you go, make an appointment with a curator or guide who can show you how the fossils are preserved and prepared for display. (b) Visit a structure in your area that was built using fossiliferous rocks. Determine what kind of rock was used and tell your counselor the kinds of fossil evidence you found there. (c) Visit a rock outcrop that contains fossils. Determine what kind of rock contains the fossils, and tell your counselor the kinds of fossil evidence you found at the outcrop. (d) Prepare a display or presentation on your state fossil. Include an image of the fossil, the age of the fossil, and its classification. You may use maps, books, articles from periodicals, and research found on the internet (with your parent or guardian's permission). Share the display with your counselor or a small group (such as your class at school). If your state does not have a state fossil, you may select a state fossil from a neighboring state.

children.text: Do ONE of the following: (a) Visit a science museum or the geology department of a local university that has fossils on display. With your parent or guardian's and counselor's approval, before you go, make an appointment with a curator or guide who can show you how the fossils are preserved and prepared for display. (b) Visit a structure in your area that was built using fossiliferous rocks. Determine what kind of rock was used and tell your counselor the kinds of fossil evidence you found there. (c) Visit a rock outcrop that contains fossils. Determine what kind of rock contains the fossils, and tell your counselor the kinds of fossil evidence you found at the outcrop. (d) Prepare a display or presentation on your state fossil. Include an image of the fossil, the age of the fossil, and its classification. You may use maps, books, articles from periodicals, and research found on the internet (with your parent or guardian's permission). Share the display with your counselor or a small group (such as your class at school). If your state does not have a state fossil, you may select a state fossil from a neighboring state.

sub_requirements.sub_req_text: Option D, Earth History. Do ALL of the following: (1) Create a chart showing suggested geological eras and periods. Determine which period the rocks in your region might have been formed. (2) Explain the theory of plate tectonics. Make a chart explaining, or discuss with your counselor, how the processes of plate tectonics work. Discuss how plate tectonics determines the distribution of most of the Earth's volcanoes, earthquakes, and mountain belts. (3) Explain to your counselor the processes of burial and fossilization, and discuss the concept of extinction. (4) Explain to your counselor how fossils provide information about ancient life, environment, climate, and geography. Discuss the following terms and explain how animals from each habitat obtain food: benthonic, pelagic, littoral, lacustrine, open marine, brackish, fluvial, eolian, and protected reef. (5) Collect 10 different fossil plants or animals OR (with your counselor's assistance) identify 15 different fossil plants or animals. Record in a notebook where you obtained (found, bought, traded) each one. Classify each specimen to the best of your ability, and explain how each one might have survived and obtained food. Tell what else you can learn from these fossils. (6) Do ONE of the following: (a) Visit a science museum or the geology department of a local university that has fossils on display. With your parent or guardian's and counselor's approval, before you go, make an appointment with a curator or guide who can show you how the fossils are preserved and prepared for display. (b) Visit a structure in your area that was built using fossiliferous rocks. Determine what kind of rock was used and tell your counselor the kinds of fossil evidence you found there. (c) Visit a rock outcrop that contains fossils. Determine what kind of rock contains the fossils, and tell your counselor the kinds of fossil evidence you found at the outcrop. (d) Prepare a display or presentation on your state fossil. Include an image of the fossil, the age of the fossil, and its classification. You may use maps, books, articles from periodicals, and research found on the internet (with your parent or guardian's permission). Share the display with your counselor or a small group (such as your class at school). If your state does not have a state fossil, you may select a state fossil from a neighboring state.

Careers & Professional Pathways Principle 2: Knowledge of geology makes Earth even more interesting (p. 89).

step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Careers & Professional Pathways): Hydrogeologists help find water underground and can plan how much to use so you will not run (p. 89).
Step 2 (Careers & Professional Pathways): Many geologists are involved in the exploration of and/orthe production of natural resources, like oil and gas, coal, ironore, copper, gold (p. 89).
Step 3 (Careers & Professional Pathways): A professional geologist must earn at least a four-year college degree (bachelor's degree) in geology, geophysics, environmental geology (p. 89).
Step 4 (Careers & Professional Pathways): In many fields a master's degree (two years beyond a bachelor's degree) may be necessary (p. 89).

patrol_quiz_bank.question: In Geology Requirement 1, how does James Hutton's principle of uniformitarianism ('the present is the key to the past') help geologists interpret the rock cycle?
options: A. It states that all rocks on Earth formed simultaneously during a single afternoon and have never changed since.

B. It explains that the physical, chemical, and biological geological processes observable today (such as volcanic cooling forming igneous rock, weathering and deposition forming sedimentary rock, and heat and pressure forming metamorphic rock) operated by the same natural laws throughout Earth's history.
C. It proves that sedimentary sandstone only forms deep inside the molten outer core of the planet.
D. It states that fossils found in upper rock layers are always millions of years older than undisturbed rock layers buried far beneath them.
choices: A. It states that all rocks on Earth formed simultaneously during a single afternoon and have never changed since.

B. pamphlet_excerpts: Safety on the golf course: You may have seen golfers lick the dirt off their golf ball so the ball will roll true or to hold a used tee in their mouth (p. 53).
Safety on the golf course Principle 2: Toxic substances on the courses may cling to the ball and tee (p. 53).
Safety on the golf course Principle 3: These include fertilizers, pesticides, weed killers, and animal excrement (p. 53).
Safety on the golf course Principle 4: Some golfers who have a habit of cleaning their golf balls by licking them develop hepatitis, an inflammation of the liver (p. 53).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Safety on the golf course): It is best to always carry a towel in your golf bag and dampen it to wipe your ball clean (p. 53).
Step 2 (Safety on the golf course): There are a few first-aid issues that apply especially to golfers and golfing (p. 53).
Step 3 (Safety on the golf course): When we lose more water than we take in, we become dehydrated (p. 53).
Step 4 (Safety on the golf course): Symptoms of mild dehydration include increased thirst, dry lips, and dark yellow urine (p. 53).
