quiz_item.scenario_prompt: Your patrol is on the 6th fairway when dark thunderclouds build and you hear thunder 20 seconds after seeing a lightning flash. What must your group do immediately?
quiz_item.question: Your patrol is on the 6th fairway when dark thunderclouds build and you hear thunder 20 seconds after seeing a lightning flash. What must your group do immediately?
options: A. Finish playing the current hole quickly while holding metal golf umbrellas overhead.
B. Take shelter together under the tallest oak tree along the fairway edge until the rain passes.

C. Suspend play immediately under the 30/30 lightning rule, leave golf bags/metal clubs behind if needed, and move to the clubhouse or a designated lightning-safe building, waiting 30 minutes after the last thunder before resuming.
D. Sit inside an open-sided golf cart parked on the elevated 7th tee box while holding a 1-iron.
choices: A. Finish playing the current hole quickly while holding metal golf umbrellas overhead.
B. Take shelter together under the tallest oak tree along the fairway edge until the rain passes.

C. Suspend play immediately under the 30/30 lightning rule, leave golf bags/metal clubs behind if needed, and move to the clubhouse or a designated lightning-safe building, waiting 30 minutes after the last thunder before resuming.
D. Sit inside an open-sided golf cart parked on the elevated 7th tee box while holding a 1-iron.
quiz_item.correct_answer: C. Suspend play immediately under the 30/30 lightning rule, leave golf bags/metal clubs behind if needed, and move to the clubhouse or a designated lightning-safe building, waiting 30 minutes after the last thunder before resuming.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (C): A 20-second flash-to-bang count means lightning is 4 miles away (within the 6-mile / 30-second strike zone); isolated trees and metal clubs/umbrellas are acute lightning hazards.

requirements.lead_text: Complete ONE of the following options:
requirements.req_text: Complete ONE of the following options: (a) Option A, Traditional Golf. Do ALL of the following: (1) Study the USGA Rules of Golf now in use. (a) Tell about the three categories of golf etiquette. (b) Demonstrate that you understand the definitions of golf terms. (c) Show that you understand the Rules of Amateur Status. (2) Tell about your understanding of the World Handicap System. (3) Do the following: (a) Tell about the early history of golf. (b) Describe golf's early years in the United States. (c) Tell about the accomplishments of a top golfer of your choice. (4) Do the following: (a) Tell how golf can contribute to a healthy lifestyle, mentally and physically. (b) Tell how a golf exercise plan can help you play better. Show two exercises that would help improve your game. (5) Show the following: (a) The proper grip, stance, posture, and key fundamentals of a good swing (b) Driver played from a tee (c) The fairway wood shot (d) The long iron shot (e) The short iron shot (f) The approach, chip-and-run, and pitch shots (g) A recovery shot from a bunker or heavy rough (h) A sound putting stroke (6) Play a minimum of two nine-hole rounds or one 18-hole round of golf with another golfer about your age and with your counselor, or an adult approved by your counselor. Do the following: (a) Follow the Rules of Golf. (b) Practice good golf etiquette. (c) Show respect to fellow golfers, committee, sponsor, and gallery. (7) Find out about three careers related to traditional golf. Pick one and identify the education, training, and experience required for this profession. Discuss this with your counselor, and explain why this interests you. (b) Option B, Disc Golf. Do ALL of the following: (1) Study the PDGA Official Rules of Disc Golf now in use. (a) Tell about the six areas of Courtesy (812). (b) Describe the seven areas of Scoring (808). (2) Tell about the history of disc golf and why it is an inclusive game. (3) Do the following: (a) Tell about the history of disc golf and why it is an inclusive game. (b) Discuss with your counselor the contributions Ed Headrick made to the sport of disc golf. (c) Describe the evolution of disc design. (d) Tell about the accomplishments of a top disc golfer of your choice. (4) Do the following: (a) Tell how disc golf can contribute to a healthy lifestyle, mentally and physically. (b) Tell how a disc golf exercise plan can help you play better. Show two exercises that would help improve your game. (5) Show the following: (a) A good throwing grip (b) A good runup (X-step) when throwing a disc (c) Backhand shot (d) Forehand shot (e) Overhand shot (f) Rolling shot (g) A good (in-line) putting stance (h) A good straddle putting stance (i) A good putting grip (j) A good putting motion and follow through (k) The proper use of a mini-marking disc (6) Play a minimum of 18-holes of disc golf with another disc golfer about your age and with your counselor, or an adult approved by your counselor. Do the following: (a) Follow the PDGA Official Rules of Disc Golf. (b) Practice good disc golf etiquette. (c) Show respect to fellow disc golfers and other people in the park along with any wildlife, trees, and plants on the property. (7) Find out about three careers related to disc golf. Pick one and identify the education, training, and experience required for this profession. Discuss this with your counselor, and explain why this interests you.

sub_requirements.sub_req_text: Option A, Traditional Golf. Do ALL of the following: (1) Study the USGA Rules of Golf now in use. (a) Tell about the three categories of golf etiquette. (b) Demonstrate that you understand the definitions of golf terms. (c) Show that you understand the Rules of Amateur Status. (2) Tell about your understanding of the World Handicap System. (3) Do the following: (a) Tell about the early history of golf. (b) Describe golf's early years in the United States. (c) Tell about the accomplishments of a top golfer of your choice. (4) Do the following: (a) Tell how golf can contribute to a healthy lifestyle, mentally and physically. (b) Tell how a golf exercise plan can help you play better. Show two exercises that would help improve your game. (5) Show the following: (a) The proper grip, stance, posture, and key fundamentals of a good swing (b) Driver played from a tee (c) The fairway wood shot (d) The long iron shot (e) The short iron shot (f) The approach, chip-and-run, and pitch shots (g) A recovery shot from a bunker or heavy rough (h) A sound putting stroke (6) Play a minimum of two nine-hole rounds or one 18-hole round of golf with another golfer about your age and with your counselor, or an adult approved by your counselor. Do the following: (a) Follow the Rules of Golf. (b) Practice good golf etiquette. (c) Show respect to fellow golfers, committee, sponsor, and gallery. (7) Find out about three careers related to traditional golf. Pick one and identify the education, training, and experience required for this profession. Discuss this with your counselor, and explain why this interests.

sub_requirements.label: (b)
sub_requirements.text: Option B, Disc Golf. Do ALL of the following: (1) Study the PDGA Official Rules of Disc Golf now in use. (a) Tell about the six areas of Courtesy (812). (b) Describe the seven areas of Scoring (808). (2) Tell about the history of disc golf and why it is an inclusive game. (3) Do the following: (a) Tell about the history of disc golf and why it is an inclusive game. (b) Discuss with your counselor the contributions Ed Headrick made to the sport of disc golf. (c) Describe the evolution of disc design. (d) Tell about the accomplishments of a top disc golfer of your choice. (4) Do the following: (a) Tell how disc golf can contribute to a healthy lifestyle, mentally and physically. (b) Tell how a disc golf exercise plan can help you play better. Show two exercises that would help improve your game. (5) Show the following: (a) A good throwing grip (b) A good runup (X-step) when throwing a disc (c) Backhand shot (d) Forehand shot (e) Overhand shot (f) Rolling shot (g) A good (in-line) putting stance (h) A good straddle putting stance (i) A good putting grip (j) A good putting motion and follow through (k) The proper use of a mini-marking disc (6) Play a minimum of 18-holes of disc golf with another disc golfer about your age and with your counselor, or an adult approved by your counselor. Do the following: (a) Follow the PDGA Official Rules of Disc Golf. (b) Practice good disc golf etiquette. (c) Show respect to fellow disc golfers and other people in the park along with any wildlife, trees, and plants on the property. (7) Find out about three careers related to disc golf. Pick one and identify the education, training, and experience required for this profession. Discuss this with your counselor, and explain why this interests.

sub_requirements.sub_req_text: Option B, Disc Golf. Do ALL of the following: (1) Study the PDGA Official Rules of Disc Golf now in use. (a) Tell about the six areas of Courtesy (812). (b) Describe the seven areas of Scoring (808). (2) Tell about the history of disc golf and why it is an inclusive game. (3) Do the following: (a) Tell about the history of disc golf and why it is an inclusive game. (b) Discuss with your counselor the contributions Ed Headrick made to the sport of disc golf. (c) Describe the evolution of disc design. (d) Tell about the accomplishments of a top disc golfer of your choice. (4) Do the following: (a) Tell how disc golf can contribute to a healthy lifestyle, mentally and physically. (b) Tell how a disc golf exercise plan can help you play better. Show two exercises that would help improve your game. (5) Show the following: (a) A good throwing grip (b) A good runup (X-step) when throwing a disc (c) Backhand shot (d) Forehand shot (e) Overhand shot (f) Rolling shot (g) A good (in-line) putting stance (h) A good straddle putting stance (i) A good putting grip (j) A good putting motion and follow through (k) The proper use of a mini-marking disc (6) Play a minimum of 18-holes of disc golf with another disc golfer about your age and with your counselor, or an adult approved by your counselor. Do the following: (a) Follow the PDGA Official Rules of Disc Golf. (b) Practice good disc golf etiquette. (c) Show respect to fellow disc golfers and other people in the park along with any wildlife, trees, and plants on the property. (7) Find out about three careers related to disc golf. Pick one and identify the education, training, and experience required for this profession. Discuss this with your counselor, and explain why this interests.

Traditional Golf / Disc Golf Principle 2: The Professional Disc Golf Association (PDGA) oversees both amateur events and a professional tour (p. 50).
Traditional Golf / Disc Golf Principle 3: The PDGA sanctions more than 9,000 events each year and hasan active membership of more than 129,000 competitive disc golfers from 70+ countries (p. 50).
Traditional Golf / Disc Golf Principle 4: The roots of disc golf are firmly grounded with the Frisbee® and date to early disc golf promoters like "Steady" Ed Head rick and George Sappenfield (p. 50).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Traditional Golf / Disc Golf): Soon the days of using a simple Frisbee® graduated to the modern golf disc, with the triangular beveled-edge disc patented by Dave Dunipace in 1983 (p. 50).
Step 2 (Traditional Golf / Disc Golf): This disc provides the player a next-level experience (p. 50).
Step 3 (Traditional Golf / Disc Golf): With most of the disc'sweight in the rim, the golf disc flies farther and more accurately, even in the wind (p. 50).
Step 4 (Traditional Golf / Disc Golf): Only one disc is needed to enjoy the game, but as players improve and get more active in the sport, a range of discs can come into play (p. 50).

patrol_quiz_bank.question: Your patrol is on the 6th fairway when dark thunderclouds build and you hear thunder 20 seconds after seeing a lightning flash. What must your group do immediately?
options: A. Finish playing the current hole quickly while holding metal golf umbrellas overhead.
B. Take shelter together under the tallest oak tree along the fairway edge until the rain passes.

C. Suspend play immediately under the 30/30 lightning rule, leave golf bags/metal clubs behind if needed, and move to the clubhouse or a designated lightning-safe building, waiting 30 minutes after the last thunder before resuming.
D. Sit inside an open-sided golf cart parked on the elevated 7th tee box while holding a 1-iron.

quiz_item.question: In Graphic Arts Requirement 1, how do the four traditional printing processes (relief, intaglio, planographic, and porous) transfer ink to a substrate?
options: A. All four processes carve deep grooves into wooden blocks and melt solid wax crayons onto the paper using laser beams.
B. Offset lithography forces ink through a woven silk mesh, while screen printing etches microscopic wells into a heavy copper cylinder.

C. Relief prints from raised surfaces, gravure/intaglio prints from recessed ink-filled cells etched into a cylinder, offset lithography prints from a flat plate using the mutual repulsion of oil-based ink and water, and screen printing squeegees ink through open mesh areas of a stencil.
D. Gravure uses raised rubber stamps for corrugated cardboard, while flexography uses only home inkjet cartridges.

pamphlet_excerpts: Differences Between Continuous Tone Line: The half tone dots are so small, the human eye cannot see the individual dots unless they are magnified, but the eye does see an overall effect (p. 44).
Differences Between Continuous Tone Line Principle 2: The arrangement of the half tone dots creates this effect (p. 44).
Differences Between Continuous Tone Line Principle 3: The half tone dots in the part of an image that is supposed to look dark are big and fill most of the half tone dot area (p. 44).
Differences Between Continuous Tone Line Principle 4: The half tone dots in the part of an image that is supposed to look light are small and fill very little of thehalftone dot area (p. 44).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Differences Between Continuous Tone Line): Generally, half tones are made from a continuous-tone image, such as a traditional photograph (p. 44).
Step 2 (Differences Between Continuous Tone Line): In the past, the continuous-tone image was photographed through a special screen that created a half tone version of the original (p. 44).
Step 3 (Differences Between Continuous Tone Line): Today it is more common to take a continuous-tone image and scan it into a computer or to take a picture with a digital camera (p. 44).
Step 4 (Differences Between Continuous Tone Line): The computer software then converts the digital file into a pattern of small half tone dots that make up an image (p. 44).

requirements.lead_text: Produce the design you created for requirement 3 using one of the following printing processes:
requirements.req_text: Produce the design you created for requirement 3 using one of the following printing processes: (a) Offset lithography. Make a layout, and produce a plate using a process approved by your counselor. Run the plate and print at least 50 copies. (b) Screen printing. Make a hand-cut or photographic stencil and attach it to a screen that you have prepared. Mask the screen and print at least 20 copies. Resource: Screen Printing Tutorial (video) (c) Electronic/digital printing. Create a layout in electronic form, download it to the press or printer, and run 50 copies. If no electronic interface to the press or printer is available, you may print and scan a paper copy of the layout. (d) Relief printing. Create a layout in electronic form, download it to the press or printer, and run 50 copies. If no electronic interface to the press or printer is available, you may print and scan a paper copy of the layout.

pamphlet_excerpts: Post press Operations: A harder paper cover is wrapped around the glued pages, covering the front, spine, and back (p. 73).
Post press Operations Principle 2: Perfect-bound books are less costly than case-bound books, but they will not withstand bending or other hard use (p. 73).
Post press Operations Principle 3: Saddle stitching, or stapling through the fold of a multiple page publication, is another method of binding smaller pamphlets or booklets (p. 73).
Post press Operations Principle 4: Saddle stitching is used for smaller publications (p. 73).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Post press Operations): Other methods of binding generally are for single-sheet printed material, where each page is printed on a separate sheet (p. 73).
Step 2 (Post press Operations): These binding methods are spiral, plastic comb, flat stitching, and stapling (p. 73).
Step 3 (Post press Operations): Spiral and plastic comb binding require the pages to be punched with holes before the wire or plastic binding is applied (p. 73).
Step 4 (Post press Operations): Stitching, a one-step operation using a thin wire called spool wire, is the oldest of the methods and the most economical (p. 73).

pamphlet_excerpts: Careers & Professional Pathways: A bindery supervisor coordinates operations in the bindery, schedules jobs, and supervises and trains workers (p. 81).
Careers & Professional Pathways Principle 2: A bindery worker may prepare and tend one or more automated machines that do cutting, scoring, folding, stitching, taping, and gluing (p. 81).
Careers & Professional Pathways Principle 3: In large binderies, the work is done on an assembly line, with workers performing one or two types of tasks (p. 81).

Careers & Professional Pathways Principle 4: A perfect-binder setter sets up and controls a binding machine that gathers magazine or book signatures, glues them, and adds the cover to magazines (p. 81).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Careers & Professional Pathways): A book binder hand binds books, usually working on special editions and custom binding, and repairs old and rare books (p. 81).
Step 2 (Careers & Professional Pathways): Book binders learn by training with the relatively few experts in the field (p. 81).
Step 3 (Careers & Professional Pathways): A distribution specialist coordinates the mailing and shipping of printed products and uses computers to organize mailings and to control (p. 81).
Step 4 (Careers & Professional Pathways): Use a reference in this booklet to identify three career opportunities of interest (p. 81).

patrol_quiz_bank.question: In Graphic Arts Requirement 1, how do the four traditional printing processes (relief, intaglio, planographic, and porous) transfer ink to a substrate?
options: A. All four processes carve deep grooves into wooden blocks and melt solid wax crayons onto the paper using laser beams.
B. Offset lithography forces ink through a woven silk mesh, while screen printing etches microscopic wells into a heavy copper cylinder.

C. Relief prints from raised surfaces, gravure/intaglio prints from recessed ink-filled cells etched into a cylinder, offset lithography prints from a flat plate using the mutual repulsion of oil-based ink and water, and screen printing squeegees ink through open mesh areas of a stencil.
D. Gravure uses raised rubber stamps for corrugated cardboard, while flexography uses only home inkjet cartridges.

options: A. Each professional operates within a defined education, state licensure, and legal scope of practice: physicians and PAs diagnosing and prescribing, pharmacists verifying medication safety and interactions, RNs delivering and coordinating bedside patient care, and allied health specialists performing diagnostic imaging, lab analysis, and physical rehabilitation.
B. Every member of a hospital team performs open-heart surgery interchangeably without specialized board certification or state licensing.
C. Pharmacists only work at retail cash registers and have no clinical training in drug dosing, pharmacology, or adverse chemical interactions.
D. Registered nurses and respiratory therapists work only in administrative billing offices and never assess patients directly.

Step 3 (Health Care Professions Careers and Pathways): Step 3 (Select three of the professions): Some PAprograms will require the applicant to have had some experience in a health care setting (p. 16).
Step 4 (Health Care Professions Careers and Pathways): Step 4 (Select three of the professions): Hospital, outpatient clinics, community health clinics, private practices, and prisons (p. 16).

pamphlet_excerpts: Hazards, First Aid & Safety: Water is essential for nearly every bodily function (p. 48).
Hazards, First Aid & Safety Principle 2: People who lose more water than they take in risk becoming dehydrated (p. 48).
Hazards, First Aid & Safety Principle 3: The first sign of dehydration usually is dark urine (p. 48).
Hazards, First Aid & Safety Principle 4: Other signs can include weariness, headache, body aches, and confusion (p. 48).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Hazards, First Aid & Safety): Heat exhaustion, heatstroke, and hypothermia might all be caused in part by dehydration (p. 48).
Step 2 (Hazards, First Aid & Safety): Prevent dehydration and heat reactions by drinking plenty of fluids (p. 48).
Step 3 (Hazards, First Aid & Safety): That is easy to do on hot summer days when you are thirsty (p. 48).
Step 4 (Hazards, First Aid & Safety): It is just as important in cold weather when you might not feel thirsty (p. 48).

pamphlet_excerpts: Leave No Trace and Outdoor Ethics: Caring for the environment is an important responsibility of every hiker (p. 28).
Leave No Trace and Outdoor Ethics Principle 2: Leave No Trace is just one set of principles that can help you live up to that responsibility and enjoy the outdoors fully by knowing (p. 28).
Leave No Trace and Outdoor Ethics Principle 3: As you and your group plan a hike, ask yourselves how you can follow each of the principles of Leave No Trace (p. 28).

Leave No Trace and Outdoor Ethics Principle 4: Leave No Trace and The Outdoor Code are principles that help you respect the environment and be considerate to others who are enjoying the outdoors (p. 28).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Leave No Trace and Outdoor Ethics): Explain your desired route and ask how you can best implement Leave No Trace (p. 28).
Step 2 (Leave No Trace and Outdoor Ethics): Here are some additional guidelines to remember (p. 28).
Step 3 (Leave No Trace and Outdoor Ethics): Remember this solid guideline: Pack it in, pack (p. 28).
Step 4 (Leave No Trace and Outdoor Ethics): Make it easier on yourself by limiting the amount of potential trash you take (p. 28).

pamphlet_excerpts: Hiking is an aerobic activity: Setting off on a hike without properly preparing can have disastrous results (p. 33).
Hiking is an aerobic activity Principle 2: Make sure you are ready, from your physical condition to the best gear for the trip (p. 33).
Hiking is an aerobic activity Principle 3: To enjoy hiking to the fullest, you will want to be in good shape (p. 33).
Hiking is an aerobic activity Principle 4: That is why requirement 3 calls for developing a plan for conditioning yourself (p. 33).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Hiking is an aerobic activity): Begin with short trips, increasing the length of your journeys as you become more fit (p. 33).
Step 2 (Hiking is an aerobic activity): A good way to prepare for Scout hikes is to walk whenever you can rather than riding in a car or relying on public transit (p. 33).
Step 3 (Hiking is an aerobic activity): The word aerobic means "with oxygen." Aerobic activities increase the rate of your breathing and your heartbeat, and push your body to use oxygen (p. 33).
Step 4 (Hiking is an aerobic activity): Aerobic training can strengthen your circulatory and respiratory systems, add mass to muscles and bones, burn excess fat, and lead to improvements (p. 33).

requirements.lead_text: Take four 10-mile hikes and one 20-mile hike, each on a different day, and each of continuous miles. Prepare a written hike plan before each hike and share it with your counselor or a designee for approval before starting the hike. Include map routes, a clothing and equipment list, and a list of items for a trail lunch. You may stop for as many short rest periods as needed, as well as one meal, during each hike, but not for an extended period such as overnight.

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: Before replacing a leaking compression faucet washer or repairing a damaged electrical wall switch for Home Repairs Requirement 1, what safety step is required first?
quiz_item.question: Before replacing a leaking compression faucet washer or repairing a damaged electrical wall switch for Home Repairs Requirement 1, what safety step is required first?
options: A. Open the faucet handle all the way so water pressure flushes the pipe while you unscrew the valve stem.

B. Shut off the fixture or main water supply valve (and relieve line pressure) before disassembling plumbing, or switch off the specific circuit breaker at the service panel and verify the wires are dead with a non-contact voltage tester before touching electrical terminals.
C. Tape the wall toggle switch in the 'off' position with masking tape and work on the live brass terminal screws with bare fingers.
D. Stand on the top cap of a folding step ladder while leaning two feet outside the side rails to reach an overhead ceiling fixture.

pamphlet_excerpts: Under the supervision of your parent: Wall Works, Caulking, and Weather-Stripping PAINT TRAY ROLLERS Using rollers gets a paint job done quickly (p. 45).
Under the supervision of your parent Principle 2: The fibers on the roller covers are known ROLLER as the nap, usually described by the fiber length, COVERS which ranges from 1⁄4" to 13⁄4 (p. 45).
Under the supervision of your parent Principle 3: Generally, the rougher the surface you are painting, the longer the nap you should use (p. 45).
Under the supervision of your parent Principle 4: The longer nap makes it possible to work paint into irregular surfaces such as concrete block and highly textured walls like stucco (p. 45).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Under the supervision of your parent): The smoother the surface you are painting, and the smoother the finish you want, the shorter the nap you should use (p. 45).
Step 2 (Under the supervision of your parent): Lead-based paint can cause serious health problems (p. 45).
Step 3 (Under the supervision of your parent): Removing it is such a high-risk job that it is best left to aprofessional (p. 45).
Step 4 (Under the supervision of your parent): Structures built prior to 1978 are likely to have been painted with lead-based paint (p. 45).

pamphlet_excerpts: Under the supervision of your parent: Toggles in a circuit breaker flip to "off" or to a center position for both short circuits and circuit overloads (p. 24).

Under the supervision of your parent Principle 2: To reset the circuit and restore power, flip the switch to full "off" and then back to "on." Circuit breaker fuses have a reset button or switch (p. 24).
Under the supervision of your parent Principle 3: When blown, they can be reactivated with the button or switch (p. 24).
Under the supervision of your parent Principle 4: Push the switch to the "off" position, then back to the "on" position (p. 24).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Under the supervision of your parent): The main electrical service entrance to your home is through a service panel containing fuses, circuit breakers, or both (p. 24).
Step 2 (Under the supervision of your parent): The panel usually is located in the basement or utility room, or in a closet on an outside wall (p. 24).

Step 3 (Under the supervision of your parent): An older home can have more than one service entrance, and many homes have additional disconnect panels for outside supplies, such as airconditioner (p. 24).
Step 4 (Under the supervision of your parent): Never replace a fuse with one that has the improper amperage rating or size (p. 24).

pamphlet_excerpts: Under the supervision of your parent: Use caustic commercial drain cleaner only as a last resort, and never in a completely clogged drain (p. 32).
Under the supervision of your parent Principle 2: These products are highly corrosive to plumbing systems (p. 32).
Under the supervision of your parent Principle 3: The drainage systems in homes have two parts: traps in the shapes of a drum or J, S, or P, plus pipes to which the traps are connected (p. 32).
Under the supervision of your parent Principle 4: When water or waste won't run out of a sink, tub, or toilet, debris is blocking the route in the pipe or trap (p. 32).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Under the supervision of your parent): Remove the stopper or drain cover and clean off any accumulation of soap scum and hair with paper towels and pipe cleaners. 2 (p. 32).
Step 2 (Under the supervision of your parent): Try a commercial drain cleaner on slow-draining sinks or tubs (p. 32).
Step 3 (Under the supervision of your parent): Give it plenty of time to work, a few minutes longer than specified on the package (p. 32).
Step 4 (Under the supervision of your parent): If the drain is still slow, don't risk a chemical burn by immediately trying repairs involving augers or trap removal (p. 32).

requirements.lead_text: Under the supervision of your parent, guardian, or counselor, do THREE of the following:
requirements.req_text: Under the supervision of your parent, guardian, or counselor, do THREE of the following: (a) Paint a wall or ceiling. (b) Repair or replace damaged tile, linoleum, or vinyl flooring. (c) Install drapery or curtain rods and then hang drapes or curtains. (d) Repair a hole in drywall. (e) Secure a picture, plant hanger, or other object approved by your parent or guardian to drywall using anchors. (f) Reinforce a picture frame. (g) Mend an object made of china, glass, or pottery. (h) Fix a drawer slide or fix/replace cabinet pulls.

pamphlet_excerpts: Careers & Professional Pathways: Wall Works, Caulking, and Weather-Stripping PAINT TRAY ROLLERS Using rollers gets a paint job done quickly (p. 45).
Careers & Professional Pathways Principle 2: The fibers on the roller covers are known ROLLER as the nap, usually described by the fiber length, COVERS which ranges from 1⁄4" to 13⁄4 (p. 45).
Careers & Professional Pathways Principle 3: Generally, the rougher the surface you are painting, the longer the nap you should use (p. 45).
Careers & Professional Pathways Principle 4: The longer nap makes it possible to work paint into irregular surfaces such as concrete block and highly textured walls like stucco (p. 45).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Careers & Professional Pathways): The smoother the surface you are painting, and the smoother the finish you want, the shorter the nap you should use (p. 45).
Step 2 (Careers & Professional Pathways): Lead-based paint can cause serious health problems (p. 45).
Step 3 (Careers & Professional Pathways): Removing it is such a high-risk job that it is best left to aprofessional (p. 45).
Step 4 (Careers & Professional Pathways): Structures built prior to 1978 are likely to have been painted with lead-based paint (p. 45).

pamphlet_excerpts: Safety precautions you should take: Before you handle a horse, you should know afew safety rules (p. 25).
Safety precautions you should take Principle 2: Because horses can sense if you are afraid, be confident yet careful around them (p. 25).
Safety precautions you should take Principle 3: Prevent accidents and injuries by following these rules. Ground Safety -Never startle a horse (p. 25).
Safety precautions you should take Principle 4: You might startle it and cause it to kick, which could result in a serious injury (p. 25).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Safety precautions you should take): Free-choice salt can be provided by securing to the stall wall a white salt block that they can access as needed (p. 25).
Step 2 (Safety precautions you should take): Horses left to pasture spend much of their time grazing on grass (p. 25).
Step 3 (Safety precautions you should take): They often have to eat a lot of grass to gain enough nutrients (p. 25).
Step 4 (Safety precautions you should take): If the pasture grass is poor in nutrients and vitamins, concentrated feedmix can help provide a more balanced diet (p. 25).

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: When approaching, haltering, and leading a horse in Horsemanship Requirement 1, which technique keeps both handler and horse safe?
quiz_item.question: When approaching, haltering, and leading a horse in Horsemanship Requirement 1, which technique keeps both handler and horse safe?
options: A. Walk silently directly behind the horse's hindquarters and slap its croup so it knows you have entered the stall.
B. Wrap the excess lead rope tightly around your hand and wrist in three loops so the horse cannot pull away if it spooks.

C. Approach calmly at an angle toward the horse's left (near) shoulder while speaking softly to stay out of its blind spots (directly in front of the nose and directly behind the tail), wear an ASTM/SEI equestrian helmet and sturdy boots, and hold the folded excess lead rope in a figure-eight (never coiled around your hand).
D. Duck underneath the horse's neck or belly to cross from the left side to the right side quickly.
choices: A. Walk silently directly behind the horse's hindquarters and slap its croup so it knows you have entered the stall.
B. Wrap the excess lead rope tightly around your hand and wrist in three loops so the horse cannot pull away if it spooks.

C. Approach calmly at an angle toward the horse's left (near) shoulder while speaking softly to stay out of its blind spots (directly in front of the nose and directly behind the tail), wear an ASTM/SEI equestrian helmet and sturdy boots, and hold the folded excess lead rope in a figure-eight (never coiled around your hand).
D. Duck underneath the horse's neck or belly to cross from the left side to the right side quickly.
quiz_item.correct_answer: C. Approach calmly at an angle toward the horse's left (near) shoulder while speaking softly to stay out of its blind spots (directly in front of the nose and directly behind the tail), wear an ASTM/SEI equestrian helmet and sturdy boots, and hold the folded excess lead rope in a figure-eight (never coiled around your hand).
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (C): Because horses have blind spots directly behind their hindquarters and directly in front of their noses, handlers approach calmly toward the shoulder while speaking softly, wear ASTM/SEI helmets when riding, and fold (never loop) the lead rope around the hand.

pamphlet_excerpts: Importance of Hoof Care: A horse's usefulness depends greatly on the condition of its hooves, which need daily inspection and attention to stay healthy (p. 39).
Importance of Hoof Care Principle 2: In addition, long-term exposure to bacteria can lead to infections (p. 39).
Importance of Hoof Care Principle 3: Starting when a horse is about 6 weeks old, the hooves should be leveled with a rasp (file) by a horseshoer (farrier) to prevent the bones from growing (p. 39).
Importance of Hoof Care Principle 4: Lifting, inspecting, and cleaning the hooves daily will prepare the horse for the possible next step of shoeing (p. 39).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Importance of Hoof Care): Use the hoof pick to carefully clean the bottom of each hoof from heel to toe (p. 39).
Step 2 (Importance of Hoof Care): Rasping and shoeing should be done only by a farrier (p. 39).
Step 3 (Importance of Hoof Care): A hoof pick probably will be the most important item in your grooming kit (p. 39).
Step 4 (Importance of Hoof Care): Shoes help prevent excessive hoof wear under rocky conditions (p. 39).

pamphlet_excerpts: Groom A Horse: Here are the steps to help you care for the hooves (p. 40).
Groom A Horse Principle 2: Step 1, Put a halter on the horse and tie it to a secure fence, rail, or post attachment with a quick-release knot (p. 40).
Groom A Horse Principle 3: Make sure the horse is standing square with its weight evenly distributed (p. 40).
Groom A Horse Principle 4: Step 2, Stand beside the horse's left foreleg, facing toward the tail (p. 40).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Groom A Horse): Run your left hand down the leg so the horse is aware that you are going to do something (p. 40).
Step 2 (Groom A Horse): Many horses will lift the foot when the hand reaches the pastern (just below the fetlock joint and above the hoof) (p. 40).
Step 3 (Groom A Horse): Step 4, If your horse still does not pick up its foot, lean against the horse slightly, pushing its weight to the other foreleg while trying steps (p. 40).
Step 4 (Groom A Horse): A professional shoer at work A shod horse's hooves should be picked daily (p. 40).

pamphlet_excerpts: Determine What and How Much: Although horses are built to forage, it is not always practical to put a horse out to pasture (p. 52).
Determine What and How Much Principle 2: When feeding, there are a few rules to follow. Provide an amount of feed appropriate to the horse's activity level (p. 52).
Determine What and How Much Principle 3: Too much feed can cause digestive and circulatory problems (p. 52).
Determine What and How Much Principle 4: Too little feed can lead to a loss of energy, and it could harm the horse's overall condition (p. 52).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Determine What and How Much): If your horse is stabled, give it clean water before feeding. Do not feed a horse that is tired or overheated (p. 52).
Step 2 (Determine What and How Much): Let a horse cool off sufficiently after exercise or work before allowing it to eat. Water is critical for a horse's health (p. 52).
Step 3 (Determine What and How Much): It helps produce saliva and other fluids, regulates body temperature, carries nutrients through the body, and is important for digestion (p. 52).
Step 4 (Determine What and How Much): A horse can drink from 4 to 15 or more gallons of water each day, depending on the weather, amount of work, and its age and size (p. 52).

pamphlet_excerpts: Safety With Horses: Before you handle a horse, you should know afew safety rules (p. 9).
Safety With Horses Principle 2: Because horses can sense if you are afraid, be confident yet careful around them (p. 9).
Safety With Horses Principle 3: Prevent accidents and injuries by following these rules. Ground Safety -Never startle a horse (p. 9).
Safety With Horses Principle 4: You might startle it and cause it to kick, which could result in a serious injury (p. 9).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Safety With Horses): The leader of a wild herd usually is an older mare that the other horses respect (p. 9).
Step 2 (Safety With Horses): She leads the herd to food and safety and even settles disputes, sometimes using discipline (p. 9).
Step 3 (Safety With Horses): If a stallion is part of the herd, he protects the herd and leads it to food and water while the lead mare still leads the herd in social (p. 9).
Step 4 (Safety With Horses): To practice good horsemanship, you will need to Humans and horses become the leader of your horse (p. 9).

requirements.req_text: On level ground, continuously do the following movements after safely mounting the horse. Do them correctly, at ease, and in harmony with the horse. (a) Walk the horse in a straight line for 60 feet. (b) Walk the horse in a half-circle of not more than 16 feet in radius. (c) Trot or jog the horse in a straight line for 60 feet. (d) Trot or jog the horse in a half-circle of not more than 30 feet in radius. (e) Halt straight. (f) Back up straight four paces. (g) Halt and dismount.

pamphlet_excerpts: On level ground, continuously: Never back ahorse by pulling or jerking on the mouth (p. 49).
On level ground, continuously Principle 2: As you teach your horse to move backward with a halter, remember that horses dislike moving backward (p. 49).
On level ground, continuously Principle 3: Your horse'sfirst reaction might be to raise its head and plant its hind feet (p. 49).
On level ground, continuously Principle 4: However, there is an effective way to teach your horse to back (p. 49).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (On level ground, continuously): Step 1, Stand on the left side of the horse, near the withers, with the lead rope in your right hand (p. 49).
Step 2 (On level ground, continuously): Use the rope to bump the horse's forefeet back while using your left hand to keep the horse's nose straight (p. 49).
Step 3 (On level ground, continuously): Just move the horse back a step at a time while saying "back." It might help to have the horse facing a wall so that it can't go forward (p. 49).
Step 4 (On level ground, continuously): Step 2, If the horse won't move, push the horse at the chest, where the muscles join (p. 49).

patrol_quiz_bank.question: When approaching, haltering, and leading a horse in Horsemanship Requirement 1, which technique keeps both handler and horse safe?
options: A. Walk silently directly behind the horse's hindquarters and slap its croup so it knows you have entered the stall.
B. Wrap the excess lead rope tightly around your hand and wrist in three loops so the horse cannot pull away if it spooks.

pamphlet_excerpts: Different American Indian cultural areas: From the brief descriptions in this pamphlet, you have learned some of the difficulties American Indian tribes faced after the arrival of Europeans (p. 91).
Different American Indian cultural areas Principle 2: Native peoples lost so much that by the late 19th and early 20th centuries, it seemed to some observers that they must be doomed (p. 91).
Different American Indian cultural areas Principle 3: Others lost huge numbers of their people and all of their lands and possessions (p. 91).

Different American Indian cultural areas Principle 4: Some, like the Mission Indians of California, lost cultural memories, their Indian ways of living and s urviving, after being under missionary (p. 91).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Different American Indian cultural areas): Some people predicted that eventually all Indian cultures and their traditional ways would be lost and that finally the Indians themselves (p. 91).
Step 2 (Different American Indian cultural areas): Native peoples endured, and today there are about 2 million American Indians living in the United States (p. 91).
Step 3 (Different American Indian cultural areas): Today, more than half of American Indians live outside the reservations that were set aside for them by the federal government (p. 91).
Step 4 (Different American Indian cultural areas): Many live in big cities; others live in smaller communities and rural areas (p. 91).

pamphlet_excerpts: American Indian Tribe: An American Indian tribe, group: Indians are relearning lost traditions and languages and reviving their arts and crafts, their songs, dances, and stories (p. 71).

American Indian Tribe Principle 2: An American Indian tribe, group Principle 2: Many have chosen not to disappear into America's "melting pot." Indians are reclaiming control over what happens to them (p. 71).
American Indian Tribe Principle 3: An American Indian tribe, group Principle 3: They want to decide for themselves how they will live in the modern world (p. 71).

American Indian Tribe Principle 4: An American Indian tribe, group Principle 4: The question is, how can they keep cultural roots alive and protect and preserve tribal identities, yet still be a part of modern society (p. 71).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (American Indian Tribe): Step 1 (An American Indian tribe, group): There is no easy answer, and no one knows what the future holds (p. 71).

Step 2 (American Indian Tribe): Step 2 (An American Indian tribe, group): The history of American Indians is filled with the names ofmen and women who are remembered for deeds that set them apart from others (p. 71).
Step 3 (American Indian Tribe): Step 3 (An American Indian tribe, group): They may have been renowned leaders, peacemakers, or lawmakers (p. 71).
Step 4 (American Indian Tribe): Step 4 (An American Indian tribe, group): Some, like Pocahontas, Sacajawea, Hahyonhwatha (known as "Hiawatha"), and Tecumseh, lived centuries ago (p. 71).

pamphlet_excerpts: Learn Common Terms in An: Learn 10 Common Terms: Indians are relearning lost traditions and languages and reviving their arts and crafts, their songs, dances, and stories (p. 91).

Learn Common Terms in An Principle 2: Learn 10 Common Terms Principle 2: Many have chosen not to disappear into America's "melting pot." Indians are reclaiming control over what happens to them (p. 91).
Learn Common Terms in An Principle 3: Learn 10 Common Terms Principle 3: They want to decide for themselves how they will live in the modern world (p. 91).

Learn Common Terms in An Principle 4: Learn 10 Common Terms Principle 4: The question is, how can they keep cultural roots alive and protect and preserve tribal identities, yet still be a part of modern society (p. 91).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Learn Common Terms in An): Step 1 (Learn 10 Common Terms): There is no easy answer, and no one knows what the future holds (p. 91).

Step 2 (Learn Common Terms in An): Step 2 (Learn 10 Common Terms): The history of American Indians is filled with the names ofmen and women who are remembered for deeds that set them apart from others (p. 91).
Step 3 (Learn Common Terms in An): Step 3 (Learn 10 Common Terms): They may have been renowned leaders, peacemakers, or lawmakers (p. 91).
Step 4 (Learn Common Terms in An): Step 4 (Learn 10 Common Terms): Some, like Pocahontas, Sacajawea, Hahyonhwatha (known as "Hiawatha"), and Tecumseh, lived centuries ago (p. 91).

step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Life Might Have Been): Step 1 (Describe How Life): You might also investigate how Indians live and work today and carry on their ancient traditions (p. 9).
Step 2 (Life Might Have Been): Step 2 (Describe How Life): Ask your school or public librarian for books and other materials about different Indian groups (p. 9).
Step 3 (Life Might Have Been): Step 3 (Describe How Life): If you have anatural history museum in your area, ask the curator or person in charge for information (p. 9).
Step 4 (Life Might Have Been): Step 4 (Describe How Life): See if your town or city has an American Indian center, oran Indian tribal council or similar governing group (p. 9).

pamphlet_excerpts: Museum Either In-person or Virtually: Visit a museum either in-person: Indians are relearning lost traditions and languages and reviving their arts and crafts, their songs, dances, and stories (p. 37).

Museum Either In-person or Virtually Principle 2: Visit a museum either in-person Principle 2: Many have chosen not to disappear into America's "melting pot." Indians are reclaiming control over what happens to them (p. 37).
Museum Either In-person or Virtually Principle 3: Visit a museum either in-person Principle 3: They want to decide for themselves how they will live in the modern world (p. 37).

Museum Either In-person or Virtually Principle 4: Visit a museum either in-person Principle 4: The question is, how can they keep cultural roots alive and protect and preserve tribal identities, yet still be a part of modern society (p. 37).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Museum Either In-person or Virtually): Step 1 (Visit a museum either in-person): There is no easy answer, and no one knows what the future holds (p. 37).

Step 2 (Museum Either In-person or Virtually): Step 2 (Visit a museum either in-person): The history of American Indians is filled with the names ofmen and women who are remembered for deeds that set them apart from others (p. 37).
Step 3 (Museum Either In-person or Virtually): Step 3 (Visit a museum either in-person): They may have been renowned leaders, peacemakers, or lawmakers (p. 37).

Step 4 (Museum Either In-person or Virtually): Step 4 (Visit a museum either in-person): Some, like Pocahontas, Sacajawea, Hahyonhwatha (known as "Hiawatha"), and Tecumseh, lived centuries ago (p. 37).

Step 3 (Hazards, First Aid & Safety): Be careful when walking through areas where spiders and biting insects might be lurking (p. 36).
Step 4 (Hazards, First Aid & Safety): Watch out for fire ants, which live in loose mounds of dirt (p. 36).

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: While observing insects in the field for Insect Study Requirement 1, what morphological traits distinguish true insects (Class Insecta) from spiders and ticks (Class Arachnida), and how should you treat a honeybee sting?
quiz_item.question: While observing insects in the field for Insect Study Requirement 1, what morphological traits distinguish true insects (Class Insecta) from spiders and ticks (Class Arachnida), and how should you treat a honeybee sting?
options: A. Adult insects have two body regions, eight legs, and no antennae; if stung by a honeybee, squeeze the venom sac firmly between tweezers to inject the remaining venom.
B. Insects and spiders both have internal vertebrate backbones and six wings; bee stings should be treated by applying a tourniquet above the knee.
C. Spiders have three body segments and compound eyes with antennae, whereas insects have a cephalothorax and abdomen with eight legs.

D. Adult insects have three body regions (head, thorax, abdomen), three pairs of jointed legs (six total), one pair of antennae, and usually one or two pairs of wings (unlike eight-legged arachnids); scrape a honeybee stinger out sideways with a flat edge, wash the site, apply a cold pack, and watch closely for signs of anaphylaxis.

quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (D): True insects possess a three-part body (head, thorax, abdomen), six legs, and antennae; if stung by a honeybee, scraping the barbed stinger away avoids squeezing extra venom from the attached sac, while monitoring for severe allergic reactions (anaphylaxis).

requirements.req_text: Life Cycles. Do the following: (a) Compare the life histories of a butterfly and a grasshopper. Tell how they are different. (b) Raise an insect through complete metamorphosis from its larval stage to its adult stage (e. g., raise a butterfly or moth from a caterpillar). (Some insects are endangered species and are protected by federal or state law. Every species is found only in its own special type of habitat. Be sure to check natural resources authorities in advance to be sure that you will not be collecting any species that is known to be protected or endangered, or in any habitat where collecting is prohibited. In most cases, all specimens should be returned at the location of capture after the requirement has been met. Check with your counselor for those instances where the return of these specimens would not be appropriate.)

pamphlet_excerpts: Life Cycles: The most accurate observation of an insect in nature comes from watching it undisturbed (p. 35).
Life Cycles Principle 2: When observing insects in their habitat, be careful to leave them unharmed in the place that you found them (p. 35).
Life Cycles Principle 3: The Seven Principles of Leave No Trace and the Outdoor Code apply to all outdoor activities, including insect study (p. 35).
Life Cycles Principle 4: Requirements for the Insect Study merit badge call for you to not only observe insects, but in some cases, to collect them (p. 35).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Life Cycles): As with any trek in the outdoors, there are some basic guidelines to follow when searching for insects. 1 (p. 35).
Step 2 (Life Cycles): When you embark on your insect safari, prepare a trip plan, or at the very least, tell an adult where you are going (p. 35).
Step 3 (Life Cycles): It is also a good idea to take a friend with you. 2 (p. 35).
Step 4 (Life Cycles): It is a good idea to wear long pants, a long-sleeved shirt, ahat, and closed shoes to keep ticks, chiggers, and insects from biting you or hitching (p. 35).

requirements.lead_text: Observation and Analysis. Do the following:
requirements.req_text: Observation and Analysis. Do the following: (a) Discuss the importance of the Leave No Trace Seven Principles and the Outdoor Code as they relate to insect study. Explain how you have followed the Leave No Trace Seven Principles and the Outdoor Code during field observation, specimen collection, and identification. (b) Observe 20 different live species of insects in their habitat. In your observations, include at least four orders of insects. (c) Make a scrapbook of the 20 insects you observe in 4(b). Include photographs, sketches, illustrations, and articles. Label each insect with its common and scientific names, where possible. Share your scrapbook with your counselor. Resources: How To Start a Bug Collection (video) How To Make an Insect Collection: Spreading (video) Collecting Insects: Tools and Supplies (video) Insect Collecting, Tools & Tips (video) (d) From your scrapbook collection, select eight species of insects and identify what role they play in the ecosystem.

Food Plants of Butterfly and Moth Larvae Principle 2: They also are valuable in studies of pollution problems and of ecology, the relationship of living things to their surroundings (p. 46).
Food Plants of Butterfly and Moth Larvae Principle 3: Many birds and some mammals live almost entirely on insects (p. 46).
Food Plants of Butterfly and Moth Larvae Principle 4: Some people say insects make tasty snacks, like thesemealworm larvae (p. 46).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Food Plants of Butterfly and Moth Larvae): In South Africa, some people roast termites and eat them by the handful, like popcorn (p. 46).
Step 2 (Food Plants of Butterfly and Moth Larvae): Some people in Mexico make a cake from the eggs of water boatmen (p. 46).
Step 3 (Food Plants of Butterfly and Moth Larvae): In Australia, grubs are roasted and eaten by the Aborigines (p. 46).
Step 4 (Food Plants of Butterfly and Moth Larvae): Studying insects can help you discover how closely connected all living things (p. 46).

pamphlet_excerpts: Insects and People: The work of entomologists can prevent the spread of disease, help farmers grow crops, save endangered species, and help solve crimes (p. 75).
Insects and People Principle 2: Here are some examples of what entomologists can achieve and where they find employment (p. 75).
Insects and People Principle 3: At least one-sixth of the human race suffers from insect-borne diseases (p. 75).
Insects and People Principle 4: A crop duster sprays pesticide on a crop of peas near Walla Walla, Washington (p. 75).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Insects and People): Entomologists work to reduce the crop losses that insects cause, which can help to relieve some of the food shortages that exist in many parts (p. 75).
Step 2 (Insects and People): Entomologists also work with foresters to battle the insect pests that injure trees, destroy timber, and damage the biological riches found (p. 75).
Step 3 (Insects and People): Plant protection entomologists study insect pests and figure out ways to protect crops, trees, flowers, and other plants from attack and injury (p. 75).
Step 4 (Insects and People): Others work outside, gathering pollen and nectar to provide the raw material for the colony's food (p. 75).

pamphlet_excerpts: Conservation Migration Route Insect: Conservation: Monarch butterfly chrysalis The chrysalis is a shiny, transparent green with several spots of gold (p. 22).
Conservation Migration Route Insect Principle 2: Conservation Principle 2: It hangs from the leaf for several days to about three weeks, depending on the weather (p. 22).

Conservation Migration Route Insect Principle 3: Conservation Principle 3: Near the end of this period, the chrysalis turns very dark (almost black), and the wing pattern of the adult butterfly can be seen beneath the thin skin (p. 22).
Conservation Migration Route Insect Principle 4: Conservation Principle 4: Finally, the bottom of the chrysalis splits and out crawls the adult monarch butterfly (p. 22).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Conservation Migration Route Insect): Step 1 (Conservation): Its wings gradually expand and harden, and the butterfly starts to use its long, hollow, coiled "tongue" to suck nectar from flowers (p. 22).
Step 2 (Conservation Migration Route Insect): Step 2 (Conservation): Usually, the adult will live four to six weeks, feeding occasionally but mostly just wandering from field to field (p. 22).
Step 3 (Conservation Migration Route Insect): Step 3 (Conservation): The last brood of summer, however, will migrate south, often in large numbers and journeying an incredible 2,500 miles (p. 22).
Step 4 (Conservation Migration Route Insect): Step 4 (Conservation): This brood lives longer, some of the monarchs live through the winter in Mexico or along the southern coast of California (p. 22).

pamphlet_excerpts: Careers & Professional Pathways: By identifying endangered insect species and studying their habitats, conservation entomologists can help rebuild threatened ecosystems (p. 91).

Careers & Professional Pathways Principle 2: Many are involved in education and outreach programs at natural history museums, nature centers, zoos, conservation agencies, and extension offices (p. 91).
Careers & Professional Pathways Principle 3: Forensic entomologists help in police investigations by examining insects that inhabit decomposing remains (p. 91).
Careers & Professional Pathways Principle 4: For example, insects can help establish the time of death (p. 91).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Careers & Professional Pathways): Among the first insects to arrive on a newly dead body are blow flies, and a femaleblowfly usually lays eggs within a very short time after arriving (p. 91).
Step 2 (Careers & Professional Pathways): A researcher who knows how long it takes blowfly eggs to reach these different stages can estimate the time of the victim's death (p. 91).
Step 3 (Careers & Professional Pathways): Few people are employed full-time as forensic entomologists (p. 91).
Step 4 (Careers & Professional Pathways): Most are affiliated with colleges or universities, teach entomology or biology, and do research (p. 91).

patrol_quiz_bank.question: While observing insects in the field for Insect Study Requirement 1, what morphological traits distinguish true insects (Class Insecta) from spiders and ticks (Class Arachnida), and how should you treat a honeybee sting?
options: A. Adult insects have two body regions, eight legs, and no antennae; if stung by a honeybee, squeeze the venom sac firmly between tweezers to inject the remaining venom.
B. Insects and spiders both have internal vertebrate backbones and six wings; bee stings should be treated by applying a tourniquet above the knee.
C. Spiders have three body segments and compound eyes with antennae, whereas insects have a cephalothorax and abdomen with eight legs.

D. Adult insects have three body regions (head, thorax, abdomen), three pairs of jointed legs (six total), one pair of antennae, and usually one or two pairs of wings (unlike eight-legged arachnids); scrape a honeybee stinger out sideways with a flat edge, wash the site, apply a cold pack, and watch closely for signs of anaphylaxis.

pamphlet_excerpts: In your own words, define inventing: Impact of Inventing on Humankind Impact of Inventing on Humankind The impact of inventing on humankind is inestimable (p. 21).
In your own words, define inventing Principle 2: Not only have inventions improved the quality of life for countless people around the world, they have also changed the course of history (p. 21).
In your own words, define inventing Principle 3: Technology has become such a large part of our daily lives that we cannot imagine surviving without the conveniences it has brought to us (p. 21).
In your own words, define inventing Principle 4: Texting would not exist, and to make phone calls you would have to use a landline (p. 21).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (In your own words, define inventing): There are countless opportunities for new products and services that take advantage of high-speed worldwide communications and transportation (p. 21).

Step 2 (In your own words, define inventing): We live in an exciting time with a global environment for knowledge sharing and distance learning, both of which foster opportunities for working (p. 21).
Step 3 (In your own words, define inventing): Recounting all of the inventions that have impacted humankind could fill a library (p. 21).
Step 4 (In your own words, define inventing): Let'slook at three "historical" inventors and their inventions to see how they changed our world (p. 21).

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: In Inventing Requirement 1, what is the difference between an invention and an innovation, and why does an inventor maintain a bound, chronologically dated inventor's logbook?
quiz_item.question: In Inventing Requirement 1, what is the difference between an invention and an innovation, and why does an inventor maintain a bound, chronologically dated inventor's logbook?
options: A. An invention is a marketing slogan, while an innovation is a trademark logo; the logbook is used only to record employee vacation days.

B. An invention is the creation of a novel device, process, or composition that did not exist before, whereas an innovation improves, adapts, or applies an existing invention to solve problems in a practical new way; a signed, dated logbook documents design iterations, test data, and conception history alongside prior art searches for patent protection.
C. Inventions cannot be patented in the United States, whereas innovations automatically receive eternal copyright protection without filing an application.
D. An inventor's logbook must be written on loose sticky notes that are thrown away each time a prototype fails a test.
choices: A. An invention is a marketing slogan, while an innovation is a trademark logo; the logbook is used only to record employee vacation days.

B. An invention is the creation of a novel device, process, or composition that did not exist before, whereas an innovation improves, adapts, or applies an existing invention to solve problems in a practical new way; a signed, dated logbook documents design iterations, test data, and conception history alongside prior art searches for patent protection.
C. Inventions cannot be patented in the United States, whereas innovations automatically receive eternal copyright protection without filing an application.
D. An inventor's logbook must be written on loose sticky notes that are thrown away each time a prototype fails a test.
quiz_item.correct_answer: B. An invention is the creation of a novel device, process, or composition that did not exist before, whereas an innovation improves, adapts, or applies an existing invention to solve problems in a practical new way; a signed, dated logbook documents design iterations, test data, and conception history alongside prior art searches for patent protection.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (B): Inventing creates something fundamentally new while innovating refines or applies existing technology effectively; keeping a permanent, dated engineering notebook records the inventive process and supports U.S. patent applications.

Interview an adult who has invented Principle 2: However, be prepared to spend sometime learning it well enough to build an invention from your 3D model (p. 65).

step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Interview an adult who has invented): Professionals usually begin by building scale models of new things like boats, vehicles, or airplanes that are expensive to create (p. 65).
Step 2 (Interview an adult who has invented): Inventor Carl Dietrich did not begin by building his "road-able aircraft" at full scale (p. 65).
Step 3 (Interview an adult who has invented): By making models, inventors can refine design and mechanical issues and correct mistakes and make improvements before building the final product (p. 65).
Step 4 (Interview an adult who has invented): Models can be made from a variety of materials: Clay, cardboard, wood, fabric, LEGO® blocks, metal conduit, and PVC pipe all are useful (p. 65).

pamphlet_excerpts: Types of Inventions: Impact of Inventing on Humankind Impact of Inventing on Humankind The impact of inventing on humankind is inestimable (p. 21).
Types of Inventions Principle 2: Not only have inventions improved the quality of life for countless people around the world, they have also changed the course of history (p. 21).
Types of Inventions Principle 3: Technology has become such a large part of our daily lives that we cannot imagine surviving without the conveniences it has brought to us (p. 21).
Types of Inventions Principle 4: Texting would not exist, and to make phone calls you would have to use a landline (p. 21).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Types of Inventions): There are countless opportunities for new products and services that take advantage of high-speed worldwide communications and transportation (p. 21).
Step 2 (Types of Inventions): We live in an exciting time with a global environment for knowledge sharing and distance learning, both of which foster opportunities for working (p. 21).
Step 3 (Types of Inventions): Recounting all of the inventions that have impacted humankind could fill a library (p. 21).
Step 4 (Types of Inventions): Let'slook at three "historical" inventors and their inventions to see how they changed our world (p. 21).

requirements.req_text: Think of an item you would like to invent that would solve a problem for your family, troop, chartered organization, community, or a special-interest group. Then do the following, while keeping a notebook to record your progress. (a) Talk to potential users of your invention and determine their needs. Then, based on what you have learned, write a statement describing the invention and how it would help solve a problem. This statement should include a detailed sketch of the invention. (b) Create a model of the invention using clay, cardboard, or any other readily available material. List the materials necessary to build a working prototype of the invention. (c) Share the idea and the model with your counselor and potential users of your invention. Record their feedback in your notebook.

pamphlet_excerpts: Participate with a club or team: The Lemelson-MIT Inven Team initiative is the premier national grants initiative for inventive high school students (p. 54).

Participate with a club or team Principle 2: Teams of students and mentors receive grants of up to $10,000 each to conceptualize, design, and build technological solutions to real-world problems (p. 54).
Participate with a club or team Principle 3: Projects are collaborative efforts, driven by the students (p. 54).
Participate with a club or team Principle 4: Inven Teams research intellectual property issues, design parts, build models, and make modifications as they develop prototypes (p. 54).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Participate with a club or team): Inven Teams showcase their prototypes each June at MIT (p. 54).
Step 2 (Participate with a club or team): Dalton Oesterreich is a member of the Omro (Wisconsin) High School Inven Team (p. 54).
Step 3 (Participate with a club or team): He's a technical designer with a team working on a local problem: to keep people and vehicles from falling through thin ice on lakes in the winter (p. 54).
Step 4 (Participate with a club or team): This Inven Team is inventing an "Internet of Things" (Io T) device that will measure and reportice thickness from on top of the ice (p. 54).

pamphlet_excerpts: Careers and Professional Pathways: Earning your Eagle Scout rank takes years of preparation just as being an accomplished athlete requires years of training (p. 53).
Careers and Professional Pathways Principle 2: Building your academic and technical foundation will greatly help you prepare for your journey of inventive thinking and doing (p. 53).
Careers and Professional Pathways Principle 3: The king wanted Archimedes to determine if his newcrown was made of pure gold, as specified, or of acheaper alloy (p. 53).
Careers and Professional Pathways Principle 4: If he could determine the volume of the irregularly shaped crown, he could calculate the density by dividing the mass by the volume (p. 53).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Careers and Professional Pathways): Thus, he could compare the crown's density to that of pure gold (p. 53).
Step 2 (Careers and Professional Pathways): As the story goes, he discovered how to determine the volume when getting into a bath and displacing the water (p. 53).
Step 3 (Careers and Professional Pathways): This illustrative story about breakthrough thinking and a Eureka! moment has endured over time (p. 53).
Step 4 (Careers and Professional Pathways): They recognize problems in their world and seek solutions (p. 53).

options: A. An invention is a marketing slogan, while an innovation is a trademark logo; the logbook is used only to record employee vacation days.

B. An invention is the creation of a novel device, process, or composition that did not exist before, whereas an innovation improves, adapts, or applies an existing invention to solve problems in a practical new way; a signed, dated logbook documents design iterations, test data, and conception history alongside prior art searches for patent protection.
C. Inventions cannot be patented in the United States, whereas innovations automatically receive eternal copyright protection without filing an application.
D. An inventor's logbook must be written on loose sticky notes that are thrown away each time a prototype fails a test.

pamphlet_excerpts: Freedom of the press: Journalists should never write something they know in advance to be false, nor should they write something carelessly, with reckless disregard for the truth (p. 20).
Freedom of the press Principle 2: Doing so can be used in a civil court as evidence of malice, the intention of doing someone harm (p. 20).
Freedom of the press Principle 3: Journalists must be careful to avoid committing defamation, or damaging someone's reputation with false statements (p. 20).
Freedom of the press Principle 4: When the damage comes from written words or photographs, it is called libel (p. 20).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Freedom of the press): When the offending words are spoken, it is called slander (p. 20).
Step 2 (Freedom of the press): Libel or slander happens, for example, when a journalist falsely reports that someone has committed a crime (p. 20).
Step 3 (Freedom of the press): The person falsely accused can sue the journalist and news organization in civil court (p. 20).
Step 4 (Freedom of the press): Journalists should respect people's privacy, their right to be left alone, out of public view (p. 20).

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: In Journalism Requirement 1, why does the First Amendment protect freedom of the press in a democracy, and how must a responsible journalist distinguish straight news reporting from an editorial or opinion column?
quiz_item.question: In Journalism Requirement 1, why does the First Amendment protect freedom of the press in a democracy, and how must a responsible journalist distinguish straight news reporting from an editorial or opinion column?
options: A. Freedom of the press allows reporters to publish fabricated quotes and defamatory falsehoods without checking any sources.
B. A straight news article should express the reporter's personal political endorsements in the opening paragraph and omit opposing viewpoints.

C. An independent press informs citizens and holds government and institutions accountable; straight hard news must verify facts across multiple credible sources and answer the 5 Ws and H objectively, while personal commentary and advocacy belong in clearly labeled editorials or op-eds.
D. Journalists are required by federal law to submit every local newspaper article to city hall for censorship before printing.
choices: A. Freedom of the press allows reporters to publish fabricated quotes and defamatory falsehoods without checking any sources.
B. A straight news article should express the reporter's personal political endorsements in the opening paragraph and omit opposing viewpoints.

C. An independent press informs citizens and holds government and institutions accountable; straight hard news must verify facts across multiple credible sources and answer the 5 Ws and H objectively, while personal commentary and advocacy belong in clearly labeled editorials or op-eds.
D. Journalists are required by federal law to submit every local newspaper article to city hall for censorship before printing.
quiz_item.correct_answer: C. An independent press informs citizens and holds government and institutions accountable; straight hard news must verify facts across multiple credible sources and answer the 5 Ws and H objectively, while personal commentary and advocacy belong in clearly labeled editorials or op-eds.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (C): A free press enables informed self-governance, and journalistic ethics require rigorous multi-source fact verification, fairness, and a clear separation between objective news reporting and labeled opinion/editorial writing.

requirements.lead_text: Do ONE of the following:
requirements.req_text: Do ONE of the following: (a) Option A, Newspaper, Magazine, and Online Journalism. (Ask your parent or guardian's permission for the online option.) Do ALL of the following: (1) On the same day, read a local news source or newspaper, a national news source or newspaper, a news magazine (online or printed), and a social media news feed. From each source, clip, read, and compare a story about the same event. Tell your counselor how long each story is and how fair and accurate the stories are in presenting different points of view. Tell how each source handled the story. (2) Visit the office of a newspaper, magazine, or internet news site. Ask for a tour of the various divisions (editorial, business, and printing). During your tour, talk to an executive from the business side about management's relations with reporters, editors, and photographers, and what makes a "good" newspaper, magazine, or internet news site. Note: If there are no opportunities for in-person visits in your community, a virtual visit is acceptable with the news site of your choice, provided your counselor approves this option in advance. (You can request a virtual visit with Scout Life magazine ) (b) Option B, Radio and Television Journalism. Do ALL of the following: (1) All on the same day, watch a local and national network newscast, listen to a radio newscast, and (with your parent or guardian's permission) view a national broadcast news source online. List the different news items and features presented, the different elements used, and the time in minutes and seconds and the online space devoted to each story. Compare the story lists and discuss whether the stories are fair and accurate. Explain why different news outlets treated the stories differently and/or presented a different point of view. (2) Visit a radio or television station. Ask for a tour of the various departments, concentrating on those related to news broadcasts. During your tour, talk to the station manager or other station management executive about station operations, particularly how management and the news staff work together, and what makes a "good" station. If possible, go with a reporter to cover a news event.

sub_requirements.sub_req_text: Option B, Radio and Television Journalism. Do ALL of the following: (1) All on the same day, watch a local and national network newscast, listen to a radio newscast, and (with your parent or guardian's permission) view a national broadcast news source online. List the different news items and features presented, the different elements used, and the time in minutes and seconds and the online space devoted to each story. Compare the story lists and discuss whether the stories are fair and accurate. Explain why different news outlets treated the stories differently and/or presented a different point of view. (2) Visit a radio or television station. Ask for a tour of the various departments, concentrating on those related to news broadcasts. During your tour, talk to the station manager or other station management executive about station operations, particularly how management and the news staff work together, and what makes a "good" station. If possible, go with a reporter to cover a news event.

pamphlet_excerpts: Journalism Specialized Field Options: In 1987, the Federal Communication Commission, which grants radio and television stations licenses to broadcast, repealed the Fairness Doctrine (p. 27).
Journalism Specialized Field Options Principle 2: This rule had required stations to present news of controversial issues of public importance, with all viewpoints given fair treatment (p. 27).
Journalism Specialized Field Options Principle 3: After the repeal, many stations reduced or eliminated their news staffs (p. 27).
Journalism Specialized Field Options Principle 4: Radio ranks second only to television in how much time people use it each day (p. 27).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Journalism Specialized Field Options): Broadcast radio reaches some 93 percent of all Americans (p. 27).
Step 2 (Journalism Specialized Field Options): In 2015, there were 15,470 licensed broadcast radio stations in the United States, a number that has been slowly increasing over the past (p. 27).
Step 3 (Journalism Specialized Field Options): The other important development was consolidation (p. 27).
Step 4 (Journalism Specialized Field Options): A single company owning dozens or even hundreds of radio stations could combine staffs and broadcast national, instead of local, programming (p. 27).

requirements.lead_text: Discuss the differences between a hard news story and a feature story. Explain what the five W's and H are. Then do ONE of the following:
requirements.req_text: Discuss the differences between a hard news story and a feature story. Explain what the five W's and H are. Then do ONE of the following: (a) Choose a current or an unusual event of interest to you, and write either a hard news article OR a feature article about the event. Gear the article for print OR online OR audio OR video journalism. Share your article with your counselor. (b) With your parent or guardian's permission and counselor's approval, interview someone in your community who is influential because of his or her leadership, talent, career, or life experiences. Then present to your counselor either a written or oral report telling what you learned about this person. (c) With your parent or guardian's permission and counselor's approval, read an autobiography written by a journalist you want to learn more about. Write an article that tells what you learned about this person and the contributions this person has made to the field of journalism. (d) Attend a Scouting event and write a 200-word article (feature or hard news) about the event. Use either the inverted pyramid style or the chronological style. Review the article with your counselor, then submit it to your community newspaper or Scouting America local council or district newsletter for consideration.
