pamphlet_excerpts: Cinematic Elements to Remember: Here are some points to consider as you begin shooting your first film (p. 36).
Cinematic Elements to Remember Principle 2: Imagine entering an elevator where two people are already in conversation (p. 36).
Cinematic Elements to Remember Principle 3: The individual on your left, a man, is looking to your right (p. 36).
Cinematic Elements to Remember Principle 4: The other person, a woman, is looking to your left to respond (p. 36).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Cinematic Elements to Remember): If you were filming this conversation in close-upshots, only one person might be seen speaking at a time (p. 36).
Step 2 (Cinematic Elements to Remember): If the man changes the direction he is looking, the audience will be confused as to who is talking (p. 36).
Step 3 (Cinematic Elements to Remember): When you develop a scripted conversation between two actors, there is an imaginary line called the axis line (p. 36).
Step 4 (Cinematic Elements to Remember): A scene will be easier for an audience to follow if the camera position does not cross this line (p. 36).

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: When filming a conversation between two characters on set, why must you maintain the 180-degree axis of action rule as you switch camera setups?
quiz_item.question: When filming a conversation between two characters on set, why must you maintain the 180-degree axis of action rule as you switch camera setups?
options: A. To ensure the camera microphone stays pointed away from background wind noise during outdoor shoots.
B. To keep the shutter speed locked at exactly double the frame rate when panning across a room.
C. To prevent lens flare by keeping the key light directly behind the camera on every shot.
D. To keep both characters looking toward each other on consistent sides of the frame so the audience does not become spatially disoriented when shots are cut together.
choices: A. To ensure the camera microphone stays pointed away from background wind noise during outdoor shoots.
B. To keep the shutter speed locked at exactly double the frame rate when panning across a room.
C. To prevent lens flare by keeping the key light directly behind the camera on every shot.
D. To keep both characters looking toward each other on consistent sides of the frame so the audience does not become spatially disoriented when shots are cut together.
quiz_item.correct_answer: D. To keep both characters looking toward each other on consistent sides of the frame so the audience does not become spatially disoriented when shots are cut together.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (D): Keeping all camera positions on one side of the imaginary 180-degree line of action preserves consistent screen direction and eyelines across cuts.

patrol_quiz_bank.question: When filming a conversation between two characters on set, why must you maintain the 180-degree axis of action rule as you switch camera setups?
options: A. To ensure the camera microphone stays pointed away from background wind noise during outdoor shoots.
B. To keep the shutter speed locked at exactly double the frame rate when panning across a room.
C. To prevent lens flare by keeping the key light directly behind the camera on every shot.
D. To keep both characters looking toward each other on consistent sides of the frame so the audience does not become spatially disoriented when shots are cut together.
choices: A. To ensure the camera microphone stays pointed away from background wind noise during outdoor shoots.
B. To keep the shutter speed locked at exactly double the frame rate when panning across a room.
C. To prevent lens flare by keeping the key light directly behind the camera on every shot.
D. To keep both characters looking toward each other on consistent sides of the frame so the audience does not become spatially disoriented when shots are cut together.
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: D. To keep both characters looking toward each other on consistent sides of the frame so the audience does not become spatially disoriented when shots are cut together.
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (D): Keeping all camera positions on one side of the imaginary 180-degree line of action preserves consistent screen direction and eyelines across cuts.

pamphlet_excerpts: Hazards, First Aid & Safety: Multi sport SAfety (p. 14).
Hazards, First Aid & Safety Principle 2: Note where busy roads are and look both ways before continuing (p. 14).
Hazards, First Aid & Safety Principle 3: Although athletes have the right of way at most pedestrian crossings, be safe and watch out for people who may not see you coming (p. 14).
Hazards, First Aid & Safety Principle 4: An abrasion is a wound that occurs as a result of the outer layers of the skin being rubbed or scraped (p. 14).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Hazards, First Aid & Safety): Abrasions may happen when the skin is scraped against a hard surface, for example, when a bicyclist falls onto the pavement (p. 14).
Step 2 (Hazards, First Aid & Safety): The greatest danger lies in contamination and possible infection of the wound (p. 14).
Step 3 (Hazards, First Aid & Safety): Treat a minor cut or scrape by flushing the area with clean water for at least five minutes or until all foreign matter appears to be washed away (p. 14).
Step 4 (Hazards, First Aid & Safety): Blisters are pockets of fluid that form when the skin is injured by friction (p. 14).

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: During the swim-to-bike and bike-to-run transitions in a triathlon, what rule applies to handling your CPSC-approved cycling helmet?
quiz_item.question: During the swim-to-bike and bike-to-run transitions in a triathlon, what rule applies to handling your CPSC-approved cycling helmet?
options: A. You may unrack the bike first and buckle your helmet chin strap while coasting through the transition exit chute.
B. Your helmet must be on your head with the chin strap securely buckled before you unrack or touch your bike, and it must stay buckled until the bike is re-racked.
C. A helmet is only required on road courses with hills steeper than five percent and is optional inside the transition zone.
D. You should leave the chin strap unbuckled for the first mile after the swim so water can drain from your ears.
choices: A. You may unrack the bike first and buckle your helmet chin strap while coasting through the transition exit chute.
B. Your helmet must be on your head with the chin strap securely buckled before you unrack or touch your bike, and it must stay buckled until the bike is re-racked.
C. A helmet is only required on road courses with hills steeper than five percent and is optional inside the transition zone.
D. You should leave the chin strap unbuckled for the first mile after the swim so water can drain from your ears.
quiz_item.correct_answer: B. Your helmet must be on your head with the chin strap securely buckled before you unrack or touch your bike, and it must stay buckled until the bike is re-racked.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (B): Multisport safety rules require athletes to put on and securely buckle a CPSC-approved helmet before touching or unracking the bicycle in T1 and to keep it buckled until the bike is fully racked in T2.

pamphlet_excerpts: Pre-Participation Physical & Health Check: Section 0. document a participant's medical history and recent medical examination (p. 23).

Pre-Participation Physical & Health Check Principle 2: To keep up with possible changes in health status, the form needs to be updated annually or when a participant'shealth information changes (p. 23).
Pre-Participation Physical & Health Check Principle 3: Discuss the form with your doctor during your physical exam (p. 23).
Pre-Participation Physical & Health Check Principle 4: To be a strong, healthy performer in multi sport and in life, avoid tobacco, alcohol, and other harmful substances (p. 23).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Pre-Participation Physical & Health Check): Smoking makes you cough and wheeze, andit interferes with proper lung growth and function (p. 23).
Step 2 (Pre-Participation Physical & Health Check): Using tobacco can leave you gasping for air when you need (p. 23).
Step 3 (Pre-Participation Physical & Health Check): Smoking not only reduces athletic performance and stamina, but it also damages nearly every organ in the body (p. 23).
Step 4 (Pre-Participation Physical & Health Check): The blood carries the poisons from smoking to all parts of the body, damaging internal organs from the brain to the bladder (p. 23).

pamphlet_excerpts: Discuss With Your Counselor Your: Your level of familiarity and experience: Multi sport is a racing competition that consists of any combination of running, biking, or swimming (p. 7).
Discuss With Your Counselor Your Principle 2: Your level of familiarity and experience Principle 2: For the most part, it's pretty simple: The fastest combined time of all three events wins (p. 7).

Discuss With Your Counselor Your Principle 3: Your level of familiarity and experience Principle 3: However, the time it takes you to transition from one sport to the next is included in your overall time, making multi sport a truly unique (p. 7).

Discuss With Your Counselor Your Principle 4: Your level of familiarity and experience Principle 4: If you know how to swim, ride a bike, and run, even casually, completing a triathlon is within your grasp (p. 7).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Discuss With Your Counselor Your): Step 1 (Your level of familiarity and experience): The sport is beginner friendly, welcoming, and rewarding (p. 7).
Step 2 (Discuss With Your Counselor Your): Step 2 (Your level of familiarity and experience): And with so many versions of those three sports, there are many different ways to compete (p. 7).
Step 3 (Discuss With Your Counselor Your): Step 3 (Your level of familiarity and experience): The most common multi sport event is the triathlon (p. 7).

Step 4 (Discuss With Your Counselor Your): Step 4 (Your level of familiarity and experience): You can find triathlon events in every state and around the world at a wide variety of distances, from shorter sprints to longer endurance races (p. 7).

step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Triathlon / Duathlon / Aquathlon): Instead, jog slowly or walk for at least a half mile, then continue to move and stretch (p. 32).

Step 3 (Triathlon / Duathlon / Aquathlon): Don't neglect this part: After astrenuous run, your total cool down routine could take as long as 10 minutes (p. 32).
Step 4 (Triathlon / Duathlon / Aquathlon): When it comes to running or walking, however, experts recommend going against the flow of traffic (p. 32).

requirements.lead_text: Do the following:
requirements.req_text: Do the following: (a) With guidance from your counselor, establish a four-week training plan that combines your chosen multisport format to develop proper techniques, gain self-confidence, and increase endurance. Each session should last at least 25 minutes and include a proper warmup before the session and stretching afterward. (b) Use a chart or other tracking method to monitor your training and development during this period. (c) Set a personal goal for improvement based on one or more of the following criteria: time, technique, or distance. (d) At the end of four weeks, discuss your progress with your counselor and tell how your development has affected you mentally and physically.

pamphlet_excerpts: Establish a four-week training: Take dedicated easy or off days each week, with a recovery week every three to five weeks. 2 (p. 44).
Establish a four-week training Principle 2: A recovery day can include exercise done at a low to moderate effort (p. 44).
Establish a four-week training Principle 3: For triathletes, something like an easy swim, a short jog, or yoga class. 3 (p. 44).
Establish a four-week training Principle 4: A recovery week does not mean you sit and do nothing, just reduce the overall training by 30%-50% and keep your efforts light for a few days. 4 (p. 44).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Establish a four-week training): Stay on top of sleep and nutrition, including post-workout nutrition. 6 (p. 44).
Step 2 (Establish a four-week training): Sleep 7 to 8 hours each night, and you might need more as your training intensity increases (p. 44).
Step 3 (Establish a four-week training): A rule of thumb is to add 30 minutes to one hour of sleep per night for every 10 hours of exercise per week. 7 (p. 44).
Step 4 (Establish a four-week training): On the nutrition front, unless you're actively trying to lose weight, you need your increased calorie expenditure to match intake. 8 (p. 44).

step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Careers and Professional Pathways): This is going to take time, and rushing it does more harm than good (p. 45).
Step 2 (Careers and Professional Pathways): The fix lies in consistent and frequent training, balancing intensity with easy runs (p. 45).
Step 3 (Careers and Professional Pathways): A general guideline says that if you are running and still able to hold a conversation with another person, you are probably training efficiently (p. 45).
Step 4 (Careers and Professional Pathways): Running at high intensity for most runs leads to fatigue, muscular damage, and stagnant fitness gains (p. 45).

options: A. Play three measures per line at a tempo of four beats per second.
B. Divide the ensemble into three vocal parts and raise the pitch by four half-steps.
C. There are three beats in each measure, and a quarter note receives one full beat.
D. There are four beats in each measure, and a dotted half note receives three beats.
choices: A. Play three measures per line at a tempo of four beats per second.

quiz_item.correct_answer: C. There are three beats in each measure, and a quarter note receives one full beat.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (C): In a time signature, the top number indicates how many beats are in each measure (three), while the bottom number indicates which note value receives one beat (4 stands for a quarter note).

requirements.lead_text: Do TWO of the following:
requirements.req_text: Do TWO of the following: (a) Attend a live performance, or listen to three hours of recordings from any two of the following musical styles: blues, jazz, classical, country, bluegrass, ethnic, gospel, musical theater, opera. Describe the sound of the music and the instruments used. Identify the composers or songwriters, the performers, and the titles of the pieces you heard. If it was a live performance, describe the setting and the reaction of the audience. Discuss your thoughts about the music. (b) Interview an adult member of your family about music. Find out what the most popular music was when he or she was your age. Find out what his or her favorite music is now, and listen to three of your relative's favorite tunes with him or her. How do those favorites sound to you? Had you ever heard any of them? Play three of your favorite songs for your relative, and explain why you like these songs. Ask what he or she thinks of your favorite music. (c) Serve for six months as a member of a school band, choir, or other organized musical group, or perform as a soloist in public six times. (d) List five people who are important in the history of American music and explain to your counselor why they continue to be influential. Include at least one composer, one performer, one innovator, and one person born more than 100 years ago.

requirements.lead_text: Do ONE of the following:
requirements.req_text: Do ONE of the following: (a) Explore careers related to this merit badge. Research one career to learn about the training and education needed, costs, job prospects, salary, job duties, and career advancement. Your research methods may include, with your parent or guardian's permission, an internet or library search, an interview with a professional in the field, or a visit to a location where people in this career work. Discuss with your counselor both your findings and what about this profession might make it an interesting career. (b) Explore how you could use knowledge and skills from this merit badge to pursue a hobby. Research any training needed, expenses, and organizations that promote or support it. Discuss with your counselor what short-term and long-term goals you might have if you pursued this.

intro_notes: NOTE: In any of the collection requirements, if collecting is permitted, do so ethically and sustainably. Scouts must remember to follow the Leave No Trace Seven Principles and the Outdoor Code while on field trips and when collecting. Collect sparingly, only taking what you need, and ensure that your collection practices do not harm the surrounding environment. Make sure you have permission from the land manager prior to taking any samples for your collections and be aware of and adhere to local laws regarding collection. (Note that collecting is prohibited in most National and State Parks.) Consider purchasing rock, mineral and fossil specimens from commercial rock and mineral shops or from home garden stores. Pictures or sketches may suffice for a collection and limit impacted disturbances. In most cases all specimens should be returned to the wild at the location of original capture after the requirements have been met. Check with your counselor for those instances where the return of these specimens would not be appropriate. Under the Endangered Species Act of 1973, some plants and animals are or may be protected by federal law. The same ones and/or others may be protected by state law. Be sure that you do not collect protected species. Your state may require that you purchase and carry a license to collect certain species. Check with the wildlife and fish and game officials in your state regarding species regulations before you begin to collect.
NOTE: The official merit badge pamphlets are now free and downloadable HERE or can be purchased at the Scout Shop.

B. Plants absorb nitrogen gas directly through their leaves and convert animal predators into decomposers.
C. Photosynthesis consumes excess oxygen from the atmosphere and releases carbon monoxide to warm forest soil.
D. Green plants rely on herbivorous insects to manufacture chlorophyll before roots can absorb soil minerals.

requirements.lead_text: Do ALL the requirements in FIVE of the following fields:
requirements.req_text: Do ALL the requirements in FIVE of the following fields: (a) Birds. Do ALL of the following: (1) In the field, identify eight species of birds. (2) Make and set out a birdhouse OR a feeding station OR a birdbath. List what birds used it during a period of one month. (b) Mammals. Do ALL of the following: (1) In the field, identify three species of wild mammals. (2) Make plaster casts of the tracks of a wild mammal. (c) Reptiles and Amphibians. Do ALL of the following: (1) Show that you can recognize the venomous snakes in your area. (2) In the field, identify three species of reptiles or amphibians. (3) Recognize one species of toad or frog by voice; OR identify one reptile or amphibian by eggs, den, burrow, or other signs. (d) Insects and Spiders. Do ALL of the following: (1) Collect and identify either in the field or through photographs 10 species of insects or spiders. Photos may be taken with your own equipment or gathered from other sources. (2) Hatch an insect from the pupa or cocoon; OR hatch adults from nymphs; OR keep larvae until they form pupae or cocoons; OR keep a colony of ants or bees through one season. (e) Fish. Do ALL of the following: (1) Identify two species of fish native to your area. (2) Collect four kinds of animal food eaten by fish in the wild. (f) Mollusks and Crustaceans. Do ALL of the following: (1) Identify five species of mollusks and crustaceans. (2) Collect, mount, and label six shells. (g) Plants. Do ALL of the following: (1) In the field, identify 15 species of wild plants. (2) Do ONE of the following: (a) Collect and label the seeds of six plants OR the leaves of 12 plants. (b) Photograph the seeds of six plants OR the leaves of 12 plants and create a catalog of your photos. (h) Soils and Rocks. Do ALL of the following: (1) Collect and identify three different types of soil that represent soils high in sand, clay and humus. (2) Collect and identify five different types of rocks from your area.

B. Plants absorb nitrogen gas directly through their leaves and convert animal predators into decomposers.
C. Photosynthesis consumes excess oxygen from the atmosphere and releases carbon monoxide to warm forest soil.
D. Green plants rely on herbivorous insects to manufacture chlorophyll before roots can absorb soil minerals.

pamphlet_excerpts: Radiation Radiation Ionizing Nonionizing: Although we know much about the dangers of radiation to humans, its effects on wildlife are less understood (p. 67).
Radiation Radiation Ionizing Nonionizing Principle 2: Radiation Principle 2: Scientists have tended to assume that as long as people were protected, animals and plants would be, too (p. 67).
Radiation Radiation Ionizing Nonionizing Principle 3: Radiation Principle 3: But that idea is changing, and more research is now being done to learn how best to safeguard wildlife (p. 67).

Radiation Radiation Ionizing Nonionizing Principle 4: Radiation Principle 4: Many researchers are focusing on how wild plants and animals have been affected by the radioactivity released from the exploded nuclear reactor at (p. 67).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Radiation Radiation Ionizing Nonionizing): Step 1 (Radiation): A person exposed to radiation does not become radioactive (p. 67).
Step 2 (Radiation Radiation Ionizing Nonionizing): Step 2 (Radiation): When you get an X-ray at the doctor's office, it does not make you radioactive (p. 67).
Step 3 (Radiation Radiation Ionizing Nonionizing): Step 3 (Radiation): Getting radiation exposure is just like going to the beach and being exposed to sunshine (p. 67).

Step 4 (Radiation Radiation Ionizing Nonionizing): Step 4 (Radiation): The light rays may deposit enough energy into your body to cause an effect, like asunburn, but when you turn off the lights that night (p. 67).

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: Under the ALARA (As Low As Reasonably Achievable) radiation safety principle, what are the three primary methods used to minimize exposure to ionizing radiation?
quiz_item.question: Under the ALARA (As Low As Reasonably Achievable) radiation safety principle, what are the three primary methods used to minimize exposure to ionizing radiation?
options: A. Ventilation, grounding, and magnetic deflection.
B. Filtration, chemical neutralization, and thermal cooling.
C. Compression, humidification, and ultraviolet sterilization.
D. Minimizing time spent near the source, maximizing distance from the source, and placing appropriate shielding between yourself and the source.
choices: A. Ventilation, grounding, and magnetic deflection.
B. Filtration, chemical neutralization, and thermal cooling.
C. Compression, humidification, and ultraviolet sterilization.
D. Minimizing time spent near the source, maximizing distance from the source, and placing appropriate shielding between yourself and the source.
quiz_item.correct_answer: D. Minimizing time spent near the source, maximizing distance from the source, and placing appropriate shielding between yourself and the source.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (D): Radiation protection relies on Time, Distance, and Shielding: reducing exposure duration, increasing distance (which follows the inverse-square law), and using proper absorber materials.

pamphlet_excerpts: Basic Nuclear Science: Begin by studying pictures of the three isotopes of hydrogen (p. 12).
Basic Nuclear Science Principle 2: Ordinary hydrogen has one proton, one electron, and no neutrons (p. 12).
Basic Nuclear Science Principle 3: There are two other hydrogen isotopes: deuterium (written in isotope notation as 2D) with 1 proton and 1 neutron, andtritium (3T or 3H) with 1 proton (p. 12).
Basic Nuclear Science Principle 4: Now use your imagination (and whatever materials are handy) to make a 3-D model of each isotope (p. 12).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Basic Nuclear Science): Successful atomic models have been made with pizza or cookies or Styrofoam balls (p. 12).
Step 2 (Basic Nuclear Science): On the next page is an example to get you thinking about the three isotopes of hydrogen (p. 12).
Step 3 (Basic Nuclear Science): If you wish, you can make models of three isotopes of an element other than hydrogen, like carbon (p. 12).
Step 4 (Basic Nuclear Science): He explained electric current as the movement of extremely small, negatively charged particles (p. 12).

pamphlet_excerpts: Modern Particle Physics: Particle accelerators, sometimes called atom smashers, are machines that can create beams of electrically charged particles and accelerate them (p. 23).
Modern Particle Physics Principle 2: This acceleration increases the particles' energy of motion (p. 23).
Modern Particle Physics Principle 3: Think of the difference between catching a baseball that is gently underhanded to you and catching a fast ball fired at youby a major-league pitcher (p. 23).
Modern Particle Physics Principle 4: Energy is the universal container that holds things together (p. 23).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Modern Particle Physics): If you want to break open a container such as an atom or a proton to see what's inside, you must overcome that container'senergy (p. 23).
Step 2 (Modern Particle Physics): From accelerators, scientists get the energy they need to break open and explore the makeup of atomic and subatomic particles (p. 23).
Step 3 (Modern Particle Physics): The Large Had ron Collider (LHC) in Geneva, Switzerland, is the world's largest and highest-energy particle accelerator (p. 23).
Step 4 (Modern Particle Physics): Scientists use the LHC's 17-mile-long underground ring to smash beams of protons or heavy ions into one another (p. 23).

requirements.lead_text: Radiation Safety. Do ONE of the following:
requirements.req_text: Radiation Safety. Do ONE of the following: (a) Using a radiation survey meter and a radioactive source, show how the counts per minute change as the source gets closer to or farther from the radiation detector. Adults must handle radioactive materials. Place three different materials between the source and the detector, then explain any differences in the measurements per minute. Explain how time, distance, and shielding can reduce an individual's radiation dose. (b) Describe how radon is detected in homes. Discuss the steps taken for the long-term and short-term test methods, tell how to interpret the results, and explain when each type of test should be used. Explain the health concerns related to radon gas and tell what steps can be taken to reduce radon in buildings. (c) Visit a place where X-rays are used. Draw a floor plan of this room. Show where the unit, the unit operator, and the patient would be when the X-ray unit is operated. Explain the precautions taken and the importance of those precautions for the safety of the operator.

pamphlet_excerpts: Nuclear Energy: Hahn and Strassmann wrote to Lise Meitner about their research (p. 53).
Nuclear Energy Principle 2: She concluded that when uranium is hit with a neutron, it must break in half (p. 53).
Nuclear Energy Principle 3: An American biologist, William Arnold, read the paper and decided to call the splitting of atoms fission, the word biologists used for the splitting (p. 53).
Nuclear Energy Principle 4: Fission would not be useful for producing energy if we had to shoot each nucleus with a neutron to break (p. 53).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Nuclear Energy): Fermi found that with the element he was using, uranium, slow neutrons hit nuclei better than fast onesdid (p. 53).
Step 2 (Nuclear Energy): In December 1942, Fermi and a group of other scientists completed the first atomic pile (p. 53).
Step 3 (Nuclear Energy): This was a stack of blocks of graphite containing uranium in carefully spaced lumps (p. 53).
Step 4 (Nuclear Energy): Rods of cadmium in the pile soakedup neutrons before they could hit the uranium (p. 53).

pamphlet_excerpts: Beneficial Applications of Nuclear Science: Putting Radiation to Work: Nuclear Technologies Radiation in Science The uses of radiation in science and research are many and varied (p. 42).
Beneficial Applications of Nuclear Science Principle 2: All living things have some radioactive carbon-14 in them (p. 42).
Beneficial Applications of Nuclear Science Principle 3: Archaeologists and paleontologists use this measurement in their studies (p. 42).
Beneficial Applications of Nuclear Science Principle 4: The carbon-14 technique is an essential tool in many fields including atmospheric science, oceanography, geology, and climatology (p. 42).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Beneficial Applications of Nuclear Science): The Mars rover Sojourner used alpha particles to identify chemical elements in Martian rocks (p. 42).
Step 2 (Beneficial Applications of Nuclear Science): An instrument on the rover bombarded selected rocks with alpha particles, then read the X-rays generated from the rocks (p. 42).
Step 3 (Beneficial Applications of Nuclear Science): Because each chemical element produces a distinctive X-ray, the instrument could determine the composition of the rocks (p. 42).
Step 4 (Beneficial Applications of Nuclear Science): Ask what types of medical images are used to help in the planning process (p. 42).

Research one career to learn about the training and education needed, costs, job prospects, salary, job duties, and career advancement. step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Careers & Professional Pathways): The path to this degree takes many years of study and research (p. 78).
Step 2 (Careers & Professional Pathways): As college students majoring in physics or chemistry, they may take one or two specialized nuclear science courses and participate (p. 78).
Step 3 (Careers & Professional Pathways): Then, after graduation from college, they enter a doctoral program, taking courses for the first year or two, then beginning full-time research (p. 78).
Step 4 (Careers & Professional Pathways): Almost all nuclear science graduate students are paid to go to school through fellowships, teaching assistants hips, research assistants hips (p. 78).

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: How do marine phytoplankton and the global ocean interact with Earth's atmosphere to support life and regulate climate?
quiz_item.question: How do marine phytoplankton and the global ocean interact with Earth's atmosphere to support life and regulate climate?
options: A. Deep-sea hydrothermal vents produce most atmospheric oxygen, while surface currents reflect all incoming solar heat back into space.
B. Marine phytoplankton generate at least half of Earth's atmospheric oxygen through photosynthesis, while ocean waters absorb vast amounts of solar heat and carbon dioxide.
C. Saltwater evaporation removes carbon dioxide from the ocean and locks it permanently into stratospheric clouds.
D. Ocean tides generate geothermal heat that warms polar air masses without transferring moisture to the atmosphere.
choices: A. Deep-sea hydrothermal vents produce most atmospheric oxygen, while surface currents reflect all incoming solar heat back into space.
B. Marine phytoplankton generate at least half of Earth's atmospheric oxygen through photosynthesis, while ocean waters absorb vast amounts of solar heat and carbon dioxide.
C. Saltwater evaporation removes carbon dioxide from the ocean and locks it permanently into stratospheric clouds.
D. Ocean tides generate geothermal heat that warms polar air masses without transferring moisture to the atmosphere.
quiz_item.correct_answer: B. Marine phytoplankton generate at least half of Earth's atmospheric oxygen through photosynthesis, while ocean waters absorb vast amounts of solar heat and carbon dioxide.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (B): Microscopic marine phytoplankton produce over half of the world's oxygen and anchor marine food webs, while the ocean stores and redistributes solar heat and absorbs atmospheric carbon dioxide.

pamphlet_excerpts: Salinity, temperature, and density: The Oceans and the Atmosphere Great wind circulation systems form (p. 32).
Salinity, temperature, and density Principle 2: Close to the equator, trade winds blow from the east (p. 32).
Salinity, temperature, and density Principle 3: In the temperate zone, steady winds called westerlies blow from the west (p. 32).
Salinity, temperature, and density Principle 4: Winds blowing across the ocean's surface create currents (p. 32).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Salinity, temperature, and density): When the trade winds and westerlies blow across the oceans, they cause the currents in each ocean basin to move in acircular pattern (p. 32).
Step 2 (Salinity, temperature, and density): Both surface and deep water currents affect the world'sclimate by moving warm air from the tropics toward the poles, and cold air (p. 32).
Step 3 (Salinity, temperature, and density): As a result, London experiences much milder winters than New York City, even though Great Britain is situated at a higher latitude (p. 32).
Step 4 (Salinity, temperature, and density): As oceans circulate heat, they regulate Earth's temperatures (p. 32).

Characteristics of ocean waves Principle 4: Water also dissolves nutrients on land that eventually find their way to rivers and into the sea (p. 18).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Characteristics of ocean waves): Inside an animal's body, water also helps dissolve food and carry it to the animal's cells (p. 18).
Step 2 (Characteristics of ocean waves): Because so many substances will dissolve in water, pure water cannot be found in nature (p. 18).
Step 3 (Characteristics of ocean waves): If you want to make your ownocean water, you will need to add 35 parts of salt to 965 parts of water (p. 18).
Step 4 (Characteristics of ocean waves): That may not seem like much salt, but mix up a batch and have a taste (p. 18).

Step 2 (Main salts, gases, and nutrients): Both surface and deep water currents affect the world'sclimate by moving warm air from the tropics toward the poles, and cold air (p. 31).
Step 3 (Main salts, gases, and nutrients): As a result, London experiences much milder winters than New York City, even though Great Britain is situated at a higher latitude (p. 31).
Step 4 (Main salts, gases, and nutrients): As oceans circulate heat, they regulate Earth's temperatures (p. 31).

pamphlet_excerpts: Some of the biologically important properties: The term plankton comes from the Greek word planktos, which means "wanderer." Plankton includes marine plants and animals that drift with the currents (p. 45).

Some of the biologically important properties Principle 2: Because they drift, plankton differ from nekton, animals that actively swim or lie on or burrow into the seafloor, such as clams and worms (p. 45).
Some of the biologically important properties Principle 3: They also differ from marine plants such as large seaweeds (p. 45).
Some of the biologically important properties Principle 4: Plankton cells are seldom larger in diameter than a few tenths of an inch (p. 45).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Some of the biologically important properties): Plankton forms the basis of all major ocean food chains (p. 45).

Step 2 (Some of the biologically important properties): However, because of their small size, long spines, shell extension, and the ability to float, these drifters have adapted in different ways to slow (p. 45).
Step 3 (Some of the biologically important properties): Some plank tonic animals rise toward the surface at night and then sink to deeper waters during the day (p. 45).
Step 4 (Some of the biologically important properties): This vertical migration is probably tied to feeding strategies as well as to the avoidance of predators (p. 45).

requirements.lead_text: Do ONE of the following:
requirements.req_text: Do ONE of the following: (a) Make a plankton net. Tow the net by a dock, wade with it, hold it in a current, or tow it from a rowboat. Do this for about 20 minutes. Save the sample. Examine it under a microscope or high-power glass. Identify the three most common types of plankton in the sample. Note: May be done in lakes or streams. (b) Make a series of models (clay or plaster and wood) of a volcanic island. Show the growth of an atoll from a fringing reef through a barrier reef. Describe the Darwinian theory of coral reef formation. (c) Measure the water temperature at the surface, midwater, and bottom of a body of water four times daily for five consecutive days. You may measure depth with a rock tied to a line. Make a Secchi disk to measure turbidity (how much suspended sedimentation is in the water). Measure the air temperature. Note the cloud cover and roughness of the water. Show your findings (air and water temperature, turbidity) on a graph. Tell how the water temperature changes with air temperature. (d) Make a model showing the inshore sediment movement by littoral currents, tidal movement, and wave action. Include such formations as high and low waterlines, low-tide terrace, berm, and coastal cliffs. Show how offshore bars are built up and torn down. (e) Make a wave generator. Show reflection and refraction of waves. Show how groins, jetties, and breakwaters affect these patterns. (f) With your counselor's and parent or guardian's approval and permission, track and monitor satellite images available on the internet for a specific location for three weeks. Describe what you have learned to your counselor.

pamphlet_excerpts: Methods That Marine Scientists Use: Four Methods That Marine Scientists: A rich assortment of living things calls the ocean home (p. 36).

Methods That Marine Scientists Use Principle 2: Four Methods That Marine Scientists Principle 2: Big and small, long and short, multicolored and drab, active and inactive, sea life ranges from microscopic plankton to the largest creatures on Earth (p. 36).
Methods That Marine Scientists Use Principle 3: Four Methods That Marine Scientists Principle 3: Some organisms even light up, like ghostly neon lights (p. 36).
Methods That Marine Scientists Use Principle 4: Four Methods That Marine Scientists Principle 4: The sea is so vast that scientists have divided it into zones (p. 36).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Methods That Marine Scientists Use): Step 1 (Four Methods That Marine Scientists): The pelagic zone includes all the environments of the ocean above the bottom, or living in open oceans or seas rather than in waters next to land (p. 36).

Step 2 (Methods That Marine Scientists Use): Step 2 (Four Methods That Marine Scientists): It is divided into an inshore neritic zone (the zone of shallow water adjoining the seacoast) and the open-sea oceanic zone (p. 36).
Step 3 (Methods That Marine Scientists Use): Step 3 (Four Methods That Marine Scientists): The boundary between them occurs at the edge of the continental shelf (p. 36).
Step 4 (Methods That Marine Scientists Use): Step 4 (Four Methods That Marine Scientists): The oceanic zone is divided further according to how deep sunlight penetrates (p. 36).

pamphlet_excerpts: Orienteering First Aid: Orienteering is a physically demanding activity that takes place over several kilometers of very mixed and often rugged terrain (p. 66).
Orienteering First Aid Principle 2: Hot weather may result in sunburn, heatstroke, heat exhaustion, and dehydration, while cold weather can lead to hypothermia and dehydration (p. 66).
Orienteering First Aid Principle 3: In the hurry to be first, you might stumble onto dangerous animals or poisonous plants (p. 66).
Orienteering First Aid Principle 4: Before going out, spend a fewminutes reviewing possible injuries and their treatment (p. 66).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Orienteering First Aid): The best thing you can do to prevent injury is to be well-rested, well-fed, and physically fit before going out on an orienteeringcourse (p. 66).
Step 2 (Orienteering First Aid): A normal night's sleep and healthy meals will help you endure the rigors of the course and decrease the possibility of a physical or mental slip (p. 66).
Step 3 (Orienteering First Aid): If you are not physically fit, you may be particularly vulnerable to heat (p. 66).
Step 4 (Orienteering First Aid): Dehydration is caused by lack of water in the body (p. 66).

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: When taking a bearing from a topographic map in an area with a 12-degree west magnetic declination, why must you account for declination before following your compass in the field?
quiz_item.question: When taking a bearing from a topographic map in an area with a 12-degree west magnetic declination, why must you account for declination before following your compass in the field?
options: A. Because contour lines on a topographic map shift position seasonally as soil moisture changes.
B. Because a baseplate compass needle always points toward the geographic North Pole rather than magnetic north.
C. Because map grid lines align with true north while the compass needle points to magnetic north, and ignoring a 12-degree difference will pull you far off course over distance.
D. Because metal control flags placed at orienteering checkpoints reverse the polarity of the compass housing.
choices: A. Because contour lines on a topographic map shift position seasonally as soil moisture changes.
B. Because a baseplate compass needle always points toward the geographic North Pole rather than magnetic north.
C. Because map grid lines align with true north while the compass needle points to magnetic north, and ignoring a 12-degree difference will pull you far off course over distance.
D. Because metal control flags placed at orienteering checkpoints reverse the polarity of the compass housing.
quiz_item.correct_answer: C. Because map grid lines align with true north while the compass needle points to magnetic north, and ignoring a 12-degree difference will pull you far off course over distance.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (C): Magnetic declination is the angular difference between true north (shown on the map) and magnetic north (where the compass needle points); failing to adjust for it causes significant navigation errors.

pamphlet_excerpts: Map Symbols and Topographic Features: Using a Topographic Map. maps you will find a number on it that tells its elevation abovesea level (p. 14).

Map Symbols and Topographic Features Principle 2: On orienteering maps, the index contour line does not have an elevation number, but is thicker than the others and is used as a guide for the eye (p. 14).
Map Symbols and Topographic Features Principle 3: You can also "see" the shape of the terrain from the profile of the lines on the paper (p. 14).
Map Symbols and Topographic Features Principle 4: If a mountain is perfectly conical like a wizard's hat, the contour lines depicting the mountain will look like a bull's-eye (p. 14).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Map Symbols and Topographic Features): Each contour line will be perfectly circular, and all will be the same distance apart (p. 14).
Step 2 (Map Symbols and Topographic Features): At one part of the mountain, the contour line may intersect a valley or a depression (p. 14).
Step 3 (Map Symbols and Topographic Features): If the contour line ran into the valley, it would lose elevation and would no longer be considered the same contour line (p. 14).
Step 4 (Map Symbols and Topographic Features): When a higher point like a ridge is encountered, the contour line will "V" downward (p. 14).

pamphlet_excerpts: A compass works: Rotate the bezel until the orienting arrow or north-south lines lie parallel to and in the same direction as the magnetic north-south lines on the map (p. 10).
A compass works Principle 2: Read the bearing directly opposite of the bearing index (p. 10).
A compass works Principle 3: If the magnetic north-south lines are not drawn on the map, convert the language of the compass to that of the map (p. 10).
A compass works Principle 4: Always add the number of degrees of error for west declination and subtract for east declination (p. 10).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (A compass works): The bearing is 244 degrees from "A" to "B." (Points "A" and "B" can be seen in the top photo on page 21.) (p. 10).
Step 2 (A compass works): The thumb compass rides on the thumb and simplifies map orientation and direction finding while you are on the move (p. 10).
Step 3 (A compass works): It suffers a bit in accuracy, however, especially in the hands of a novice (p. 10).
Step 4 (A compass works): The bearing index and direction-of-travel arrow are located on the base plate (p. 10).

Step 3 (Set up a 100-meter pace course): As your stride lengthens, the distance you cover increases (p. 26).
Step 4 (Set up a 100-meter pace course): So the number of paces per 100 meters will decrease, as will the time it takes you to cover that distance (p. 26).

requirements.lead_text: Do the following:
requirements.req_text: Do the following: (a) Take part in three orienteering events. One of these must be a cross-country course. Note: While orienteering is primarily an individual sport, Scouting America Youth Protection procedures call for using the buddy system. Requirement 7(a) can be completed by pairs or groups of Scouts. (b) After each event, write a report with (1) a copy of the master map and control description sheet, (2) a copy of the route you took on the course, (3) a discussion of how you could improve your time between control points, and (4) a list of your major weaknesses on this course. Describe what you could do to improve.

Step 3 (Orienteering Events): Step 3 (Take part in three orienteering events): Unless you plan your course, you will waste time mapping areas that the course does not use (p. 30).

pamphlet_excerpts: Act as an official: Orienteering USA is the ruling body for sanctioned orienteering events in the United States (p. 35).
Act as an official Principle 2: Its rule book is comprehensive and addresses the technicalities of holding an event, as well as conduct that is expected of the participants (p. 35).
Act as an official Principle 3: A few general rules are provided below, but for detailed information, it is best to consult the rule book or to contact the OUSA. 1 (p. 35).
Act as an official Principle 4: Competitors who have prior knowledge of the course that will give them an unfair advantage should not participate (p. 35).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Act as an official): Investigation of the course before an event is forbidden. 2 (p. 35).
Step 2 (Act as an official): The use of any navigational aid other than a compass is prohibited for navigation during a race (p. 35).
Step 3 (Act as an official): This includes GPS (global positioning system) units, altimeters, and mobile mapping apps (p. 35).
Step 4 (Act as an official): Note on post-race analysis: Many modern orienteers wear GPS watches solely to record their track for later study (p. 35).

pamphlet_excerpts: Teach orienteering techniques to your patrol: More obscure handrails might be ridge lines, valleys, tree lines, forest fire burns, or avalanche scars (p. 41).
Teach orienteering techniques to your patrol Principle 2: Beginners' courses rely heavily on handrails to help the novice get to each control (p. 41).
Teach orienteering techniques to your patrol Principle 3: The route for the easiest courses may actually go right down a trail or road, the handrail (p. 41).

Teach orienteering techniques to your patrol Principle 4: Collecting, Check-Off, and Catching Features Always look around and take note of the features you pass as you move toward the next control (p. 41).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Teach orienteering techniques to your patrol): There may be some obvious features along the route, such as a large pond or small lake, that will help send you in the right direction (p. 41).
Step 2 (Teach orienteering techniques to your patrol): These are collecting features, which lie between you and the control (p. 41).
Step 3 (Teach orienteering techniques to your patrol): Equally important but less obvious are check-off features, which you will see along the way (p. 41).
Step 4 (Teach orienteering techniques to your patrol): You can constantly verify your position by making a mental note as you pass the features and moving your thumb along the map (p. 41).

patrol_quiz_bank.question: When taking a bearing from a topographic map in an area with a 12-degree west magnetic declination, why must you account for declination before following your compass in the field?
options: A. Because contour lines on a topographic map shift position seasonally as soil moisture changes.
B. Because a baseplate compass needle always points toward the geographic North Pole rather than magnetic north.
C. Because map grid lines align with true north while the compass needle points to magnetic north, and ignoring a 12-degree difference will pull you far off course over distance.
D. Because metal control flags placed at orienteering checkpoints reverse the polarity of the compass housing.
choices: A. Because contour lines on a topographic map shift position seasonally as soil moisture changes.
B. Because a baseplate compass needle always points toward the geographic North Pole rather than magnetic north.
C. Because map grid lines align with true north while the compass needle points to magnetic north, and ignoring a 12-degree difference will pull you far off course over distance.
D. Because metal control flags placed at orienteering checkpoints reverse the polarity of the compass housing.
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: C. Because map grid lines align with true north while the compass needle points to magnetic north, and ignoring a 12-degree difference will pull you far off course over distance.
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (C): Magnetic declination is the angular difference between true north (shown on the map) and magnetic north (where the compass needle points); failing to adjust for it causes significant navigation errors.

quiz_item.question: When setting up an extension ladder to scrape, prime, and paint an exterior wall, how should you position the base of the ladder according to the 4-to-1 rule?
options: A. Place the base of the ladder 1 foot away from the wall for every 4 feet of vertical height to the upper support point, on firm level ground.
B. Place the base 4 feet away from the wall for every 1 foot of vertical height so you can lean backward while rolling paint.
C. Set the ladder rails flush against the siding and tie the top rung to a rain gutter with twine.
D. Extend the ladder to its maximum length with zero overlap between sections and prop one leg on loose bricks.
choices: A. Place the base of the ladder 1 foot away from the wall for every 4 feet of vertical height to the upper support point, on firm level ground.
B. Place the base 4 feet away from the wall for every 1 foot of vertical height so you can lean backward while rolling paint.
C. Set the ladder rails flush against the siding and tie the top rung to a rain gutter with twine.
D. Extend the ladder to its maximum length with zero overlap between sections and prop one leg on loose bricks.
quiz_item.correct_answer: A. Place the base of the ladder 1 foot away from the wall for every 4 feet of vertical height to the upper support point, on firm level ground.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (A): The 4-to-1 ladder safety rule places the base 1 foot out from the wall for every 4 feet of working height, providing a stable 75-degree climbing angle that prevents tipping backward or sliding out.

Step 3 (Coatings Can Improve A Surface): Step 3 (Explain Three Ways That Coatings): A flat finish is most often used for ceilings and on interior walls (p. 43).

pamphlet_excerpts: Paint Two Different Surfaces Using: Prepare and paint two different surfaces: Applying primer, the first coat of paint, also is the last stage of surface preparation (p. 51).

Paint Two Different Surfaces Using Principle 2: Prepare and paint two different surfaces Principle 2: The primer makes the next coat stick to the surface, protects the substrate, and seals the surface (p. 51).

Paint Two Different Surfaces Using Principle 3: Prepare and paint two different surfaces Principle 3: There are different primers for wood, concrete and masonry, plaster and drywall, steel, and other metals (p. 51).

Paint Two Different Surfaces Using Principle 4: Prepare and paint two different surfaces Principle 4: Wood primers are available in oil-based or water-based products and can be used indoors or outdoors (p. 51).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Paint Two Different Surfaces Using): Step 1 (Prepare and paint two different surfaces): Exterior masonry surfaces are often highly alkaline, so be sure to use primers on surfaces that are alkali-resistant (p. 51).

Step 2 (Paint Two Different Surfaces Using): Step 2 (Prepare and paint two different surfaces): Make sure primers for plaster surfaces are alkali-resistant and that plaster dust is removed first (p. 51).
Step 3 (Paint Two Different Surfaces Using): Step 3 (Prepare and paint two different surfaces): The best primers for drywall or gypsum board are water based, such as vinyl and acrylic (p. 51).

Step 4 (Paint Two Different Surfaces Using): Step 4 (Prepare and paint two different surfaces): The type of primer you choose depends on the surface preparation required as well as the topcoat to be applied over the primer (p. 51).

pamphlet_excerpts: Right Way to Use Clean: Show The Right Way: Care and Storage of Equipment The most important part of taking care of any paint application tool or equipment is cleaning it immediately (p. 54).
Right Way to Use Clean Principle 2: Show The Right Way Principle 2: Failure to do so can cost you more time and more money spent on special cleaners, which in some cases may ruin the tool (p. 54).
Right Way to Use Clean Principle 3: Show The Right Way Principle 3: If you clean your brushes after each use, they will last along time (p. 54).
Right Way to Use Clean Principle 4: Show The Right Way Principle 4: Cleaning takes only a few minutes and saves hours of work and, quite possibly, the cost of replacement (p. 54).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Right Way to Use Clean): Step 1 (Show The Right Way): If paint is allowed to harden in a brush, cleaning that brush becomes adifficult and time-consuming task, one that could have been easily avoided (p. 54).

Step 2 (Right Way to Use Clean): Step 2 (Show The Right Way): If the same brush and paint have been used over several days, store the brush for the night (with most of the paint wiped off) in tightly folded aluminum (p. 54).
Step 3 (Right Way to Use Clean): Step 3 (Show The Right Way): Carefully smooth down the bristles and wrap the brush in its original packaging or heavy paper tied around the ferrule (p. 54).
Step 4 (Right Way to Use Clean): Step 4 (Show The Right Way): A good paint job requires the right equipment and following the right procedures (p. 54).

pamphlet_excerpts: Some of the environmental and health: Solvents, paints, paint chips, and dust that may contain lead must be disposed of properly (p. 14).
Some of the environmental and health Principle 2: Paint ingredients, when mishandled, can be dangerous (p. 14).

Some of the environmental and health Principle 3: Solvents, such as mineral spirits, xylol, and naphtha, are present in some paints and are used to reduce or thin the paint and during cleanup (p. 14).
Some of the environmental and health Principle 4: Solvents are particularly hazardous to the painter and others who may be exposed to them (p. 14).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Some of the environmental and health): Follow the same safety guidelines for solvents and solvent-based paints (p. 14).
Step 2 (Some of the environmental and health): Inhaling too many solvent vapors can make breathing difficult, lowering the oxygen level in the body (p. 14).
Step 3 (Some of the environmental and health): Always keep the work area well-ventilated by opening all the windows (p. 14).
Step 4 (Some of the environmental and health): If part of your body comes in contact with a solvent, the result could be harmful (p. 14).

Step 4 (Careers & Professional Pathways): Check community colleges in your area to find trade courses in the construction and painting industries (p. 69).

requirements.lead_text: Your Fitness Knowledge and Habits. Do the following with your counselor:
requirements.req_text: Your Fitness Knowledge and Habits. Do the following with your counselor: (a) Explain the physical exercise you regularly do, whether your routine includes all four components of physical fitness (cardiorespiratory fitness, muscular strength and endurance, flexibility, and body composition), and how your current practices increase or decrease your likelihood of developing cardiovascular disease or other conditions in adulthood. (b) Discuss what harmful substances you consciously avoid, and how these actions affect your risk factors now and in the future. (c) Explain what common diseases can be prevented or mitigated by vaccinations, and whether you are immunized according to the advice of your healthcare provider and the direction of your parent or guardian. (d) Discuss how good nutrition is related to the other components of personal fitness, and if you follow a nutritious, balanced diet. (e) Discuss what a healthy weight is for you, and what you do to maintain a healthy weight. (f) Explain why getting adequate sleep is important, and whether you get enough hours of sleep each night. (g) Discuss whether you spend quality time with your family and friends in social and recreational activities, and how you contribute to creating and maintaining a good home life.

requirements.lead_text: Measures of Physical Fitness. Determine with your counselor the assessments of physical fitness and nutrition you will do before, during, and after completing the 12-week program in requirement 7.
requirements.req_text: Measures of Physical Fitness. Determine with your counselor the assessments of physical fitness and nutrition you will do before, during, and after completing the 12-week program in requirement 7. (a) Include a measure of cardiorespiratory (aerobic) fitness: Record the time required to complete a mile walk or run as fast as you can. If you are unable to walk or run as a result of a disability that is permanent or is expected to last for longer than two years, work with your counselor to define a test with a similar degree of aerobic challenge. (b) Include two measures of muscular strength and endurance: Record either the number of sit-ups done in 60 seconds OR how long a plank was held; AND, record the number of either push-ups OR pull-ups done in 60 seconds. If you are unable to complete one of these exercises safely and correctly, work with your counselor to replace it with a different exercise that measures strength and endurance. (c) Include at least one measure of flexibility, such as a back-saver sit-and-reach test or a back scratch test.

pamphlet_excerpts: Measures of Physical Fitness: Creating a Personal Fitness Program Physical Fitness Tests It is important to know your current level of fitness to create the best possible (p. 65).
Measures of Physical Fitness Principle 2: The following tests will help you measure your physical fitness (p. 65).
Measures of Physical Fitness Principle 3: You will also use these tests to fulﬁll your merit badge requirements (p. 65).
Measures of Physical Fitness Principle 4: After you'vecompleted the fitness testing, compare your scores to the tables that begin on page 76 (p. 65).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Measures of Physical Fitness): If you scored at or below the 20thpercentile, work on improving in that test (p. 65).
Step 2 (Measures of Physical Fitness): If you scored above the 20th percentile and would like to do even better, you might want to consider including this in your 12 weeks (p. 65).
Step 3 (Measures of Physical Fitness): Using a sit-and-reach box constructed according to specifications in this pamphlet, make four repetitions and record the fourth reach (p. 65).
Step 4 (Measures of Physical Fitness): You may also do all three for extra experience and benefit. (Measurements should be in numbers and repetitions.) 1 (p. 65).

step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Pre-Assessment of Physical Fitness): Decide what you want to achieve on each of the aerobic, ﬂexibility, and strength measurements (p. 74).
Step 2 (Pre-Assessment of Physical Fitness): Be realistic, but challenge yourself to make asubstantial improvement on each measure (p. 74).
Step 3 (Pre-Assessment of Physical Fitness): Then ﬁgure out what routines will get you from your starting measurements to your goals (p. 74).
Step 4 (Pre-Assessment of Physical Fitness): You may want to adjust and revise your program every week or twoas you progress (p. 74).

requirements.lead_text: Plan the Program. Outline with your counselor a comprehensive 12-week physical fitness and nutrition program that you will complete based on your improvement goals and ability. The program must incorporate the following:
requirements.req_text: Plan the Program. Outline with your counselor a comprehensive 12-week physical fitness and nutrition program that you will complete based on your improvement goals and ability. The program must incorporate the following: (a) Warm-up: low-intensity movement or gentle muscle stretching before each more rigorous workout (b) Cardiorespiratory (aerobic) element: an activity that raises your heart and respiratory rate for 15 to 30 minutes at least three times per week (c) Muscular strength and endurance element: repetitive exercises that target different muscles, upper body, core, and/or legs, based on your improvement goals and potential (d) Flexibility element: movements that arch/lower/stretch/relax your back, rotate your trunk, or stretch your hamstrings (e) Cool-down: low-intensity movement or gentle stretching to prevent muscle cramps and enhance the benefits of exercise (f) A plan for achieving your two improvement goals related to diet and nutrition

requirements.lead_text: Complete the Program. Do the following:
requirements.req_text: Complete the Program. Do the following: (a) Complete and keep a log, over 12 consecutive weeks, of the physical fitness and nutrition program you have outlined. (If your program is interrupted by illness or unavoidable conflicts for less than two weeks, you may resume where you left off, adding the missed days or weeks at the end.) (b) During week 4 and week 8 of your program, repeat the assessments you did in requirement 5(a) before you began. Repeat the same tests for a final assessment within two weeks after completing the 12-week program. Show improvement over your pre-assessment results. (c) For three days during week 8, and again during week 12, keep a log of what you eat and drink. Show improvement toward the diet and nutrition goals you set in requirement 5(d). (d) Discuss your results, improvements, insights, and experiences with your counselor after completing the program and assessments.

step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Careers & Professional Pathways): They should hold first-aid and CPR certifications (p. 84).
Step 2 (Careers & Professional Pathways): People who have trouble moving or performing everyday activities need the help of a physical therapist (p. 84).
Step 3 (Careers & Professional Pathways): These health professionals use exercises and many other techniques to get their patients moving (p. 84).
Step 4 (Careers & Professional Pathways): They also teach them how to get around using crutches and wheelchairs, and using prosthetic limbs (p. 84).

pamphlet_excerpts: Family Might Want to Purchase: Choose An Item: Your family must take care of needs such as food, housing, insurance, car payments, school expenses, utilities, and clothes before making a major purchase (p. 15).
Family Might Want to Purchase Principle 2: Choose An Item Principle 2: Once these needs are met, you can set the goal of saving for an item that your family has agreed to purchase (p. 15).
Family Might Want to Purchase Principle 3: Choose An Item Principle 3: Many factors must be considered before making a big purchase (p. 15).
Family Might Want to Purchase Principle 4: Choose An Item Principle 4: To determine the answers, read articles about televisions in magazines, consumer guides, and on the internet (p. 15).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Family Might Want to Purchase): Step 1 (Choose An Item): Talk to salespeople in consumer electronics stores, and, if you can, also talk to technicians who work on TVs (p. 15).

Step 2 (Family Might Want to Purchase): Step 2 (Choose An Item): Do not rely on only one source of information, and remember that salespeople might highlight slow-selling or high-profit items rather than the best (p. 15).
Step 3 (Family Might Want to Purchase): Step 3 (Choose An Item): For instance, check how long the manufacturer guarantees components (p. 15).
Step 4 (Family Might Want to Purchase): Step 4 (Choose An Item): Learn what customers must do to make sure the warranty and/or guarantee stays valid (p. 15).

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: When planning a major family purchase under Requirement 1, why should you compare total cost of ownership and financing options across multiple retailers rather than looking only at the monthly payment?
quiz_item.question: When planning a major family purchase under Requirement 1, why should you compare total cost of ownership and financing options across multiple retailers rather than looking only at the monthly payment?
options: A. Because a lower monthly payment always guarantees a lower total purchase price and zero interest charges.
B. Because long-term financing with high interest rates, fees, maintenance, and operating costs can make a low monthly payment far more expensive overall than saving up to pay cash.
C. Because retail stores are legally required to match the lowest monthly payment offered by any online auction site.
D. Because comparison shopping only applies to consumable groceries and does not affect durable goods or warranties.
choices: A. Because a lower monthly payment always guarantees a lower total purchase price and zero interest charges.
B. Because long-term financing with high interest rates, fees, maintenance, and operating costs can make a low monthly payment far more expensive overall than saving up to pay cash.
C. Because retail stores are legally required to match the lowest monthly payment offered by any online auction site.
D. Because comparison shopping only applies to consumable groceries and does not affect durable goods or warranties.
quiz_item.correct_answer: B. Because long-term financing with high interest rates, fees, maintenance, and operating costs can make a low monthly payment far more expensive overall than saving up to pay cash.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (B): Evaluating needs versus wants, comparison shopping for quality and price, and calculating interest, warranties, and operating expenses reveals the true total cost of a major purchase.

requirements.lead_text: Do the following:
requirements.req_text: Do the following: (a) Prepare a budget reflecting your expected income (allowance, gifts, wages), expenses, and savings for a period of 13 consecutive weeks. (b) Compare expected income with expected expenses. (1) If expenses exceed budget income, determine steps to balance your budget. (2) If income exceeds budget expenses, state how you would use the excess money (new goal, savings). (c) Track and record your actual income, expenses, and savings for 13 consecutive weeks (the same 13-week period for which you budgeted). (You may use the forms provided in the Personal Management merit badge pamphlet, devise your own, or use a computer-generated version.) When complete, present the records showing the results to your counselor. (d) Compare your budget with your actual income and expenses to understand when your budget worked and when it did not work. With your counselor, discuss what you might do differently the next time.

Step 3 (Budget Reflecting Your Expected Income): Step 3 (Prepare A Budget Reflecting): It's important to show where all of your money goes (p. 22).

Step 4 (Budget Reflecting Your Expected Income): Step 4 (Prepare A Budget Reflecting): This will give a better idea of where you spend your money and where you can reduce spending, if necessary (p. 22).

requirements.req_text: Discuss with your counselor FIVE of the following concepts: (a) The emotions you feel when you receive money. pamphlet_excerpts: Saving and Investing Including Reasons: Your counselor: Investments are subject to different levels of risk, the extent to which an investment goes up and down over time (p. 29).
Saving and Investing Including Reasons Principle 2: Your counselor Principle 2: The value of investments with higher risk, such as stocks, will tend to go up and down a lot (p. 29).
Saving and Investing Including Reasons Principle 3: Your counselor Principle 3: The value of less risky investments, such as bonds, will rise and fall less dramatically (p. 29).
Saving and Investing Including Reasons Principle 4: Your counselor Principle 4: Diversification means owning many different investments instead just one or a few (p. 29).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Saving and Investing Including Reasons): Step 1 (Your counselor): In general, having a very diversified portfolio is best (p. 29).
Step 2 (Saving and Investing Including Reasons): Step 2 (Your counselor): Yield is what an investment pays directly in income (p. 29).
Step 3 (Saving and Investing Including Reasons): Step 3 (Your counselor): Yield might bein the form of interest, dividends, or rental income from property (p. 29).
Step 4 (Saving and Investing Including Reasons): Step 4 (Your counselor): Financial investments take two basic forms: owned investments or loaned investments (p. 29).

Saving Versus Investing Principle 2: The value of investments with higher risk, such as stocks, will tend to go up and down a lot (p. 30).
Saving Versus Investing Principle 3: The value of less risky investments, such as bonds, will rise and fall less dramatically (p. 30).
Saving Versus Investing Principle 4: Diversification means owning many different investments instead just one or a few (p. 30).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Saving Versus Investing): In general, having a very diversified portfolio is best (p. 30).
Step 2 (Saving Versus Investing): Yield is what an investment pays directly in income (p. 30).
Step 3 (Saving Versus Investing): Yield might bein the form of interest, dividends, or rental income from property (p. 30).
Step 4 (Saving Versus Investing): Financial investments take two basic forms: owned investments or loaned investments (p. 30).

pamphlet_excerpts: People Might Purchase The Following: Most adults in the U. S. already have life insurance in the form of Social Security survivor benefits (p. 58).
People Might Purchase Principle 2: People Might Purchase The Following Principle 2: There are two main types of life insurance: term and whole life (p. 58).
People Might Purchase Principle 3: People Might Purchase The Following Principle 3: Term insurance pays a specified amount if you die during the covered term (for example, a 10-year period) (p. 58).
People Might Purchase Principle 4: People Might Purchase The Following Principle 4: Whole life insurance pays a specified amount regardless of when you die (p. 58).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (People Might Purchase): Step 1 (People Might Purchase The Following): Term insurance costs much less than whole life insurance (p. 58).

Step 2 (People Might Purchase): Step 2 (People Might Purchase The Following): Whole life insurance, however, is aggressively sold by insurance companies because they make significant profits from selling (p. 58).

Step 3 (People Might Purchase): Step 3 (People Might Purchase The Following): Most people who need life insurance at all should buy term insurance, shopping around for the least expensive policy that provides the coverage (p. 58).

Step 4 (People Might Purchase): Step 4 (People Might Purchase The Following): The main reason that most people buy most types of insurance is because they would need help paying large bills associated with an insured event (p. 58).

pamphlet_excerpts: Personal Management Core Field Standard: By the time you reach your late teens, you probably will have received numerous offers from credit card companies to apply for their cards (p. 39).
Personal Management Core Field Standard Principle 2: Just remember that you are personally responsible and legally obligated to pay back all amounts charged to your card (p. 39).
Personal Management Core Field Standard Principle 3: A credit card is a form of loan, just as if you had borrowed cash from a financial institution (p. 39).
Personal Management Core Field Standard Principle 4: It can be a convenient substitute for carrying checks or a large amount of cash and especially useful in emergencies (p. 39).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Personal Management Core Field Standard): In fact, credit cards do represent real money; using them unwisely can lead to financial difficulties (p. 39).

Step 2 (Personal Management Core Field Standard): A credit card, issued by a financial institution or credit card company, can be used to pay for any product or service as long as the seller accepts (p. 39).
Step 3 (Personal Management Core Field Standard): Not all sellers accept credit cards or a particular type of credit card, however (p. 39).
Step 4 (Personal Management Core Field Standard): In addition, credit cards have a charge limit, which means you can charge only up to the amount the credit card issuerallows (p. 39).

requirements.lead_text: Demonstrate to your counselor your understanding of time management by doing the following:
requirements.req_text: Demonstrate to your counselor your understanding of time management by doing the following: (a) Write a to-do list of tasks or activities, such as homework assignments, chores, and personal projects, that must be done in the coming week. List these in order of importance to you. (b) Make a seven-day calendar or schedule. Put in your set activities, such as school classes, sports practices or games, jobs or chores, and/or Scout or place of worship or club meetings, then plan when you will do all the tasks from your to-do list between your set activities. (c) Follow the one-week schedule you planned. Keep a daily diary or journal during each of the seven days of this week's activities, writing down when you completed each of the tasks on your to-do list compared to when you scheduled them. (d) With your counselor, review your to-do list, one-week schedule, and diary/journal to understand when your schedule worked and when it did not work. Discuss what you might do differently the next time.

Careers and Professional Pathways Principle 2: Experts say that, on average, people go through 10 different positions and three different careers during their working lives (p. 52).
Careers and Professional Pathways Principle 3: But a career should be more than a way to make a living (p. 52).
Careers and Professional Pathways Principle 4: Ideally, it should be emotionally, spiritually, and intellectually satisfying as well (p. 52).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Careers and Professional Pathways): Try choosing acareer that you are good at doing and one that you truly (p. 52).
Step 2 (Careers and Professional Pathways): It can be tough to work in a position that you do not like, even if you are earning a lot of money (p. 52).
Step 3 (Careers and Professional Pathways): If you are still trying to decide what career you would like to pursue, do not worry (p. 52).
Step 4 (Careers and Professional Pathways): Sometimes career decisions are not made until college or later (p. 52).

D. Because comparison shopping only applies to consumable groceries and does not affect durable goods or warranties.

B. Because long-term financing with high interest rates, fees, maintenance, and operating costs can make a low monthly payment far more expensive overall than saving up to pay cash.

Evidence That You Have Cared Principle 4: Present evidence that you have cared Principle 4: You must take the time to properly train your pet so that it does not become a nuisance (p. 7).

Step 3 (Evidence That You Have Cared): Step 3 (Present evidence that you have cared): Municipal laws may restrict the types of pets (p. 7).
Step 4 (Evidence That You Have Cared): Step 4 (Present evidence that you have cared): Give baby canaries all the egg food (available at pet stores) and conditioning food they want (p. 7).

step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Hazards, First Aid & Safety): Generally, a wide-angle lens will give a larger angle of view, while a telephoto lens compresses the subject and gives a smaller angle of view (p. 33).
Step 2 (Hazards, First Aid & Safety): A wide-angle lens is a good choice when you are close to your subject (p. 33).
Step 3 (Hazards, First Aid & Safety): A telephoto lens is best for subjects when you can't get up close (p. 33).
Step 4 (Hazards, First Aid & Safety): Earlier we discussed the importance of f-stops in controlling your depth of field and what is in focus (p. 33).

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: While composing photographs outdoors near a canyon rim, roadway, or approaching thunderstorm, what safety rule takes priority over capturing the shot?
quiz_item.question: While composing photographs outdoors near a canyon rim, roadway, or approaching thunderstorm, what safety rule takes priority over capturing the shot?
options: A. Maintain situational awareness of your footing and surroundings before stepping while looking through the viewfinder, and seek shelter immediately if lightning or severe weather approaches.
B. Walk backward while looking continuously through the viewfinder to frame a wider angle near ledges or moving traffic.
C. Hold a carbon-fiber tripod high overhead in an open field during a thunderstorm to keep the camera dry.
D. Climb over safety guardrails at scenic overlooks so foreground fences do not appear in the frame.
choices: A. Maintain situational awareness of your footing and surroundings before stepping while looking through the viewfinder, and seek shelter immediately if lightning or severe weather approaches.

quiz_item.correct_answer: A. Maintain situational awareness of your footing and surroundings before stepping while looking through the viewfinder, and seek shelter immediately if lightning or severe weather approaches.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (A): Photographers frequently get injured when stepping backward or sideways while focused on a viewfinder or LCD screen; always check footing and surroundings before moving, and never use tripods as lightning rods in storms.
