requirements.req_text: Do FOUR of the following, each under the supervision of a knowledgeable adult: (a) Visit the plumbing section of a hardware store or home center and identify: (1) PVC pipe and fittings (2) CPVC pipe and fittings (3) PEX pipe and fittings (4) Copper pipe and fittings (5) Steel pipe and fittings (6) Specialty plumbing tools (b) Cut, clean (deburr), PVC or CPVC pipe; solvent weld at least three connections to include a coupling, tee, and elbow. pamphlet_excerpts: Careers & Professional Pathways: Plumbing, including pipe fitting, is an important and well-paid occupation (p. 8).
Careers & Professional Pathways Principle 2: It covers installations and repairs in homes, commercial properties, and factories (p. 8).
Careers & Professional Pathways Principle 3: Plumbing pipelines are used for water supply, waste drainage, natural-gas heating, and many other purposes (p. 8).
Careers & Professional Pathways Principle 4: As a Scout, your major interest in plumbing probably will be in the field of home repairs (p. 8).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Careers & Professional Pathways): If a faucet leaks, a pipe freezes, or a plumbing fixture does not operate properly, you will want to know how to evaluate the problem (p. 8).
Step 2 (Careers & Professional Pathways): Then you will be able to decide on the proper steps to take to fix the problem, or determine that the job requires a professional plumber (p. 8).
Step 3 (Careers & Professional Pathways): When you discover a plumbing problem, you can often take care of basic plumbing needs, but remember that a plumber is like a doctor (p. 8).
Step 4 (Careers & Professional Pathways): For serious trouble or problems beyond your ability, you should get help from a trained specialist (p. 8).

patrol_quiz_bank.question: What is the primary purpose of the curved P-trap installed directly beneath every household sink, shower, and floor drain?
options: A. To boost incoming municipal water pressure before it reaches the hot and cold faucet valves.
B. To grind up solid food waste so it does not enter the septic tank or city sewer main.
C. To hold a standing water seal that blocks toxic, flammable, and foul-smelling sewer gases from rising out of the drain-waste-vent system into the building.
D. To filter dissolved calcium and magnesium minerals out of potable drinking water.
choices: A. To boost incoming municipal water pressure before it reaches the hot and cold faucet valves.
B. To grind up solid food waste so it does not enter the septic tank or city sewer main.
C. To hold a standing water seal that blocks toxic, flammable, and foul-smelling sewer gases from rising out of the drain-waste-vent system into the building.
D. To filter dissolved calcium and magnesium minerals out of potable drinking water.
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: C. To hold a standing water seal that blocks toxic, flammable, and foul-smelling sewer gases from rising out of the drain-waste-vent system into the building.
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (C): A P-trap retains a small volume of water after each use, creating an airtight liquid barrier that prevents hazardous sewer gases (such as methane and hydrogen sulfide) from entering living spaces.

pamphlet_excerpts: Precautions That Must Be Followed: Carving and modeling tools come in an amazing array, and most are made of wood, metal, or plastic (p. 39).
Precautions That Must Be Followed Principle 2: Discarded (and sterilized) steel dental tools are excellent for detailing, as are wood-carving tools (p. 39).
Precautions That Must Be Followed Principle 3: Restaurant suppliers and hardware and kitchenware stores are great sources for tools that can be used in pottery making (p. 39).
Precautions That Must Be Followed Principle 4: An experienced potter probably has collected a variety of tools, but beginners will do well with a basic tool set from aclay supplier (p. 39).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Precautions That Must Be Followed): These sets commonly contain a sponge, a metalrib, a rubber rib, a metal loop tool, a wooden stick, a metal needle tool, a fettling knife (p. 39).
Step 2 (Precautions That Must Be Followed): Pottery tools should be kept handy and safe in a sturdy container (p. 39).
Step 3 (Precautions That Must Be Followed): For instance, small, very smooth rivers tones are useful for burnishing and compressing clay surfaces, as are spoons (p. 39).
Step 4 (Precautions That Must Be Followed): Use seashells or pineconesto make interesting textures on pottery (p. 39).

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: Why should a pottery studio always be cleaned with wet sponges and mops rather than dry sweeping or blowing away dried clay scraps?
quiz_item.question: Why should a pottery studio always be cleaned with wet sponges and mops rather than dry sweeping or blowing away dried clay scraps?
options: A. Dry sweeping launches fine crystalline silica dust into the air, which can cause permanent lung damage (silicosis) when inhaled over time.
B. Broom bristles scratch the glaze off bisque-fired pottery sitting on drying shelves.
C. Dry clay dust reacts with room humidity to make the potter's wheel motor overheat.
D. Wet mopping is the only way to dissolve lead oxide out of raw earthenware clay bodies.
choices: A. Dry sweeping launches fine crystalline silica dust into the air, which can cause permanent lung damage (silicosis) when inhaled over time.
B. Broom bristles scratch the glaze off bisque-fired pottery sitting on drying shelves.
C. Dry clay dust reacts with room humidity to make the potter's wheel motor overheat.
D. Wet mopping is the only way to dissolve lead oxide out of raw earthenware clay bodies.
quiz_item.correct_answer: A. Dry sweeping launches fine crystalline silica dust into the air, which can cause permanent lung damage (silicosis) when inhaled over time.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (A): Clay and glaze powders contain fine silica particles that stay suspended in the air when dry-swept; wiping surfaces and mopping floors with water traps dust safely.

pamphlet_excerpts: Scope of The Ceramic Industry: The ceramics industry is one of the largest industries in the United States (p. 89).
Scope of The Ceramic Industry Principle 2: Ceramics are useful because of their chemical, electrical, mechanical, thermal, magnetic, and structural properties (p. 89).
Scope of The Ceramic Industry Principle 3: The ceramics industry is vital to the successful operation of other industries (p. 89).
Scope of The Ceramic Industry Principle 4: Abrasive materials made from silica are essential to the machine-tool and automotive industry (p. 89).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Scope of The Ceramic Industry): Glass products are essential to the automobile industry and to architectural, electronic, medical, and agricultural industries (p. 89).
Step 2 (Scope of The Ceramic Industry): Uranium oxide fuels are packaged in ceramic rods for useby nuclear power plants (p. 89).
Step 3 (Scope of The Ceramic Industry): The chips in every computer are ceramic, as are the tiles that covered NASA's space shuttles (p. 89).
Step 4 (Scope of The Ceramic Industry): Even the coating on paper used for magazines and books is ceramic (p. 89).

pamphlet_excerpts: Counselor's Approval Do ONE: Your Parent or Guardian's Permission: Because many high-fire kilns are built by individuals, each kiln follows a unique schedule (p. 25).
Counselor's Approval Do ONE Principle 2: Your Parent or Guardian's Permission Principle 2: Do not attempt to fire any fuel-burning kiln without close supervision from the owner (p. 25).

Counselor's Approval Do ONE Principle 3: Your Parent or Guardian's Permission Principle 3: Copper oxide can produce a brilliantred in a reduction firing, but it would produce greens inan oxidation firing (p. 25).
Counselor's Approval Do ONE Principle 4: Your Parent or Guardian's Permission Principle 4: Fuel must have a sufficient amount of oxygen to burn (p. 25).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Counselor's Approval Do ONE): Step 1 (Your Parent or Guardian's Permission): The dampers in fuel-burning kilns enable the potter to adjust the amount of oxygen inside the kiln (p. 25).

Step 2 (Counselor's Approval Do ONE): Step 2 (Your Parent or Guardian's Permission): When the kiln contains more than enough oxygen needed to completely burn the amount of fuel being used, the atmosphere inside the kiln is oxidized (p. 25).

Step 3 (Counselor's Approval Do ONE): Step 3 (Your Parent or Guardian's Permission): In a reduction firing, the flame is seeking oxygen inside the kiln, and because there isn't enough, it "steals" oxygen from the clay and glazes (p. 25).
Step 4 (Counselor's Approval Do ONE): Step 4 (Your Parent or Guardian's Permission): This chemical reaction darkens the clay and changes the look and texture of some glazes (p. 25).

pamphlet_excerpts: Programming Core Field Standard: You might not think that writing programs could cause injuries (p. 88).

Programming Core Field Standard Principle 2: But in fact, injuries from programming have much in common with sports injuries and can be prevented using some of the same techniques that athletes use (p. 88).
Programming Core Field Standard Principle 3: The main programming-related injuries are repetitive stress injuries, or RSIs (p. 88).
Programming Core Field Standard Principle 4: Just as in athletic activities, an RSI occurs when stress is placed on a joint, pulling on the tendons and muscles around the joint (p. 88).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Programming Core Field Standard): When the stress happens repeatedly, the body does not have time to recover and becomes irritated (p. 88).
Step 2 (Programming Core Field Standard): The body reacts to the irritation by increasing the amount of fluid in that area to reduce the stress placed on the tendon or muscle (p. 88).
Step 3 (Programming Core Field Standard): And just as athletes are trained to do, you can avoid issues like the following by developing good habits (p. 88).
Step 4 (Programming Core Field Standard): Proper equipment and preparation are the keys to prevention (p. 88).

pamphlet_excerpts: Historical Origins and Evolution: As of the printing of this merit badge pamphlet, more than 2,500 programming languages have been developed (p. 18).
Historical Origins and Evolution Principle 2: By the 1950s and 1960s, many new languages were being introduced, including BASIC, Fortran, and LISP (p. 18).
Historical Origins and Evolution Principle 3: These languages took programming beyond binary and assembly to allow portability of languages beyond just the processor hardware of the time (p. 18).
Historical Origins and Evolution Principle 4: That is, programs written in these languages could runon two or more kinds of processors or with two or more kinds of operating systems (p. 18).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Historical Origins and Evolution): Many languages, such as Pascal, we recreated to capture new concepts of computer science (p. 18).
Step 2 (Historical Origins and Evolution): Others, such as Fortran and COBOL, were developed to meet specific needs of science or business (p. 18).
Step 3 (Historical Origins and Evolution): FORTRAN (Formula Translation), originally developed in the 1950s, was among the earliest programming languages (p. 18).
Step 4 (Historical Origins and Evolution): Well-suited for mathematical calculations, FORTRAN was used mainly for scientific and engineering programming (p. 18).

pamphlet_excerpts: Intellectual Property: The value of software is in its electronically coded instructions, not in the plastic disc or other tangible media upon which the instructions are stored (p. 84).
Intellectual Property Principle 2: Software developers do not sell DVDs or other storage media (p. 84).
Intellectual Property Principle 3: What they actually sell is permission touse the programs they have created (p. 84).
Intellectual Property Principle 4: Licensing is more like renting a bike than buying one (p. 84).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Intellectual Property): When you buy a bike, you own it outright and can do what you want (p. 84).
Step 2 (Intellectual Property): When you rent a bike, however, you have the right to use it, but you may have some restrictions on how long and where you can ride (p. 84).
Step 3 (Intellectual Property): Similarly, with software, you purchase alicense to use the software in a manner specified by the terms and conditions of the license (p. 84).
Step 4 (Intellectual Property): Software may be licensed in several ways, including: Freeware (p. 84).

pamphlet_excerpts: Programming Core Field Standard: A program is a set of instructions that tells a processor how to do aparticular task (p. 14).
Programming Core Field Standard Principle 2: A programming language is the tool that converts the programmer'sinstructions into a form the processor can understand (p. 14).
Programming Core Field Standard Principle 3: The roots of modern programming stretch back to before the first computers (p. 14).
Programming Core Field Standard Principle 4: Most programming languages have their origins in early efforts to automate machines like calculating machines (p. 14).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Programming Core Field Standard): Before the development of modern programming languages, developers used binary code, which is the "native language" of amachine/computer (p. 14).
Step 2 (Programming Core Field Standard): These two numerals used in binary language were numeric codes for the operations a particular computer could execute (carry out) directly (p. 14).
Step 3 (Programming Core Field Standard): Binary code allowed programmers to turn pieces of computer hardware (circuits) "on" (represented with a 1) or "off" (represented by the numeral 0) (p. 14).
Step 4 (Programming Core Field Standard): All modern programming languages are built off the concept of trying to turn human commands into binary or machine code (p. 14).

intro_notes: Scouts BSA Test Lab Pilot Badge (Valid through 2026-12-31). This badge takes you on an exciting journey to understand how psychology impacts everyday life and leadership. You’ll learn about famous psychologists and their contributions, create and perform a skit showing psychology in action, explore mental health and resilience, and track your own activities and emotions to see how they shape your well-being. Along the way, you’ll practice empathy, reflect on the Scout Oath and Law, and even design your own pledge to inspire hope and support in your community. Finally, dive into career paths in psychology and discover what it takes to succeed in this fascinating field. Expand your mind, build resilience, and make a difference—start your Psychology Badge adventure today!

NOTE: Any registered adult Scouting America volunteer may serve as the counselor/reviewer for a Test Lab badge. Upon completion of all requirements and the official Scouting America Test Lab survey, Scouts receive an official Certificate of Completion that converts to Merit Badge credit if the badge graduates to permanent status.

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: While preparing for a high-adventure trek, a patrol leader notices a Scout becoming overwhelmed when trying to memorize 15 wilderness safety rules all at once. Using cognitive psychology principles of working memory, what teaching strategy works best?
quiz_item.question: While preparing for a high-adventure trek, a patrol leader notices a Scout becoming overwhelmed when trying to memorize 15 wilderness safety rules all at once. Using cognitive psychology principles of working memory, what teaching strategy works best?
options: A. Read all 15 rules faster without pausing so they enter long-term memory immediately.
B. Use chunking and spaced practice: group the 15 rules into 3 meaningful categories (such as S.T.O.P. or ABCDE) and practice retrieving them across multiple hands-on scenarios.
C. Skip practice and rely only on passive re-reading right before the trek.
D. Test the Scout on all 15 rules simultaneously while playing loud background distractions.
choices: A. Read all 15 rules faster without pausing so they enter long-term memory immediately.
B. Use chunking and spaced practice: group the 15 rules into 3 meaningful categories (such as S.T.O.P. or ABCDE) and practice retrieving them across multiple hands-on scenarios.
C. Skip practice and rely only on passive re-reading right before the trek.
D. Test the Scout on all 15 rules simultaneously while playing loud background distractions.
quiz_item.correct_answer: B. Use chunking and spaced practice: group the 15 rules into 3 meaningful categories (such as S.T.O.P. or ABCDE) and practice retrieving them across multiple hands-on scenarios.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (B): Human working memory holds only a few chunks at once; grouping items into meaningful frameworks and practicing active recall builds durable neural pathways.

options: A. Read all 15 rules faster without pausing so they enter long-term memory immediately.
B. Use chunking and spaced practice: group the 15 rules into 3 meaningful categories (such as S.T.O.P. or ABCDE) and practice retrieving them across multiple hands-on scenarios.
C. Skip practice and rely only on passive re-reading right before the trek.
D. Test the Scout on all 15 rules simultaneously while playing loud background distractions.

patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: B. Use chunking and spaced practice: group the 15 rules into 3 meaningful categories (such as S.T.O.P. or ABCDE) and practice retrieving them across multiple hands-on scenarios.

Step 2 (Public health): Following are some diseases that are common concerns for public health in the United States (p. 18).
Step 3 (Public health): People with viral respiratory infections are contagious one day before and up to two weeks after they show symptoms (p. 18).

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: How do safe drinking water treatment, sanitary sewage disposal, handwashing, and vector control work together in public health?
quiz_item.question: How do safe drinking water treatment, sanitary sewage disposal, handwashing, and vector control work together in public health?
options: A. They treat genetic disorders by altering human DNA after symptoms appear.
B. They break the chain of infection by eliminating reservoirs and blocking waterborne, fecal-oral, and insect-borne transmission pathways before pathogens can spread across a community.
C. They replace the need for childhood vaccinations against airborne viruses like measles and influenza.
D. They increase antibiotic resistance in bacteria by sterilizing outdoor soil ecosystems.
choices: A. They treat genetic disorders by altering human DNA after symptoms appear.
B. They break the chain of infection by eliminating reservoirs and blocking waterborne, fecal-oral, and insect-borne transmission pathways before pathogens can spread across a community.
C. They replace the need for childhood vaccinations against airborne viruses like measles and influenza.
D. They increase antibiotic resistance in bacteria by sterilizing outdoor soil ecosystems.
quiz_item.correct_answer: B. They break the chain of infection by eliminating reservoirs and blocking waterborne, fecal-oral, and insect-borne transmission pathways before pathogens can spread across a community.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (B): Public health sanitation, clean water, hygiene, and mosquito/tick vector control prevent epidemics by interrupting disease transmission routes between reservoirs and susceptible hosts.

pamphlet_excerpts: Immunization B Name Eight Diseases: Explain The Meaning of Immunization: The immune system makes antibodies for each particular disease that it meets (p. 20).
Immunization B Name Eight Diseases Principle 2: Explain The Meaning of Immunization Principle 2: Therefore, a different vaccine is needed for each disease (p. 20).

Immunization B Name Eight Diseases Principle 3: Explain The Meaning of Immunization Principle 3: Immunizations also are available for many other diseases that are uncommon in the United States but common in other parts of the world (p. 20).

Immunization B Name Eight Diseases Principle 4: Explain The Meaning of Immunization Principle 4: Americans typically receive these immunizations when they travel out of the country or join the armed forces (p. 20).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Immunization B Name Eight Diseases): Step 1 (Explain The Meaning of Immunization): Immunization is suggested for very young children, with periodic booster injections as recommended (p. 20).
Step 2 (Immunization B Name Eight Diseases): Step 2 (Explain The Meaning of Immunization): Antibodies are long-lasting, but the protection they give may decrease with time (p. 20).
Step 3 (Immunization B Name Eight Diseases): Step 3 (Explain The Meaning of Immunization): A second exposure to a pathogen will increase the level of antibodies a person's body will produce (p. 20).
Step 4 (Immunization B Name Eight Diseases): Step 4 (Explain The Meaning of Immunization): So a second injection, or booster shot, often is given to help strengthen immunity (p. 20).

pamphlet_excerpts: Importance of Safe Drinking Water: Soil can contain lead, too, from deteriorating buildings and from the lead in car exhaust (p. 32).
Importance of Safe Drinking Water Principle 2: Lead pipes and solder use din older homes can add lead to the water (p. 32).
Importance of Safe Drinking Water Principle 3: In older homes that have lead pipes, lead poisoning can be avoided by using cold water for drinking and making baby formula (p. 32).
Importance of Safe Drinking Water Principle 4: Hot water that runs through old pipes will contain more lead than will cold water (p. 32).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Importance of Safe Drinking Water): Food or drink held in lead-glazed pottery is another source of lead buildup in a person's body (p. 32).
Step 2 (Importance of Safe Drinking Water): Escherichia coli is a bacterium that causes a type of food poisoning (p. 32).
Step 3 (Importance of Safe Drinking Water): Different strains of E. coli normally live in the intestines of humans and other animals and help with digestion (p. 32).
Step 4 (Importance of Safe Drinking Water): But some strains cause illness and others produce toxins that are among the most poisonous substances known (p. 32).

Step 3 (A vector is and how insects): In urban areas, the landfill might be far from the city that creates the waste (p. 49).
Step 4 (A vector is and how insects): There are accepted laws and regulations for creating and operating landfills (p. 49).

requirements.lead_text: With your parent or guardian's and counselor's approval, do ONE of the following:
requirements.req_text: With your parent or guardian's and counselor's approval, do ONE of the following: (a) Visit a municipal wastewater treatment facility or a solid-waste management operation in your community. (1) Describe how the facility safely treats and disposes of sewage or solid waste. (2) Discuss your visit and what you learned with your counselor. (3) Describe how sewage and solid waste should be disposed of under wilderness camping conditions. (b) Visit a food service facility, such as a restaurant or school cafeteria. (1) Observe food preparation, handling, and storage. Learn how the facility keeps food from becoming contaminated. (2) Find out what conditions allow microorganisms to multiply in food, what can be done to help prevent them from growing and spreading, and how to kill them. (3) Discuss the importance of using a thermometer to check food temperatures. (4) Discuss your visit and what you learned with your counselor.

pamphlet_excerpts: Municipal Wastewater Treatment Facility: Do ONE of The Following: Municipal sewage treatment systems are designed to handle large volumes of sewage and liquid wastes (p. 44).
Municipal Wastewater Treatment Facility Principle 2: Do ONE of The Following Principle 2: The raw sewage flows to a treatment plant through underground pipes (mains) (p. 44).
Municipal Wastewater Treatment Facility Principle 3: Do ONE of The Following Principle 3: Sewage is screened, allowed to settle, processed, dried, and disinfected before disposal (p. 44).
Municipal Wastewater Treatment Facility Principle 4: Do ONE of The Following Principle 4: Screening removes objects larger than an inch or two in size that have entered sewage mains (p. 44).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Municipal Wastewater Treatment Facility): Step 1 (Do ONE of The Following): Debris is removed and then taken to a landfill or burned (p. 44).

Step 2 (Municipal Wastewater Treatment Facility): Step 2 (Do ONE of The Following): By the time incoming waste reaches the sewage treatment plant, it is mostly liquid with particles suspended (p. 44).
Step 3 (Municipal Wastewater Treatment Facility): Step 3 (Do ONE of The Following): Many suspended particles drop out of the liquid portion as the screened sewage is allowed to settle (p. 44).
Step 4 (Municipal Wastewater Treatment Facility): Step 4 (Do ONE of The Following): Processing or treatment is done by two basic methods: activated sludge and trickling (p. 44).

pamphlet_excerpts: Health dangers from air, water: The World Health Organization considers tobacco use to be an epidemic because it kills 6 million people every year (p. 70).
Health dangers from air, water Principle 2: Using these substances can damage the body, lead to accompanying diseases, and cause great numbers of injuries and accidents (p. 70).
Health dangers from air, water Principle 3: Tobacco contains more than 4,000 chemical compounds, many of which cause emphysema and cancer (p. 70).
Health dangers from air, water Principle 4: In fact, cigarette smoking causes 87 percent of lung cancer, a rarely cured disease with poor survival rates (p. 70).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Health dangers from air, water): It is one of the leading causes of death worldwide (p. 70).
Step 2 (Health dangers from air, water): Smoking contributes greatly to heart disease and stroke as well (p. 70).
Step 3 (Health dangers from air, water): Most smokers began smoking before they were 18 year sold (p. 70).
Step 4 (Health dangers from air, water): Because nicotine is one of the most addictive substances known to humans, young adults who start using tobacco often become hooked for life (p. 70).

Explain how the public health agency you visited is trying to reduce the mortality and morbidity rates of these leading causes of illness and death. (2) Explain the role of your health agency as it relates to the outbreak of diseases. (3) Discuss the kinds of public assistance the agency is able to provide in case of disasters such as floods, storms, tornadoes, earthquakes, and other acts of destruction. Your discussion can include the cleanup necessary after the disaster.

City County State or Federal Principle 2: Do The Following Principle 2: But individuals also can help maintain public health, and their own health, by learning about diseases (p. 18).

City County State or Federal Principle 4: Do The Following Principle 4: Benzene, a chemical found in tobacco smoke, vehicle exhaust, detergents, and other sources, can cause leukemia (p. 18).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (City County State or Federal): Step 1 (Do The Following): Diseases that are passed through the genes, from parents to offspring, are known as hereditary diseases (p. 18).
Step 2 (City County State or Federal): Step 2 (Do The Following): Examples include sickle-cell anemia and hemophilia (p. 18).
Step 3 (City County State or Federal): Step 3 (Do The Following): Still other diseases may be caused by poor lifestyle choices (p. 18).

Step 4 (City County State or Federal): Step 4 (Do The Following): Encouraging healthy dietary habits and regular physical activity can markedly reduce the numbers of deaths from heart attacks each year (p. 18).

options: A. Read your speech word-for-word from a full sheet of paper held in front of your face while speaking as rapidly as possible.
B. Stare at a single spot on the back wall above the audience's heads and speak in a flat monotone to avoid sounding nervous.
C. Use brief keyword outline notes to stay organized while maintaining natural eye contact across the audience, projecting your voice clearly, and varying your pace and pitch.
D. Pace continuously back and forth across the stage while looking down at the floor to remember memorized sentences.
choices: A. Read your speech word-for-word from a full sheet of paper held in front of your face while speaking as rapidly as possible.
B. Stare at a single spot on the back wall above the audience's heads and speak in a flat monotone to avoid sounding nervous.

pamphlet_excerpts: You know parliamentary procedure by leading: Come to Order, Parliamentary Procedure Made Easy In formal meetings, the chair, or leader, conducts all business (p. 45).
You know parliamentary procedure by leading Principle 2: While the leader of an informal meeting may participate in the discussion, the chair of a formal meeting only conducts the meeting (p. 45).
You know parliamentary procedure by leading Principle 3: Speakers must be recognized by the chair and technically, all remarks are directed to the chair (p. 45).
You know parliamentary procedure by leading Principle 4: Questions from individual to individual also are directed via the chair (p. 45).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (You know parliamentary procedure by leading): The formal meeting is more a debate of opposing ideas, each of which strives for audience approval (p. 45).

Step 2 (You know parliamentary procedure by leading): The chair enforces the rules equally on all participants to ensure that each person has a fair opportunity to present his or her point of view (p. 45).
Step 3 (You know parliamentary procedure by leading): Responsibility for keeping the meeting going also means keeping it focused (p. 45).

Step 4 (You know parliamentary procedure by leading): When the discussion While informal discussions do not have rules, the chair must apply common sense ideas for a successful meeting to take place (p. 45).

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: In papermaking, what is the primary difference between mechanical pulping and chemical (kraft) pulping of wood chips?
quiz_item.question: In papermaking, what is the primary difference between mechanical pulping and chemical (kraft) pulping of wood chips?
options: A. Mechanical pulping grinds wood into high-yield short fibers that retain lignin (suited for newsprint), whereas chemical kraft pulping dissolves lignin with heat and chemicals to preserve long, strong cellulose fibers.
B. Mechanical pulping dissolves all cellulose fibers in acid, whereas chemical pulping uses only cold water and sanders.
C. Mechanical pulping works only on recycled cotton rags, whereas chemical pulping requires synthetic polyester fibers.
D. Chemical pulping leaves all bark and lignin intact so the finished paper turns yellow within a few days in sunlight.
choices: A. Mechanical pulping grinds wood into high-yield short fibers that retain lignin (suited for newsprint), whereas chemical kraft pulping dissolves lignin with heat and chemicals to preserve long, strong cellulose fibers.
B. Mechanical pulping dissolves all cellulose fibers in acid, whereas chemical pulping uses only cold water and sanders.
C. Mechanical pulping works only on recycled cotton rags, whereas chemical pulping requires synthetic polyester fibers.
D. Chemical pulping leaves all bark and lignin intact so the finished paper turns yellow within a few days in sunlight.
quiz_item.correct_answer: A. Mechanical pulping grinds wood into high-yield short fibers that retain lignin (suited for newsprint), whereas chemical kraft pulping dissolves lignin with heat and chemicals to preserve long, strong cellulose fibers.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (A): Mechanical pulping physically separates fibers with high yield but leaves lignin behind (which weakens and yellows paper), while chemical kraft pulping dissolves lignin to yield strong, durable cellulose fibers.

requirements.lead_text: With your parent or guardian's and counselor's approval, do ONE of the following:
requirements.req_text: With your parent or guardian's and counselor's approval, do ONE of the following: (a) Visit a pulp mill. Describe how the mill converts wood to cellulose fibers. (b) Visit a paper mill and get a sample of the paper made there. Describe the processes used for making this paper. Tell how it will be used. (c) Visit a container plant or box plant. Describe how the plant's products are made. (d) Visit a recycled paper collection or sorting facility. Describe the operations there. (e) Using books, magazines, your local library, the internet (with your parent or guardian's permission), and any other suitable research tool, find out how paper products are developed. Find out what role research and development play in the papermaking industry. Share what you learned with your counselor.

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: In papermaking, what is the primary difference between mechanical pulping and chemical (kraft) pulping of wood chips?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: In papermaking, what is the primary difference between mechanical pulping and chemical (kraft) pulping of wood chips?
options: A. Mechanical pulping grinds wood into high-yield short fibers that retain lignin (suited for newsprint), whereas chemical kraft pulping dissolves lignin with heat and chemicals to preserve long, strong cellulose fibers.
B. Mechanical pulping dissolves all cellulose fibers in acid, whereas chemical pulping uses only cold water and sanders.
C. Mechanical pulping works only on recycled cotton rags, whereas chemical pulping requires synthetic polyester fibers.
D. Chemical pulping leaves all bark and lignin intact so the finished paper turns yellow within a few days in sunlight.
choices: A. Mechanical pulping grinds wood into high-yield short fibers that retain lignin (suited for newsprint), whereas chemical kraft pulping dissolves lignin with heat and chemicals to preserve long, strong cellulose fibers.
B. Mechanical pulping dissolves all cellulose fibers in acid, whereas chemical pulping uses only cold water and sanders.
C. Mechanical pulping works only on recycled cotton rags, whereas chemical pulping requires synthetic polyester fibers.
D. Chemical pulping leaves all bark and lignin intact so the finished paper turns yellow within a few days in sunlight.
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: A. Mechanical pulping grinds wood into high-yield short fibers that retain lignin (suited for newsprint), whereas chemical kraft pulping dissolves lignin with heat and chemicals to preserve long, strong cellulose fibers.
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (A): Mechanical pulping physically separates fibers with high yield but leaves lignin behind (which weakens and yellows paper), while chemical kraft pulping dissolves lignin to yield strong, durable cellulose fibers.

pamphlet_excerpts: Radio Safety: All equipment must be connected to a good ground, preferably to a long metal rod driven into the earth (which is why it is called a "ground") (p. 35).
Radio Safety Principle 2: But most amateur radio operators prefer to drive a separate ground rod close by, just for their station (p. 35).
Radio Safety Principle 3: Also, a good RF ground is important to make the whole station work at its best; the ground provides the "return path" for the radio waves you are sending (p. 35).
Radio Safety Principle 4: Antennas may be hit by lightning and you must provide a path to ground for the energy from lightning strikes (p. 35).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Radio Safety): Ground antenna feed lines to safely bleed off static buildup during electrical storms (p. 35).
Step 2 (Radio Safety): Many operators put lightning protectors in their feed lines where the lines enter the house (p. 35).
Step 3 (Radio Safety): These devices provide a safe path for static to discharge to ground, even if the feed line is still connected to the radio (p. 35).
Step 4 (Radio Safety): Nothing can protect your radio against a direct lightning hit, or even a nearby strike (p. 35).

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: What is the single most critical safety rule when choosing a location to erect an outdoor amateur radio mast or wire antenna?
quiz_item.question: What is the single most critical safety rule when choosing a location to erect an outdoor amateur radio mast or wire antenna?
options: A. Mount the antenna directly onto an electric utility pole so the coax shield shares the power company ground wire.
B. String dipole wires directly underneath high-voltage overhead distribution lines to shield the receiver from lightning.
C. Erect the mast only during rainstorms so moist soil improves radio-frequency grounding.
D. Locate the antenna and mast far enough from all overhead power lines that even if the mast or wire falls in any direction, it cannot come within 10 feet of a power line.
choices: A. Mount the antenna directly onto an electric utility pole so the coax shield shares the power company ground wire.
B. String dipole wires directly underneath high-voltage overhead distribution lines to shield the receiver from lightning.
C. Erect the mast only during rainstorms so moist soil improves radio-frequency grounding.
D. Locate the antenna and mast far enough from all overhead power lines that even if the mast or wire falls in any direction, it cannot come within 10 feet of a power line.
quiz_item.correct_answer: D. Locate the antenna and mast far enough from all overhead power lines that even if the mast or wire falls in any direction, it cannot come within 10 feet of a power line.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (D): Contact between an antenna or mast and overhead electrical power lines is a leading cause of fatal electrocution in radio operations; antennas must never be placed where they could fall onto or near power lines.

step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Information by Radio): You can see that the amplitude of the overall waveform varies according to the frequency and amplitude of the tone (p. 29).
Step 2 (Information by Radio): Unlike shortwave stations, many medium-wave stations do not offer QSL cards, but they can confirm your reception viaemail or even with a letter (p. 29).
Step 3 (Information by Radio): Check astation's website for an email address or aphysical address for sending your reception report (p. 29).
Step 4 (Information by Radio): On the other hand, medium-wave broadcasters are assigned only one frequency (p. 29).

step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Cell Phones): In a real sense, the phone is a computer that includes a display to show text messages, photos, etc (p. 32).
Step 2 (Cell Phones): The cell-phone network consists of cell towers placed close enough together that you never lose radio coverage as you travel, well, almost (p. 32).
Step 3 (Cell Phones): Sometimes, when you're camping or on a road trip, you may lose cell coverage (p. 32).
Step 4 (Cell Phones): The cell towers pick up your signal and send signals back to your cell phone (p. 32).

requirements.lead_text: Amateur and Professional Radio. Do ONE of the following options:
requirements.req_text: Amateur and Professional Radio. Do ONE of the following options: (a) Option A, Amateur Radio. Do ALL of the following: (1) Tell why the FCC has an amateur radio service. Describe activities that amateur radio operators can do on the air, once they have earned an amateur radio license. (2) Explain differences between the Technician, General, and Extra Class license requirements and privileges. Explain who administers amateur radio exams. (3) Explain at least five Q signals or amateur radio terms. (4) Explain how you would make an emergency call on voice or Morse code. Resources: How To Use Your VHF Marine Radio To Call for Help in a Boat Emergency (video) Ham Radio Disaster Messaging Demo (video) Using Ham Radio To Call for Help in an Emergency, What You Should Do! (video) (5) Explain the differences between handheld, mobile, and base station transceivers and their uses. Explain the use of amateur radio repeaters. (6) Using proper call signs, Q signals, and abbreviations, carry on a 10-minute real or simulated amateur radio contact using voice, Morse code, or digital mode. Properly log the real or simulated amateur radio contact, and record the signal report. Note: Licensed amateur radio operators may substitute five QSL cards as evidence of contacts with five amateur radio operators. (b) Option B, Radio Broadcasting. Do ALL of the following: (1) Discuss with your counselor FCC broadcast regulations. Include power levels, frequencies, and the regulations for low-power stations. (2) Prepare a program schedule for radio station "KBSA" of exactly one-half hour, including music, news, commercials, and proper station identification. Record your program on audiotape or in a digital audio format, using proper techniques. (3) Listen to and properly log 15 broadcast stations. Determine the program format and target audience for five of these stations. (4) Explain to your counselor at least eight terms used in commercial broadcasting, such as segue, cut, fade, continuity, remote, Emergency Alert System, network, cue, dead air, PSA, and playlist. (5) Discuss with your counselor alternative radio platforms such as internet streaming, satellite radio, and podcasts. (c) Option C, Shortwave and Medium-Wave Listening. Do ALL of the following: (1) Listen across several shortwave bands for four one-hour periods-at least one period during daylight hours and at least one period at night. Log the stations properly and locate them geographically on a map, globe, or web-based mapping service. (2) Listen to several medium-wave stations for two one-hour periods, one period during daylight hours and one period at night. Log the stations properly and locate them on a map, globe, or web-based mapping service. (3) Compare your daytime and nighttime logs; note the frequencies on which your selected stations were loudest during each session. Explain differences in the signal strength from one period to the next. (4) Compare your medium-wave broadcast station logs and explain why some distant stations are heard at your location only during the night. (5) Demonstrate listening to a radio broadcast using a smartphone/cell phone. Include international broadcasts in your demonstration. (d) Option D, Amateur Radio Direction Finding. Do ALL of the following: (1) Describe amateur radio direction finding and explain why direction finding is important as both an activity and in competition. (2) Describe what frequencies and equipment are used for ARDF or fox hunting. (3) Build a simple directional antenna for either of the two frequencies used in ARDF. (4) Participate in a simple fox hunt using your antenna along with a provided receiver. (5) Show, on a map, how you located the "fox" using your receiver. (e) Option E, Family Radio Service (FRS) and General Mobile Radio Service (GMRS) Walkie Talkies. Do ALL of the following: (1) Explain what the Family Radio Service (FRS) and General Mobile Radio Service (GMRS) are and how they are different from each other, from other commercial two-way radios, and from Citizens Band (CB) and amateur radio (ham). (2) Explain each of the following for using a FRS radio or GMRS walkie talkie: (a) Is any type of license needed to use these radios? If so: what kind? (b) What radio frequencies are used and how is information encoded? (c) How much power can be used when transmitting? (d) What type of antenna can be used? (e) What is the effective range and what limits it? (f) What are common everyday uses for these radios? (g) How can these radios be useful in an emergency? (3) Use the FRS radios or GMRS walkie talkies with family, friends, or Scouts on a hike, at an event, or in a team game. Discuss what you learned with your counselor.

sub_requirements.sub_req_text: Option A, Amateur Radio. Do ALL of the following: (1) Tell why the FCC has an amateur radio service. Describe activities that amateur radio operators can do on the air, once they have earned an amateur radio license. (2) Explain differences between the Technician, General, and Extra Class license requirements and privileges. Explain who administers amateur radio exams. (3) Explain at least five Q signals or amateur radio terms. (4) Explain how you would make an emergency call on voice or Morse code. Resources: How To Use Your VHF Marine Radio To Call for Help in a Boat Emergency (video) Ham Radio Disaster Messaging Demo (video) Using Ham Radio To Call for Help in an Emergency, What You Should Do! (video) (5) Explain the differences between handheld, mobile, and base station transceivers and their uses. Explain the use of amateur radio repeaters. (6) Using proper call signs, Q signals, and abbreviations, carry on a 10-minute real or simulated amateur radio contact using voice, Morse code, or digital mode. Properly log the real or simulated amateur radio contact, and record the signal report. Note: Licensed amateur radio operators may substitute five QSL cards as evidence of contacts with five amateur radio operators.

sub_requirements.label: (b)
sub_requirements.text: Option B, Radio Broadcasting. Do ALL of the following: (1) Discuss with your counselor FCC broadcast regulations. Include power levels, frequencies, and the regulations for low-power stations. (2) Prepare a program schedule for radio station "KBSA" of exactly one-half hour, including music, news, commercials, and proper station identification. Record your program on audiotape or in a digital audio format, using proper techniques. (3) Listen to and properly log 15 broadcast stations. Determine the program format and target audience for five of these stations. (4) Explain to your counselor at least eight terms used in commercial broadcasting, such as segue, cut, fade, continuity, remote, Emergency Alert System, network, cue, dead air, PSA, and playlist. (5) Discuss with your counselor alternative radio platforms such as internet streaming, satellite radio, and podcasts.

sub_requirements.label: (c)
sub_requirements.text: Option C, Shortwave and Medium-Wave Listening. Do ALL of the following: (1) Listen across several shortwave bands for four one-hour periods-at least one period during daylight hours and at least one period at night. Log the stations properly and locate them geographically on a map, globe, or web-based mapping service. (2) Listen to several medium-wave stations for two one-hour periods, one period during daylight hours and one period at night. Log the stations properly and locate them on a map, globe, or web-based mapping service. (3) Compare your daytime and nighttime logs; note the frequencies on which your selected stations were loudest during each session. Explain differences in the signal strength from one period to the next. (4) Compare your medium-wave broadcast station logs and explain why some distant stations are heard at your location only during the night. (5) Demonstrate listening to a radio broadcast using a smartphone/cell phone. Include international broadcasts in your demonstration.

sub_requirements.label: (e)
sub_requirements.text: Option E, Family Radio Service (FRS) and General Mobile Radio Service (GMRS) Walkie Talkies. Do ALL of the following: (1) Explain what the Family Radio Service (FRS) and General Mobile Radio Service (GMRS) are and how they are different from each other, from other commercial two-way radios, and from Citizens Band (CB) and amateur radio (ham). (2) Explain each of the following for using a FRS radio or GMRS walkie talkie: (a) Is any type of license needed to use these radios? If so: what kind? (b) What radio frequencies are used and how is information encoded? (c) How much power can be used when transmitting? (d) What type of antenna can be used? pamphlet_excerpts: Careers and Professional Pathways: Using relatively simple receivers, you can pick up many shortwave broadcast (SWB) stations (p. 72).
Careers and Professional Pathways Principle 2: These stations are fun to listen to, and many shortwave listeners (SWLs) spend all of their listening time on SWB stations (p. 72).
Careers and Professional Pathways Principle 3: These stations broadcast in every conceivable language, often 24 hours a day (p. 72).
Careers and Professional Pathways Principle 4: Some are religious in nature, some present political viewpoints, and others are primarily for entertainment (p. 72).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Careers and Professional Pathways): Each station tries to put the best face on its country, and this can lead to fascinating comparisons (p. 72).
Step 2 (Careers and Professional Pathways): Listen to the world news on the Voice of America, then follow with China Radio International (Beijing), and finish up with Radio Havana (Cuba) (p. 72).
Step 3 (Careers and Professional Pathways): It may be hard to believe that those broadcasts describe the same world (p. 72).
Step 4 (Careers and Professional Pathways): The major SWB stations, such as the BBC, Voice of America (VOA), and China Radio International (CRI), each transmit on many frequencies (p. 72).

requirements.req_text: Careers. Do ONE of the following: (a) Explore careers related to radio. Research one career to learn about the training and education needed, costs, job prospects, salary, job duties, and advancement. With permission of your parent or guardian, your research methods may include an internet or library search, an interview with a professional in the field, or a visit to a location where people in this career work or train. Discuss your findings and career interest with your counselor. (b) Explore how you could use radio knowledge and skills to develop a hobby or to serve as a volunteer. If possible, with permission of your parent or guardian, interview a radio hobbyist or volunteer. Research training and licensing needed, expenses, and organizations that promote or support your objectives. Discuss with your counselor what short-term and long-term goals you might have if you pursue this.

patrol_quiz_bank.question: What is the single most critical safety rule when choosing a location to erect an outdoor amateur radio mast or wire antenna?
options: A. Mount the antenna directly onto an electric utility pole so the coax shield shares the power company ground wire.
B. String dipole wires directly underneath high-voltage overhead distribution lines to shield the receiver from lightning.
C. Erect the mast only during rainstorms so moist soil improves radio-frequency grounding.
D. Locate the antenna and mast far enough from all overhead power lines that even if the mast or wire falls in any direction, it cannot come within 10 feet of a power line.
choices: A. Mount the antenna directly onto an electric utility pole so the coax shield shares the power company ground wire.
B. String dipole wires directly underneath high-voltage overhead distribution lines to shield the receiver from lightning.
C. Erect the mast only during rainstorms so moist soil improves radio-frequency grounding.
D. Locate the antenna and mast far enough from all overhead power lines that even if the mast or wire falls in any direction, it cannot come within 10 feet of a power line.
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: D. Locate the antenna and mast far enough from all overhead power lines that even if the mast or wire falls in any direction, it cannot come within 10 feet of a power line.
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (D): Contact between an antenna or mast and overhead electrical power lines is a leading cause of fatal electrocution in radio operations; antennas must never be placed where they could fall onto or near power lines.

pamphlet_excerpts: Types of Modern Freight Trains: Name three types of modern freight: Electric locomotives (without a diesel engine) collect current from overhead wires, orcatenary, through metal arms called pantographs mounted on (p. 15).

Types of Modern Freight Trains Principle 2: Name three types of modern freight Principle 2: Others use a pickup shoe to collect current from an electrified third rail placed next to the running rails (p. 15).
Types of Modern Freight Trains Principle 3: Name three types of modern freight Principle 3: The locomotive's internal equipment converts high-voltage current to lower voltage current (p. 15).
Types of Modern Freight Trains Principle 4: Name three types of modern freight Principle 4: Locomotives, especially on passenger commuter trains, often push as well as pull their trains (p. 15).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Types of Modern Freight Trains): Step 1 (Name three types of modern freight): The train has a locomotive on one end and a passenger car equipped with an engineer's cab and duplicate controls on the other end (p. 15).

Step 2 (Types of Modern Freight Trains): Step 2 (Name three types of modern freight): A train stops by using an air brake system, which allows the engineer to apply the brakes to all cars at once (p. 15).
Step 3 (Types of Modern Freight Trains): Step 3 (Name three types of modern freight): An aircompressor fills a main air reservoir, located in the locomotive, with compressed air (p. 15).

Step 4 (Types of Modern Freight Trains): Step 4 (Name three types of modern freight): Then the air is piped through the brake pipe from the locomotive to the cars, one after the other, by hoses (p. 15).

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: Why does Operation Lifesaver emphasize that pedestrians and drivers must never walk along railroad tracks or drive around lowered crossing gates?
quiz_item.question: Why does Operation Lifesaver emphasize that pedestrians and drivers must never walk along railroad tracks or drive around lowered crossing gates?
options: A. Trains can easily swerve onto adjacent tracks, making it hard to predict which rail they will use.
B. A freight train overhangs the rails by at least three feet on both sides, can approach quietly, and often requires more than a mile to stop even with emergency braking.
C. Railroad tracks carry high-voltage third-rail traction power on all rural diesel freight lines across North America.
D. Crossing gates lower only after the locomotive is within 50 feet of the intersection.
choices: A. Trains can easily swerve onto adjacent tracks, making it hard to predict which rail they will use.
B. A freight train overhangs the rails by at least three feet on both sides, can approach quietly, and often requires more than a mile to stop even with emergency braking.
C. Railroad tracks carry high-voltage third-rail traction power on all rural diesel freight lines across North America.
D. Crossing gates lower only after the locomotive is within 50 feet of the intersection.
quiz_item.correct_answer: B. A freight train overhangs the rails by at least three feet on both sides, can approach quietly, and often requires more than a mile to stop even with emergency braking.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (B): Trains cannot steer, overhang the crossties, appear slower and farther away than they actually are, and require a mile or more to come to a full stop.

pamphlet_excerpts: Formation of Amtrak: Explain The Purpose and Formation: Today Amtrak carries more than 31 million passengers ayear over more than 22,000 miles of track, almost all of it owned by the Class I freight railroads (p. 27).

Formation of Amtrak Principle 2: Explain The Purpose and Formation Principle 2: The exception is the Northeast Corridor (NEC), where Amtrak owns and maintains most of this high-speed electrified rail line between Boston (p. 27).

Formation of Amtrak Principle 3: Explain The Purpose and Formation Principle 3: Long-term plans are under way to extend this rail corridor south to Richmond, Virginia, and add other high-speed lines in California, the upper (p. 27).
Formation of Amtrak Principle 4: Explain The Purpose and Formation Principle 4: It also owns a 97-mile segment between Porter, Indiana, and Kalamazoo, Michigan (p. 27).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Formation of Amtrak): Step 1 (Explain The Purpose and Formation): On long-distance routes, Amtrak is replacing older diesel locomotives with fuel efficient and cleaner-burning ALC-42 locomotives from Siemens (p. 27).
Step 2 (Formation of Amtrak): Step 2 (Explain The Purpose and Formation): These engines emit 89% less nitrogen oxide and 95% less particulate matter than the old diesels (p. 27).
Step 3 (Formation of Amtrak): Step 3 (Explain The Purpose and Formation): Before this nation's "iron network" connected communities across North America, each town set its clocks by the sun (p. 27).

Step 4 (Formation of Amtrak): Step 4 (Explain The Purpose and Formation): So time varied from place to place, with the time in towns to the west running minutes behind the time in towns to the east (p. 27).

pamphlet_excerpts: Operation Lifesaver and Its Mission: Explain The Purpose of Operation: In America's cities and beyond, nothing connects us to work, play, and each other like public transit, today's safest, most reliable way to travel (p. 38).

Operation Lifesaver and Its Mission Principle 2: Explain The Purpose of Operation Principle 2: The American Public Transportation Association (APTA) estimates that people use public transportation 34 million times each weekday (p. 38).
Operation Lifesaver and Its Mission Principle 3: Explain The Purpose of Operation Principle 3: Six things to know about light rail and commuter train safety: 1 (p. 38).
Operation Lifesaver and Its Mission Principle 4: Explain The Purpose of Operation Principle 4: Trains can come from either direction at anytime and can be very quiet (p. 38).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Operation Lifesaver and Its Mission): Step 1 (Explain The Purpose of Operation): Obey all warning signs and signals, and use caution when using headsets or cell phones. 2 (p. 38).
Step 2 (Operation Lifesaver and Its Mission): Step 2 (Explain The Purpose of Operation): Trains are wider than the tracks; never sit on the edge of a station platform. 3 (p. 38).

Step 3 (Operation Lifesaver and Its Mission): Step 3 (Explain The Purpose of Operation): Pay attention to painted or raised markings at the platform edge, and stay at least 3 feet from the train while it is coming (p. 38).

Step 4 (Operation Lifesaver and Its Mission): Step 4 (Explain The Purpose of Operation): Hold on tight to poles or seats, and listen carefully to directions from the train operator or conductor. 5 (p. 38).

pamphlet_excerpts: Appearance Rail Signs Signals: Appearance and Meaning: Reminds the driver to slowdown, look, and listen for a train (p. 39).
Appearance Rail Signs Signals Principle 2: Appearance and Meaning Principle 2: No train horn A Quiet Zone has been established and normally the train will not sound the horn (p. 39).

Appearance Rail Signs Signals Principle 3: Appearance and Meaning Principle 3: The locomotive engineer can still sound the horn in emergency situations or if workers are near the tracks. grade crossing Raised crossing ahead (p. 39).

Appearance Rail Signs Signals Principle 4: Appearance and Meaning Principle 4: If you drive alow-clearance vehicle (lowboy), trailer or anything else low to the ground, you are at risk of getting hung upon the tracks (p. 39).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Appearance Rail Signs Signals): Step 1 (Appearance and Meaning): All drivers need to make sure that their vehicle has cleared the tracks once they cross (p. 39).

Step 2 (Appearance Rail Signs Signals): Step 2 (Appearance and Meaning): Advance warning for side streets Warns that a highway rail intersection will appear immediately after making either a right or left turn (p. 39).
Step 3 (Appearance Rail Signs Signals): Step 3 (Appearance and Meaning): Reminds the driver to be prepared to stop if a train is approaching (p. 39).

Step 4 (Appearance Rail Signs Signals): Step 4 (Appearance and Meaning): If you attempt to ride an ATV or asnowmobile; hike on the tracks, a bridge, or a trestle; or even walk near the tracks, you can be arrested and fined (p. 39).

pamphlet_excerpts: Railroad signals operate: All employees involved with train operations must learn the signal techniques defined in their railroad's operating rules book and carry the book (p. 30).
Railroad signals operate Principle 2: Since the early days of railroading, train crew members have used hand signals (p. 30).
Railroad signals operate Principle 3: The old oil- or kerosene-powered lanterns have become collectibles (p. 30).
Railroad signals operate Principle 4: Today's train crews carry battery-powered railroad lanterns as part of their standard equipment (p. 30).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Railroad signals operate): Railroad employees rarely use hand signals and now use walkie-talkiesto communicate directly (p. 30).
Step 2 (Railroad signals operate): Horn signals also are used to alert the public when a train is nearing a highway-rail grade crossing as well as approaching or departing (p. 30).
Step 3 (Railroad signals operate): The chart shown here summarizes the different horn signals that have been used over the years (p. 30).
Step 4 (Railroad signals operate): In the past, trains left stations, one after another, on apaced schedule (p. 30).

requirements.lead_text: Do ONE of the following special-interest options:
requirements.req_text: Do ONE of the following special-interest options: (a) Option A, Model Railroading. With your parent or guardian's and counselor's approval, do TWO of the following: (1) Draw a layout of your own model railroad or one that could be built in your home. Design a point-to-point track or loop with different routings. Include one of the following: turnaround or terminal or yard or siding. (2) Build one model railroad car kit or one locomotive kit. (3) Name the scale of four popular model railroad gauges. Identify the scale of four model cars or locomotives. (4) Locate the websites of four model railroad-related manufacturers or magazine publishers. Print information about their products and services, and discuss the information with your counselor. (5) Build one railroad structure (from scratch or using a kit), paint and weather the structure, mount it on your layout or diorama, and make the surrounding area on the diorama scenic. (6) Alone or with others, build a model railroad or modular layout including ballast and scenery. Make electrical connections and operate a train. Describe what you enjoyed most. (7) Participate in a switching contest on a timesaver layout and record your time. (8) Explain the difference between powering and controlling a model railroad by using direct current, and powering and controlling a model railroad using digital command control. (b) Option B, Railfanning. With your parent or guardian's and counselor's approval, do TWO of the following: (1) Visit a railroad museum, historical display, or a prototype railroad-sponsored public event. With permission, photograph, digitally record, or sketch items of interest. Explain what you saw and describe your photos, sketches, or video. (2) Purchase tickets and ride a scenic or historic railroad. Under supervision, photograph the equipment and discuss with your counselor the historic significance of the operation. (3) Locate the websites of four rail historical groups, then find information on the history of the rail preservation operations and purpose of each group. Talk with a member of one of the groups and find out how you might help. (4) Plan a trip by rail between two points. Obtain a schedule and explain when the train should arrive at two intermediate points. Purchase the tickets and make the trip. Explain to your counselor what you saw.

(3) Name the scale of four popular model railroad gauges. Identify the scale of four model cars or locomotives. (4) Locate the websites of four model railroad-related manufacturers or magazine publishers. Print information about their products and services, and discuss the information with your counselor. (5) Build one railroad structure (from scratch or using a kit), paint and weather the structure, mount it on your layout or diorama, and make the surrounding area on the diorama scenic. (6) Alone or with others, build a model railroad or modular layout including ballast and scenery. Make electrical connections and operate a train. Describe what you enjoyed most. (7) Participate in a switching contest on a timesaver layout and record your time. (8) Explain the difference between powering and controlling a model railroad by using direct current, and powering and controlling a model railroad using digital command control.

sub_requirements.text: Option B, Railfanning. With your parent or guardian's and counselor's approval, do TWO of the following: (1) Visit a railroad museum, historical display, or a prototype railroad-sponsored public event. With permission, photograph, digitally record, or sketch items of interest. Explain what you saw and describe your photos, sketches, or video. (2) Purchase tickets and ride a scenic or historic railroad. Under supervision, photograph the equipment and discuss with your counselor the historic significance of the operation. (3) Locate the websites of four rail historical groups, then find information on the history of the rail preservation operations and purpose of each group. Talk with a member of one of the groups and find out how you might help. (4) Plan a trip by rail between two points. Obtain a schedule and explain when the train should arrive at two intermediate points. Purchase the tickets and make the trip. Explain to your counselor what you saw.

requirements.lead_text: Do the following:
requirements.req_text: Do the following: (a) Take a tour of a library. Discuss with your counselor how the library is organized and what resources and/or services are offered in the library. (b) Learn how to search for material using a library's card catalog or computerized catalog by author, title, and subject. (c) In a library, search the card catalog or computerized catalog for six books of four different types, such as poetry, fiction, nonfiction, and biographies. (d) With the assistance of your counselor or the librarian, see if you can locate on the shelves the six books you selected. (e) Explain what a library card is, why it is needed, and how to get one.

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: When using a library catalog to locate nonfiction research materials, how does the Dewey Decimal Classification system organize books on the shelves?
quiz_item.question: When using a library catalog to locate nonfiction research materials, how does the Dewey Decimal Classification system organize books on the shelves?
options: A. Alphabetically by the publisher's city of origin, followed by the book's page count.
B. Chronologically by the year the book was acquired by the local library branch.
C. Numerically by subject into ten main classes (000 to 999) with decimal subdivisions, followed by the author's cutter code so books on the same topic sit together.
D. By cover size and binding color so reference encyclopedias are shelved next to paperback fiction.
choices: A. Alphabetically by the publisher's city of origin, followed by the book's page count.
B. Chronologically by the year the book was acquired by the local library branch.
C. Numerically by subject into ten main classes (000 to 999) with decimal subdivisions, followed by the author's cutter code so books on the same topic sit together.
D. By cover size and binding color so reference encyclopedias are shelved next to paperback fiction.
quiz_item.correct_answer: C. Numerically by subject into ten main classes (000 to 999) with decimal subdivisions, followed by the author's cutter code so books on the same topic sit together.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (C): The Dewey Decimal system groups nonfiction books by subject using three-digit numbers (000-999) and decimal extensions, making it easy to browse related works on the same topic.

pamphlet_excerpts: Careers & Professional Pathways: Careers that center around reading can be incredibly fulfilling for those who have apassion for books, literature, or gathering and interpreting (p. 12).
Careers & Professional Pathways Principle 2: Such careers often involve skills like analysis, communication, and creative thinking (p. 12).

Careers & Professional Pathways Principle 3: Many reading-focused roles allow individuals to immerse themselves in stories, ideas, or academic research, making them ideal for lifelong learners (p. 12).
Careers & Professional Pathways Principle 4: Examples of careers in this realm include librarians, who manage collections of books and digital resources while guiding others in their reading (p. 12).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Careers & Professional Pathways): Editors and proofreaders are another path; they play a critical role in refining written content for publication (p. 12).
Step 2 (Careers & Professional Pathways): Writers and authors, of course, craft compelling works for readers to enjoy, while literary critics analyze and review books to provide (p. 12).
Step 3 (Careers & Professional Pathways): Other options include careers in academia, where professors and researchers frequently engage with texts to educate and innovate in their fields (p. 12).
Step 4 (Careers & Professional Pathways): Lawyers and paralegals also have careers deeply intertwined with reading, as they analyze legal documents, contracts, and case studies (p. 12).

intro_notes: NOTE: Scouts must remember to follow the Leave No Trace Seven Principles and the Outdoor Code while on field trips and when collecting specimens. Make sure you have permission of the land manager prior to taking any samples for your collections. Collecting is prohibited in most National and State Parks. Scouts must not use venomous reptiles in fulfilling requirement 8(a). When you decide that keeping your specimen is no longer possible or desired, be sure to find another appropriate home for it or return it to the wild at the location of capture. Check with your counselor for those instances where the return of these specimens would not be appropriate. Under the Endangered Species Act of 1973, some plants and animals are, or may be, protected by federal law. The same ones and/or others may be protected by state law. Be sure that you do not collect protected species. Your state may require that you purchase and carry a license to collect certain species. Check with the wildlife and fish and game officials in your state regarding species regulations before you begin to collect.
NOTE: The official merit badge pamphlets are now free and downloadable HERE or can be purchased at the Scout Shop.

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: Which biological traits distinguish reptiles (such as snakes, lizards, and turtles) from amphibians (such as frogs, toads, and salamanders)?
quiz_item.question: Which biological traits distinguish reptiles (such as snakes, lizards, and turtles) from amphibians (such as frogs, toads, and salamanders)?
options: A. Reptiles have dry skin covered in scales or scutes and lay shelled amniotic eggs on land, whereas amphibians have moist, permeable skin without scales and typically lay shell-less eggs in water before undergoing metamorphosis.
B. Reptiles are warm-blooded endothermic vertebrates that nurse their young, whereas amphibians are cold-blooded invertebrates.
C. Amphibians breathe exclusively through lungs from the moment they hatch, whereas reptiles breathe through external gills throughout adulthood.
D. Reptiles must keep their skin wet in freshwater ponds to absorb oxygen, whereas amphibians have waterproof keratin claws and shells.
choices: A. Reptiles have dry skin covered in scales or scutes and lay shelled amniotic eggs on land, whereas amphibians have moist, permeable skin without scales and typically lay shell-less eggs in water before undergoing metamorphosis.
B. Reptiles are warm-blooded endothermic vertebrates that nurse their young, whereas amphibians are cold-blooded invertebrates.
C. Amphibians breathe exclusively through lungs from the moment they hatch, whereas reptiles breathe through external gills throughout adulthood.
D. Reptiles must keep their skin wet in freshwater ponds to absorb oxygen, whereas amphibians have waterproof keratin claws and shells.
quiz_item.correct_answer: A. Reptiles have dry skin covered in scales or scutes and lay shelled amniotic eggs on land, whereas amphibians have moist, permeable skin without scales and typically lay shell-less eggs in water before undergoing metamorphosis.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (A): Both groups are ectothermic vertebrates, but reptiles possess dry scaly skin and amniotic eggs adapted to land, while amphibians have scaleless permeable skin and an aquatic larval stage.

requirements.lead_text: Do ONE of the following:
requirements.req_text: Do ONE of the following: (a) Take custody of one or more reptiles or amphibians in a manner approved by your counselor. Maintain one or more reptiles or amphibians for at least a month. Record food accepted, eating methods, changes in coloration, shedding of skins, and general habits; or keep the eggs of a reptile from the time of laying until hatching; or keep the eggs of an amphibian from the time of laying until their transformation into tadpoles (frogs) or larvae (salamanders). Whichever you choose, keep records of and report to your counselor how you cared for your animal, eggs, or larvae, including lighting, habitat, temperature and humidity maintenance, and any veterinary care requirements. Unless you are the long-term owner, at the conclusion of this study, turn the animal(s) over to another responsible party approved by your counselor. (b) Choose a reptile or amphibian that you can observe or foster at a local zoo, aquarium, nature center, local rescue, or other such exhibit (such as your classroom or school). Study the specimen weekly for a period of three months. At each visit, sketch the specimen in its captive habitat and note any changes in its coloration, shedding of skins, and general habits and behavior. Discuss with your counselor how the animal you observed was cared for to include its housing and habitat, how the lighting, temperature, and humidity were maintained, and any veterinary care requirements. Find out, either from information you locate on your own or by talking to the caretaker, what this species eats and what are its native habitat and home range, preferred climate, average life expectancy, and natural predators. Also, identify any human-caused threats to its population and any laws that protect the species and its habitat. After the observation period, share what you have learned with your counselor.

patrol_quiz_bank.question: Which biological traits distinguish reptiles (such as snakes, lizards, and turtles) from amphibians (such as frogs, toads, and salamanders)?
options: A. Reptiles have dry skin covered in scales or scutes and lay shelled amniotic eggs on land, whereas amphibians have moist, permeable skin without scales and typically lay shell-less eggs in water before undergoing metamorphosis.
B. Reptiles are warm-blooded endothermic vertebrates that nurse their young, whereas amphibians are cold-blooded invertebrates.
C. Amphibians breathe exclusively through lungs from the moment they hatch, whereas reptiles breathe through external gills throughout adulthood.
D. Reptiles must keep their skin wet in freshwater ponds to absorb oxygen, whereas amphibians have waterproof keratin claws and shells.
choices: A. Reptiles have dry skin covered in scales or scutes and lay shelled amniotic eggs on land, whereas amphibians have moist, permeable skin without scales and typically lay shell-less eggs in water before undergoing metamorphosis.
B. Reptiles are warm-blooded endothermic vertebrates that nurse their young, whereas amphibians are cold-blooded invertebrates.
C. Amphibians breathe exclusively through lungs from the moment they hatch, whereas reptiles breathe through external gills throughout adulthood.
D. Reptiles must keep their skin wet in freshwater ponds to absorb oxygen, whereas amphibians have waterproof keratin claws and shells.
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: A. Reptiles have dry skin covered in scales or scutes and lay shelled amniotic eggs on land, whereas amphibians have moist, permeable skin without scales and typically lay shell-less eggs in water before undergoing metamorphosis.
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (A): Both groups are ectothermic vertebrates, but reptiles possess dry scaly skin and amniotic eggs adapted to land, while amphibians have scaleless permeable skin and an aquatic larval stage.

requirements.lead_text: Do the following:
requirements.req_text: Do the following: (a) Explain what a projectile is, and why any device that shoots a projectile at high speed must be handled with care and respect, and used only in approved locations. (b) Explain the basic rules of safe gun handling that apply to all firearms. (c) Describe how you would react if a friend visiting your home asked to see your or your family's firearm. (d) Explain the need for, types, and use of eye protection and hearing protection. (e) Explain the main points of the laws for owning and using guns in your community and state. (f) Explain how hunting is related to the wise use of renewable wildlife resources. (g) Successfully complete a state hunter education course, or obtain a copy of the hunting laws for your state, then do the following: (1) Explain the main points of hunting laws in your state, and any special laws on the use of guns and ammunition, AND (2) List the kinds of wildlife that can be legally hunted in your state. (h) Explain to your counselor the proper hygienic guidelines followed while shooting. (i) Identify places in your community where you can join or be a part of range and target activities. (j) Discuss with your counselor a list of sources you could contact for information on firearms and their use.

pamphlet_excerpts: Projectile Safety, Range Rules & Wildlife: In marksmanship, nothing is more important than safety (p. 17).
Projectile Safety, Range Rules & Wildlife Principle 2: Participants in shooting sports assume a vital responsibility that affects the lives of others (p. 17).
Projectile Safety, Range Rules & Wildlife Principle 3: It is critically important to learn and practice all of the rifle safety rules (p. 17).
Projectile Safety, Range Rules & Wildlife Principle 4: When handled correctly and used properly, a rifle is not dangerous (p. 17).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Projectile Safety, Range Rules & Wildlife): A rifle, like any other precision machine, instrument, or piece of sports equipment, is manufactured to perform a specific task (p. 17).
Step 2 (Projectile Safety, Range Rules & Wildlife): If arifle is handled incorrectly or recklessly, without regard for the safety rules, then accidents can happen (p. 17).
Step 3 (Projectile Safety, Range Rules & Wildlife): You must first acquire knowledge of how to handle rifles safely, then develop and maintain proper safe-handling skills through practice (p. 17).
Step 4 (Projectile Safety, Range Rules & Wildlife): The most important element to being safe is attitude (p. 17).
