quiz_item.scenario_prompt: On the firing line, you squeeze the trigger on a loaded .22 rimfire rifle and hear an audible 'click' with no discharge. What is the mandatory misfire safety procedure?
quiz_item.question: On the firing line, you squeeze the trigger on a loaded .22 rimfire rifle and hear an audible 'click' with no discharge. What is the mandatory misfire safety procedure?
options: A. Immediately open the bolt to eject the cartridge and inspect the firing pin indent.
B. Keep the rifle muzzle pointed safely downrange, raise your non-shooting hand to notify the Range Safety Officer, and wait at least 30 seconds before opening the action in case of a hangfire.
C. Lay the closed rifle down on the shooting mat pointed toward the waiting bench and walk over to the instructor.
D. Look down the muzzle end of the barrel to verify whether a bullet is lodged in the bore.
choices: A. Immediately open the bolt to eject the cartridge and inspect the firing pin indent.
B. Keep the rifle muzzle pointed safely downrange, raise your non-shooting hand to notify the Range Safety Officer, and wait at least 30 seconds before opening the action in case of a hangfire.
C. Lay the closed rifle down on the shooting mat pointed toward the waiting bench and walk over to the instructor.
D. Look down the muzzle end of the barrel to verify whether a bullet is lodged in the bore.
quiz_item.correct_answer: B. Keep the rifle muzzle pointed safely downrange, raise your non-shooting hand to notify the Range Safety Officer, and wait at least 30 seconds before opening the action in case of a hangfire.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (B): A delayed ignition (hangfire) can detonate seconds after the trigger pull; opening the breech immediately exposes the shooter's face and hands to a live rupture outside the chamber.

requirements.lead_text: Working under the supervision of a certified National Rifle Association (NRA) rifle instructor and a certified range safety officer, at a nationally authorized camp property or at a commercial firearm range (as defined in the Scouting America National Range and Target Activities Manual ), do ONE of the following options:
requirements.req_text: Working under the supervision of a certified National Rifle Association (NRA) rifle instructor and a certified range safety officer, at a nationally authorized camp property or at a commercial firearm range (as defined in the Scouting America National Range and Target Activities Manual ), do ONE of the following options: (a) Option A, Rifle Shooting (Modern Cartridge Type). Do ALL of the following: (1) Identify the three main parts of a rifle, and tell how they function. (2) Identify and demonstrate the rules for safely storing and handling a rifle. (3) Identify the two types of cartridges, their parts, and how they function. (4) Explain to your counselor what a misfire, hangfire, and squib fire are, and explain the procedures to follow in response to each. (5) Explain and demonstrate the five fundamentals of shooting a rifle: aiming, breath control, hold control, trigger control, and follow-through. (6) Demonstrate the knowledge, skills, and attitude necessary to safely shoot a rifle on a range, including understanding and following range procedures and commands. (7) Explain the basic safety rules for cleaning a rifle, and identify the materials needed. (8) Demonstrate how to clean a rifle properly and safely. (9) Discuss what points you would consider in selecting a rifle. (10) Using a bolt-action.22 caliber rimfire rifle, and shooting from a benchrest or supported prone position at 50 feet, fire five groups (three shots per group) that can be touched by a quarter. Using these targets, explain how to adjust sights to zero a rifle. (11) Adjust sights to center the group on the target and fire five groups (five shots per group). In the event that your instructor determines it is not practical to adjust the sights, for instance, on a borrowed rifle, you may explain (rather than doing) how to adjust the sights, and then fire five groups (five shots per group) in which all shots can be touched by a quarter. According to the target used, each shot in the group must meet the following minimum score: A-32 targets: 9; A-17 or TQ-1 targets: 7; A-36 targets: 5. Note: Other suitable NRA targets may be used if the specified targets are unavailable. (b) Option B, Air Rifle Shooting (BB or Pellet). Do ALL of the following: (1) Identify the three main parts of an air rifle, and explain how they function. (2) Identify and demonstrate the rules for safely storing and handling an air rifle. (3) Identify the two most common types of air rifle ammunition. (4) Explain and demonstrate the five fundamentals of shooting an air rifle: aiming, breath control, hold control, trigger control, and follow-through. (5) Demonstrate the knowledge, skills, and attitude necessary to safely shoot on a range, including understanding and following range procedures and commands. (6) Explain the basic safety rules for cleaning an air rifle, and identify the materials needed. (7) Demonstrate how to clean an air rifle properly and safely. (8) Discuss what points you would consider in selecting an air rifle. (9) Using a BB gun or pellet rifle and shooting from a benchrest or supported prone position at 15 feet for BB guns or 33 feet for pellet rifles, fire five groups (three shots per group) that can be touched by a quarter. (10) Adjust sights to center the group on the target and fire five groups (five shots per group). In the event that your instructor determines it is not practical to adjust the sights, for instance, on a borrowed air rifle, you may explain (rather than doing) how to adjust the sights, and then fire five groups (five shots per group) in which all shots can be touched by a quarter. According to the target used, each shot in the group must meet the following minimum score: BB rifle at 15 feet (or 5 meters) using TQ-5 targets: 8; Pellet rifle at 25 feet using TQ-5 targets: 8; Pellet rifle at 33 feet (or 10 meters) using AR-1 targets: 6. Note: Other suitable NRA targets may be used if the specified targets are unavailable. (c) Option C, Muzzleloading Rifle Shooting. Do ALL of the following: (1) Discuss with your counselor a brief history of the development of muzzleloading rifles. (2) Identify principal parts of muzzleloading rifles and discuss how they function. (3) Identify and demonstrate the rules for safely storing and handling a muzzleloading rifle. (4) Identify the various grades of black powder and explain their proper and safe use. (5) Discuss proper safety procedures pertaining to black powder storage. (6) Discuss proper components of a load. (7) Identify proper procedures and accessories used for safely loading a muzzleloading rifle. (8) Identify the causes of a muzzleloading rifle's failure to fire, and explain what a misfire, hangfire, and squib fire are. Explain and demonstrate proper preventive measures, and the procedures to follow in response to each. (9) Demonstrate the knowledge, skills, and attitude necessary to safely shoot a muzzleloading rifle on a range, including understanding and following range procedures and commands. (10) Explain the basic safety rules for cleaning a muzzleloading rifle, and identify the materials needed. (11) Demonstrate how to clean a muzzleloading rifle properly and safely. (12) Discuss what points you would consider in selecting a muzzleloading rifle. (13) Using a muzzleloading rifle of.45 or.50 caliber and shooting from a benchrest or supported prone position, fire three groups (three shots per group) at 50 feet that can be covered by the base of a standard-size soft drink can. (14) Adjust the sights to center the group on the target and fire three groups (five shots per group). In the event that your instructor determines it is not practical to adjust the sights, for instance, on a borrowed muzzleloading rifle, you may explain (rather than doing) how to adjust the sights, and then fire three groups (five shots per group) in which all shots can be covered by the base of a standard-size soft drink can. According to the target used, each shot in the group must meet the following minimum score: at 25 yards using NRA A-23 or NMLRA 50-yard targets: 7; at 50 yards using NRA A-25 or NMLRA 100-yard targets: 7. Note: Other suitable NRA targets may be used if the specified targets are unavailable.

sub_requirements.sub_req_text: Option A, Rifle Shooting (Modern Cartridge Type). Do ALL of the following: (1) Identify the three main parts of a rifle, and tell how they function. (2) Identify and demonstrate the rules for safely storing and handling a rifle. (3) Identify the two types of cartridges, their parts, and how they function. (4) Explain to your counselor what a misfire, hangfire, and squib fire are, and explain the procedures to follow in response to each. (5) Explain and demonstrate the five fundamentals of shooting a rifle: aiming, breath control, hold control, trigger control, and follow-through. (6) Demonstrate the knowledge, skills, and attitude necessary to safely shoot a rifle on a range, including understanding and following range procedures and commands. (7) Explain the basic safety rules for cleaning a rifle, and identify the materials needed. (8) Demonstrate how to clean a rifle properly and safely. (9) Discuss what points you would consider in selecting a rifle. (10) Using a bolt-action.22 caliber rimfire rifle, and shooting from a benchrest or supported prone position at 50 feet, fire five groups (three shots per group) that can be touched by a quarter. Using these targets, explain how to adjust sights to zero a rifle. (11) Adjust sights to center the group on the target and fire five groups (five shots per group). In the event that your instructor determines it is not practical to adjust the sights, for instance, on a borrowed rifle, you may explain (rather than doing) how to adjust the sights, and then fire five groups (five shots per group) in which all shots can be touched by a quarter. According to the target used, each shot in the group must meet the following minimum score: A-32 targets: 9; A-17 or TQ-1 targets: 7; A-36 targets: 5. Note: Other suitable NRA targets may be used if the specified targets are unavailable.

sub_requirements.text: Option B, Air Rifle Shooting (BB or Pellet). Do ALL of the following: (1) Identify the three main parts of an air rifle, and explain how they function. (2) Identify and demonstrate the rules for safely storing and handling an air rifle. (3) Identify the two most common types of air rifle ammunition. (4) Explain and demonstrate the five fundamentals of shooting an air rifle: aiming, breath control, hold control, trigger control, and follow-through. (5) Demonstrate the knowledge, skills, and attitude necessary to safely shoot on a range, including understanding and following range procedures and commands. (6) Explain the basic safety rules for cleaning an air rifle, and identify the materials needed. (7) Demonstrate how to clean an air rifle properly and safely. (8) Discuss what points you would consider in selecting an air rifle. (9) Using a BB gun or pellet rifle and shooting from a benchrest or supported prone position at 15 feet for BB guns or 33 feet for pellet rifles, fire five groups (three shots per group) that can be touched by a quarter. (10) Adjust sights to center the group on the target and fire five groups (five shots per group). In the event that your instructor determines it is not practical to adjust the sights, for instance, on a borrowed air rifle, you may explain (rather than doing) how to adjust the sights, and then fire five groups (five shots per group) in which all shots can be touched by a quarter. According to the target used, each shot in the group must meet the following minimum score: BB rifle at 15 feet (or 5 meters) using TQ-5 targets: 8; Pellet rifle at 25 feet using TQ-5 targets: 8; Pellet rifle at 33 feet (or 10 meters) using AR-1 targets: 6. Note: Other suitable NRA targets may be used if the specified targets are unavailable.

sub_requirements.sub_req_text: Option B, Air Rifle Shooting (BB or Pellet). Do ALL of the following: (1) Identify the three main parts of an air rifle, and explain how they function. (2) Identify and demonstrate the rules for safely storing and handling an air rifle. (3) Identify the two most common types of air rifle ammunition. (4) Explain and demonstrate the five fundamentals of shooting an air rifle: aiming, breath control, hold control, trigger control, and follow-through. (5) Demonstrate the knowledge, skills, and attitude necessary to safely shoot on a range, including understanding and following range procedures and commands. (6) Explain the basic safety rules for cleaning an air rifle, and identify the materials needed. (7) Demonstrate how to clean an air rifle properly and safely. (8) Discuss what points you would consider in selecting an air rifle. (9) Using a BB gun or pellet rifle and shooting from a benchrest or supported prone position at 15 feet for BB guns or 33 feet for pellet rifles, fire five groups (three shots per group) that can be touched by a quarter. (10) Adjust sights to center the group on the target and fire five groups (five shots per group). In the event that your instructor determines it is not practical to adjust the sights, for instance, on a borrowed air rifle, you may explain (rather than doing) how to adjust the sights, and then fire five groups (five shots per group) in which all shots can be touched by a quarter. According to the target used, each shot in the group must meet the following minimum score: BB rifle at 15 feet (or 5 meters) using TQ-5 targets: 8; Pellet rifle at 25 feet using TQ-5 targets: 8; Pellet rifle at 33 feet (or 10 meters) using AR-1 targets: 6. Note: Other suitable NRA targets may be used if the specified targets are unavailable.

sub_requirements.text: Option C, Muzzleloading Rifle Shooting. Do ALL of the following: (1) Discuss with your counselor a brief history of the development of muzzleloading rifles. (2) Identify principal parts of muzzleloading rifles and discuss how they function. (3) Identify and demonstrate the rules for safely storing and handling a muzzleloading rifle. (4) Identify the various grades of black powder and explain their proper and safe use. (5) Discuss proper safety procedures pertaining to black powder storage. (6) Discuss proper components of a load. (7) Identify proper procedures and accessories used for safely loading a muzzleloading rifle. (8) Identify the causes of a muzzleloading rifle's failure to fire, and explain what a misfire, hangfire, and squib fire are. Explain and demonstrate proper preventive measures, and the procedures to follow in response to each. (9) Demonstrate the knowledge, skills, and attitude necessary to safely shoot a muzzleloading rifle on a range, including understanding and following range procedures and commands. (10) Explain the basic safety rules for cleaning a muzzleloading rifle, and identify the materials needed. (11) Demonstrate how to clean a muzzleloading rifle properly and safely. (12) Discuss what points you would consider in selecting a muzzleloading rifle. (13) Using a muzzleloading rifle of.45 or.50 caliber and shooting from a benchrest or supported prone position, fire three groups (three shots per group) at 50 feet that can be covered by the base of a standard-size soft drink can. (14) Adjust the sights to center the group on the target and fire three groups (five shots per group). In the event that your instructor determines it is not practical to adjust the sights, for instance, on a borrowed muzzleloading rifle, you may explain (rather than doing) how to adjust the sights, and then fire three groups (five shots per group) in which all shots can be covered by the base of a standard-size soft drink can. According to the target used, each shot in the group must meet the following minimum score: at 25 yards using NRA A-23 or NMLRA 50-yard targets: 7; at 50 yards using NRA A-25 or NMLRA 100-yard targets: 7. Note: Other suitable NRA targets may be used if the specified targets are unavailable.

sub_requirements.sub_req_text: Option C, Muzzleloading Rifle Shooting. Do ALL of the following: (1) Discuss with your counselor a brief history of the development of muzzleloading rifles. (2) Identify principal parts of muzzleloading rifles and discuss how they function. (3) Identify and demonstrate the rules for safely storing and handling a muzzleloading rifle. (4) Identify the various grades of black powder and explain their proper and safe use. (5) Discuss proper safety procedures pertaining to black powder storage. (6) Discuss proper components of a load. (7) Identify proper procedures and accessories used for safely loading a muzzleloading rifle. (8) Identify the causes of a muzzleloading rifle's failure to fire, and explain what a misfire, hangfire, and squib fire are. Explain and demonstrate proper preventive measures, and the procedures to follow in response to each. (9) Demonstrate the knowledge, skills, and attitude necessary to safely shoot a muzzleloading rifle on a range, including understanding and following range procedures and commands. (10) Explain the basic safety rules for cleaning a muzzleloading rifle, and identify the materials needed. (11) Demonstrate how to clean a muzzleloading rifle properly and safely. (12) Discuss what points you would consider in selecting a muzzleloading rifle. (13) Using a muzzleloading rifle of.45 or.50 caliber and shooting from a benchrest or supported prone position, fire three groups (three shots per group) at 50 feet that can be covered by the base of a standard-size soft drink can. (14) Adjust the sights to center the group on the target and fire three groups (five shots per group). In the event that your instructor determines it is not practical to adjust the sights, for instance, on a borrowed muzzleloading rifle, you may explain (rather than doing) how to adjust the sights, and then fire three groups (five shots per group) in which all shots can be covered by the base of a standard-size soft drink can. According to the target used, each shot in the group must meet the following minimum score: at 25 yards using NRA A-23 or NMLRA 50-yard targets: 7; at 50 yards using NRA A-25 or NMLRA 100-yard targets: 7. Note: Other suitable NRA targets may be used if the specified targets are unavailable.

pamphlet_excerpts: Hazards, First Aid & Safety: For more information about first aid, see the First Aid merit badge pamphlet (p. 26).
Hazards, First Aid & Safety Principle 2: Discuss with your counselor all the potential hazards stemming from your project (p. 26).
Hazards, First Aid & Safety Principle 3: Know the proper first aid for cuts, burns, and eye injuries (p. 26).
Hazards, First Aid & Safety Principle 4: To avoid minor cuts and scrapes, be sure you dress appropriately when working on your robot, for instance, jeans, boots, gloves (p. 26).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Hazards, First Aid & Safety): Treat minor cuts and scrapes by flushing the area with clean water for at least five minutes, or until all foreign matter appears to be washed away (p. 26).
Step 2 (Hazards, First Aid & Safety): Apply triple antibiotic ointment (if appropriate and if there are no known allergies) and cover with a dry, sterile bandage (p. 26).
Step 3 (Hazards, First Aid & Safety): Working under close supervision of a responsible adult and being careful when you work with materials that can cause burns will help prevent (p. 26).
Step 4 (Hazards, First Aid & Safety): For chemical burns, it'simportant to quickly brush off as much of the chemical as possible using a gloved hand (p. 26).

quiz_item.question: While adjusting a jammed spur-gear drive train in the robotics lab, a Scout notices white dry residue from a damaged battery cell and has a minor sheet-metal cut on a forearm. What safety and first-aid procedure does the Robotics Merit Badge Pamphlet require?
options: A. Leave the battery connected so the servo motors hold torque while clearing the jammed gear teeth with bare fingers.

B. Wear ANSI Z87.1 safety glasses, disconnect the main battery before touching drive gears, brush off dry battery or flux chemicals with a gloved hand before flushing, and wash minor cuts with soap and running water for 5 minutes.
C. Pour water directly onto dry battery powder with bare hands and wrap the unwashed cut with electrical tape.
D. Remove safety glasses for a closer view of the spinning pinion gear while toggling the transmitter stick.

quiz_item.correct_answer: B. Wear ANSI Z87.1 safety glasses, disconnect the main battery before touching drive gears, brush off dry battery or flux chemicals with a gloved hand before flushing, and wash minor cuts with soap and running water for 5 minutes.

Step 4 (Robotics Industry): Teach pendants are similar to a handheld video-game controller that has a small video screen (p. 16).

requirements.lead_text: Design, Build, Program, Test. Do the following:
requirements.req_text: Design, Build, Program, Test. Do the following: (a) With your counselor's approval, choose a task for the robot or robotic subsystem that you plan to build. Include sensor feedback and programming in the task. Document this information in your robot engineering notebook. (b) Design your robot. The robot design should use sensors and programming and have at least 2 degrees of freedom. Document the design in your robot engineering notebook using drawings and a written description. (c) Build a robot or robotic subsystem of your original design to accomplish the task you chose for requirement 4(a). (d) Discuss with your counselor the programming options available for your robot. Then do ONE of the following: (1) Program your robot to perform the task you chose for your robot in 4(a). Include a sample of your program's source code in your robot engineering notebook. (2) Prepare a flowchart of the desired steps to program your robot for accomplishing the task in 4(a). Include procedures that show activities based on sensor inputs. Place this in your robot engineering notebook. (e) Test your robot and record the results in your robot engineering notebook. Include suggestions on how you could improve your robot, as well as pictures or sketches of your finished robot.

requirements.lead_text: Do ONE of the following:
requirements.req_text: Do ONE of the following: (a) Identify three career opportunities that would use skills and knowledge in robotics. Pick one and research the training, education, certification requirements, experience, and expenses associated with entering the field. Research the prospects for employment, starting salary, advancement opportunities and career goals associated with this career. Discuss what you learned with your counselor and whether you might be interested in this career. (b) Identify how you might use the skills and knowledge in robotics to pursue a personal hobby. Research the additional training required, expenses, and affiliation with organizations that would help you maximize the enjoyment and benefit you might gain from it. Discuss what you learned with your counselor and share what short-term and long-term goals you might have if you pursued this.

Careers & Professional Pathways Principle 2: Only a few of the possible career paths are discussed here (p. 31).
Careers & Professional Pathways Principle 3: Take as many classes as possible in math, physics, computers, and design (p. 31).
Careers & Professional Pathways Principle 4: Get as much practical, hands-on experience as possible by participating in clubs or organizations pertaining to robotics or engineering (p. 31).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Careers & Professional Pathways): You will need more than a high school degree to work with robots (p. 31).
Step 2 (Careers & Professional Pathways): If you want to be a robotics technician, many junior or community colleges offer robotics and automation associate degrees (p. 31).
Step 3 (Careers & Professional Pathways): Robotics technicians operate and maintain the robots; if you want to design robots you will need to get an engineering degree (p. 31).
Step 4 (Careers & Professional Pathways): Most people who seek a career in robotics major in mechanical, electrical, structural, biomedical, or industrial engineering or computer science (p. 31).

patrol_quiz_bank.question: While adjusting a jammed spur-gear drive train in the robotics lab, a Scout notices white dry residue from a damaged battery cell and has a minor sheet-metal cut on a forearm. What safety and first-aid procedure does the Robotics Merit Badge Pamphlet require?
options: A. Leave the battery connected so the servo motors hold torque while clearing the jammed gear teeth with bare fingers.

B. Wear ANSI Z87.1 safety glasses, disconnect the main battery before touching drive gears, brush off dry battery or flux chemicals with a gloved hand before flushing, and wash minor cuts with soap and running water for 5 minutes.
C. Pour water directly onto dry battery powder with bare hands and wrap the unwashed cut with electrical tape.
D. Remove safety glasses for a closer view of the spinning pinion gear while toggling the transmitter stick.

requirements.lead_text: Do the following:
requirements.req_text: Do the following: (a) Explain to your counselor the most likely hazards you may encounter while participating in rowing activities, including weather- and water-related hazards, and what you should do to anticipate, help prevent, mitigate, and respond to these hazards. (b) Review prevention, symptoms, and first-aid treatment for the following injuries or illnesses that can occur while rowing: blisters, hypothermia, heat-related illnesses, dehydration, sunburn, sprains, and strains. (c) Review the Scouting America Safety Afloat policy. Explain to your counselor how this applies to rowing activities.

pamphlet_excerpts: Hazards, First Aid & Safety: In rowing, blisters are most likely to occur on the hands (p. 13).
Hazards, First Aid & Safety Principle 2: Pay attention to any tender or sensitive areas (hot spots) that indicate the start of a blister (p. 13).
Hazards, First Aid & Safety Principle 3: You may be able to adjust or relax your grip to avoid friction on the sensitive area (p. 13).
Hazards, First Aid & Safety Principle 4: If you are prone to blisters, prevent them by wearing rowing gloves (p. 13).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Hazards, First Aid & Safety): If you do get a blister, cover and protect the area from further irritation (p. 13).
Step 2 (Hazards, First Aid & Safety): A sprain occurs when an ankle, wrist, or other joint is bent farenough to over stretch the ligaments, the tough bands that hold joints together (p. 13).

Step 4 (Hazards, First Aid & Safety): Minor sprains and strains cause only mild discomfort, but more serious sprains and strains might be temporarily disabling (p. 13).

requirements.lead_text: Do ONE of the following:
requirements.req_text: Do ONE of the following: (a) Alone or with a passenger, do the following in either a fixed-seat or sliding-seat rowboat: (1) Launch. (2) Row in a straight line for 100 yards. Stop, pivot, and return to the starting point. (3) Backwater in a straight line for 25 yards. Make a turn underway and return to the starting point. (4) Land and moor or rack your craft. (5) Tie the following mooring knots, clove hitch, roundturn with two half-hitches, bowline, Wellman's knot, and mooring hitch. (b) Participate as a rowing team member in a competitive rowing meet. The team may be sponsored by a school, club, or Scout unit. The meet must include competition between two or more teams with different sponsors. Complete at least 10 hours of team practice prior to the meet.

Stop, pivot, and return to the starting point. (3) Backwater in a straight line for 25 yards. Make a turn underway and return to the starting point. (4) Land and moor or rack your craft. (5) Tie the following mooring knots, clove hitch, roundturn with two half-hitches, bowline, Wellman's knot, and mooring hitch.

requirements.lead_text: Do ONE of the following:
requirements.req_text: Do ONE of the following: (a) In a fixed-seat rowboat, come alongside a pier and help a passenger into the boat. Pull away from the pier, change positions with your passenger, and demonstrate sculling over the stern or side. Resume your rowing position, return alongside the pier, and help your passenger out of the boat. (b) In a sliding-seat rowboat, come alongside a pier and, with your buddy assisting you, get out onto the pier. Help your buddy into the boat. Reverse roles with your buddy and repeat the procedure.

pamphlet_excerpts: In a fixed-seat rowboat, come alongside: The strokes and maneuvers of rowing alone are the same as rowing with a passenger, except that you sit on the midshipseat to maintain trim (p. 67).
In a fixed-seat rowboat, come alongside Principle 2: When doing a single-person launch from a mooring where the bow is tied out, it is a good idea to ask another boater for help (p. 67).

In a fixed-seat rowboat, come alongside Principle 3: The person assisting will play the role of the passenger, except that instead of getting in when you are ready, he or she will give you a gentle push (p. 67).
In a fixed-seat rowboat, come alongside Principle 4: If no one is available to help out, begin by loading your gear into the boat, then untying the stern painter (p. 67).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (In a fixed-seat rowboat, come alongside): Sit on the dock and ease in over the transom while being careful to not lose your balance (p. 67).
Step 2 (In a fixed-seat rowboat, come alongside): Move forward to the bow and untie the bowpainter (p. 67).
Step 3 (In a fixed-seat rowboat, come alongside): When the boat is free and you have pulled the painters into the boat, take your rowing position and move the boat away from the pier (p. 67).

Step 4 (In a fixed-seat rowboat, come alongside): If there is not enough space for you to rowout, use one oar over the stern or at the bow to scull or paddle yourself clear of obstacles, then begin (p. 67).

Participate in a swamped boat drill Principle 2: Even experienced rowers may occasionally capsize in shells, so you should always have someone in a fixed-seat rowboat or powerboat on the water to assist (p. 29).

Step 3 (Participate in a swamped boat drill): Begin by placing the oar blades on abreast plate out of your way (p. 29).
Step 4 (Participate in a swamped boat drill): Then move along the gunwale to a midship point where there is an open compartment (p. 29).

pamphlet_excerpts: Alone in A Rowboat Push: If you are with a friend and your boat capsizes, pull yourself up over the side of the swamped boat while your friend holds down the other side (p. 65).
Alone in A Rowboat Push Principle 2: Push down on the gunwale with both hands so that you bring yourself up to where your hips are about level with the gunwale (p. 65).
Alone in A Rowboat Push Principle 3: Then roll over so that you fall into the bottom of the swamped boat, landing on your backside (p. 65).
Alone in A Rowboat Push Principle 4: You can then lean over the side to counterbalance as your friend follows the same steps to come in over the opposite side (p. 65).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Alone in A Rowboat Push): Remember that when you pull yourself up on the gunwale, the gunwale will be forced down into the water (p. 65).
Step 2 (Alone in A Rowboat Push): After you roll in and get your weightoff the gunwale, it will rise back (p. 65).
Step 3 (Alone in A Rowboat Push): Even when fully awash, the gunwale of most boats will be a few inches above the level of the water (p. 65).
Step 4 (Alone in A Rowboat Push): If you are alone and your boat swamps and yougo over the side, the best way toget back in is over the transom (p. 65).

Step 3 (Rowing Core Field Standard): Remember also that waves or rough water can make launching from shore dangerous (p. 67).

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: In risk management and personal safety at home, school, or camp, what is the difference between a hazard and a risk, and why must both smoke and carbon monoxide (CO) alarms be maintained?
quiz_item.question: In risk management and personal safety at home, school, or camp, what is the difference between a hazard and a risk, and why must both smoke and carbon monoxide (CO) alarms be maintained?
options: A. A hazard and a risk mean the exact same thing, and smoke detectors automatically detect odorless carbon monoxide gas without a separate CO sensor.

B. A hazard is an unsafe condition or source of potential harm, while risk is the likelihood and severity of injury from that hazard; smoke alarms detect fire early while CO alarms detect colorless, odorless carbon monoxide from fuel-burning appliances.
C. A hazard only exists outdoors during camping trips, and carbon monoxide alarms should be installed inside attic vents rather than near sleeping areas.
D. Risk can be eliminated only by avoiding all physical activity, and smoke alarm batteries only need testing once every ten years.
choices: A. A hazard and a risk mean the exact same thing, and smoke detectors automatically detect odorless carbon monoxide gas without a separate CO sensor.

B. A hazard is an unsafe condition or source of potential harm, while risk is the likelihood and severity of injury from that hazard; smoke alarms detect fire early while CO alarms detect colorless, odorless carbon monoxide from fuel-burning appliances.
C. A hazard only exists outdoors during camping trips, and carbon monoxide alarms should be installed inside attic vents rather than near sleeping areas.
D. Risk can be eliminated only by avoiding all physical activity, and smoke alarm batteries only need testing once every ten years.
quiz_item.correct_answer: B. A hazard is an unsafe condition or source of potential harm, while risk is the likelihood and severity of injury from that hazard; smoke alarms detect fire early while CO alarms detect colorless, odorless carbon monoxide from fuel-burning appliances.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (B): Identifying hazards allows you to reduce risk before an accident happens, and installing working smoke and CO alarms on every level and near sleeping areas protects against both fire and invisible carbon monoxide poisoning.

requirements.lead_text: Family and Home Safety. Do the following:
requirements.req_text: Family and Home Safety. Do the following: (a) Explain common causes of and prevention of home injuries. (b) Discuss the dangers involved with the use of fireworks. (c) Explain common causes of and prevention of home fires. (d) Using the Home Safety Checklist in the Safety merit badge pamphlet, or one approved by your counselor, inspect your home or a similar building for hazards with an adult. Review your checklist and findings with your counselor. (e) Develop a fire-escape plan for your home or for a similar building. Include in your drawings exit routes from each room and a meeting place outside. Conduct a fire-escape drill. Review your plan and your drill with your counselor. (f) Develop a family emergency action plan for evacuation because of weather or other natural disasters that occur in your area. Using a checklist in the Safety merit badge pamphlet or one approved by your counselor, assemble or inspect an emergency supplies kit. Explain to your counselor how a family would use the plan and the kit supplies in an emergency.

pamphlet_excerpts: Safety from Assault: Candles are carefully extinguished after use, before bedtime, or before leaving home (p. 17).
Safety from Assault Principle 2: Do not The National Fire Protection leave a room that has a lit candle (p. 17).
Safety from Assault Principle 3: When replacing the battery, write the date on it with a permanent marker (p. 17).
Safety from Assault Principle 4: Learning how drugs can affect you may help prevent accidents (p. 17).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Safety from Assault): Of course, do not take illegal drugs in the first place (p. 17).
Step 2 (Safety from Assault): Also, avoid people who do drugs, because they can be violent and are unsafe drivers (p. 17).
Step 3 (Safety from Assault): As you collect clippings about accidents in the home and workplace, look for stories that give you clues about unsafe conditions or acts (p. 17).
Step 4 (Safety from Assault): Doing so will help you determine how these accidents could have been prevented (p. 17).

pamphlet_excerpts: Online Safety: Never share your internet password with anyone other than your parent, guardian, or other responsible adults in your family (p. 18).
Online Safety Principle 2: Do not do anything that harms others or is against the law (p. 18).
Online Safety Principle 3: Any information posted online, such as notes and personal remarks, can be shared with others (p. 18).
Online Safety Principle 4: A good rule of thumb is to not post information you do not want others, including strangers, to see (p. 18).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Online Safety): Never give outpersonal information to anyone you meet online or without your parent or guardian's permission (p. 18).
Step 2 (Online Safety): Identity theft is the fastest-growing crime in the United States (p. 18).
Step 3 (Online Safety): When a criminal steals someone's personal information to impersonate this person and make legal transactions, it is identity theft (p. 18).
Step 4 (Online Safety): A criminal can use this information to apply for credit cards that can be sent directly to the criminal's address (p. 18).

requirements.req_text: Careers. Do ONE of the following: (a) Explore careers related to Safety merit badge. Research one career to learn about the training and education needed, costs, job prospects, salary, job duties, and career advancement. With permission of your parent or guardian, your research methods may include an internet or library search, an interview with a professional in the field, or a visit to a location where people in this career work. Discuss with your counselor both your findings and what about this profession might make it an interesting career. (b) Explore how you could use knowledge and skills related to safety to pursue a hobby, lifestyle, or service as a volunteer. Research any training needed, expenses, and organizations that promote or support it. Discuss with your counselor what short-term and long-term goals you might have if you pursue this.

pamphlet_excerpts: Careers & Professional Pathways: Saving and protecting the lives of other people can be are warding career (p. 77).
Careers & Professional Pathways Principle 2: Firefighters rescue people, but they also raise ladders, hook hoses to water hydrants, and enter burning buildings (p. 77).
Careers & Professional Pathways Principle 3: Fire inspectors help prevent fires from happening by checking buildings to be sure fire ordinances, laws, and codes are followed (p. 77).
Careers & Professional Pathways Principle 4: By using clues left after the fire, they determine the starting point and cause of the fire (p. 77).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Careers & Professional Pathways): Fire safety technicians also work to prevent fires by planning fire protection systems like the ceiling sprinkler systems in public buildings (p. 77).
Step 2 (Careers & Professional Pathways): To be a firefighter, you must have a high school diploma and advanced first-aid training (p. 77).
Step 3 (Careers & Professional Pathways): In many areas, firefighters must also be trained as paramedics (p. 77).
Step 4 (Careers & Professional Pathways): In addition, a position may require state fire protection certification, paramedic certification, public education specialist certification (p. 77).

options: A. A hazard and a risk mean the exact same thing, and smoke detectors automatically detect odorless carbon monoxide gas without a separate CO sensor.

C. A hazard only exists outdoors during camping trips, and carbon monoxide alarms should be installed inside attic vents rather than near sleeping areas.
D. Risk can be eliminated only by avoiding all physical activity, and smoke alarm batteries only need testing once every ten years.

quiz_item.question: In ethical, customer-focused salesmanship, what is the primary goal when asking questions and listening to a prospective buyer?
options: A. To pressure the buyer into purchasing the highest-priced item in stock regardless of whether it fits their situation.
B. To memorize a rigid script so you can talk continuously without letting the customer raise objections.
C. To understand the customer's actual needs and budget so you can honestly recommend a product or service that provides genuine value and builds long-term trust.
D. To exaggerate product performance claims during the pitch and clarify limitations only after payment is completed.
choices: A. To pressure the buyer into purchasing the highest-priced item in stock regardless of whether it fits their situation.
B. To memorize a rigid script so you can talk continuously without letting the customer raise objections.
C. To understand the customer's actual needs and budget so you can honestly recommend a product or service that provides genuine value and builds long-term trust.
D. To exaggerate product performance claims during the pitch and clarify limitations only after payment is completed.
quiz_item.correct_answer: C. To understand the customer's actual needs and budget so you can honestly recommend a product or service that provides genuine value and builds long-term trust.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (C): Successful salesmanship is built on integrity and helping the customer solve a problem by discovering their needs, presenting honest facts, and answering objections respectfully.

requirements.req_text: Do ONE of the following and keep a record (cost sheet). Use the sales techniques you have learned, and share your experience with your counselor: (a) Help your unit raise funds through sales of merchandise or of tickets to a Scout event. (b) Sell your services, such as lawn raking or mowing, pet sitting, dog walking, snow shoveling, or car washing, to your neighbors. Follow up after completing the service to determine the customer satisfaction. (c) Earn money through retail selling.

pamphlet_excerpts: Careers & Professional Pathways: As you research sales career opportunities, check the classifiedads in the newspaper (p. 42).
Careers & Professional Pathways Principle 2: Notice how many positions are sales based and how many different types of products people sell (p. 42).
Careers & Professional Pathways Principle 3: In a free-enterprise society like the United States, selling is the fundamental way business gets done (p. 42).
Careers & Professional Pathways Principle 4: Now think about your favorite products, such as a favorite brand of athletic shoes or type of jeans (p. 42).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Careers & Professional Pathways): Pick a company you particularly like or a brand name that you always buy (p. 42).
Step 2 (Careers & Professional Pathways): Research that company on the internet (with your parent or guardian's permission) or at your local library (p. 42).
Step 3 (Careers & Professional Pathways): Find out what you can about the company, its philosophy, and its products (p. 42).
Step 4 (Careers & Professional Pathways): Summer sales positions provide valuable experience that many companies seek when hiring for career sales positions (p. 42).

options: A. Tracking assignments in a planner, studying in a distraction-free workspace, taking structured notes in class, reviewing material regularly, and asking teachers questions early when concepts are unclear.
B. Waiting until the night before each exam to cram all chapters at once while multitasking with social media and television.
C. Copying a classmate's homework assignments verbatim so you can spend evenings re-reading the textbook cover to cover without taking notes.
D. Skipping note-taking during lectures and relying solely on memorizing boldface vocabulary words five minutes before class.

requirements.lead_text: Do TWO of the following:
requirements.req_text: Do TWO of the following: (a) Make a list of educational places located where you live (other than schools). Visit one, and report on how you used the place for self-education. (b) With your counselor's and your parent or guardian's approval, interview two professionals (other than teachers or other professionals at your school) with established careers. Find out where they were educated, what training they received, and how their education and training have helped prepare them for the career they have chosen. Find out how they continue to educate themselves. Discuss what you find out with your counselor. (c) Using a daily planner, show your counselor how you keep track of assignments and activities, and discuss how you manage your time. (d) Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of the different methods of research available to you for school assignments, such as the library, books and periodicals, and the internet.

pamphlet_excerpts: Life and Times of Lord: The divide between rich and poor was widening, and most families were poor or close (p. 9).
Life and Times of Lord Principle 2: As people migrated to dirty, overcrowded cities, they were more likely to become sick and less likely to be able to enjoy nature or get physical exercise (p. 9).
Life and Times of Lord Principle 3: In fact, when Britain went to war in 1899, more than half the men who volunteered for the army weren't fit enough to fight (p. 9).
Life and Times of Lord Principle 4: Children on both sides of the Atlantic Ocean suffered right along with their parents (p. 9).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Life and Times of Lord): Beyond the YMCA and some church-based programs, few organized activities or sports leagues were available for them to enjoy (p. 9).
Step 2 (Life and Times of Lord): Even worse, at least 1.7 million American children under the age of 16 worked full time, sometimes working as many as 12 hours a day in factories (p. 9).
Step 3 (Life and Times of Lord): Many adults grew deeply concerned about the problems of English and Child laborer, circa early 20th century American children (p. 9).
Step 4 (Life and Times of Lord): Among them were Robert Baden-Powell, Ernest Thompson Seton, and Daniel Carter Beard (p. 9).

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: What historic event did Lord Robert Baden-Powell organize in August 1907 on Brownsea Island in Poole Harbour, England, and what did it lead to in 1908?
quiz_item.question: What historic event did Lord Robert Baden-Powell organize in August 1907 on Brownsea Island in Poole Harbour, England, and what did it lead to in 1908?
options: A. He convened the first World Scout Jamboree with 50,000 Scouts from thirty nations and founded the Order of the Arrow.
B. He wrote the United States congressional charter for the Boy Scouts of America alongside William D. Boyce and Ernest Thompson Seton.
C. He established the Philmont Scout Ranch in New Mexico and published the first American Scout Handbook.
D. He held an experimental camp with 20 boys from diverse social backgrounds organized into four patrols to test his outdoor training ideas, which led to publishing Scouting for Boys in 1908.
choices: A. He convened the first World Scout Jamboree with 50,000 Scouts from thirty nations and founded the Order of the Arrow.
B. He wrote the United States congressional charter for the Boy Scouts of America alongside William D. Boyce and Ernest Thompson Seton.
C. He established the Philmont Scout Ranch in New Mexico and published the first American Scout Handbook.
D. He held an experimental camp with 20 boys from diverse social backgrounds organized into four patrols to test his outdoor training ideas, which led to publishing Scouting for Boys in 1908.
quiz_item.correct_answer: D. He held an experimental camp with 20 boys from diverse social backgrounds organized into four patrols to test his outdoor training ideas, which led to publishing Scouting for Boys in 1908.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (D): Baden-Powell's 1907 Brownsea Island experimental camp proved the effectiveness of the Patrol Method and outdoor skills training, inspiring his 1908 publication of Scouting for Boys and the global Scouting movement.

Short Biographical Summary Principle 3: Give A Short Biographical Summary Principle 3: Hill court attended the first World Jamboree in London in 1920 (p. 17).

Short Biographical Summary Principle 4: Give A Short Biographical Summary Principle 4: In 1925, he went to New York, where he connected with Scouting friends and soon earned a job with the BSA Supply Service (p. 17).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Short Biographical Summary): Step 1 (Give A Short Biographical Summary): West hired Hill court to write the first of many influential publications, the Handbook for Patrol Leaders (p. 17).

Step 2 (Short Biographical Summary): Step 2 (Give A Short Biographical Summary): Toadd a little mystery, he adopted the nickname "Green Bar Bill" in reference to the two green bars on a patrol leader's badge (p. 17).
Step 3 (Short Biographical Summary): Step 3 (Give A Short Biographical Summary): In 1935, to test ideas for his Scouting writing, he founded Troop 1 in Mendham, New Jersey (p. 17).

Step 4 (Short Biographical Summary): Step 4 (Give A Short Biographical Summary): In 1936 he was part of the first Wood Badge courses in the United States, and in 1948 was Scoutmaster for the first two standard American courses (p. 17).

pamphlet_excerpts: Scouting's Programs Have Developed: In 1935, the BSA created a program called Explorer Scouts asone option in Senior Scouting (p. 38).
Scouting's Programs Have Developed Principle 2: It offered to older Boy Scouts a land-based alternative to Sea Scouting (p. 38).
Scouting's Programs Have Developed Principle 3: Explorer Scouts initially wore the same uniform as Boy Scouts, although it featured an "Explorer Scout, BSA" strip over the right pocket (p. 38).
Scouting's Programs Have Developed Principle 4: In the 1940s, a forest-green uniform was introduced, and Explorer Scout units began to be called posts instead of troops (p. 38).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Scouting's Programs Have Developed): Explorer Scouts got their own advancement program in 1944 (p. 38).
Step 2 (Scouting's Programs Have Developed): The four ranks, Apprentice, Woodsman, Frontiersman, and Ranger, corresponded to the four ranks in Sea Scouting (p. 38).
Step 3 (Scouting's Programs Have Developed): In 1949, Explorer Scouts became simply Explorers, and the program's focus was expanded to include social activities, service opportunities (p. 38).
Step 4 (Scouting's Programs Have Developed): More and more, posts began to specialize in specific careers or hobbies (p. 38).

(c) Visit an exhibit of Scouting memorabilia or a local museum with a Scouting history gallery, or (with your parent or guardian's permission and counselor's approval) visit with someone in your council who is recognized as a dedicated Scouting historian or memorabilia collector. Step 3 (Scouting America National Jamboree): Step 3 (Attend either a Scouting America National): That changed when a lodge was built on the shore of Moose Lake (p. 46).
Step 4 (Scouting America National Jamboree): Step 4 (Attend either a Scouting America National): Dedicated on May 17, 1942, it was named for Charles (p. 46).

History of Your Unit Council Principle 2: Research The History Principle 2: There's only one National Scouting Museum, but many local councils and other groups have created Scouting museums (p. 59).
History of Your Unit Council Principle 3: Research The History Principle 3: Some fit into small rooms in council service centers; others house hundreds of thousands of items (p. 59).

History of Your Unit Council Principle 4: Research The History Principle 4: A new, ever-growing official website, The Scouting Memories Project atscoutingmemories. org, is an interactive archive of Scouting (p. 59).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (History of Your Unit Council): Step 1 (Research The History): The collection contains indexes of at least 2,323 councils (current and past), 3,550 camps, and 1,002 Order of the Arrow lodges (p. 59).
Step 2 (History of Your Unit Council): Step 2 (Research The History): It's a great place to start (or continue) your Scouting heritage journey (p. 59).
Step 3 (History of Your Unit Council): Step 3 (Research The History): Requirements 5 and 8 ask you to interview several people who were involved in Scouting in the past (p. 59).

Step 4 (History of Your Unit Council): Step 4 (Research The History): Talking with these people can open a window into Scouting heritage in ways an old Scout handbook or a patch collection never (p. 59).

pamphlet_excerpts: Reproduce the equipment for an old-time: Baden-Powell, Seton, Beard, and the Birth of Scouting ing concepts from The Birch Bark Roll of the Woodcraft Indians (1906) by Ernest Thompson Seton (p. 8).

Reproduce the equipment for an old-time Principle 2: Aids to Scouting focused on military scouting and self-reliance skills learned from Frederick Russell Burnham, the British Army Chief of Scouts (p. 8).

Reproduce the equipment for an old-time Principle 3: Baden-Powell recruited and trained boys as cadets during the siege, leading to Aids to Scouting's use in British schools for teaching observation (p. 8).
Reproduce the equipment for an old-time Principle 4: The book's publication sparked widespread interest, leading to the formation of Scout patrols worldwide (p. 8).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Reproduce the equipment for an old-time): By the end of the 20th century, nearly 150 million copies of Scouting for Boys had been published, making it one of the best-selling books ofall time (p. 8).
Step 2 (Reproduce the equipment for an old-time): Thanks to Scouting for Boys, Scouting quickly spread through England, the British colonies, and beyond (p. 8).
Step 3 (Reproduce the equipment for an old-time): As early as 1908, people in America were buying copies of the book and starting their owntroops (p. 8).
Step 4 (Reproduce the equipment for an old-time): A woman in Burnside, Kentucky, started agroup she called the "Eagle Troop" that year (p. 8).

requirements.req_text: Careers. Do ONE of the following: (a) Explore careers related to Scouting. Research one career to learn about the training and education needed, costs, job prospects, salary, job duties, and career advancement. With permission of your parent or guardian, your research methods may include an internet or library search, an interview with a professional in the field, or a visit to a location where people in this career work. Discuss with your counselor both your findings and what about this profession might make it an interesting career. (b) Explore how you could use knowledge and skills from this merit badge to serve as a Scouting volunteer. Research any training needed, expenses, and how you could serve as a unit, district, council, regional, or national volunteer. Discuss with your counselor what short-term and long-term goals you might have if you pursued this.

pamphlet_excerpts: Careers & Professional Pathways: In 1984, the BSA introduced Varsity Scouting, aimed at boys ages 14 but not yet 18 years old (p. 38).
Careers & Professional Pathways Principle 2: Varsity Scouting used sports terminology and offered high adventure activities geared for older Scouts (p. 38).
Careers & Professional Pathways Principle 3: Varsity Scouts used the same advancement program as Boy Scouts, but they could also earn the Denali Award (p. 38).
Careers & Professional Pathways Principle 4: The first older-youth program, Sea Scouting, came to the United States in 1912, when Arthur (p. 38).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Careers & Professional Pathways): Carey of Massachusetts started a Sea Scout group using his schooner, the Pioneer (p. 38).
Step 2 (Careers & Professional Pathways): The program limped along until Commander Thomas (p. 38).
Step 3 (Careers & Professional Pathways): Keane revamped the program, introducing an advancement program that included four ranks: Apprentice, Ordinary, Able, and Quartermaster (p. 38).
Step 4 (Careers & Professional Pathways): Sea Scouting became known as Sea Exploring in 1949, but the program didn't change much (p. 38).

pamphlet_excerpts: First aid for injuries or illnesses: Hyperventilation is the result of over breathing, either deliberately or because of panic (p. 21).
First aid for injuries or illnesses Principle 2: The likely result of hyperventilation is dizziness and fainting, and victims will feel as if they are being suffocated (p. 21).
First aid for injuries or illnesses Principle 3: Such a condition is unlikely in diving if the participants are properly prepared for each new skill level (p. 21).

First aid for injuries or illnesses Principle 4: If a diver shows signs of panic at any time, bring that person back into the boat or onto shore, calm the person, and encourage slow breathing (p. 21).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (First aid for injuries or illnesses): Make sure the person rests in a comfortable position and has plenty of open, fresh air (p. 21).
Step 2 (First aid for injuries or illnesses): Before resuming any activity, find out and resolve the cause of the panic (p. 21).
Step 3 (First aid for injuries or illnesses): Ifyou feel sinus pain while descending, stop your descent and end the dive (p. 21).
Step 4 (First aid for injuries or illnesses): A scuba diver may be injured by failing to equalize these air spaces, either while descending or ascending (p. 21).

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: Why is the most important rule in scuba diving to breathe continuously and never hold your breath while ascending with compressed air?
quiz_item.question: Why is the most important rule in scuba diving to breathe continuously and never hold your breath while ascending with compressed air?
options: A. Holding your breath causes nitrogen gas to freeze inside the first-stage regulator valve.
B. As water pressure decreases during ascent, trapped air in the lungs expands according to Boyle's Law and can rupture lung tissue (pulmonary barotrauma) if not exhaled.
C. Exhaling underwater fogs the inside of your dive mask and drains the buoyancy compensator vest.
D. Breathing continuously allows you to ascend faster than 60 feet per minute without making a safety stop.
choices: A. Holding your breath causes nitrogen gas to freeze inside the first-stage regulator valve.
B. As water pressure decreases during ascent, trapped air in the lungs expands according to Boyle's Law and can rupture lung tissue (pulmonary barotrauma) if not exhaled.
C. Exhaling underwater fogs the inside of your dive mask and drains the buoyancy compensator vest.
D. Breathing continuously allows you to ascend faster than 60 feet per minute without making a safety stop.
quiz_item.correct_answer: B. As water pressure decreases during ascent, trapped air in the lungs expands according to Boyle's Law and can rupture lung tissue (pulmonary barotrauma) if not exhaled.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (B): Under Boyle's Law, gas volume increases as surrounding water pressure drops during ascent; holding your breath while breathing compressed air traps expanding gas in the lungs, risking life-threatening pulmonary barotrauma.

An ecosystem Principle 2: Food webs and food pyramids illustrate the flow of energy (p. 73).

An ecosystem Principle 4: In this way, the sun's energy is passed from organism to organism in the ecosystem (p. 73).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (An ecosystem): The entire tropical zone receives the sun's rays more directly than area sin higher latitudes, so the average annual temperature (p. 73).
Step 2 (An ecosystem): Seasonal temperatures vary less than in other places on Earth (p. 73).
Step 3 (An ecosystem): Of all Earth's ecosystems, few compare to the coral reef (p. 73).
Step 4 (An ecosystem): A coral reef consists of the hard outer skeletons of tiny animals called corals (p. 73).

patrol_quiz_bank.question: Why is the most important rule in scuba diving to breathe continuously and never hold your breath while ascending with compressed air?
options: A. Holding your breath causes nitrogen gas to freeze inside the first-stage regulator valve.
B. As water pressure decreases during ascent, trapped air in the lungs expands according to Boyle's Law and can rupture lung tissue (pulmonary barotrauma) if not exhaled.
C. Exhaling underwater fogs the inside of your dive mask and drains the buoyancy compensator vest.
D. Breathing continuously allows you to ascend faster than 60 feet per minute without making a safety stop.
choices: A. Holding your breath causes nitrogen gas to freeze inside the first-stage regulator valve.
B. As water pressure decreases during ascent, trapped air in the lungs expands according to Boyle's Law and can rupture lung tissue (pulmonary barotrauma) if not exhaled.
C. Exhaling underwater fogs the inside of your dive mask and drains the buoyancy compensator vest.
D. Breathing continuously allows you to ascend faster than 60 feet per minute without making a safety stop.
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: B. As water pressure decreases during ascent, trapped air in the lungs expands according to Boyle's Law and can rupture lung tissue (pulmonary barotrauma) if not exhaled.
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (B): Under Boyle's Law, gas volume increases as surrounding water pressure drops during ascent; holding your breath while breathing compressed air traps expanding gas in the lungs, risking life-threatening pulmonary barotrauma.

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: When carving plaster or soft stone with chisels and rasps, or modeling clay over a wire armature, what studio safety precautions must you take?
quiz_item.question: When carving plaster or soft stone with chisels and rasps, or modeling clay over a wire armature, what studio safety precautions must you take?
options: A. Blow carving dust off your workbench with compressed air and leave wire armature ends unlooped at eye level.
B. Heat vinyl modeling clays in a kitchen oven above 500 degrees Fahrenheit without ventilation to soften them.
C. Wear impact-rated safety goggles when chipping or carving, loop or pad sharp armature wire ends, and clean up plaster or stone dust with a damp sponge or HEPA vacuum rather than dry sweeping.
D. Hold small stone blocks between your knees while striking a cold chisel toward your body.
choices: A. Blow carving dust off your workbench with compressed air and leave wire armature ends unlooped at eye level.
B. Heat vinyl modeling clays in a kitchen oven above 500 degrees Fahrenheit without ventilation to soften them.
C. Wear impact-rated safety goggles when chipping or carving, loop or pad sharp armature wire ends, and clean up plaster or stone dust with a damp sponge or HEPA vacuum rather than dry sweeping.
D. Hold small stone blocks between your knees while striking a cold chisel toward your body.
quiz_item.correct_answer: C. Wear impact-rated safety goggles when chipping or carving, loop or pad sharp armature wire ends, and clean up plaster or stone dust with a damp sponge or HEPA vacuum rather than dry sweeping.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (C): Sculpting requires eye protection against flying chips and sharp armature wires, plus wet cleanup and ventilation to avoid inhaling hazardous silica or plaster dust and solvent fumes.

requirements.lead_text: Do TWO of the following:
requirements.req_text: Do TWO of the following: (a) Model in clay a life-size human head. Then sculpt in modeling clay, carve in wood or plaster, or use 3D modeling software to make a small-scale model of an animal or person. Explain to your counselor the method and tools you used to sculpt the figure. (b) Make a plaster mold of a fruit or vegetable. In this mold, make a copy of the fruit or vegetable. Explain to your counselor the method and tools you used to make the copy. (c) With your parent or guardian's permission and your counselor's approval, visit a museum, art exhibit, art gallery, artists' co-op, or artist's studio. After your visit, share with your counselor what you have learned. Discuss the importance of visual arts and how it strengthens social tolerance and helps stimulate cultural, intellectual, and personal development.

pamphlet_excerpts: Careers & Professional Pathways: If you want to pursue a career as aprofessional sculptor, you will need some studio lessons and hands-on training (p. 59).

Careers & Professional Pathways Principle 2: You can start by findingout if your high school offers shop classes that will introduce you to the techniques for working with metal, wood, and plastics (p. 59).
Careers & Professional Pathways Principle 3: Later, you can get hands-on training by working for another artist as an apprentice or assistant (p. 59).
Careers & Professional Pathways Principle 4: If you intend to supplement your income in a related field, you might have to earn advanced degrees (p. 59).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Careers & Professional Pathways): Colleges and universities offer four- and five-year programs that lead to bachelor of fine arts (BFA) or master of fine arts (MFA) degrees (p. 59).
Step 2 (Careers & Professional Pathways): Beyond the core courses common to all major areas of study, these programs include art history and studio art classes (p. 59).
Step 3 (Careers & Professional Pathways): Independent schools of art and design offer two-year programs that lead to an associate of arts or bachelor of fine arts degree (p. 59).
Step 4 (Careers & Professional Pathways): Anyone who wants to teach art in public schools must have a bachelor's degree; you might also need a teaching certificate (p. 59).

options: A. Blow carving dust off your workbench with compressed air and leave wire armature ends unlooped at eye level.
B. Heat vinyl modeling clays in a kitchen oven above 500 degrees Fahrenheit without ventilation to soften them.
C. Wear impact-rated safety goggles when chipping or carving, loop or pad sharp armature wire ends, and clean up plaster or stone dust with a damp sponge or HEPA vacuum rather than dry sweeping.
D. Hold small stone blocks between your knees while striking a cold chisel toward your body.

requirements.lead_text: Hazards and First Aid. Do the following:
requirements.req_text: Hazards and First Aid. Do the following: (a) Show or explain first aid for, and prevention of, injuries and conditions that searchers and subjects could develop during an SAR situation, including: (1) Dehydration (2) Heatstroke (3) Hypothermia (4) Shock (5) Blisters (6) Eye injuries (7) Ankle and knee sprains (8) Bug bites of chiggers, ticks, mosquitoes, and biting gnats (9) Bee stings (10) Bites of spiders (11) Sting of a scorpion (12) Bite of a wild mammal (13) Bite of a venomous snake (b) Explain how the Scout Basic Essentials address hazards outdoors and help lost Scouts stay safe before they are rescued. (c) Discuss how the safety gear carried by SAR team members in their field packs addresses SAR hazards.

step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Hazards and First): Keep the victim warm with blankets, coats, or sleeping bags (p. 43).
Step 2 (Hazards and First): Do not make any cuts on or apply suction to the bite, apply a tourniquet, or use electric shock such as from a car battery (p. 43).
Step 3 (Hazards and First): These methods could cause more harm to the victim or are not proven to be effective (p. 43).
Step 4 (Hazards and First): For more information about first aid, see the First Aid merit badge pamphlet and the Scouts BSA Handbook (p. 43).

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: In Search and Rescue (SAR) operations, why is the searcher's personal safety and self-sufficiency with a prepared SAR pack considered the highest priority before entering the field?
quiz_item.question: In Search and Rescue (SAR) operations, why is the searcher's personal safety and self-sufficiency with a prepared SAR pack considered the highest priority before entering the field?
options: A. An unprepared or injured searcher becomes a second victim, diverting rescue teams and resources away from finding the original missing subject.
B. Searchers are required to hike alone off-trail without radio contact so they can cover twice as much ground.
C. Carrying the Ten Essentials allows a searcher to bypass Incident Command System (ICS) check-in at base camp.
D. Personal safety gear is only needed during night searches and can be left behind on warm summer afternoons.
choices: A. An unprepared or injured searcher becomes a second victim, diverting rescue teams and resources away from finding the original missing subject.
B. Searchers are required to hike alone off-trail without radio contact so they can cover twice as much ground.
C. Carrying the Ten Essentials allows a searcher to bypass Incident Command System (ICS) check-in at base camp.
D. Personal safety gear is only needed during night searches and can be left behind on warm summer afternoons.
quiz_item.correct_answer: A. An unprepared or injured searcher becomes a second victim, diverting rescue teams and resources away from finding the original missing subject.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (A): In SAR, responder safety comes first: checking in through the Incident Command System, working in teams, and carrying essential gear ensures rescuers do not become additional casualties.

pamphlet_excerpts: Staying and Getting Found: If your plans must change while on an outing, be sure to alert your parent or guardian (p. 41).
Staying and Getting Found Principle 2: Call ahead to your destination ifsomeone is expecting (p. 41).
Staying and Getting Found Principle 3: And finally, discuss safety and good decision making with all the members of your patrol and troop (p. 41).
Staying and Getting Found Principle 4: The buddy system is a way for Scouts to look after one another, especially during outdoor adventures (p. 41).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Staying and Getting Found): You keep track of your buddy, and your buddy keeps track (p. 41).
Step 2 (Staying and Getting Found): The buddy system should always be used when a troop or patrol is hiking, camping, and participating in any aquatic activities (p. 41).
Step 3 (Staying and Getting Found): The chances of a Scout becoming lost decrease when use of the buddy system is encouraged (p. 41).
Step 4 (Staying and Getting Found): After you discover how search and rescue missions for lost people are reported in your area, discuss the procedure with your parent or guardian (p. 41).

requirements.lead_text: Maps. Using a map, a compass and a GPS device or app approved by your counselor, do the following:
requirements.req_text: Maps. Using a map, a compass and a GPS device or app approved by your counselor, do the following: (a) Point out and explain the 5 D's (Date, Description, Details, Direction or Declination, Distance) of the map. (b) Choose a location on the map and record the altitude, latitude, longitude, and US National Grid coordinates. Describe how these coordinate systems differ. (c) Orient the map and take a bearing to another map location. Estimate the distance between, and describe the terrain between, the two locations. (d) Show a hypothetical place last seen and point out an area on your map that could be used for containment using natural or human-made boundaries.

pamphlet_excerpts: Incident Command System: FEMA offers a series of courses for those involved in emergency planning and response activities (p. 14).
Incident Command System Principle 2: Introduction to the Incident Command System, or ICS 100, is a foundational course that provides instruction on the history, organizational structure (p. 14).
Incident Command System Principle 3: This course serves as the basis for more advanced courses in emergency management (p. 14).
Incident Command System Principle 4: The Incident Command System uses five key concepts (p. 14).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Incident Command System): Unity of command refers to the concept that each person or resource responding to a scene reports to only one supervisor (p. 14).
Step 2 (Incident Command System): This eliminates the potential for individuals to receive conflicting orders from multiple supervisors (p. 14).
Step 3 (Incident Command System): Unity of command increases accountability, prevents resources from working without the knowledge of command, improves the flow of information (p. 14).
Step 4 (Incident Command System): This concept is fundamental to the ICS chain of command structure (p. 14).

pamphlet_excerpts: SAR Teams: Ground teams and dog teams search on foot, while other teams search from horseback, ATVs, mountain bikes, or aircraft (p. 75).
SAR Teams Principle 2: Dogs trained to deploy to disaster situations must have all the qualities of previously described search dogs and must also be acclimated to stressful (p. 75).
SAR Teams Principle 3: Many strong odors are present in a disaster setting, and the dogs work intensely (p. 75).
SAR Teams Principle 4: For this reason, they are worked for short periods such as 30 to 60 minutes, then rested and rehydrated before working another session (p. 75).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (SAR Teams): Disaster dogs are trained to search in the same way as area air scent dogs (p. 75).
Step 2 (SAR Teams): They are used off leash but without ID vest or collar to prevent entrapment by debris (p. 75).
Step 3 (SAR Teams): They search areas of rubble and destruction, moving quickly to search and clear the area (p. 75).
Step 4 (SAR Teams): The dogs are carefully trained in obedience and will search areas as directed by the handler from a distance (p. 75).

requirements.lead_text: Plan and Complete a Search. Do the following with a team of Scouts, friends, or family to execute a practice SAR exercise:
requirements.req_text: Plan and Complete a Search. Do the following with a team of Scouts, friends, or family to execute a practice SAR exercise: (a) Choose a hypothetical SAR scenario, either one presented in the Search and Rescue merit badge pamphlet or one approved by your counselor. (b) Develop an Incident Action Plan (IAP) for a hasty search using the scenario information. (c) Before the search begins, conduct a PAUSE briefing to review hazards, safety concerns, personal and shared Scout Basic Essentials, and other gear. (d) Execute the search. (e) After the search, hold a team debriefing to discuss the search, problems, successful and unsuccessful tactics, and ideas for improvement.

requirements.lead_text: Careers. Do ONE of the following:
requirements.req_text: Careers. Do ONE of the following: (a) Explore careers related to Search and Rescue merit badge or emergency management. Research one career to learn about the training and education needed, costs, job prospects, salary, job duties, and career advancement. With permission of your parent or guardian, your research methods may include an internet or library search, an interview with a professional in the field, or a visit to a location where people in this career work. Discuss with your counselor both your findings and what about this profession might make it an interesting career. (b) Explore how you could use knowledge and skills from this merit badge to serve as a volunteer on a disaster relief team, a wilderness rescue team, or a ski patrol. Research any training needed, expenses, and organizations that promote or support it. Discuss with your counselor what short-term and long-term goals you might have if you pursue this.

pamphlet_excerpts: Careers & Professional Pathways: Search and rescue operations in the United States are primarily conducted by volunteer teams (p. 77).
Careers & Professional Pathways Principle 2: Many of these teams are members of professional organizations such as the National Association for Search and Rescue or the Mountain Rescue (p. 77).
Careers & Professional Pathways Principle 3: They usually are run by local sheriff's offices or city or state agencies and may have paid positions (p. 77).
Careers & Professional Pathways Principle 4: The Las Vegas Metropolitan Police Department Search and Rescue is a prime example (p. 77).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Careers & Professional Pathways): The National Park Service also employs SAR personnel throughout many national parks, most notably Denali, Grand Canyon, and Yosemite national parks (p. 77).
Step 2 (Careers & Professional Pathways): Many of these national and state park positions require emergency medical, law enforcement, and fire/rescue credentials (p. 77).
Step 3 (Careers & Professional Pathways): They may also prefer certifications from organizations like the American Mountain Guides Association (p. 77).
Step 4 (Careers & Professional Pathways): If you are thinking about a military career, you may want to look into the U. S. Air Force Pararescuemen (PJs) or Combat Rescue Officers (CROs) (p. 77).

options: A. An unprepared or injured searcher becomes a second victim, diverting rescue teams and resources away from finding the original missing subject.
B. Searchers are required to hike alone off-trail without radio contact so they can cover twice as much ground.
C. Carrying the Ten Essentials allows a searcher to bypass Incident Command System (ICS) check-in at base camp.
D. Personal safety gear is only needed during night searches and can be left behind on warm summer afternoons.
choices: A. An unprepared or injured searcher becomes a second victim, diverting rescue teams and resources away from finding the original missing subject.
B. Searchers are required to hike alone off-trail without radio contact so they can cover twice as much ground.

D. Personal safety gear is only needed during night searches and can be left behind on warm summer afternoons.
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: A. An unprepared or injured searcher becomes a second victim, diverting rescue teams and resources away from finding the original missing subject.
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (A): In SAR, responder safety comes first: checking in through the Incident Command System, working in teams, and carrying essential gear ensures rescuers do not become additional casualties.

intro_notes: Scouts BSA Test Lab Pilot Badge (Valid through 2026-12-31). Sewing is using a needle and thread to make stitches and combine textiles by hand or machine. Needlework is decorative sewing and other textile arts. In this badge, you will investigate several types of sewing and needlework. You will learn basic hand and machine sewing skills and make several small, practical projects using your new skills!

NOTE: Any registered adult Scouting America volunteer may serve as the counselor/reviewer for a Test Lab badge. Upon completion of all requirements and the official Scouting America Test Lab survey, Scouts receive an official Certificate of Completion that converts to Merit Badge credit if the badge graduates to permanent status.
