quiz_item.scenario_prompt: How do farming and land-management practices like contour plowing, cover crops, and vegetated riparian buffers along streams protect soil and water resources?
quiz_item.question: How do farming and land-management practices like contour plowing, cover crops, and vegetated riparian buffers along streams protect soil and water resources?
options: A. They slow down surface water runoff, anchor the nutrient-rich topsoil (A horizon) with plant roots, and filter out sediment and fertilizers before runoff reaches streams.
B. They strip away the organic O and A soil horizons so rainwater can flow rapidly over bare subsoil into rivers.
C. They compact clay particles into an impermeable crust that prevents groundwater aquifers from recharging.
D. They channel agricultural runoff directly into storm drains to speed up stream erosion downstream.
choices: A. They slow down surface water runoff, anchor the nutrient-rich topsoil (A horizon) with plant roots, and filter out sediment and fertilizers before runoff reaches streams.
B. They strip away the organic O and A soil horizons so rainwater can flow rapidly over bare subsoil into rivers.
C. They compact clay particles into an impermeable crust that prevents groundwater aquifers from recharging.
D. They channel agricultural runoff directly into storm drains to speed up stream erosion downstream.
quiz_item.correct_answer: A. They slow down surface water runoff, anchor the nutrient-rich topsoil (A horizon) with plant roots, and filter out sediment and fertilizers before runoff reaches streams.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (A): Contour farming, cover crops, and streamside buffer strips reduce water velocity, hold topsoil in place against wind and water erosion, and trap sediment and nutrient pollution.

pamphlet_excerpts: Soil Erosion B Tell Why: Soil and water conservation projects help control the rate of this kind of soil erosion, which some call the greatest scourge the world has ever known (p. 39).
Soil Erosion B Tell Why Principle 2: Define soil erosion Principle 2: You don't want to play in it and you certainly don't want to drink (p. 39).
Soil Erosion B Tell Why Principle 3: Define soil erosion Principle 3: In many small streams, sediment fills the deep pools that provide arefuge for fish during the dry season (p. 39).
Soil Erosion B Tell Why Principle 4: Define soil erosion Principle 4: Sediment often damages the spawning beds of game fish, ruins their eggs, and reduces their food supply (p. 39).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Soil Erosion B Tell Why): Step 1 (Define soil erosion): It has caused oysters to disappear from the Chesapeake Bay, affecting commercial fisheries (p. 39).
Step 2 (Soil Erosion B Tell Why): Step 2 (Define soil erosion): When flood-prevention and other types of reservoirs are built, allowance must be made for the sedimentation (p. 39).
Step 3 (Soil Erosion B Tell Why): Step 3 (Define soil erosion): Much of the cost for removal is passed on to taxpayers (p. 39).

Step 4 (Soil Erosion B Tell Why): Step 4 (Define soil erosion): But when billions of raindrops together hammer against bare ground, they tear clumps of soil apart and separate the tiny particles from each (p. 39).

pamphlet_excerpts: Meant By Conservation: Tell What Is Meant: Fire also can remove plant cover from the land and expose bare soil to beating rains; then, muddy runoff flows down slopes and fills streams and lakes (p. 45).
Meant By Conservation Principle 2: Tell What Is Meant Principle 2: The damage to a city's water supply can be devastating (p. 45).
Meant By Conservation Principle 3: Tell What Is Meant Principle 3: Plant cover is important in controlling runoff, but in many instances it is not possible to keep plants growing on the land (p. 45).
Meant By Conservation Principle 4: Tell What Is Meant Principle 4: Sometimes the surface of the land needs to be shaped to guide and control runoff (p. 45).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Meant By Conservation): Step 1 (Tell What Is Meant): Small dams and other types of water-retarding structures often must be built to control runoff so that the land and the water are not damaged (p. 45).

Step 2 (Meant By Conservation): Step 2 (Tell What Is Meant): Learning more about soil and water conservation will help you become aware of some of the conservation problems your community might face (p. 45).

Step 3 (Meant By Conservation): Step 3 (Tell What Is Meant): Aim: Protect footpaths in camp areas, hiking and nature trails, and primitive roads from damage caused by erosion and from earth slides caused (p. 45).
Step 4 (Meant By Conservation): Step 4 (Tell What Is Meant): In laying out new trails or dirt roads, avoid trouble by locating them as nearly as possible on the contour (p. 45).

A watershed Principle 2: But this area is also called a river basin, an area of land drained by a river and all its large and small tributaries (p. 58).
A watershed Principle 3: All river basins are large watersheds, but not all watersheds can be called river basins, some watersheds are very small and their runoff is collected (p. 58).
A watershed Principle 4: Today, attention is being focused on river basins as areas for large-scale planning, development, and conservation of natural resources (p. 58).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (A watershed): The way people in cities along a river use water and the kinds of wastes they put into the river will affect industries, businesses, and cities farther (p. 58).
Step 2 (A watershed): Remember, the care and use of land in your watershed is important (p. 58).
Step 3 (A watershed): Fires that have swept through watersheds in the western United States and have been followed by heavy and prolonged rains have washed huge amounts (p. 58).
Step 4 (A watershed): In some places, mudslides have carried houses and other buildings (p. 58).

pamphlet_excerpts: Drawing to show the hydrologic cycle: Evaporation is one of nature's ways of purifying water, because most of the dissolved substances in it, such as the salt inseawater, remain behind (p. 30).
Drawing to show the hydrologic cycle Principle 2: Chemical reactions return small amounts of water to the atmosphere (p. 30).
Drawing to show the hydrologic cycle Principle 3: People, animals, and plants return some through the process of respiration (breathing), and the combustion, or burning, of fuels in cars (p. 30).
Drawing to show the hydrologic cycle Principle 4: Let's begin with the sea, where the sun's energy draws up into the atmosphere most of the water that travels through thehydrologic cycle (p. 30).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Drawing to show the hydrologic cycle): Much of the moisture evaporated into the air soon falls back into the sea during storms, but winds eventually do carryair masses with moisture (p. 30).
Step 2 (Drawing to show the hydrologic cycle): A small part of the moisture, or water vapor, in the air at any time might be visible to us as clouds, fog, or mist (p. 30).
Step 3 (Drawing to show the hydrologic cycle): When the water vapor in clouds condenses, we get the rain, snow, sleet, or hail that falls on Earth, called precipitation (p. 30).
Step 4 (Drawing to show the hydrologic cycle): As air masses move across the land, the air picks up more moisture (p. 30).

pamphlet_excerpts: Meant By Water Pollution: Tell What Is Meant: Often, the effluent resulting from primary treatment requires secondary treatment (p. 78).

Meant By Water Pollution Principle 2: Tell What Is Meant Principle 2: The wastewater repeats all the steps of primary treatment and then one of two processes for further organic waste decomposition (p. 78).
Meant By Water Pollution Principle 3: Tell What Is Meant Principle 3: Both processes depend on biological action and both require oxygen (p. 78).
Meant By Water Pollution Principle 4: Tell What Is Meant Principle 4: The oxygen is supplied through aeration, that is, by spraying the effluent into the air or by pumping air (p. 78).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Meant By Water Pollution): Step 1 (Tell What Is Meant): In one process, the effluent goes from the primary settling tank to a trickling filter (p. 78).
Step 2 (Meant By Water Pollution): Step 2 (Tell What Is Meant): There, it passes slowly over stones or other material where biological growths decompose the waste left in the effluent (p. 78).

Step 3 (Meant By Water Pollution): Step 3 (Tell What Is Meant): The stones and other material in the trickling filter provide as much surface area as possible with oxygen so that the biological growths can live (p. 78).
Step 4 (Meant By Water Pollution): Step 4 (Tell What Is Meant): While the effluent remains in the sludge tank, it is continuously aerated (p. 78).

requirements.lead_text: Do TWO of the following:
requirements.req_text: Do TWO of the following: (a) Make a trip to TWO of the following places. Write a report of more than 500 words about the soil and water and energy conservation practices you saw. (1) An agricultural experiment (2) A managed forest or woodlot, range, or pasture (3) A wildlife refuge or a fish or game management area (4) A conservation-managed farm or ranch (5) A managed watershed (6) A waste-treatment plant (7) A public drinking water treatment plant (8) An industry water use installation (9) A desalinization plant (b) Plant 100 trees, bushes, and/or vines for a good purpose. (c) Seed an area of at least one-fifth acre for some worthwhile conservation purposes, using suitable grasses or legumes alone or in a mixture. (d) Study a soil survey report. Describe the things in it. Using tracing paper and a pen, trace over any of the soil maps, and outline an area with three or more different kinds of soil. List each kind of soil by full name and map symbol. (e) Make a list of places in your neighborhood, camps, school ground, or park that have erosion, sedimentation, or pollution problems. Describe how these could be corrected through individual or group action. (f) Carry out any other soil and water conservation project approved by your counselor.

patrol_quiz_bank.question: How do farming and land-management practices like contour plowing, cover crops, and vegetated riparian buffers along streams protect soil and water resources?
options: A. They slow down surface water runoff, anchor the nutrient-rich topsoil (A horizon) with plant roots, and filter out sediment and fertilizers before runoff reaches streams.
B. They strip away the organic O and A soil horizons so rainwater can flow rapidly over bare subsoil into rivers.
C. They compact clay particles into an impermeable crust that prevents groundwater aquifers from recharging.
D. They channel agricultural runoff directly into storm drains to speed up stream erosion downstream.
choices: A. They slow down surface water runoff, anchor the nutrient-rich topsoil (A horizon) with plant roots, and filter out sediment and fertilizers before runoff reaches streams.

patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: A. They slow down surface water runoff, anchor the nutrient-rich topsoil (A horizon) with plant roots, and filter out sediment and fertilizers before runoff reaches streams.

pamphlet_excerpts: Purpose of Space Exploration: The United States, Russia, and other countries wanted alarger, longer-lasting facility to do long-term research in space (p. 69).
Purpose of Space Exploration Principle 2: The space shuttle had supported some research, but flights had been too few and too short (p. 69).
Purpose of Space Exploration Principle 3: A bigger space station also would provide better research support services (such as data transmission) than the shuttle could ever provide (p. 69).
Purpose of Space Exploration Principle 4: Purposes of the ISS The million-pound ISS is the largest construction project ever attempted in space (p. 69).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Purpose of Space Exploration): The International Space Station has several purposes (p. 69).
Step 2 (Purpose of Space Exploration): One of the most important is that the ISS provides a constant presence in space (p. 69).
Step 3 (Purpose of Space Exploration): Since November 2000, there have been from two to 13 (when the space shuttleorbiter was docked) astronauts and cosmonauts at a time living in space (p. 69).
Step 4 (Purpose of Space Exploration): The research done aboard the ISS may lead to breakthroughs in medicine, engineering, and technology that will have practical uses for humanity (p. 69).

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: Under the National Association of Rocketry (NAR) Model Rocket Safety Code, how must a model rocket be constructed and launched?
quiz_item.question: Under the National Association of Rocketry (NAR) Model Rocket Safety Code, how must a model rocket be constructed and launched?
options: A. Build the airframe from lightweight steel tubing and ignite the engine with a hand-held match before stepping back five feet.
B. Pack the parachute directly against the motor nozzle without recovery wadding and launch into low clouds to test altitude.
C. Aim the launch rod horizontally at a 30-degree angle to clear nearby trees and power lines.

D. Use only lightweight non-metallic materials (paper, wood, plastic), install flame-resistant recovery wadding, verify a clear sky and safe standoff distance, and launch electrically using a controller with a removable safety interlock key.
choices: A. Build the airframe from lightweight steel tubing and ignite the engine with a hand-held match before stepping back five feet.

quiz_item.correct_answer: D. Use only lightweight non-metallic materials (paper, wood, plastic), install flame-resistant recovery wadding, verify a clear sky and safe standoff distance, and launch electrically using a controller with a removable safety interlock key.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (D): The NAR Model Rocket Safety Code mandates non-metallic airframes, recovery systems protected by flameproof wadding, vertical launches away from hazards, a loud 5-second countdown, and an electrical launch system with a safety key.

pamphlet_excerpts: Collector's Card With A Picture: Design a collector's card: Richard Branson (1950- ) and Burt Rutan (1943- ) founded Virgin Galactic, an early commercial spaceflight company offering customers suborbital flights (p. 23).

Collector's Card With A Picture Principle 2: Design a collector's card Principle 2: They used an innovative launch system designed by Rutan featuring a carrier aircraft and a suborbital rocket-powered space plane as a second stage (p. 23).

Collector's Card With A Picture Principle 3: Design a collector's card Principle 3: Overcoming a number of technical setbacks including a fatal crash, the company would lead the way in commercial spaceflight (p. 23).
Collector's Card With A Picture Principle 4: Design a collector's card Principle 4: Its test pilots earned the first commercial astronaut wings, award by the FAA in 2004 (p. 23).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Collector's Card With A Picture): Step 1 (Design a collector's card): Elon Musk (1971- ) formed Space Exploration Technologies (Space X) in 2002 to build rockets that could inexpensively carry payloads to low Earth orbit (p. 23).

Step 2 (Collector's Card With A Picture): Step 2 (Design a collector's card): After years of successful rocket launches, the company began transporting cargo to the International Space Station in October 2012 in its Dragon (p. 23).
Step 3 (Collector's Card With A Picture): Step 3 (Design a collector's card): For requirement 2, create a collector's card of your favorite space pioneer (p. 23).
Step 4 (Collector's Card With A Picture): Step 4 (Design a collector's card): Give details of the person's contribution to spaceflight, including dates, missions, and other accomplishments (p. 23).

Step 3 (Launch and Recover A Model): Step 3 (Build, launch, and recover a model): You can purchase model rocket kits and engines online, through mail-order catalogs, and in toy and hobby shops (p. 25).

Step 4 (Launch and Recover A Model): Step 4 (Build, launch, and recover a model): Ifyou can borrow a rocket launcher, you can buy everything you need to complete requirement 3 for less than $20 (p. 25).

requirements.req_text: Do TWO of the following: (a) Discuss with your counselor a robotic space exploration mission and a historic crewed mission. Step 3 (Purpose, operation, and components): Space X developed the Dragon capsule for both cargo and crew transportation, launching on the reusable Falcon 9 rocket (p. 76).
Step 4 (Purpose, operation, and components): The first cargo mission occurred in May 2012, followed by the first crewed mission in May 2020 (p. 76).

step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Risks in sports): If you feel a hot spot developing, stop immediately and protect the tender area by applying an adhesive bandage or moleskin (p. 87).
Step 2 (Risks in sports): If a blister must be drained, first wash the blister with mild soap and water (p. 87).
Step 3 (Risks in sports): Prick the edge of the blister with a needle that has been sterilized in a flame (p. 87).
Step 4 (Risks in sports): Cover it with an adhesive bandage or other sterile dressing (p. 87).

quiz_item.question: If an athlete receives a blow to the head or body during practice or competition and shows signs of dizziness, confusion, headache, or balance problems, what action must be taken immediately?
options: A. Have the athlete drink cold water on the sideline for five minutes and return to the game if the score is close.
B. Remove the athlete from play immediately to prevent second-impact syndrome, notify parents and coaches, and do not allow a return to play until cleared by a licensed healthcare professional.
C. Have the athlete perform vigorous sprint intervals to test whether their vision clears up.
D. Give the athlete aspirin on the bench and let them finish the current half before evaluating symptoms.

quiz_item.correct_answer: B. Remove the athlete from play immediately to prevent second-impact syndrome, notify parents and coaches, and do not allow a return to play until cleared by a licensed healthcare professional.

pamphlet_excerpts: Sports Core Field Standard: To be a strong, healthy performer in sports and in life, avoid tobacco, alcohol, and other harmful substances (p. 10).
Sports Core Field Standard Principle 2: Tobacco smoke interferes with proper lung growth and function (p. 10).
Sports Core Field Standard Principle 3: It coats the lungs with sticky tars and injures the airways and air sacs of the lungs (p. 10).
Sports Core Field Standard Principle 4: Athletes need their lungs working at peak capacity (p. 10).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Sports Core Field Standard): Using tobacco can leave you gasping for air when you need (p. 10).
Step 2 (Sports Core Field Standard): Being tobacco-free gives you the stamina to plays ports (p. 10).
Step 3 (Sports Core Field Standard): The blood carries the poisons from smoking to all parts of the body, from the brain to the bladder (p. 10).
Step 4 (Sports Core Field Standard): Scientists now know that smoking causes cancers of the mouth, the larynx (voice box), the lungs, and the kidneys (p. 10).

pamphlet_excerpts: Warm-Up, Cool-Down, and Hydration: Sometimes good sportsmanship means accepting what might be a poor decision made by an official, referee, or umpire (p. 22).
Warm-Up, Cool-Down, and Hydration Principle 2: Remember, when you are struggling to be a good sport, that you have promised to exhibit the Scout spirit (p. 22).
Warm-Up, Cool-Down, and Hydration Principle 3: You show your Scout spirit with a cheerful smile and living by the Scout Oath, which includes helping other people at all times (p. 22).
Warm-Up, Cool-Down, and Hydration Principle 4: It can be hard to be a good sport but you can always take pride (p. 22).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Warm-Up, Cool-Down, and Hydration): If you are having difficulty with the officials' rulings, try to putyourself in their shoes (p. 22).
Step 2 (Warm-Up, Cool-Down, and Hydration): From the official's point of view, the decision was consistent and fair (p. 22).
Step 3 (Warm-Up, Cool-Down, and Hydration): If you truly disagree with the officiating after the game, it is acceptable to write a letter to the league commissioner or officiating (p. 22).
Step 4 (Warm-Up, Cool-Down, and Hydration): Also consider taking a course to qualify as an official (p. 22).

requirements.req_text: Do the following: (a) With guidance from your counselor, establish a suitable personal training program that you will follow throughout your competition season (or for three months). (f) Draw and explain a diagram of the playing area for each sport. (g) Participate in each sport as a competitive individual or as a member of an organized team for one season (or for three months). (h) At the end of the season, share your completed chart with your counselor and discuss how your participation in the sports you chose has affected you mentally and physically.

options: A. Have the athlete drink cold water on the sideline for five minutes and return to the game if the score is close.
B. Remove the athlete from play immediately to prevent second-impact syndrome, notify parents and coaches, and do not allow a return to play until cleared by a licensed healthcare professional.
C. Have the athlete perform vigorous sprint intervals to test whether their vision clears up.
D. Give the athlete aspirin on the bench and let them finish the current half before evaluating symptoms.
choices: A. Have the athlete drink cold water on the sideline for five minutes and return to the game if the score is close.
B. Remove the athlete from play immediately to prevent second-impact syndrome, notify parents and coaches, and do not allow a return to play until cleared by a licensed healthcare professional.
C. Have the athlete perform vigorous sprint intervals to test whether their vision clears up.
D. Give the athlete aspirin on the bench and let them finish the current half before evaluating symptoms.
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: B. Remove the athlete from play immediately to prevent second-impact syndrome, notify parents and coaches, and do not allow a return to play until cleared by a licensed healthcare professional.
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (B): Any suspected concussion requires immediate removal from play ('when in doubt, sit them out') and formal medical clearance before returning, as a second head impact before recovery can be catastrophic.

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: Why do philatelists always handle postage stamps with smooth-tipped stamp tongs rather than their bare fingers, and never use household tape to mount stamps in an album?
quiz_item.question: Why do philatelists always handle postage stamps with smooth-tipped stamp tongs rather than their bare fingers, and never use household tape to mount stamps in an album?
options: A. Stamp tongs magnetize the iron oxide ink on commemorative stamps so they cling to album pages without glue.
B. Bare fingers erase the postmark cancellation ink, while household tape increases a stamp's catalog value.
C. Natural skin oils, sweat, and dirt transfer from fingers to delicate stamp paper and gum, while household tape stains and permanently ruins stamps compared to archival philatelic hinges or mounts.
D. Stamp tongs are sharp enough to trim damaged perforations off the edges of rare imperforate stamps.
choices: A. Stamp tongs magnetize the iron oxide ink on commemorative stamps so they cling to album pages without glue.
B. Bare fingers erase the postmark cancellation ink, while household tape increases a stamp's catalog value.
C. Natural skin oils, sweat, and dirt transfer from fingers to delicate stamp paper and gum, while household tape stains and permanently ruins stamps compared to archival philatelic hinges or mounts.
D. Stamp tongs are sharp enough to trim damaged perforations off the edges of rare imperforate stamps.
quiz_item.correct_answer: C. Natural skin oils, sweat, and dirt transfer from fingers to delicate stamp paper and gum, while household tape stains and permanently ruins stamps compared to archival philatelic hinges or mounts.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (C): Skin oils and moisture degrade stamp paper and original gum, and pressure-sensitive household tape causes irreversible chemical staining; philatelists use smooth stamp tongs and archival hinges or mounts.

pamphlet_excerpts: Topical Stamp Collecting: Define topical stamp collecting: Most experienced collectors have more than one interest in stamps (p. 20).

Topical Stamp Collecting Principle 2: Define topical stamp collecting Principle 2: A collector can, for example, focus on stamps of the United States while specializing in trains as a topical collection (p. 20).

Topical Stamp Collecting Principle 3: Define topical stamp collecting Principle 3: A variety of definitive and commemorative stamps and postal stationery can make an interesting and inexpensive type of collection (p. 20).
Topical Stamp Collecting Principle 4: Define topical stamp collecting Principle 4: Covers, or envelopes, showing different postal rates and classes make a challenging collection (p. 20).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Topical Stamp Collecting): Step 1 (Define topical stamp collecting): Even advertising covers used to promote different products can be collected (p. 20).

Step 2 (Topical Stamp Collecting): Step 2 (Define topical stamp collecting): Without spending a cent, you can easily collect 50 to a hundred items that reflect the complexity of the modern mail system, from your family's (p. 20).
Step 3 (Topical Stamp Collecting): Step 3 (Define topical stamp collecting): Some collectors specialize in meter imprints and labels (p. 20).

Step 4 (Topical Stamp Collecting): Step 4 (Define topical stamp collecting): These can be collected historically, going back to the many types used since the 1920s or focusing on current use alone (p. 20).

pamphlet_excerpts: Standard Catalog for Several Different: Demonstrate The Use of ONE: The Scott catalog value is a retail price that reflects recent selling prices (p. 37).
Standard Catalog for Several Different Principle 2: Demonstrate The Use of ONE Principle 2: The value of stamps also depends on supply and demand (p. 37).
Standard Catalog for Several Different Principle 3: Demonstrate The Use of ONE Principle 3: Common stamps often sell for less than catalog value (p. 37).
Standard Catalog for Several Different Principle 4: Demonstrate The Use of ONE Principle 4: Values also rise and fall as conditions in the stamp market change (p. 37).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Standard Catalog for Several Different): Step 1 (Demonstrate The Use of ONE): To look up a stamp in a catalog, first determine the country that issued the stamp (p. 37).
Step 2 (Standard Catalog for Several Different): Step 2 (Demonstrate The Use of ONE): Then compare its design with the stamp illustrations in the catalog (p. 37).
Step 3 (Standard Catalog for Several Different): Step 3 (Demonstrate The Use of ONE): Time to identify the stamp can be saved by looking at it for clues (p. 37).

Step 4 (Standard Catalog for Several Different): Step 4 (Demonstrate The Use of ONE): Because there are so many factors in the value of stamps, it is best to collect what you can afford and what you enjoy (p. 37).

requirements.lead_text: Do TWO of the following:
requirements.req_text: Do TWO of the following: (a) Design a stamp, cancellation, or cachet. (b) Visit a post office, stamp club, or stamp show with an experienced collector. Explain what you saw and learned. (c) Write a review of an interesting article from a stamp newspaper, magazine, book, or website (with your parent or guardian's permission). (d) Research and report on a famous stamp-related personality or the history behind a particular stamp. (e) Describe the steps taken to produce a stamp. Include the methods of printing, types of paper, perforation styles, and how they are gummed. (f) Prepare a two- to three-page display involving stamps. Using ingenuity, as well as clippings, drawings, etc., tell a story about the stamps and how they relate to history, geography, or a favorite topic of yours.

step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Stamp Cancellation or Cachet): Step 1 (Design a stamp, cancellation, or cachet): A cachet is a design that is usually hand-drawn, rubbers tamped, or printed on the left side of an envelope (p. 22).

Step 2 (Stamp Cancellation or Cachet): Step 2 (Design a stamp, cancellation, or cachet): Cachets are usually created to draw attention to the stamp on the envelope or to an event you are promoting (p. 22).
Step 3 (Stamp Cancellation or Cachet): Step 3 (Design a stamp, cancellation, or cachet): To make a cachet on a photocopy machine, open a 63⁄4-inch envelope completely (p. 22).
Step 4 (Stamp Cancellation or Cachet): Step 4 (Design a stamp, cancellation, or cachet): Using your imagination, draw your own design or select a picture to place on the open envelope (p. 22).

requirements.lead_text: Mount and show, in a purchased or homemade album, ONE of the following:
requirements.req_text: Mount and show, in a purchased or homemade album, ONE of the following: (a) A collection of 250 or more different stamps from at least 15 countries (b) A collection of a stamp from each of 50 different countries, mounted on maps to show the location of each (c) A collection of 100 or more different stamps from either one country or a group of closely related countries (d) A collection of 75 or more different stamps on a single topic. (Some interesting topics include Scouting, birds, insects, the Olympics, sports, flowers, animals, ships, holidays, trains, famous people, space, and medicine.) Stamps may be from different countries. (e) A collection of postal items discovered in your mail by monitoring it over a period of 30 days. Include at least five different types listed in requirement 3.

patrol_quiz_bank.question: Why do philatelists always handle postage stamps with smooth-tipped stamp tongs rather than their bare fingers, and never use household tape to mount stamps in an album?

B. Bare fingers erase the postmark cancellation ink, while household tape increases a stamp's catalog value.
C. Natural skin oils, sweat, and dirt transfer from fingers to delicate stamp paper and gum, while household tape stains and permanently ruins stamps compared to archival philatelic hinges or mounts.
D. Stamp tongs are sharp enough to trim damaged perforations off the edges of rare imperforate stamps.

B. Stand in the active travel lane without warning signs so your line of sight is straight, and use an aluminum leveling rod to push low-hanging wires out of the way.
C. Leave tripod legs unlatched on steep pavement so one person can carry the mounted total station over their shoulder near power lines.
D. Apply insect repellent directly onto the optical lenses of the transit to keep gnats away from the crosshairs.

pamphlet_excerpts: Emerging surveying technology such as drones: Each township is divided into 36 one-mile squares, called sections, which are numbered as shown in the diagram shown here (p. 12).
Emerging surveying technology such as drones Principle 2: This diagram shows the numbering of a township's 36 sections (p. 12).
Emerging surveying technology such as drones Principle 3: Except in a fewspecial cases, each section is approximately one mile square and contains approximately 640 acres (p. 12).

Emerging surveying technology such as drones Principle 4: Each section may be divided into halves, quarters, and smaller subdivisions, all according to rigidly standardized directions from the government (p. 12).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Emerging surveying technology such as drones): Irregularly shaped subdivisions may be called lots (p. 12).
Step 2 (Emerging surveying technology such as drones): The following diagram shows how one particular section was divided according to the needs of the landowners (p. 12).

Step 3 (Emerging surveying technology such as drones): This particular section is divided into eight approximately 40-acre 16th sections, three approximately 80-acre eighth sections, and two lake (p. 12).
Step 4 (Emerging surveying technology such as drones): Old surveys are very helpful because they show what other surveyors have found in past years (p. 12).

pamphlet_excerpts: Careers & Professional Pathways: Surveying principles are used in mapping land features and to lay out the positions for what is to be built on land (buildings, parking lots) (p. 10).
Careers & Professional Pathways Principle 2: While earning this badge, you will barely scratch the surface of surveying (p. 10).
Careers & Professional Pathways Principle 3: Becoming a surveyor generally takes several years of study in college and even more years of training and experience (p. 10).
Careers & Professional Pathways Principle 4: Furthermore, surveying involves extensive knowledge of law as well as measurements and mathematics (p. 10).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Careers & Professional Pathways): Your experience might, however, entice you to learn more about it in college or at a summer job (p. 10).
Step 2 (Careers & Professional Pathways): You also will learn about other fields that use surveying instruments and methods (p. 10).
Step 3 (Careers & Professional Pathways): Best of all, earning the Surveying merit badge will expose you to hand's-on use of surveying instruments and methods (p. 10).
Step 4 (Careers & Professional Pathways): If you like mathematics, you will enjoy working on this merit badge (p. 10).

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: What does sustainability mean in Scouting and global resource management, and what are its three interconnected pillars?
quiz_item.question: What does sustainability mean in Scouting and global resource management, and what are its three interconnected pillars?
options: A. Stopping all agricultural and industrial production immediately so natural resources are never used by humans.
B. Maximizing short-term corporate profit by extracting nonrenewable fossil fuels as rapidly as possible.
C. Focusing exclusively on recycling aluminum cans while ignoring water usage, energy grids, and community well-being.

D. Meeting the needs of the present generation without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs, balancing environmental stewardship, economic vitality, and social community well-being.
choices: A. Stopping all agricultural and industrial production immediately so natural resources are never used by humans.
B. Maximizing short-term corporate profit by extracting nonrenewable fossil fuels as rapidly as possible.
C. Focusing exclusively on recycling aluminum cans while ignoring water usage, energy grids, and community well-being.

D. Meeting the needs of the present generation without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs, balancing environmental stewardship, economic vitality, and social community well-being.
quiz_item.correct_answer: D. Meeting the needs of the present generation without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs, balancing environmental stewardship, economic vitality, and social community well-being.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (D): Sustainability balances environmental protection, economic viability, and social responsibility so natural systems and communities can thrive now and for future generations.

requirements.req_text: Water. Do ONE of the following and discuss with your counselor: (a) Evaluate your household water usage. If available, review water bills from the past year and evaluate the seasonal changes in water use. Identify three ways to help reduce water consumption. Tell two ways to preserve your community's access to clean water in the future. (c) Different areas of the world are affected by either too much (flooding) or too little (drought) water. Explore whether either or both affect where you live. Identify three water conservation or flood mitigation practices (successful or unsuccessful) that have been tried where you live or in an area of the world that interests you.

requirements.lead_text: Energy. Do ONE of the following and discuss with your counselor:
requirements.req_text: Energy. Do ONE of the following and discuss with your counselor: (a) Learn about the sustainability of different energy sources, including coal, gas, geothermal, hydro power, nuclear, petroleum, solar, and wind. Identify three common energy sources in the United States and describe how the production and consumption of each of these energy sources affects sustainability. (b) List eight ways your family consumes energy, such as gas appliances, electricity, heating systems or cooling systems, and transportation. For one home- and one transportation-related energy use, list three ways to help reduce consumption, reduce your carbon footprint, and be a better steward of this resource. (c) List five ways you and your family could reduce energy consumption in your home, such as adjusting your thermostat, window shades, opening windows, reducing hot-water temperature, and minimizing water consumption. Identify the benefits and risks of each idea and implement if possible.

pamphlet_excerpts: Sustain ability Core Field Standard: Close window drapes to keep heat out in summer, and open the drapes to letin the warm sunin wintertime (p. 62).
Sustain ability Core Field Standard Principle 2: By using less fuel and less electricity and reducing the amount of trash you create, you can reduce your carbon footprint dramatically (p. 62).
Sustain ability Core Field Standard Principle 3: Start by turning off computers, televisions, and lights when you are not using them (p. 62).
Sustain ability Core Field Standard Principle 4: Unplug small appliances and phone chargers, etc., when they are not in use (p. 62).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Sustain ability Core Field Standard): Lower the temperature in your home to 68 degrees or lower in winter, and raise it to 78 degrees or higher when running an air conditioner in (p. 62).
Step 2 (Sustain ability Core Field Standard): Turn off your heat or air conditioner entirely and open screened windows for natural ventilation when the weather is comfortable (p. 62).
Step 3 (Sustain ability Core Field Standard): Here are more tips for reducing your carbon footprint: Buy local and buy organic (p. 62).
Step 4 (Sustain ability Core Field Standard): When possible, buy organic or "fair trade." There's a better chance the food was grown inan eco-friendly way (p. 62).

requirements.lead_text: Stuff. Do ONE of the following and discuss with your counselor:
requirements.req_text: Stuff. Do ONE of the following and discuss with your counselor: (a) Create a list of 15 items of your personal "stuff." Classify each item as an essential need (such as soap) or a desirable want (such as a video game). Identify any excess "stuff" you no longer need, working with your family, if possible. Donate, repurpose, or recycle those items you can. (b) List five ways having too much "stuff" affects you, your family, your community, AND the world. For each of the five ways, consider the following aspects: the financial impact, time spent, maintenance, health, storage, and waste generation. Identify practices that can be used to avoid accumulating too much "stuff." (c) Research the impact waste has on the environment (land, water, air). Find out what the trash vortex is and how it was formed. Explain the number system for plastic recyclables and which plastics are more commonly recycled. Identify the average lifespan of one electronic device in your household, and whether it can be recycled in whole or part.

requirements.lead_text: Do TWO of the following and discuss with your counselor:
requirements.req_text: Do TWO of the following and discuss with your counselor: (a) The United Nations lists 17 Sustainable Development Goals. These include Zero Hunger, Clean Water and Sanitation, Affordable and Clean Energy, Sustainable Cities and Communities, Responsible Consumption and Production, Climate Action, Life Below Water, and Life on Land. Pick one of these eight and summarize the goal and its current and future impact on you, your family, community, and the world. (b) Identify how the planetary life-support systems (soil, climate, freshwater, atmospheric, nutrient, oceanic, ecosystems, and species) support life on Earth and interact with one another. Share what happens to the planet's sustainability when these systems are disrupted by natural events or human activity. (c) Identify how product life cycles (the cycle of design, sourcing, production, use, and disposal or reuse) influence current and future sustainability. Choose one common product to demonstrate how the full product life cycle would apply. (d) Learn how the world's population affects the sustainability of Earth. Discuss three human activities that may contribute to putting Earth at risk, now and in the future. (e) Explain the term species (plant or animal) decline. Share the human activities that contribute to species decline, what can be done to help reverse the decline, and its impact on a sustainable environment. (f) Find a world map that shows the pattern of temperature change for a period of at least 100 years. Identify three factors that scientists believe affect the global weather and temperature. Discuss how climate change impacts sustainability of food, water, or other resources.

pamphlet_excerpts: Discuss United Nations Sustainable: Do TWO of The Following: You can also work with your Scout troop and local schools to transform school property into an educational wildlife garden (p. 81).

Discuss United Nations Sustainable Principle 2: Do TWO of The Following Principle 2: Discuss with your counselor how human activities can endanger animals and plants and contribute to species extinction (p. 81).
Discuss United Nations Sustainable Principle 3: Do TWO of The Following Principle 3: What do you think can be done to stop the decline in wildlife and its impact on a sustainable environment (p. 81).

Discuss United Nations Sustainable Principle 4: Do TWO of The Following Principle 4: The diverse life on Earth is interconnected in a "vast web of life." Maintaining biodiversity is essential to the welfare and future of humanity (p. 81).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Discuss United Nations Sustainable): Step 1 (Do TWO of The Following): Biodiversity contributes significantly to the quality of life on Earth, providing climate regulation, food, clean water, and clean air (p. 81).
Step 2 (Discuss United Nations Sustainable): Step 2 (Do TWO of The Following): When a species becomes extinct, it diminishes our lives and those of future generations (p. 81).
Step 3 (Discuss United Nations Sustainable): Step 3 (Do TWO of The Following): Consider how the world's growing human population impacts biodiversity (p. 81).

Step 4 (Discuss United Nations Sustainable): Step 4 (Do TWO of The Following): Before meeting with your counselor, you might want to research how the needs and demands of people affect the sustain ability of life on Earth (p. 81).

requirements.req_text: Do the following: (a) On a campout or other outdoor Scouting activity that you attend, make notes on the sustainability practices you and your fellow Scouts practice. Observe transportation, forestry, soil conservation, water resources, habitat, buildings, campsites, and sanitation. Share what you observed and learned with your counselor. (b) Discuss with your counselor how living by the Scout Oath, Scout Law, Leave No Trace Seven Principles, and the Outdoor Code in your daily life helps promote sustainability. (c) Identify 5 behavioral changes that you and your family can make to improve the sustainability of your household. Share and discuss each with your counselor.

pamphlet_excerpts: Safe Swim Defense and Safety Afloat: Review with your counselor how Scouting: Spinal injuries can occur from diving into shallow or obstructed water (p. 25).
Safe Swim Defense and Safety Afloat Principle 2: Review with your counselor how Scouting Principle 2: Rescuers must be very careful when a spinal injury is suspected (p. 25).
Safe Swim Defense and Safety Afloat Principle 3: Review with your counselor how Scouting Principle 3: Spinal injuries can be fatal or can cause paralysis (p. 25).
Safe Swim Defense and Safety Afloat Principle 4: Review with your counselor how Scouting Principle 4: If the victim is not handled properly, additional serious injury could result (p. 25).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Safe Swim Defense and Safety Afloat): Step 1 (Review with your counselor how Scouting): Moving a victim is an extremely delicate task best left to trained emergency personnel, but if no one else is present you may need to act (p. 25).

Step 2 (Safe Swim Defense and Safety Afloat): Step 2 (Review with your counselor how Scouting): In a swimming accident, you may have to move the victim to prevent drowning or to perform rescue breathing (p. 25).

Step 3 (Safe Swim Defense and Safety Afloat): Step 3 (Review with your counselor how Scouting): When tending to a suspected spinal injury victim, move the victim's head, neck, and back as little as possible (p. 25).
Step 4 (Safe Swim Defense and Safety Afloat): Step 4 (Review with your counselor how Scouting): The technique used to limit this movement is called in-line stabilization (p. 25).

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: While swimming at an ocean beach, a Scout feels a narrow, fast-moving current pulling them straight offshore through a break in the sandbar. What is the safest way to escape this rip current?
quiz_item.question: While swimming at an ocean beach, a Scout feels a narrow, fast-moving current pulling them straight offshore through a break in the sandbar. What is the safest way to escape this rip current?
options: A. Sprint-swim straight back toward the beach directly against the outgoing current.
B. Stay calm to conserve energy, swim parallel to the shoreline until out of the narrow seaward pull, and then angle back to the beach with the breaking waves.
C. Dive to the sandy bottom and try to crawl toward shore underwater.
D. Remove your swim goggles and tread water while pulling another swimmer into the center of the rip channel.
choices: A. Sprint-swim straight back toward the beach directly against the outgoing current.
B. Stay calm to conserve energy, swim parallel to the shoreline until out of the narrow seaward pull, and then angle back to the beach with the breaking waves.
C. Dive to the sandy bottom and try to crawl toward shore underwater.
D. Remove your swim goggles and tread water while pulling another swimmer into the center of the rip channel.
quiz_item.correct_answer: B. Stay calm to conserve energy, swim parallel to the shoreline until out of the narrow seaward pull, and then angle back to the beach with the breaking waves.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (B): Rip currents are narrow channels that quickly exhaust swimmers who fight them head-on; swimming parallel to the beach moves you out of the current within 50 to 100 feet.

BSA Swimmer Qualification and Safety Principle 4: Requirements Principle 4: Each group is assigned a specific swimming area with depths consistent with those abilities (p. 8).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (BSA Swimmer Qualification and Safety): Step 1 (Requirements): The classification tests should be renewed annually, preferably at the beginning of the season even if the Scout has earned the Swimming (p. 8).
Step 2 (BSA Swimmer Qualification and Safety): Step 2 (Requirements): Swimmers pass this test: Jump feet first into water over the head in depth (p. 8).
Step 3 (BSA Swimmer Qualification and Safety): Step 3 (Requirements): The 100 yards must be completed in one swim without stops and must include at least one sharp turn (p. 8).
Step 4 (BSA Swimmer Qualification and Safety): Step 4 (Requirements): One of the most important elements of safety in the water is the ability to swim (p. 8).

Swimming Strokes Principle 4: You also are required to swim the specified strokes in a "strong manner." This means no rest stops and no gasping, panting finishes (p. 41).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Swimming Strokes): The stroke sequence begins with the more strenuous strokes and moves through to the more restful strokes, with the last stroke (p. 41).

Step 3 (Swimming Strokes): Ifyou complete the swim "in a strong manner" in the specified sequence, then you should be rested and able to continue well beyond the 150-yard (p. 41).
Step 4 (Swimming Strokes): On the following pages, you will find the required strokes illustrated and explained as you should swim them to complete requirement 3 (p. 41).

pamphlet_excerpts: Water rescue methods by reaching: Spinal injuries can occur from diving into shallow or obstructed water (p. 22).
Water rescue methods by reaching Principle 2: Rescuers must be very careful when a spinal injury is suspected (p. 22).
Water rescue methods by reaching Principle 3: Spinal injuries can be fatal or can cause paralysis (p. 22).
Water rescue methods by reaching Principle 4: If the victim is not handled properly, additional serious injury could result (p. 22).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Water rescue methods by reaching): Moving a victim is an extremely delicate task best left to trained emergency personnel, but if no one else is present you may need to act (p. 22).
Step 2 (Water rescue methods by reaching): In a swimming accident, you may have to move the victim to prevent drowning or to perform rescue breathing (p. 22).
Step 3 (Water rescue methods by reaching): When tending to a suspected spinal injury victim, move the victim's head, neck, and back as little as possible (p. 22).
Step 4 (Water rescue methods by reaching): The technique used to limit this movement is called in-line stabilization (p. 22).

pamphlet_excerpts: In Water Over Your Head: The easiest way to do the headfirst pike surface dive is while moving forward with a breaststroke (p. 56).
In Water Over Your Head Principle 2: Then reverse the direction of your arm stroke while lifting your legs out of the water and into the air (p. 56).
In Water Over Your Head Principle 3: In this streamlined position, the weight of your legs above the water will drive you downward (p. 56).
In Water Over Your Head Principle 4: It all should happen quickly inone smooth motion (p. 56).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (In Water Over Your Head): Once your feet are underwater, you can begin to swim (p. 56).
Step 2 (In Water Over Your Head): If you want to go deeper or faster after you are completely beneath the surface, use the breaststroke, which you also can use to swim along the bottom (p. 56).
Step 3 (In Water Over Your Head): A tuck surface dive is another option you can use to fulfill requirement (p. 56).
Step 4 (In Water Over Your Head): Instead of lifting your legs as you would for apike surface dive, pull your knees toward your chest and push them upward as you point your head (p. 56).

pamphlet_excerpts: Surface Dives: No elevated entry is permitted where the person must clear any obstacle, including jumping or diving over land (p. 15).
Surface Dives Principle 2: In water with less than 7 feet of unobstructed depth, diving is not permitted and water entry must be feet first (p. 15).
Surface Dives Principle 3: A leaping entry is recommended where water is at or above head level (p. 15).
Surface Dives Principle 4: A step-down or jump-down entry from a sitting position is recommended for shallower water (p. 15).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Surface Dives): Never attempt to plunge headfirst below waves at a beach (p. 15).
Step 2 (Surface Dives): Diving is permitted in clear water at least 7 feet deep from a dock, pier, or platform that is no more than 18 inches above the water surface (p. 15).
Step 3 (Surface Dives): However, if your state, city, or local community requires a water depth greater than 7 feet, it is important to abide by that mandate (p. 15).
Step 4 (Surface Dives): Remember that it is the weight of your legs above you that pushes you down into the water (p. 15).

C. Dive to the sandy bottom and try to crawl toward shore underwater.

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: How do woven fabrics and knitted fabrics differ in the way yarns are assembled, and how does that structure affect the fabric's behavior?
quiz_item.question: How do woven fabrics and knitted fabrics differ in the way yarns are assembled, and how does that structure affect the fabric's behavior?
options: A. Woven fabrics are fused directly from loose fibers using heat and glue, whereas knitted fabrics are spun without yarn.

B. Woven fabrics interlace two perpendicular sets of yarn (warp and weft) on a loom to create a firm, stable cloth, whereas knitted fabrics interlock loops of yarn to create a flexible, stretchy material.
C. Woven fabrics can only be made from synthetic polyester, whereas knitted fabrics can only be made from natural sheep wool.
D. Knitted fabrics have zero elasticity and unravel only when cut with pinking shears, whereas woven fabrics stretch easily in every direction.
choices: A. Woven fabrics are fused directly from loose fibers using heat and glue, whereas knitted fabrics are spun without yarn.

B. Woven fabrics interlace two perpendicular sets of yarn (warp and weft) on a loom to create a firm, stable cloth, whereas knitted fabrics interlock loops of yarn to create a flexible, stretchy material.
C. Woven fabrics can only be made from synthetic polyester, whereas knitted fabrics can only be made from natural sheep wool.

quiz_item.correct_answer: B. Woven fabrics interlace two perpendicular sets of yarn (warp and weft) on a loom to create a firm, stable cloth, whereas knitted fabrics interlock loops of yarn to create a flexible, stretchy material.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (B): Weaving crosses lengthwise warp yarns and crosswise weft yarns at right angles for dimensional stability, while knitting forms interlocking loops that give garments natural stretch and recovery.

Core Textile Terminology and Weaves Principle 2: Skis with aramid-fiber cores last longer and perform better (p. 27).
Core Textile Terminology and Weaves Principle 3: Racing drivers wear aramid suits that help prevent them from burning to death in fiery, high-speed crashes (p. 27).

Core Textile Terminology and Weaves Principle 4: Carbon fibers are extremely strong, stiff, lightweight fibers of nearly pure carbon made by "baking" or "charring" rayon, pitch, or acrylic fibers (p. 27).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Core Textile Terminology and Weaves): They are used to strengthen airplanes and spacecraft (p. 27).
Step 2 (Core Textile Terminology and Weaves): The exhaust nozzles of the two large booster rockets that lift the space shuttle into orbit contain 30,000 pounds of carbonized (charred) rayon (p. 27).
Step 3 (Core Textile Terminology and Weaves): Three dimensional fabrics made from carbon fibers may someday replace steel in such products as automobiles, military vehicles, and building (p. 27).
Step 4 (Core Textile Terminology and Weaves): Lyocell, first produced in the United States in 1992, is a relative of rayon (p. 27).

Step 4 (Advantages and disadvantages of natural plant): Lyocell, first produced in the United States in 1992, is a relative of rayon (p. 27).

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: In stagecraft and theater performance, why are the rear of the stage called 'upstage' and the front near the audience called 'downstage,' and what safety rule applies to overhead stage rigging?
quiz_item.question: In stagecraft and theater performance, why are the rear of the stage called 'upstage' and the front near the audience called 'downstage,' and what safety rule applies to overhead stage rigging?
options: A. Because early Greek amphitheaters placed the audience on the roof above the actors, and anyone may pull counterweight ropes at any time.
B. Because sound travels upward toward the balcony, and stage lights should be hung without safety cables so they can be aimed faster.

C. Historic raked stages sloped upward away from the audience toward the back wall; backstage, only trained crew may operate counterweight fly lines, and every overhead lighting instrument must have a secondary safety cable.
D. Upstage refers to the catwalk above the proscenium arch, where actors wait between scenes without hard hats.
choices: A. Because early Greek amphitheaters placed the audience on the roof above the actors, and anyone may pull counterweight ropes at any time.
B. Because sound travels upward toward the balcony, and stage lights should be hung without safety cables so they can be aimed faster.

C. Historic raked stages sloped upward away from the audience toward the back wall; backstage, only trained crew may operate counterweight fly lines, and every overhead lighting instrument must have a secondary safety cable.
D. Upstage refers to the catwalk above the proscenium arch, where actors wait between scenes without hard hats.
quiz_item.correct_answer: C. Historic raked stages sloped upward away from the audience toward the back wall; backstage, only trained crew may operate counterweight fly lines, and every overhead lighting instrument must have a secondary safety cable.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (C): Historical raked stages angled upward toward the back to improve audience sightlines, giving us upstage and downstage; modern theater safety requires secondary safety cables on overhead lights and trained control of rigging.

requirements.lead_text: Discuss with your counselor the safety precautions that should be practiced when working in a theater to protect the cast and crew. Then do THREE of the following:
requirements.req_text: Discuss with your counselor the safety precautions that should be practiced when working in a theater to protect the cast and crew. Then do THREE of the following: (a) Act a major part in a full-length play; or act a part in three one-act plays. (b) Direct a play. Cast, rehearse, and stage it. The play must be at least 10 minutes long. (c) Design the set for a play or a theatrical production. Make a model of it. (d) Design the costumes for five characters in a theatrical production set in a historical time. (e) Show skill in hair and makeup design. Make up yourself or a friend as a historical figure, a clown, an extraterrestrial, or a monster as directed. (f) With your counselor's approval, help with the building and painting of the scenery for a theatrical production. (g) With your counselor's approval, design the lighting for a play; or help install, focus, color, program, and operate the lighting for a theatrical production. (h) With your counselor's approval, help install, focus, equalize, program, and operate the sound for a theatrical production. (i) Serve as the stage manager for a theatrical production. Document all cues and stage setups in your calling script. (j) Serve as musical director for a musical theater production.

options: A. Because early Greek amphitheaters placed the audience on the roof above the actors, and anyone may pull counterweight ropes at any time.
B. Because sound travels upward toward the balcony, and stage lights should be hung without safety cables so they can be aimed faster.

C. Historic raked stages sloped upward away from the audience toward the back wall; backstage, only trained crew may operate counterweight fly lines, and every overhead lighting instrument must have a secondary safety cable.
D. Upstage refers to the catwalk above the proscenium arch, where actors wait between scenes without hard hats.
choices: A. Because early Greek amphitheaters placed the audience on the roof above the actors, and anyone may pull counterweight ropes at any time.

requirements.lead_text: Preventing Impaired Driving. Do the following:
requirements.req_text: Preventing Impaired Driving. Do the following: (a) Explain why a distracted driver must not operate a motor vehicle. List five common distractions, explain how driver distractions contribute to traffic accidents, and tell how drivers can minimize distractions. (b) Explain why a driver impaired by alcohol, drugs, or other substances must not operate a motor vehicle. Describe how alcohol, cold medications, and prescription and illegal drugs affect driving abilities. For the state where you live, find out what is the legal blood alcohol concentration and what are the consequences for driving while intoxicated or driving under the influence. Find out what the open-container law is in your state. (c) Explain why a fatigued driver must not operate a motor vehicle. Describe how drivers must plan to be alert for safely transporting families, friends, Scouts, and themselves. (d) Describe mistakes that new drivers make, how those mistakes increase their risk of collisions, how drivers can reduce this risk, and how driving behavior affects automobile insurance rates.

pamphlet_excerpts: Preventing Impaired Driving: Motor vehicle crashes are the leading cause of death in the United States for young people, and an alarming number of these crashes are related (p. 17).
Preventing Impaired Driving Principle 2: Alcohol impaired driving is highest among persons 21 to 24 years old, and the percentage of fatal crashes that are alcohol-related is highest (p. 17).
Preventing Impaired Driving Principle 3: However, even for the youngest drivers, alcohol-related crashes are a serious problem (p. 17).
Preventing Impaired Driving Principle 4: Alcohol and drugs are perhaps the most publicized causes of impaired driving, but they are not the only causes (p. 17).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Preventing Impaired Driving): Each year a considerable number of serious crashes occur as a result of drivers who are impaired by fatigue and drowsiness (p. 17).
Step 2 (Preventing Impaired Driving): Another serious factor in accidents is drivers using their cell phones while driving, which diverts their attention from the road (p. 17).
Step 3 (Preventing Impaired Driving): Texting while driving is extremely dangerous and is illegal in many states (p. 17).
Step 4 (Preventing Impaired Driving): Research shows that Marijuana is harmful to the brain, heart, lungs, and immune system (p. 17).

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: Why is texting or interacting with a smartphone while driving considered uniquely dangerous under traffic safety principles, and how should following distance be adjusted in rain?
quiz_item.question: Why is texting or interacting with a smartphone while driving considered uniquely dangerous under traffic safety principles, and how should following distance be adjusted in rain?
options: A. Texting combines all three types of driving distraction at once (visual, manual, and cognitive), and drivers should increase their normal three-second following distance to four or more seconds on wet pavement.
B. Texting only causes a brief manual distraction, which can be offset by driving one car length behind the vehicle ahead.
C. Using a phone at highway speeds is safe as long as you hold the phone on top of the steering wheel in your line of sight.
D. Wet roads cool down rubber tires so braking distances are shorter than on dry asphalt, allowing a one-second following gap.
choices: A. Texting combines all three types of driving distraction at once (visual, manual, and cognitive), and drivers should increase their normal three-second following distance to four or more seconds on wet pavement.
B. Texting only causes a brief manual distraction, which can be offset by driving one car length behind the vehicle ahead.
C. Using a phone at highway speeds is safe as long as you hold the phone on top of the steering wheel in your line of sight.
D. Wet roads cool down rubber tires so braking distances are shorter than on dry asphalt, allowing a one-second following gap.
quiz_item.correct_answer: A. Texting combines all three types of driving distraction at once (visual, manual, and cognitive), and drivers should increase their normal three-second following distance to four or more seconds on wet pavement.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (A): Texting takes your eyes off the road (visual), hands off the wheel (manual), and mind off driving (cognitive) simultaneously, while wet or slick conditions require expanding the 3-second following distance.

pamphlet_excerpts: Vehicle Safety: Safety belts are the most effective device for preventing serious injuries and reducing fatalities in motor vehicle crashes (p. 37).
Vehicle Safety Principle 2: Studies have shown that people who wear seat belts reduce their risk of serious injury by 50 percent and reduce the risk of fatal injury by 45 percent (p. 37).
Vehicle Safety Principle 3: Safety belts also keep passengers properly positioned to fully benefit from the protection provided by airbags (p. 37).
Vehicle Safety Principle 4: Research has shown that the chances of being killed are five times greater when the occupant is thrown from a vehicle (p. 37).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Vehicle Safety): Properly worn safety belts help prevent passengers from being ejected (p. 37).
Step 2 (Vehicle Safety): Crash victims who wear safety belts are more likely to be unhurt, alert, and able to escape quickly (p. 37).
Step 3 (Vehicle Safety): Always wear a safety belt and make sure that all other passengers are properly restrained (p. 37).
Step 4 (Vehicle Safety): The NHTSA says that growing up safe is a four-step process (p. 37).

requirements.lead_text: Auto Maintenance and Safety Checkups. With adult supervision and using a vehicle that you have access to, do the following:
requirements.req_text: Auto Maintenance and Safety Checkups. With adult supervision and using a vehicle that you have access to, do the following: (a) Demonstrate that all driving lights and signaling lights are clear and operational. Show where the switches are for these lights. Explain how drivers use lights to drive safely and courteously and to communicate with other drivers. (b) Explain issues that might affect the driver's ability to see through the front, rear, and side windows. Demonstrate with a smear-and-clear test if the windshield wiper blades will clear the windshield completely or need to be replaced. Describe instances in good and bad weather when windshield wipers are important to safe driving. (c) Demonstrate how to find the vehicle's recommended tire pressures, how to check tire pressures, and how to check for adequate tire tread depth. Explain why proper tire pressure and tread depth are important to traction, stopping distances, tire wear, and fuel economy. (d) Check the vehicle for tools needed to change a flat tire or to use tire sealant to fix a puncture. Demonstrate you know how to change a flat tire and how to use tire sealant. (e) In a location away from traffic hazards, mark off the reaction distances and braking distances that a car will travel as it makes an emergency stop at 25, 55, and 70 miles per hour on level dry and level wet pavement. Discuss how these distances change for normal and impaired drivers, for day and night driving, and for weather conditions. Note: Use the graphics template in the Traffic Safety merit badge pamphlet or one approved by your counselor to set up this demonstration.

pamphlet_excerpts: Traffic Safety and the Law: As a Scout, you understand the importance of sharing and working together to make sure things go smoothly (p. 51).
Traffic Safety and the Law Principle 2: Scouts always have backup plans in case of emergencies (p. 51).
Traffic Safety and the Law Principle 3: Safe driving means sharing the road with other drivers and being aware of those who are using the road (p. 51).

Traffic Safety and the Law Principle 4: Safe driving also means sharing the road with everybody who uses it, including pedestrians, bicycles, motorcycles, trucks, buses, and stray or wild animals (p. 51).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Traffic Safety and the Law): Riding a bike in traffic with bigger, faster, heavier four-wheeled vehicles is often dangerous and scary (p. 51).
Step 2 (Traffic Safety and the Law): The number of bicycles and vehicles sharing the road continues to grow every year andso, too, do accidents involving (p. 51).
Step 3 (Traffic Safety and the Law): In traffic, bicycles are considered vehicles and traffic laws that apply to cars also apply to bicyclists (p. 51).
Step 4 (Traffic Safety and the Law): Rules of the road to help ensure bicycle safety include the following: Always ride on the right side of the road, with traffic, just as cars (p. 51).

pamphlet_excerpts: Road Designs and Signs: Rumble strips help keep roads safe because they increase driver attention (p. 28).
Road Designs and Signs Principle 2: The textured patterns of rumble strips will not damage a vehicle and can safely be driven over at the speed limit (p. 28).
Road Designs and Signs Principle 3: Rumble strips are small indentations or raised strips on the pavement that, when driven over, make noise (p. 28).
Road Designs and Signs Principle 4: Rumble strips alert drivers when they are veering off the road or heading into a different lane (p. 28).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Road Designs and Signs): Retroreflective signs and pavement markings help nighttime drivers (p. 28).
Step 2 (Road Designs and Signs): Made from a material that bounces light from headlights back to drivers' eyes, such signs and markings are quite easy to see at night (p. 28).
Step 3 (Road Designs and Signs): About 40 percent of all crashes occur at intersections (p. 28).
Step 4 (Road Designs and Signs): To make intersections safer for drivers, pedestrians, and bicyclists, traffic engineers have made improvements to the timing mechanisms (p. 28).

pamphlet_excerpts: Sharing the Road: Always wear a helmet when you are on a motorcycle, regardless of whether your state requires them (p. 55).
Sharing the Road Principle 2: Ahelmet will help protect you from serious, often fatal, head injuries (p. 55).
Sharing the Road Principle 3: On a motorcycle, a person does not have the protection that a car's metal body structure affords, so amotorcyclist is much more vulnerable to injury (p. 55).
Sharing the Road Principle 4: For this reason, motorcyclists must drive extremely defensively (p. 55).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Sharing the Road): These safety guidelines also apply to street-legal scooters and mopeds (p. 55).
Step 2 (Sharing the Road): Vehicles that are not street legal, such as go-carts and all-terrain vehicles (ATVs), should not be used for transportation on any public road (p. 55).
Step 3 (Sharing the Road): Pedestrian safety is a serious issue because people who are walking across a roadway lose in any accident with avehicle (p. 55).
Step 4 (Sharing the Road): Each year, nearly 5,000 pedestrians die in traffic crashes (p. 55).

requirements.lead_text: Careers. Explore careers related to traffic safety. Research one career to learn about the training and education needed, costs, job prospects, salary, job duties, and career advancement. Your research methods may include, with your parent or guardian's permission, an internet or library search, an interview with a professional in the field, or a visit to a location where people in this career work. Discuss with your counselor both your findings and what about this profession might make it an interesting career.

patrol_quiz_bank.question: Why is texting or interacting with a smartphone while driving considered uniquely dangerous under traffic safety principles, and how should following distance be adjusted in rain?
options: A. Texting combines all three types of driving distraction at once (visual, manual, and cognitive), and drivers should increase their normal three-second following distance to four or more seconds on wet pavement.
B. Texting only causes a brief manual distraction, which can be offset by driving one car length behind the vehicle ahead.
C. Using a phone at highway speeds is safe as long as you hold the phone on top of the steering wheel in your line of sight.
D. Wet roads cool down rubber tires so braking distances are shorter than on dry asphalt, allowing a one-second following gap.
choices: A. Texting combines all three types of driving distraction at once (visual, manual, and cognitive), and drivers should increase their normal three-second following distance to four or more seconds on wet pavement.

patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: A. Texting combines all three types of driving distraction at once (visual, manual, and cognitive), and drivers should increase their normal three-second following distance to four or more seconds on wet pavement.
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (A): Texting takes your eyes off the road (visual), hands off the wheel (manual), and mind off driving (cognitive) simultaneously, while wet or slick conditions require expanding the 3-second following distance.

pamphlet_excerpts: Roles A Veterinarian Plays: Aquaculture medicine uses the principles of veterinary medicine to maintain healthy colonies of fish and other aquatic animals (p. 22).
Roles A Veterinarian Plays Principle 2: This field of veterinary medicine is distinct from other areas of aquatic science, such as marine biology (p. 22).
Roles A Veterinarian Plays Principle 3: As the world population grows, aquaculture will help provide an adequate food supply, and the work of aquaculture veterinarians will be critical (p. 22).
Roles A Veterinarian Plays Principle 4: Students interested in aquaculture medicine must earn a doctorate in veterinary medicine (p. 22).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Roles A Veterinarian Plays): Postgraduate training in aquaculture medicine is offered at some schools of veterinary medicine (p. 22).
Step 2 (Roles A Veterinarian Plays): Many opportunities, especially in the coming years, await individuals trained in aquaculture medicine (p. 22).
Step 3 (Roles A Veterinarian Plays): You might not hear much about public health veterinarians because most of them work for local, state, and federal agencies (p. 22).
Step 4 (Roles A Veterinarian Plays): Veterinarians who work in public health are the silent sentinels protecting America's public health and our quality of life (p. 22).

quiz_item.question: Beyond treating sick pets in a clinic, how do veterinarians protect human public health and the nation's food supply?
options: A. By prescribing human antibiotics to grocery store produce departments.
B. By controlling zoonotic diseases (such as rabies, brucellosis, and avian influenza) that can pass from animals to humans, and inspecting livestock health and food safety from farm to table.
C. By breeding wild predators to replace domestic cattle and poultry on commercial ranches.
D. By restricting vaccinations exclusively to indoor house cats and ornamental aquarium fish.
choices: A. By prescribing human antibiotics to grocery store produce departments.
B. By controlling zoonotic diseases (such as rabies, brucellosis, and avian influenza) that can pass from animals to humans, and inspecting livestock health and food safety from farm to table.

pamphlet_excerpts: Roles A Veterinarian Plays: Laboratory animal medicine and research veterinary medicine have much in common (p. 30).
Roles A Veterinarian Plays Principle 2: Both fields apply the skills learned in veterinary school to a number of areas of study (p. 30).
Roles A Veterinarian Plays Principle 3: A veterinarian working in laboratory animal medicine provides medical care for animals used in research (p. 30).
Roles A Veterinarian Plays Principle 4: The veterinarian sometimes is a member of the research team and helps design studies, interpret results, and publish articles about the research (p. 30).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Roles A Veterinarian Plays): Research veterinarians investigate new medicines, biotechnical and diagnostic tests, food technologies, and other newtechnologies (p. 30).
Step 2 (Roles A Veterinarian Plays): Research veterinarians might also investigate the exotic and infectious diseases that threaten public health (p. 30).
Step 3 (Roles A Veterinarian Plays): Or, research veterinarians might work in the emerging field of genetic research (p. 30).
Step 4 (Roles A Veterinarian Plays): Laboratory animal medicine and research veterinarians usually work on a team of scientists, much like an individual Scout works (p. 30).

pamphlet_excerpts: Registered Veterinary Technician: The American Veterinary Medical Association accredits veterinary technician programs throughout the United States (p. 30).
Registered Veterinary Technician Principle 2: Training to become a veterinary technician usually begins inone of these programs (p. 30).
Registered Veterinary Technician Principle 3: Most accredited programs lead to an associate's degree after two years of study (p. 30).
Registered Veterinary Technician Principle 4: However, veterinary technicians with a bachelor of science degree typically earn a higher salary and have more responsibilities (p. 30).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Registered Veterinary Technician): In addition to course work, students of veterinary technician programs complete a certain amount of hands-on training, which is acritical part of all (p. 30).
Step 2 (Registered Veterinary Technician): Finally, nearly every state requires that veterinary technicians pass a state and/or national examination to be eligible to practice (p. 30).
Step 3 (Registered Veterinary Technician): For a complete list of veterinary technology programs, many accredited by the American Veterinary Medical Association, visit the AVMA's website (p. 30).
Step 4 (Registered Veterinary Technician): Laboratory animal medicine and research veterinary medicine have much in common (p. 30).

pamphlet_excerpts: Role A Veterinarian Plays: The Human-Animal Bond and the Veterinarian If you have a pet, you know how special that pet (p. 41).

step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Role A Veterinarian Plays): The veterinarian's role is to recognize and understand the importance of the human-animal bond and to enhance (p. 41).

Step 3 (Role A Veterinarian Plays): This includes providing quality medical care and giving advice to people about animal care, preventive medical care, and howto choose (p. 41).
Step 4 (Role A Veterinarian Plays): Hieroglyphics on the Egyptian pyramids illustrate the human-animal bond, and Roman legends tell about it in stories such as "Romulus and Remus (p. 41).

patrol_quiz_bank.question: Beyond treating sick pets in a clinic, how do veterinarians protect human public health and the nation's food supply?
options: A. By prescribing human antibiotics to grocery store produce departments.
B. By controlling zoonotic diseases (such as rabies, brucellosis, and avian influenza) that can pass from animals to humans, and inspecting livestock health and food safety from farm to table.
C. By breeding wild predators to replace domestic cattle and poultry on commercial ranches.
D. By restricting vaccinations exclusively to indoor house cats and ornamental aquarium fish.
choices: A. By prescribing human antibiotics to grocery store produce departments.
B. By controlling zoonotic diseases (such as rabies, brucellosis, and avian influenza) that can pass from animals to humans, and inspecting livestock health and food safety from farm to table.
