D. By restricting vaccinations exclusively to indoor house cats and ornamental aquarium fish.
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: B. By controlling zoonotic diseases (such as rabies, brucellosis, and avian influenza) that can pass from animals to humans, and inspecting livestock health and food safety from farm to table.
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (B): Veterinarians play a vital One Health role by preventing zoonotic disease spillover between animals and people (such as rabies vaccination) and safeguarding livestock health and food safety.

pamphlet_excerpts: Hazards, First Aid & Safety: A body temperature of 105 degrees or greater is a life-threatening medical condition and requires immediate medical treatment by health-care (p. 28).
Hazards, First Aid & Safety Principle 2: Heatstroke is a life-threatening condition; call for medical assistance immediately (p. 28).
Hazards, First Aid & Safety Principle 3: While waiting for medical personnel to arrive, work to lower the victim's temperature (p. 28).
Hazards, First Aid & Safety Principle 4: Move the person to an air-conditioned or shady area (p. 28).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Hazards, First Aid & Safety): Loosen tight clothing and further cool the victim by fanning and applying wet towels (p. 28).
Step 2 (Hazards, First Aid & Safety): If possible, immerse or spray the person with cold water (p. 28).
Step 3 (Hazards, First Aid & Safety): Ifyou have ice packs, wrap them in a thin barrier (such as a thin towel) and place them under the armpits and against the neck and groin (p. 28).
Step 4 (Hazards, First Aid & Safety): If the person is able to drink, give small amounts of cool water (p. 28).

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: When towing a water-skier or wakeboarder behind a motorboat, what crew roles, life jacket gear, and boarding procedures are required for safety?
quiz_item.question: When towing a water-skier or wakeboarder behind a motorboat, what crew roles, life jacket gear, and boarding procedures are required for safety?
options: A. The boat driver watches the skier in a rearview mirror without a spotter, and the engine stays in neutral while the skier climbs the swim platform.
B. The skier wears an inflatable belt pack only if they cannot swim, and signals 'stop' by waving both arms up and down.

C. A dedicated observer must watch the skier and relay hand signals so the driver stays focused ahead, the skier must wear a USCG-approved PFD rated for water impact, and the engine must be shut off completely before anyone approaches the stern to board.
D. Two boats should tow the same skier side-by-side so one boat can block wakes from passing vessels.
choices: A. The boat driver watches the skier in a rearview mirror without a spotter, and the engine stays in neutral while the skier climbs the swim platform.
B. The skier wears an inflatable belt pack only if they cannot swim, and signals 'stop' by waving both arms up and down.

C. A dedicated observer must watch the skier and relay hand signals so the driver stays focused ahead, the skier must wear a USCG-approved PFD rated for water impact, and the engine must be shut off completely before anyone approaches the stern to board.
D. Two boats should tow the same skier side-by-side so one boat can block wakes from passing vessels.
quiz_item.correct_answer: C. A dedicated observer must watch the skier and relay hand signals so the driver stays focused ahead, the skier must wear a USCG-approved PFD rated for water impact, and the engine must be shut off completely before anyone approaches the stern to board.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (C): Safe water skiing and wakeboarding require a dedicated observer in addition to the operator, a USCG-approved Type III PFD, clear hand signals, and turning the engine completely off before a skier reboards near the propeller.

Step 3 (BSA Swimmer Qualification Check): Every individual must have a buddy, and every craft should have a buddy boat when on the water. 6 (p. 12).
Step 4 (BSA Swimmer Qualification Check): Skill Proficiency All participants in a water sports activity must be trained and experienced in watercraft handling skills, safety (p. 12).

pamphlet_excerpts: Signals to the safety observer: The driver may use this signal to alert the skier that the boat is about to turn (p. 20).
Signals to the safety observer Principle 2: If the skier wants the driver to turn, the skier uses the same signal followed by pointing in the direction he or she wants the driver (p. 20).
Signals to the safety observer Principle 3: Once a skier is under way, the noise from the boat makes hearing instructions difficult (p. 20).
Signals to the safety observer Principle 4: The skier must learn to give directions by using the hand signals shown here (p. 20).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Signals to the safety observer): The observer serves as the eyes and the ears for the driver and skier (p. 20).
Step 2 (Signals to the safety observer): Note that "skier" refers to both water-skiers and wake boarders (p. 20).
Step 3 (Signals to the safety observer): The observer must communicate the skier's signals to the boat driver quickly and accurately (p. 20).
Step 4 (Signals to the safety observer): To do this, the observer must watch the skier closely, tell the boat driver if the skier falls, and keep the driver alert to other boat traffic (p. 20).

pamphlet_excerpts: Showing reasonable control: To keep the board from wobbling, puts lightly more weight on your front foot than on your back foot as the boat begins Alternate Method for Deep water (p. 59).
Showing reasonable control Principle 2: You may prefer to start out with the wake board partially rotated uptoward the front foot (p. 59).
Showing reasonable control Principle 3: Begin with the wake board out in front ofyou and parallel to the water's surface (p. 59).
Showing reasonable control Principle 4: Keep your knees bent and hold the rope handle with your arms straight (p. 59).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Showing reasonable control): When you are in position and ready, shout out "Hit it!" to let the driver know to accelerate (p. 59).
Step 2 (Showing reasonable control): As soon as the boat starts to pull, twist at the hips to turn the front of the board up and toward the boat (p. 59).
Step 3 (Showing reasonable control): Keeping your knees bent, transfer more weight to your back foot as the boat pulls (p. 59).
Step 4 (Showing reasonable control): Alternate starting position to pull you out of the water (p. 59).

pamphlet_excerpts: While on shore: With wake boards, the angle of your feet on the board can be adjusted depending on your skill level (p. 17).
While on shore Principle 2: As a beginner, you'll want to follow the steps below, fine-tuning the adjustments to find a stance that feels most comfortable (p. 17).
While on shore Principle 3: Step 1, Adjust the distance between the bindings to about shoulder-width apart, with your back foot slightly more toward the rear of the board for better (p. 17).
While on shore Principle 4: Step 2, Adjust the angle of the back foot so that it is straight across the board or turned outs lightly toward the back (at zero to 9 degrees) (p. 17).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (While on shore): Step 3, Adjust the angle of the front foot so that it is slightly turned outtoward the front (9 to 27 degrees) (p. 17).
Step 2 (While on shore): Try the board on for size before you hit the water (p. 17).
Step 3 (While on shore): When riding a wake board, one foot is in front (p. 17).
Step 4 (While on shore): Having the left foot forward is called "regular-footed," and having the right foot forward is called "goofy-footed," but there is no right (p. 17).

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: Your patrol is hiking across an open alpine ridgeline when towering cumulonimbus clouds build rapidly and you hear thunder 10 seconds after seeing a lightning flash (roughly 2 miles away). What is the safest immediate action for the patrol?
quiz_item.question: Your patrol is hiking across an open alpine ridgeline when towering cumulonimbus clouds build rapidly and you hear thunder 10 seconds after seeing a lightning flash (roughly 2 miles away). What is the safest immediate action for the patrol?
options: A. Stay on the ridgeline under a tall isolated pine tree to keep dry until the rain passes.

B. Apply the 30/30 lightning rule: immediately descend off the exposed ridge and away from tall isolated trees or water, move into lower dense timber or a substantial building, and spread patrol members at least 50 feet apart if caught in the open.
C. Huddle together in a tight circle on top of metal-frame backpacks.
D. Lie flat on wet granite at the summit so the wind blows over the patrol.
choices: A. Stay on the ridgeline under a tall isolated pine tree to keep dry until the rain passes.

B. Apply the 30/30 lightning rule: immediately descend off the exposed ridge and away from tall isolated trees or water, move into lower dense timber or a substantial building, and spread patrol members at least 50 feet apart if caught in the open.
C. Huddle together in a tight circle on top of metal-frame backpacks.
D. Lie flat on wet granite at the summit so the wind blows over the patrol.
quiz_item.correct_answer: B. Apply the 30/30 lightning rule: immediately descend off the exposed ridge and away from tall isolated trees or water, move into lower dense timber or a substantial building, and spread patrol members at least 50 feet apart if caught in the open.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (B): Sound travels about 1 mile every 5 seconds; a 10-second flash-to-bang interval means lightning is within 2 miles and already in strike range, requiring immediate descent from ridges and avoidance of tall isolated objects.

options: A. A Watch means a tornado has been spotted on the ground; a Warning means conditions might become favorable tomorrow.

B. A Watch means atmospheric conditions favor severe thunderstorm and tornado development (stay alert and prepared); a Warning means hazardous weather or a tornado is imminent or occurring on radar/ground (take immediate shelter now).
C. Both Watch and Warning mean the storm has already passed your campsite and outdoor activities can resume.
D. Wait until you see hail larger than golf balls before checking your family or troop emergency shelter plan.
choices: A. A Watch means a tornado has been spotted on the ground; a Warning means conditions might become favorable tomorrow.

C. Both Watch and Warning mean the storm has already passed your campsite and outdoor activities can resume.

quiz_item.correct_answer: B. A Watch means atmospheric conditions favor severe thunderstorm and tornado development (stay alert and prepared); a Warning means hazardous weather or a tornado is imminent or occurring on radar/ground (take immediate shelter now).

pamphlet_excerpts: At least two sources of weather: The first weather satellite, known as TIROS-1, was launched in the spring of 1960 (p. 33).
At least two sources of weather Principle 2: It was highly successful at giving meteorologists their first overall view of entire storm systems (p. 33).
At least two sources of weather Principle 3: Since then, satellites have become much more sophisticated, allowing a nearly continuous watch over the entire Earth (p. 33).
At least two sources of weather Principle 4: NOAA has two satellite systems: polar-orbiting satellites and geostationary satellites (p. 33).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (At least two sources of weather): The satellite systems are named Polar Operational Environmental Satellites (POES) and Geostationary Operational Environmental Satellites (p. 33).
Step 2 (At least two sources of weather): The polar-orbiting satellites circle Earth, passing over or near the poles at a height of approximately 520 miles (p. 33).
Step 3 (At least two sources of weather): They travel around the globe several times each day (p. 33).
Step 4 (At least two sources of weather): The polar-orbiting satellites are placed in sun-synchronous orbits, which means they pass over the same spot at the same time each day (p. 33).

quiz_item.question: Looking at a surface weather map (Requirement 4), your patrol sees a blue line with triangles pointing southeast advancing toward a warm, humid air mass. What frontal system is approaching and what weather should the troop expect?
options: A. A warm front that brings several days of calm, cloudless skies and rising barometric pressure.

B. An advancing cold front where dense cold air wedges abruptly under warm moist air, forcing rapid vertical uplift, towering cumulonimbus clouds, gusty winds, and potential squall-line thunderstorms.
C. A high-pressure ridge where sinking air creates heavy blizzards and stationary fog.
D. A stationary pressure trough where wind stops completely and humidity drops to zero.
choices: A. A warm front that brings several days of calm, cloudless skies and rising barometric pressure.

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: During a summer afternoon thunderstorm (Requirement 5), your patrol observes jagged lightning bolts and half-inch hailstones. What physical mechanism inside a cumulonimbus cloud produces both hail and lightning?
quiz_item.question: During a summer afternoon thunderstorm (Requirement 5), your patrol observes jagged lightning bolts and half-inch hailstones. What physical mechanism inside a cumulonimbus cloud produces both hail and lightning?
options: A. Gentle horizontal breezes blowing across flat stratus clouds below 2,000 feet.

B. Powerful vertical updrafts and downdrafts cycling water droplets above and below the freezing level (accreting layered ice for hail) while colliding ice crystals and graupel separate electrical charges that discharge as lightning.
C. Direct solar radiation melting high-altitude cirrus clouds without any vertical air motion.
D. Ocean tides pulling warm air downward into a high-pressure center.
choices: A. Gentle horizontal breezes blowing across flat stratus clouds below 2,000 feet.

B. Powerful vertical updrafts and downdrafts cycling water droplets above and below the freezing level (accreting layered ice for hail) while colliding ice crystals and graupel separate electrical charges that discharge as lightning.
C. Direct solar radiation melting high-altitude cirrus clouds without any vertical air motion.
D. Ocean tides pulling warm air downward into a high-pressure center.
quiz_item.correct_answer: B. Powerful vertical updrafts and downdrafts cycling water droplets above and below the freezing level (accreting layered ice for hail) while colliding ice crystals and graupel separate electrical charges that discharge as lightning.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (B): Strong updrafts in cumulonimbus clouds suspend and cycle freezing droplets into layered hailstones while collisions between ice crystals and soft hail (graupel) build high-voltage charge separation that arcs as lightning (p. 34).

quiz_item.question: When tracing the hydrologic (water) cycle diagram for Requirement 7, how do evaporation, transpiration, condensation, and precipitation work together to move water between the ocean, atmosphere, and land?
options: A. Solar energy evaporates liquid water from oceans and lakes (plus plant transpiration) into invisible water vapor, which rises, cools, and condenses onto cloud condensation nuclei before falling as precipitation and returning via surface runoff and groundwater infiltration.
B. Condensation turns liquid river water directly into underground aquifers without entering the atmosphere.
C. Precipitation moves water upward from the soil into clouds, while evaporation pulls rain down to Earth.
D. The water cycle creates brand-new water molecules each summer and destroys them each winter.
choices: A. Solar energy evaporates liquid water from oceans and lakes (plus plant transpiration) into invisible water vapor, which rises, cools, and condenses onto cloud condensation nuclei before falling as precipitation and returning via surface runoff and groundwater infiltration.
B. Condensation turns liquid river water directly into underground aquifers without entering the atmosphere.
C. Precipitation moves water upward from the soil into clouds, while evaporation pulls rain down to Earth.
D. The water cycle creates brand-new water molecules each summer and destroys them each winter.
quiz_item.correct_answer: A. Solar energy evaporates liquid water from oceans and lakes (plus plant transpiration) into invisible water vapor, which rises, cools, and condenses onto cloud condensation nuclei before falling as precipitation and returning via surface runoff and groundwater infiltration.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (A): Solar heating drives evaporation and plant transpiration; rising moist air cools to its dew point (condensation) to form clouds, which release precipitation that replenishes rivers, groundwater, and oceans (p. 42).

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: For Requirement 8, how does a densely paved city ('urban heat island') alter local weather compared to surrounding rural forests, and how do sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxide emissions affect precipitation?
quiz_item.question: For Requirement 8, how does a densely paved city ('urban heat island') alter local weather compared to surrounding rural forests, and how do sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxide emissions affect precipitation?
options: A. Dark asphalt and concrete absorb and re-radiate solar heat with less vegetation cooling—raising urban temperatures by 2°F to 10°F and boosting downwind convective showers—while SO2 and NOx react with atmospheric moisture to form acid rain.
B. Concrete buildings reflect 100% of sunlight and make cities 15°F colder than surrounding forests in summer.
C. Acid rain is caused purely by natural ocean salt spray and has no connection to fossil-fuel combustion.
D. Urban heat islands eliminate all cloud formation and stop the greenhouse effect.
choices: A. Dark asphalt and concrete absorb and re-radiate solar heat with less vegetation cooling—raising urban temperatures by 2°F to 10°F and boosting downwind convective showers—while SO2 and NOx react with atmospheric moisture to form acid rain.
B. Concrete buildings reflect 100% of sunlight and make cities 15°F colder than surrounding forests in summer.
C. Acid rain is caused purely by natural ocean salt spray and has no connection to fossil-fuel combustion.
D. Urban heat islands eliminate all cloud formation and stop the greenhouse effect.
quiz_item.correct_answer: A. Dark asphalt and concrete absorb and re-radiate solar heat with less vegetation cooling—raising urban temperatures by 2°F to 10°F and boosting downwind convective showers—while SO2 and NOx react with atmospheric moisture to form acid rain.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (A): Urban heat islands retain heat in masonry and asphalt while reducing evapotranspiration, and industrial/vehicle emissions of sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides form sulfuric and nitric acids in rainwater (p. 48).

pamphlet_excerpts: Tilt of Earth's Axis Helps: Recall that weather is the condition of the atmosphere over aparticular area for a short time (p. 66).
Tilt of Earth's Axis Helps Principle 2: Climate is the average of the weather over a region for a longer time, such as 30 years (p. 66).

Tilt of Earth's Axis Helps Principle 3: The word climate comes from the Greek word klima, meaning "angle." This name was used because the angle at which the sun strikes Earth largely determines (p. 66).
Tilt of Earth's Axis Helps Principle 4: At the equator, the sun is nearly straight overhead most of the year, so most of the equatorial region is hot (p. 66).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Tilt of Earth's Axis Helps): Pole ward from the equator, the climate gradually shifts from hot to cold (p. 66).
Step 2 (Tilt of Earth's Axis Helps): This tilt (about 23.5 degrees from the perpendicular) remains the same all year as seen from deep space (top) but changes relative to the sun (p. 66).
Step 3 (Tilt of Earth's Axis Helps): At the summer solstice (the first day of summer, bottom left), the North Pole tilts toward the sun, and the sun reaches its northernmost point (p. 66).
Step 4 (Tilt of Earth's Axis Helps): This is the longest day of the year in the Northern Hemisphere (p. 66).

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: For Requirement 9, why does the Northern Hemisphere experience warm summer weather in June and cold winter weather in December, and why are polar regions colder than the equator?
quiz_item.question: For Requirement 9, why does the Northern Hemisphere experience warm summer weather in June and cold winter weather in December, and why are polar regions colder than the equator?
options: A. Earth's orbit brings the planet 50 million miles closer to the sun every June and farther away in December.

B. Earth's rotational axis is tilted 23.5 degrees relative to its orbital plane, causing sunlight to strike the equator nearly perpendicularly year-round while striking the poles at a low oblique angle and tilting the Northern Hemisphere toward the sun in June.
C. The sun burns hotter in July and cools down in January on a 12-month solar cycle.
D. Ocean currents reverse direction every six months when the moon crosses the equator.
choices: A. Earth's orbit brings the planet 50 million miles closer to the sun every June and farther away in December.

B. Earth's rotational axis is tilted 23.5 degrees relative to its orbital plane, causing sunlight to strike the equator nearly perpendicularly year-round while striking the poles at a low oblique angle and tilting the Northern Hemisphere toward the sun in June.
C. The sun burns hotter in July and cools down in January on a 12-month solar cycle.
D. Ocean currents reverse direction every six months when the moon crosses the equator.
quiz_item.correct_answer: B. Earth's rotational axis is tilted 23.5 degrees relative to its orbital plane, causing sunlight to strike the equator nearly perpendicularly year-round while striking the poles at a low oblique angle and tilting the Northern Hemisphere toward the sun in June.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (B): Earth's 23.5-degree axial tilt—not distance from the sun—governs solar incidence angle and day length across latitudes and seasons (p. 21).

requirements.lead_text: Do ONE of the following:
requirements.req_text: Do ONE of the following: (a) Make one of the following instruments: wind vane, anemometer, rain gauge, or hygrometer. Keep a daily weather log for one week using information from this instrument as well as from other sources such as local radio and television stations, NOAA Weather Radio All Hazards, and internet sources (with your parent or guardian's permission). Record the following information at the same time every day: wind direction and speed, temperature, precipitation, and types of clouds. Be sure to make a note of any morning dew or frost. In the log, also list the weather forecasts from radio or television at the same time each day and show how the weather really turned out. (b) Visit a National Weather Service office or talk with a local radio or television weathercaster, private meteorologist, local agricultural extension service officer, or university meteorology instructor. Find out what type of weather is most dangerous or damaging to your community. Determine how severe weather and flood warnings reach the homes in your community.

pamphlet_excerpts: Measuring and Recording the Weather The most obvious way to study the weather is to observe actual events and keep a record of what you see (p. 61).
Measuring and Recording the Weather Principle 2: Daily observations of temperature, wind, pressure, clouds, and rainfall can help you understand how the atmosphere behaves (p. 61).
Measuring and Recording the Weather Principle 3: Keep a daily weatherlog, similar to the one shown, for at least aweek (p. 61).
Measuring and Recording the Weather Principle 4: If possible, record observations for amonth (p. 61).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Measuring and Recording the Weather): You can obtain readings from your owninstruments, from local television or radio, and from internet sites devoted to meteorology (p. 61).
Step 2 (Measuring and Recording the Weather): By comparing readings from day to day, you can see how the various weather elements change at your location in response to passing weather (p. 61).
Step 3 (Measuring and Recording the Weather): Keep a 30-day record based on local weather forecasts and your own observations (p. 61).
Step 4 (Measuring and Recording the Weather): Make and record observations at the same time each day (p. 61).

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: When building and siting a thermometer, barometer, or rain gauge for your Requirement 10 daily weather observation log, what instrument placement rule ensures accurate readings?
quiz_item.question: When building and siting a thermometer, barometer, or rain gauge for your Requirement 10 daily weather observation log, what instrument placement rule ensures accurate readings?
options: A. Mount the thermometer in direct afternoon sunlight against a dark brick wall and place the rain gauge directly beneath a leafy maple tree.

B. Mount the thermometer in a ventilated, shaded shelter away from heat-radiating surfaces, and place the rain gauge in an open, level area at least twice as far from trees or buildings as those obstacles are tall.
C. Keep the rain gauge and wind vane inside an enclosed garage so wind cannot tip them over.
D. Record your 30-day weather log from memory on the final day instead of taking daily measurements at a consistent time.

quiz_item.question: During your 5-minute outdoor weather safety talk to your troop (Requirement 11), you explain safety rules for lightning, flash floods, and tornadoes. Which protocol is accurate?
options: A. Apply the 30/30 lightning rule (shelter when thunder follows flash within 30 seconds; wait 30 minutes after last thunder), move immediately to higher ground during flash-flood warnings ('Turn Around, Don't Drown'), and shelter in an interior basement or lowest-floor room away from windows during a tornado.
B. Lightning cannot strike unless rain is actively falling directly overhead, so clear-air thunder more than 10 seconds away is harmless.
C. During a tornado warning in the backcountry, climb to the highest exposed ridge to watch the funnel cloud.
D. If caught in a flash flood while driving to camp, drive faster through flooded low-water crossings to beat rising water.
choices: A. Apply the 30/30 lightning rule (shelter when thunder follows flash within 30 seconds; wait 30 minutes after last thunder), move immediately to higher ground during flash-flood warnings ('Turn Around, Don't Drown'), and shelter in an interior basement or lowest-floor room away from windows during a tornado.
B. Lightning cannot strike unless rain is actively falling directly overhead, so clear-air thunder more than 10 seconds away is harmless.

B. Apply the 30/30 lightning rule: immediately descend off the exposed ridge and away from tall isolated trees or water, move into lower dense timber or a substantial building, and spread patrol members at least 50 feet apart if caught in the open.
C. Huddle together in a tight circle on top of metal-frame backpacks.
D. Lie flat on wet granite at the summit so the wind blows over the patrol.
choices: A. Stay on the ridgeline under a tall isolated pine tree to keep dry until the rain passes.

B. Apply the 30/30 lightning rule: immediately descend off the exposed ridge and away from tall isolated trees or water, move into lower dense timber or a substantial building, and spread patrol members at least 50 feet apart if caught in the open.
C. Huddle together in a tight circle on top of metal-frame backpacks.

patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: B. Apply the 30/30 lightning rule: immediately descend off the exposed ridge and away from tall isolated trees or water, move into lower dense timber or a substantial building, and spread patrol members at least 50 feet apart if caught in the open.
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (B): Sound travels about 1 mile every 5 seconds; a 10-second flash-to-bang interval means lightning is within 2 miles and already in strike range, requiring immediate descent from ridges and avoidance of tall isolated objects.

patrol_quiz_bank.question: Your patrol is camping when the NOAA Weather Radio broadcasts a 'Tornado Warning' for your county, versus a 'Tornado Watch' issued two hours earlier. What is the critical difference and required action?

B. A Watch means atmospheric conditions favor severe thunderstorm and tornado development (stay alert and prepared); a Warning means hazardous weather or a tornado is imminent or occurring on radar/ground (take immediate shelter now).
C. Both Watch and Warning mean the storm has already passed your campsite and outdoor activities can resume.
D. Wait until you see hail larger than golf balls before checking your family or troop emergency shelter plan.

B. A Watch means atmospheric conditions favor severe thunderstorm and tornado development (stay alert and prepared); a Warning means hazardous weather or a tornado is imminent or occurring on radar/ground (take immediate shelter now).
C. Both Watch and Warning mean the storm has already passed your campsite and outdoor activities can resume.
D. Wait until you see hail larger than golf balls before checking your family or troop emergency shelter plan.
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: B. A Watch means atmospheric conditions favor severe thunderstorm and tornado development (stay alert and prepared); a Warning means hazardous weather or a tornado is imminent or occurring on radar/ground (take immediate shelter now).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: Looking at a surface weather map (Requirement 4), your patrol sees a blue line with triangles pointing southeast advancing toward a warm, humid air mass. What frontal system is approaching and what weather should the troop expect?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: Looking at a surface weather map (Requirement 4), your patrol sees a blue line with triangles pointing southeast advancing toward a warm, humid air mass. What frontal system is approaching and what weather should the troop expect?
options: A. A warm front that brings several days of calm, cloudless skies and rising barometric pressure.

B. An advancing cold front where dense cold air wedges abruptly under warm moist air, forcing rapid vertical uplift, towering cumulonimbus clouds, gusty winds, and potential squall-line thunderstorms.
C. A high-pressure ridge where sinking air creates heavy blizzards and stationary fog.
D. A stationary pressure trough where wind stops completely and humidity drops to zero.
choices: A. A warm front that brings several days of calm, cloudless skies and rising barometric pressure.

B. An advancing cold front where dense cold air wedges abruptly under warm moist air, forcing rapid vertical uplift, towering cumulonimbus clouds, gusty winds, and potential squall-line thunderstorms.
C. A high-pressure ridge where sinking air creates heavy blizzards and stationary fog.
D. A stationary pressure trough where wind stops completely and humidity drops to zero.
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: B. An advancing cold front where dense cold air wedges abruptly under warm moist air, forcing rapid vertical uplift, towering cumulonimbus clouds, gusty winds, and potential squall-line thunderstorms.
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (B): Cold fronts (blue triangles) push dense cold air beneath lighter warm air, causing steep vertical lifting, rapid cumulus/cumulonimbus buildup, and sudden showers or thunderstorms followed by cooler, drier air (p. 29).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: During a summer afternoon thunderstorm (Requirement 5), your patrol observes jagged lightning bolts and half-inch hailstones. What physical mechanism inside a cumulonimbus cloud produces both hail and lightning?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: During a summer afternoon thunderstorm (Requirement 5), your patrol observes jagged lightning bolts and half-inch hailstones. What physical mechanism inside a cumulonimbus cloud produces both hail and lightning?
options: A. Gentle horizontal breezes blowing across flat stratus clouds below 2,000 feet.

B. Powerful vertical updrafts and downdrafts cycling water droplets above and below the freezing level (accreting layered ice for hail) while colliding ice crystals and graupel separate electrical charges that discharge as lightning.
C. Direct solar radiation melting high-altitude cirrus clouds without any vertical air motion.
D. Ocean tides pulling warm air downward into a high-pressure center.
choices: A. Gentle horizontal breezes blowing across flat stratus clouds below 2,000 feet.

B. Powerful vertical updrafts and downdrafts cycling water droplets above and below the freezing level (accreting layered ice for hail) while colliding ice crystals and graupel separate electrical charges that discharge as lightning.
C. Direct solar radiation melting high-altitude cirrus clouds without any vertical air motion.
D. Ocean tides pulling warm air downward into a high-pressure center.
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: B. Powerful vertical updrafts and downdrafts cycling water droplets above and below the freezing level (accreting layered ice for hail) while colliding ice crystals and graupel separate electrical charges that discharge as lightning.
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (B): Strong updrafts in cumulonimbus clouds suspend and cycle freezing droplets into layered hailstones while collisions between ice crystals and soft hail (graupel) build high-voltage charge separation that arcs as lightning (p. 34).

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: Why must a welder wear a properly shaded welding helmet (such as Shade 10 to 13 for arc welding) and flame-resistant leather or heavy cotton clothing rather than synthetic polyester or fleece?
quiz_item.question: Why must a welder wear a properly shaded welding helmet (such as Shade 10 to 13 for arc welding) and flame-resistant leather or heavy cotton clothing rather than synthetic polyester or fleece?
options: A. The welding arc emits intense ultraviolet and infrared radiation that causes painful corneal flash burns ('arc eye') and skin burns, while sparks and hot slag can melt synthetic fabrics directly into the skin.
B. A clear plastic face shield blocks all ultraviolet arc rays, and polyester fleece reflects molten spatter better than leather.
C. Welding helmets are only needed to keep smoke out of your eyes, and synthetic gym shorts keep the welder cool during overhead passes.
D. Sunglasses provide enough shade protection for MIG and stick welding as long as you squint during the strike.
choices: A. The welding arc emits intense ultraviolet and infrared radiation that causes painful corneal flash burns ('arc eye') and skin burns, while sparks and hot slag can melt synthetic fabrics directly into the skin.
B. A clear plastic face shield blocks all ultraviolet arc rays, and polyester fleece reflects molten spatter better than leather.
C. Welding helmets are only needed to keep smoke out of your eyes, and synthetic gym shorts keep the welder cool during overhead passes.
D. Sunglasses provide enough shade protection for MIG and stick welding as long as you squint during the strike.
quiz_item.correct_answer: A. The welding arc emits intense ultraviolet and infrared radiation that causes painful corneal flash burns ('arc eye') and skin burns, while sparks and hot slag can melt synthetic fabrics directly into the skin.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (A): An electric welding arc produces intense UV and IR radiation that burns unprotected retinas and corneas in seconds, and hot slag ignites or melts synthetic fabrics like nylon or polyester onto skin.

requirements.lead_text: After successfully completing requirements 1 through 5, use the equipment you prepared for the welding process in 5(b) to do the following:
requirements.req_text: After successfully completing requirements 1 through 5, use the equipment you prepared for the welding process in 5(b) to do the following: (a) Using a metal scribe or soapstone, sketch your initial onto a metal plate, and weld a bead on the plate following the pattern of your initial. (b) Cover a small plate (approximately 3" x 3" x 1/4") with weld beads side by side. (c) Tack two plates together in a square groove butt joint. pamphlet_excerpts: Multi-Process Welding Shop Projects: Welding for the Novice When you are ready to close down the equipment, turn off the torch oxygen valve; then, turn off the fuel valve (p. 71).
Multi-Process Welding Shop Projects Principle 2: Close the cylinder valves, then open the torch oxygen valve to allow the oxygen to drain, and close the torch oxygen valve (p. 71).
Multi-Process Welding Shop Projects Principle 3: Release the adjusting screw on the oxygen regulator (p. 71).
Multi-Process Welding Shop Projects Principle 4: Open the torch-fuel valve to drain fuel gas, and then close (p. 71).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Multi-Process Welding Shop Projects): Release the adjusting screw on the fuel-gas regulator (p. 71).
Step 2 (Multi-Process Welding Shop Projects): Common joints are butt joints, T-joints, and lap joints (p. 71).
Step 3 (Multi-Process Welding Shop Projects): Welded joints are designed primarily on the basis of the strength and safety required of the weldment (p. 71).
Step 4 (Multi-Process Welding Shop Projects): Thicker members normally require some edge preparation to allow puddle to reach the point where the weld metal must be deposited (p. 71).

patrol_quiz_bank.question: Why must a welder wear a properly shaded welding helmet (such as Shade 10 to 13 for arc welding) and flame-resistant leather or heavy cotton clothing rather than synthetic polyester or fleece?
options: A. The welding arc emits intense ultraviolet and infrared radiation that causes painful corneal flash burns ('arc eye') and skin burns, while sparks and hot slag can melt synthetic fabrics directly into the skin.
B. A clear plastic face shield blocks all ultraviolet arc rays, and polyester fleece reflects molten spatter better than leather.
C. Welding helmets are only needed to keep smoke out of your eyes, and synthetic gym shorts keep the welder cool during overhead passes.
D. Sunglasses provide enough shade protection for MIG and stick welding as long as you squint during the strike.
choices: A. The welding arc emits intense ultraviolet and infrared radiation that causes painful corneal flash burns ('arc eye') and skin burns, while sparks and hot slag can melt synthetic fabrics directly into the skin.
B. A clear plastic face shield blocks all ultraviolet arc rays, and polyester fleece reflects molten spatter better than leather.
C. Welding helmets are only needed to keep smoke out of your eyes, and synthetic gym shorts keep the welder cool during overhead passes.
D. Sunglasses provide enough shade protection for MIG and stick welding as long as you squint during the strike.
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: A. The welding arc emits intense ultraviolet and infrared radiation that causes painful corneal flash burns ('arc eye') and skin burns, while sparks and hot slag can melt synthetic fabrics directly into the skin.
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (A): An electric welding arc produces intense UV and IR radiation that burns unprotected retinas and corneas in seconds, and hot slag ignites or melts synthetic fabrics like nylon or polyester onto skin.

requirements.lead_text: Do the following:
requirements.req_text: Do the following: (a) Explain to your counselor the most likely hazards you may encounter while participating in whitewater activities, including branches and trees in water along a shore and stretching across the stream, rocks, hydraulics over ledges or low-head dams, strong wind, low water or air temperature, and thunder and lightning storms. Explain what you should do to anticipate, help prevent, mitigate, and respond to these hazards. (b) Review with your counselor the prevention, symptoms, and first-aid treatment for the following injuries or illnesses that could occur while participating in whitewater activities: cold-water shock; hypothermia; head, neck, and back injuries; heat-related illnesses; sunburn; dehydration; blisters; bruises; cuts; sprains and strains; shoulder dislocation; and submersion injuries. (c) Discuss with your counselor the Scouting America Safety Afloat policy and the American Whitewater safety guidelines, including the use of helmet and life jackets.

pamphlet_excerpts: Hazards, First Aid & Safety: Cool the victim immediately through immersion with cold packs in the groin area and armpits (p. 21).
Hazards, First Aid & Safety Principle 2: Increase the body's fluid level by having a conscious victim sip water (p. 21).

Hazards, First Aid & Safety Principle 4: Shoulder dislocations are one of the most serious injuries associated with white water activities (p. 21).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Hazards, First Aid & Safety): A shoulder becomes dislocated when the ball at the end of the upper arm bone slips out of the socket at the shoulder (p. 21).
Step 2 (Hazards, First Aid & Safety): This can happen when a paddlerattempts a maneuver such as a high brace that involves reaching overhead to gain leverage with the paddle (p. 21).
Step 3 (Hazards, First Aid & Safety): Any stroke or maneuver in which the arm is fully extended and then rotated rearward so the elbow is behind the shoulder puts the shoulder joint (p. 21).
Step 4 (Hazards, First Aid & Safety): You can reduce the likelihood of such an injury by making sure you keep a slight bend in your elbows and by keeping your grip or upper hand (p. 21).

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: If your canoe, kayak, or raft capsizes in moving whitewater rapids deeper than knee height, why must you never attempt to stand up on the riverbed?
quiz_item.question: If your canoe, kayak, or raft capsizes in moving whitewater rapids deeper than knee height, why must you never attempt to stand up on the riverbed?
options: A. Standing up scares downstream paddlers into dropping their throw bags.
B. River rocks are too slippery to push your boat upstream against the current.
C. Standing upright causes your life jacket to lose buoyancy when splashed.

D. Your foot can wedge between rocks on the riverbed while the force of the current pushes your body downstream and holds your head underwater (foot entrapment); instead, float on your back with feet up and pointed downstream.
choices: A. Standing up scares downstream paddlers into dropping their throw bags.
B. River rocks are too slippery to push your boat upstream against the current.
C. Standing upright causes your life jacket to lose buoyancy when splashed.

D. Your foot can wedge between rocks on the riverbed while the force of the current pushes your body downstream and holds your head underwater (foot entrapment); instead, float on your back with feet up and pointed downstream.
quiz_item.correct_answer: D. Your foot can wedge between rocks on the riverbed while the force of the current pushes your body downstream and holds your head underwater (foot entrapment); instead, float on your back with feet up and pointed downstream.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (D): Foot entrapment in swift current is a deadly whitewater hazard; swimmers must assume the defensive whitewater swim position on their back with feet at the surface pointed downstream to fend off rocks until reaching an eddy.

pamphlet_excerpts: Ferrying Upstream and Downstream: Upstream (forward) ferries and downstream (back) ferries move you sideways across the current (p. 30).
Ferrying Upstream and Downstream Principle 2: In an upstream ferry, you face upstream and paddle forward with your bow at an angle to the current (p. 30).
Ferrying Upstream and Downstream Principle 3: You move across the current in the direction your bowis pointing (p. 30).
Ferrying Upstream and Downstream Principle 4: To perform a downstream ferry, you face downstream and back paddle with your stern pointed upstream at an angle to the current (p. 30).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Ferrying Upstream and Downstream): You move across the current in the direction your stern is facing (p. 30).
Step 2 (Ferrying Upstream and Downstream): To perform a successful upstream ferry, begin by turning your boat until it faces upstream (p. 30).
Step 3 (Ferrying Upstream and Downstream): As you start paddling, adjust the ferry angle, the angle of the boat compared to the upstream, to about 10 degrees (p. 30).
Step 4 (Ferrying Upstream and Downstream): If you are moving out of an eddy into the current, enter the current as if you were doing a peel out by exiting the eddy at about a 45-degree angle (p. 30).

pamphlet_excerpts: White water Swimmer and Boating Prerequisites: Canoeists and kayakers use backstrokes to back paddle, that is, to slow or reverse the forward motion of the boat (p. 56).
White water Swimmer and Boating Prerequisites Principle 2: As you paddle downstream, you will want to stop in an eddy to rest or to scout a rapid below (p. 56).
White water Swimmer and Boating Prerequisites Principle 3: The maneuver to enter an eddy while heading downstream is called an eddy turn (p. 56).
White water Swimmer and Boating Prerequisites Principle 4: Later you will learn how to exit an eddy using a peel (p. 56).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (White water Swimmer and Boating Prerequisites): When you have learned how to move in and out of eddies with confidence and ease, you will have passed a major white water skills milestone (p. 56).
Step 2 (White water Swimmer and Boating Prerequisites): Entering an eddy while moving downstream in a boat can be challenging, especially if the current is fast (p. 56).
Step 3 (White water Swimmer and Boating Prerequisites): The three important components of an eddy turn are angle, speed, and edge or tilt (p. 56).
Step 4 (White water Swimmer and Boating Prerequisites): Aim the bow so it crosses the eddy line as close as possible to the top of the eddy (p. 56).

pamphlet_excerpts: Tandem Canoeist / Solo Canoeist / Solo Kayaker: In the peel out, note how both paddlers use their left knees to lean into and tilt the boat into the turn (p. 50).
Tandem Canoeist / Solo Canoeist / Solo Kayaker Principle 2: An offside peel out incorporates all the same features of the on side peel out except that the turning strokes are different (p. 50).
Tandem Canoeist / Solo Canoeist / Solo Kayaker Principle 3: For kayakers, the opposite paddle blade is used for the turning stroke (p. 50).
Tandem Canoeist / Solo Canoeist / Solo Kayaker Principle 4: After crossing the eddy line, solo canoeists can use avariety of turning strokes, including a forward sweep or crossbow draw (p. 50).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Tandem Canoeist / Solo Canoeist / Solo Kayaker): Tandem canoeists use a combination of a cross-bowdraw in the bow while the stern paddler does a low bracing reverse sweep or simply powers (p. 50).
Step 2 (Tandem Canoeist / Solo Canoeist / Solo Kayaker): The paddle shaft should be vertical and move in a path 2 to 3 feet long next to the side of the boat (p. 50).
Step 3 (Tandem Canoeist / Solo Canoeist / Solo Kayaker): Angle the blade at 45 degrees, as if you were spreading butter on a slice of bread, and move the paddle from side to side (p. 50).
Step 4 (Tandem Canoeist / Solo Canoeist / Solo Kayaker): At the end of each stroke, move the blade back in the opposite direction with the forward edge (p. 50).

Step 3 (International Scale of River Difficulty): Step 3 (Explain The International Scale): The International Scale of River Difficulty provides a standardized classification system for rating the difficulty and risks in running rapids (p. 34).

Step 4 (International Scale of River Difficulty): Step 4 (Explain The International Scale): River runners use the scale as a rough but useful means of comparing the difficulty of one river with another (p. 34).

pamphlet_excerpts: Importance of Communication: Remember: River right an driver left always refer to the right side or the left side of the river as if you were facing downstream (p. 33).
Importance of Communication Principle 2: Teammates should discuss their run on an ongoing basis and make adjustments to any plan as needed (p. 33).
Importance of Communication Principle 3: Even as mall riffle can muffle words, and roaring rapids often drownout speech altogether (p. 33).
Importance of Communication Principle 4: For emergencies or times when talk is difficult, river runners make use of whistles and paddle signals to communicate (p. 33).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Importance of Communication): Review river signals before the beginning of every trip (p. 33).
Step 2 (Importance of Communication): To respond that you are OK to someone signaling you, return the same signal (p. 33).
Step 3 (Importance of Communication): The time of year, fallen trees, and rainfall are just several elements that can transform a normally safe route into adangerous one (p. 33).
Step 4 (Importance of Communication): Always scout ahead, plan your run, and identify several options in case your run does not goas planned (p. 33).

pamphlet_excerpts: Ability to Read A Class: Your ability to read a Class: Before you set foot in your boat, take the time to learn as much as you can about the stretch of river you will be running (p. 26).
Ability to Read A Class Principle 2: Your ability to read a Class Principle 2: Find out about the river's unique features and hazards and identify what class of rapids you will be dealing (p. 26).
Ability to Read A Class Principle 3: Your ability to read a Class Principle 3: If possible, scout your route to avoid unpleasant and potentially dangerous surprises (p. 26).
Ability to Read A Class Principle 4: Your ability to read a Class Principle 4: When scouting ariver, be sure to wear your helmet (p. 26).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Ability to Read A Class): Step 1 (Your ability to read a Class): The term white water refers to a stretch of swiftly moving water that becomes white and foamy as it passes over or around obstacles (p. 26).
Step 2 (Ability to Read A Class): Step 2 (Your ability to read a Class): A rapid is a turbulent, fast-flowing stretch of river that contains obstructions above or below the water (p. 26).
Step 3 (Ability to Read A Class): Step 3 (Your ability to read a Class): Rapids may feature drops in which the water abruptly descends over rocks or a ledge (p. 26).
Step 4 (Ability to Read A Class): Step 4 (Your ability to read a Class): Current describes the continuous movement of water in a certain direction (p. 26).

requirements.lead_text: Wearing a proper life jacket and being appropriately dressed for the weather and water conditions, perform the following skills in moving water in a properly equipped whitewater craft of your choice (tandem canoe, solo canoe, or solo kayak). If a tandem canoe is used, the skills must be demonstrated from both the bow and stern positions.
requirements.req_text: Wearing a proper life jacket and being appropriately dressed for the weather and water conditions, perform the following skills in moving water in a properly equipped whitewater craft of your choice (tandem canoe, solo canoe, or solo kayak). If a tandem canoe is used, the skills must be demonstrated from both the bow and stern positions. (a) Launch and land. (b) Paddle forward in a straight line at least 10 boat lengths. (c) Backpaddle in a straight line at least five boat lengths. (d) Ferry upstream from both sides of the river. (e) Ferry downstream from both sides of the river. (f) Eddy turn from both sides of an eddy. (g) Peel out from both sides of an eddy.

pamphlet_excerpts: Wearing a proper life jacket: Upstream (forward) ferries and downstream (back) ferries move you sideways across the current (p. 46).
Wearing a proper life jacket Principle 2: In an upstream ferry, you face upstream and paddle forward with your bow at an angle to the current (p. 46).
Wearing a proper life jacket Principle 3: You move across the current in the direction your bowis pointing (p. 46).
Wearing a proper life jacket Principle 4: To perform a downstream ferry, you face downstream and back paddle with your stern pointed upstream at an angle to the current (p. 46).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Wearing a proper life jacket): You move across the current in the direction your stern is facing (p. 46).
Step 2 (Wearing a proper life jacket): To perform a successful upstream ferry, begin by turning your boat until it faces upstream (p. 46).
Step 3 (Wearing a proper life jacket): As you start paddling, adjust the ferry angle, the angle of the boat compared to the upstream, to about 10 degrees (p. 46).
Step 4 (Wearing a proper life jacket): If you are moving out of an eddy into the current, enter the current as if you were doing a peel out by exiting the eddy at about a 45-degree angle (p. 46).

pamphlet_excerpts: Using a Throw Rope to Rescue Others As you will recall, a throw rope is a floating rope that is stored in a throw bag (p. 71).
Using a Throw Rope to Rescue Others Principle 2: The rope will pay out neatly when the bagis tossed (p. 71).

Using a Throw Rope to Rescue Others Principle 3: A throw bag or a neatly coiled throw rope should always be secured in your craft so that it will be handy in a rescue situation but is not an entrapment (p. 71).
Using a Throw Rope to Rescue Others Principle 4: Allow the remainder of the rope to stay in the bag (p. 71).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Using a Throw Rope to Rescue Others): Be sure that the mouth of the bag is only halfway open (p. 71).
Step 2 (Using a Throw Rope to Rescue Others): Step 2, Get the attention of the person in the water by yelling, "Rope!" or giving a single blast of your whistle (p. 71).
Step 3 (Using a Throw Rope to Rescue Others): Step 3, Grasp or step on the freeend of the rope and toss the bag at the swimmer (p. 71).
Step 4 (Using a Throw Rope to Rescue Others): Ifyou miss, quickly restuff the bagor make arm-length coils of rope and try again (p. 71).

requirements.lead_text: Participate in one or more whitewater trips using either a canoe or kayak on a Class I and/or Class II river. The trip(s) must involve at least six hours of paddling time. For each trip:
requirements.req_text: Participate in one or more whitewater trips using either a canoe or kayak on a Class I and/or Class II river. The trip(s) must involve at least six hours of paddling time. For each trip: (a) Help to prepare a written plan, specifying the route (put-ins and takeouts), schedule, equipment, safety precautions, and emergency procedures. (b) Determine local rules and obtain permission from landowners and land managers in advance. (c) Explain what steps have been taken to comply with Scouting America Safety Afloat and the American Whitewater safety guidelines. (d) Show how to protect personal and group equipment from water and how to load and secure the containers in boats to be used in the trip. Execute the plans with other paddlers. (e) Explain to your counselor how well your plans worked for each trip taken.

patrol_quiz_bank.question: If your canoe, kayak, or raft capsizes in moving whitewater rapids deeper than knee height, why must you never attempt to stand up on the riverbed?
options: A. Standing up scares downstream paddlers into dropping their throw bags.
B. River rocks are too slippery to push your boat upstream against the current.
C. Standing upright causes your life jacket to lose buoyancy when splashed.

D. Your foot can wedge between rocks on the riverbed while the force of the current pushes your body downstream and holds your head underwater (foot entrapment); instead, float on your back with feet up and pointed downstream.
choices: A. Standing up scares downstream paddlers into dropping their throw bags.
B. River rocks are too slippery to push your boat upstream against the current.
C. Standing upright causes your life jacket to lose buoyancy when splashed.

D. Your foot can wedge between rocks on the riverbed while the force of the current pushes your body downstream and holds your head underwater (foot entrapment); instead, float on your back with feet up and pointed downstream.
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: D. Your foot can wedge between rocks on the riverbed while the force of the current pushes your body downstream and holds your head underwater (foot entrapment); instead, float on your back with feet up and pointed downstream.
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (D): Foot entrapment in swift current is a deadly whitewater hazard; swimmers must assume the defensive whitewater swim position on their back with feet at the surface pointed downstream to fend off rocks until reaching an eddy.

requirements.lead_text: Hazards and First Aid. Do the following:
requirements.req_text: Hazards and First Aid. Do the following: (a) Show or explain first aid for, and prevention of, injuries and conditions that could occur in backcountry settings, including: (1) Dehydration (2) Heatstroke (3) Hypothermia (4) Shock (5) Blisters (6) Eye injuries (7) Ankle and knee sprains (8) Bug bites of chiggers, ticks, mosquitoes, and biting gnats (9) Bee stings (10) Bites of spiders (11) Sting of a scorpion (12) Bite of a wild mammal (13) Bite of a venomous snake (b) Explain how the Scout Basic Essentials address hazards of survival situations and are basic to a survival kit. (c) Explain how a trip plan could help prevent a wilderness survival situation.

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: While hiking back from a peak at dusk, your buddy pair realizes you missed a trail junction and are no longer sure where the main trail is. Following the BSA S.T.O.P. survival protocol, what should you do?
quiz_item.question: While hiking back from a peak at dusk, your buddy pair realizes you missed a trail junction and are no longer sure where the main trail is. Following the BSA S.T.O.P. survival protocol, what should you do?
options: A. Run downhill through the woods before total darkness falls to look for a road.
B. Stop immediately in place, Think calmly without panic, Observe your surroundings/weather/daylight/gear, and Plan shelter and signaling while staying together so searchers can find you.
C. Split up and hike in opposite directions to cover twice as much ground.
D. Climb an exposed cliff face after dark to check for distant highway lights.
choices: A. Run downhill through the woods before total darkness falls to look for a road.
B. Stop immediately in place, Think calmly without panic, Observe your surroundings/weather/daylight/gear, and Plan shelter and signaling while staying together so searchers can find you.
C. Split up and hike in opposite directions to cover twice as much ground.
D. Climb an exposed cliff face after dark to check for distant highway lights.
quiz_item.correct_answer: B. Stop immediately in place, Think calmly without panic, Observe your surroundings/weather/daylight/gear, and Plan shelter and signaling while staying together so searchers can find you.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (B): Moving randomly after losing the trail increases search radius exponentially and risks injury after dark; staying put with S.T.O.P., shelter, and 3-signal distress calls maximizes rapid rescue.

pamphlet_excerpts: Avoiding Panic: Being Prepared as a Group Being Prepared as a Group Many people keep things to themselves (p. 21).
Avoiding Panic Principle 2: They don't want to hold up the team or are worried about what others will think of them (p. 21).
Avoiding Panic Principle 3: Remember, stopping for a few moments to deal with a hot spot on a heel can avoid bringing the group to a long halt later in the day when blisters break (p. 21).
Avoiding Panic Principle 4: Most important is how you think about things when you are confronted with a survival situation (p. 21).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Avoiding Panic): Many survivors of wilderness emergencies have said that a willingness to survive is the key factor in getting through a difficult situation (p. 21).
Step 2 (Avoiding Panic): You might assume that everyone has an equal desire to survive, but that is not always the case (p. 21).
Step 3 (Avoiding Panic): Some people will endure almost unbelievable conditions while others in much less difficult situations might simply give up and quit (p. 21).
Step 4 (Avoiding Panic): Make aconscious choice to be among those who can and will endure (p. 21).

step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Wet Forests): You might need to move a short distance to a meadow, stream bank, or other open area visible from an aircraft (p. 43).
Step 2 (Wet Forests): Consider your options carefully, though, before changing locations (p. 43).
Step 3 (Wet Forests): Mark your route clearly in case you need to find your way back (p. 43).
Step 4 (Wet Forests): Rest in a high, shady spot during the day, then complete necessary activities in the cool of the evening or early morning (p. 43).

pamphlet_excerpts: Fire Building: The importance of a fire means that you should spend plenty of time getting it right (p. 31).
Fire Building Principle 2: As with most survival skills, practicing when you are not in an emergency situation is the best way to become good (p. 31).
Fire Building Principle 3: It is especially important to practice using fire-lighting methods other than matches and lighters, a magnifying lens, flint and steel, and fire (p. 31).
Fire Building Principle 4: A good way to think about a campfire is to consider it a tool to be used for specific and important uses (p. 31).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Fire Building): If you come to thebackcountry prepared not to need a fire, carrying a stove and fuel, for example, you can make an informed choice (p. 31).
Step 2 (Fire Building): Be mindful of any temporary bans against open flames in the area (p. 31).
Step 3 (Fire Building): In a survival situation, you might not have a stove or the clothing and gear to stay warm without a fire (p. 31).
Step 4 (Fire Building): Even so, take time to build your fire in a manner that does not harm the environment (p. 31).

Signaling Lost Stranded Could Principle 4: Signaling Principle 4: Flares can be found on airplanes and in some watercraft and motor vehicles and can be effective if you have a rescue aircraft in sight (p. 36).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Signaling Lost Stranded Could): Step 1 (Signaling): They are visible for only a short time, though, so save them for the right moment (p. 36).
Step 2 (Signaling Lost Stranded Could): Step 2 (Signaling): Hanging brightly colored clothing or camping gear on tree branches can catch the rescuers' attention (p. 36).
Step 3 (Signaling Lost Stranded Could): Step 3 (Signaling): Flags, banners, and contrasting colors can be part of your signaling efforts (p. 36).
Step 4 (Signaling Lost Stranded Could): Step 4 (Signaling): If you can see rescuers, wave a shirt over your head or attach it to a pole and wave it as a flag (p. 36).

pamphlet_excerpts: 6. Drink Water: Drink Water It bears repeating: Drink plenty of water (p. 40).
6. Drink Water Principle 2: You can survive for days without food, but inhot weather without water, only hours (p. 40).
6. Drink Water Principle 3: Dehydration happens in cold weather, too, even though you may not feel as thirsty (p. 40).
6. Drink Water Principle 4: The best rule is to drink plenty of water, enough so that your urine is clear, whenever you arein the outdoors (p. 40).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (6. Drink Water): Ideally you will be able to find water where you are, from a lake, a stream, or melting snow, or by guiding rainwater down a tarp or tent fly (p. 40).
Step 2 (6. Drink Water): Water may have collected in depressions in rocks, in the crotches of trees, or in seeps along cliffs (p. 40).
Step 3 (6. Drink Water): The surest means of making your water safe is by boiling (p. 40).
Step 4 (6. Drink Water): Use a pot or other metal container on a stove or over a fire and bring the water to a full boil (p. 40).

B. Fuel, weather, and topography govern wildland fire behavior; LCES stands for Lookouts, Communications, Escape routes, and Safety zones.
C. Humidity, barometric pressure, and moonlight; LCES stands for Lighting, Containment, Evacuation, and Shelter.
D. Soil depth, tree height, and road width; LCES stands for Location, Compass, Elevation, and Slope.
choices: A. Oxygen, nitrogen, and carbon dioxide; LCES stands for Ladders, Chainsaws, Engines, and Sprinklers.
B. Fuel, weather, and topography govern wildland fire behavior; LCES stands for Lookouts, Communications, Escape routes, and Safety zones.

requirements.lead_text: Taking Action. Do ONE of the following:
requirements.req_text: Taking Action. Do ONE of the following: (a) Develop a fire readiness plan for a wildland area with which you are familiar. The plan should include a map showing available resources, water supplies, natural and manmade barriers, and access. The plan should discuss fuel loads, available fire apparatus, structure protection needs, values at risk, medical and evacuation considerations, and potential fire suppression tactics. (b) Visit with a state or federal forestry official or your local fire warden. Discuss the causes of and types of wildland fire that occur in your area. Discuss the prime fire season(s) in your area. Identify the agency responsible for wildland fire suppression in your area. Discuss what you learned with your counselor. (c) Conduct a Firewise assessment of a home or a building in the wildland-urban interface, which could include a Scout camp building or facility. Identify potential risks and fire hazards. With your counselor's approval, complete a project to reduce the wildfire risk and increase the preparedness of the building. Write a brief report about what you did and learned from the assessment and project. (d) Meet with a Fire Prevention Specialist or a local fire official to learn about fire prevention efforts in your community. From what you learned, prepare a fire prevention message (skit, video, or billboard concept) and share with your counselor and troop (or other group approved by your counselor). (e) Meet with a meteorologist or someone familiar with fire weather and discuss the fire weather concerns and typical fire seasons that exist in your area. Discuss the conditions that lead to a Fire Weather Watch or a Red Flag Warning. Discuss what you learned with your counselor.

requirements.lead_text: Apply Your Learning to a Real Event. Research an historic catastrophic wildland fire incident that occurred in the United States. Discuss with your counselor and/or your troop or a group approved by your counselor the conditions that led to the incident, how the incident was managed, and how the incident could have been prevented. Explain what lessons were learned and how this incident affected future fire suppression policy or suppression tactics.

pamphlet_excerpts: Hazards, First Aid & Safety: Prevention is the best way to avoid cuts, nicks, and other injuries (p. 15).
Hazards, First Aid & Safety Principle 2: However, as a Scout working with wood and knives, you should be prepared in the event of a cut or perhaps a splinter (p. 15).
Hazards, First Aid & Safety Principle 3: If you are injured, stay calm and let the adult in charge know what has happened (p. 15).

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: Why is a sharp carving knife safer than a dull blade when whittling or relief carving, and how should you protect your holding hand?
quiz_item.question: Why is a sharp carving knife safer than a dull blade when whittling or relief carving, and how should you protect your holding hand?
options: A. A dull blade slices through wood grain effortlessly, whereas a sharp blade requires you to push with your full body weight.
B. A sharp blade lets you carve directly toward your bare thumb without wearing any protective gear.

C. A sharp blade makes clean, controlled cuts with light pressure, whereas a dull blade binds in the wood and slips unexpectedly under heavy force; always carve away from your body and wear a cut-resistant glove and thumb guard.
D. You should pass an open carving knife blade-first to another Scout so they can test its sharpness immediately.
choices: A. A dull blade slices through wood grain effortlessly, whereas a sharp blade requires you to push with your full body weight.

quiz_item.correct_answer: C. A sharp blade makes clean, controlled cuts with light pressure, whereas a dull blade binds in the wood and slips unexpectedly under heavy force; always carve away from your body and wear a cut-resistant glove and thumb guard.

Step 3 (Different Woods Are Used): Some special cuts may require a craft knife, which holds various special shaped blades (p. 29).

Step 3 (Own or Select A Project): Step 3 (Plan your own or select): Pick a new shape and repeat this in the next square down, then all around the stick (p. 42).

pamphlet_excerpts: Simple Low-relief OR A Chip: Complete a simple low-relief: Very few tools are needed to create beautiful designs, so almost anyone can create a work of art after learning the basics. with your owndesigns (p. 55).
Simple Low-relief OR A Chip Principle 2: Complete a simple low-relief Principle 2: Be sure to firmly secure the staff with avise clamp before you start to work (p. 55).

Simple Low-relief OR A Chip Principle 3: Complete a simple low-relief Principle 3: The intricate designs of chip carving are created with a combination of simple shapes like triangles, diamonds, and squares (p. 55).

Simple Low-relief OR A Chip Principle 4: Complete a simple low-relief Principle 4: A triangle is formed with three cuts made diagonally toward a central point, which creates an insideout pyramid (p. 55).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Simple Low-relief OR A Chip): Step 1 (Complete a simple low-relief): Adding two cuts from a point outside one flat side creates a diamond (p. 55).
Step 2 (Simple Low-relief OR A Chip): Step 2 (Complete a simple low-relief): One cut from each side of a square makes a square pyramid (p. 55).
Step 3 (Simple Low-relief OR A Chip): Step 3 (Complete a simple low-relief): Any pattern that can be drawn with straight lines can be made into a chip carving design (p. 55).

Step 4 (Simple Low-relief OR A Chip): Step 4 (Complete a simple low-relief): Several different knives can be use din chip carving, including a skew chisel and a gouge, but a regular carving knife will work just fine (p. 55).

patrol_quiz_bank.question: Why is a sharp carving knife safer than a dull blade when whittling or relief carving, and how should you protect your holding hand?
options: A. A dull blade slices through wood grain effortlessly, whereas a sharp blade requires you to push with your full body weight.
B. A sharp blade lets you carve directly toward your bare thumb without wearing any protective gear.

C. A sharp blade makes clean, controlled cuts with light pressure, whereas a dull blade binds in the wood and slips unexpectedly under heavy force; always carve away from your body and wear a cut-resistant glove and thumb guard.
D. You should pass an open carving knife blade-first to another Scout so they can test its sharpness immediately.
choices: A. A dull blade slices through wood grain effortlessly, whereas a sharp blade requires you to push with your full body weight.
B. A sharp blade lets you carve directly toward your bare thumb without wearing any protective gear.

C. A sharp blade makes clean, controlled cuts with light pressure, whereas a dull blade binds in the wood and slips unexpectedly under heavy force; always carve away from your body and wear a cut-resistant glove and thumb guard.
D. You should pass an open carving knife blade-first to another Scout so they can test its sharpness immediately.
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: C. A sharp blade makes clean, controlled cuts with light pressure, whereas a dull blade binds in the wood and slips unexpectedly under heavy force; always carve away from your body and wear a cut-resistant glove and thumb guard.
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (C): Dull carving blades require excessive force and are much more likely to slip off the wood; keeping tools honed sharp, carving away from yourself, and wearing a thumb guard and cut-resistant glove prevent lacerations.

quiz_item.question: Before changing a blade or bit on a power saw, router, or drill press, and when feeding narrow stock past a spinning blade, what workshop safety rules must you follow?
options: A. Unplug the tool (or lock out the power switch) before touching the blade or chuck, wear safety glasses and hearing protection, inspect wood for nails or loose knots, and use a push stick to keep hands clear of the blade.
B. Leave the machine plugged in with your finger off the trigger while wrenching the arbor nut, and wear loose knit gloves to guide wood within an inch of the saw blade.
C. Remove the blade guard permanently so you can see the pencil line better, and reach behind a spinning table saw blade to pull off scrap pieces.
D. Stand directly in line with the table saw blade without eye protection so you can hold the board down if it starts to kick back.

pamphlet_excerpts: Timber is grown, harvested, and milled: Then workers called buckers lop off the limbs and slice the trunks into shorter lengths (logs) that are easier to handle (p. 14).
Timber is grown, harvested, and milled Principle 2: The logs are trucked, floated, or carried on railroads to asawmill (p. 14).
Timber is grown, harvested, and milled Principle 3: At the mill, logs are debarked (their bark is removed), and saws cut them into boards (lumber) (p. 14).
Timber is grown, harvested, and milled Principle 4: Small logs are often cut into boards in a single pass through a set of saws (a gang saw) that makes many cuts at once (p. 14).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Timber is grown, harvested, and milled): Large logs may make several passes through one saw (a headsaw) that slices off a board at a time until the whole log is cut into lumber (p. 14).
Step 2 (Timber is grown, harvested, and milled): The new lumber, called green lumber, is edged and trimmed to straighten the sides and cut into boards of standard lengths (p. 14).
Step 3 (Timber is grown, harvested, and milled): Lumber is graded for quality, appearance, and strength (p. 14).
Step 4 (Timber is grown, harvested, and milled): Manufacturers use them to make flooring, pallets, and similar products (p. 14).

Care Use and Storage Principle 2: Show The Proper Care Use Principle 2: Rough handling will nick and dull the cutting edges (p. 34).

Care Use and Storage Principle 3: Show The Proper Care Use Principle 3: Most wood-cutting tools have two wedge shapes on their cutting edge: the main or ground bevel, and the sharpening bevel (p. 34).
Care Use and Storage Principle 4: Show The Proper Care Use Principle 4: When you are sharpening an edge, you should be working off the sharpening bevel only, not the larger ground bevel (p. 34).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Care Use and Storage): Step 1 (Show The Proper Care Use): When sharpening a blade, start with a roughs tone, followed by (in this order and as needed) a medium, fine, and smooth stone (p. 34).
Step 2 (Care Use and Storage): Step 2 (Show The Proper Care Use): Whet the edge by pushing it forward over the stone (p. 34).

Step 3 (Care Use and Storage): Step 3 (Show The Proper Care Use): To finish, turn the blade over on Correct angle for sharpening the cutting its flat side and, keeping the back flatiron of a plane on the stone, push (p. 34).
Step 4 (Care Use and Storage): Step 4 (Show The Proper Care Use): Stoning both sides produces a little wiry burr on the edge (p. 34).

pamphlet_excerpts: Using a saw, plane, hammer, brace: A mortise and tenon joint has two parts: the mortise is a hole in one piece of wood, and the tenon is the part of the second piece that is cut and shaped (p. 60).
Using a saw, plane, hammer, brace Principle 2: Simply, this joint is "a square peg in a square hole." To start the mortise, drill the holes only as deep as you want the mortise (p. 60).
Using a saw, plane, hammer, brace Principle 3: Then use a sharp wood chisel to shave out any excess wood and square the corners (p. 60).
Using a saw, plane, hammer, brace Principle 4: To make the tenon, mark its depth and width on the end of the tenon piece (p. 60).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Using a saw, plane, hammer, brace): Use a backsaw to cut the tenon, making a series of straight, square cuts to remove excess wood (p. 60).
Step 2 (Using a saw, plane, hammer, brace): Think of "tenant", someone who dwells inside a place, to help you remember that the tenon (the peg) goes inside the mortise (the hole) (p. 60).
Step 3 (Using a saw, plane, hammer, brace): For requirement 6, you might choose aproject below, take an idea from a book or website listed in the resources section, or think (p. 60).
Step 4 (Using a saw, plane, hammer, brace): You have made several butt joints in your projects so far (p. 60).

(e) Help make wooden toys for children OR help carry out a woodworking service project approved by your counselor for a charitable organization.

pamphlet_excerpts: Working Drawings of A Project: Make working drawings of a project: A mortise and tenon joint has two parts: the mortise is a hole in one piece of wood, and the tenon is the part of the second piece that is cut and shaped (p. 62).

Working Drawings of A Project Principle 2: Make working drawings of a project Principle 2: Simply, this joint is "a square peg in a square hole." To start the mortise, drill the holes only as deep as you want the mortise (p. 62).
Working Drawings of A Project Principle 3: Make working drawings of a project Principle 3: Then use a sharp wood chisel to shave out any excess wood and square the corners (p. 62).
Working Drawings of A Project Principle 4: Make working drawings of a project Principle 4: To make the tenon, mark its depth and width on the end of the tenon piece (p. 62).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Working Drawings of A Project): Step 1 (Make working drawings of a project): Use a backsaw to cut the tenon, making a series of straight, square cuts to remove excess wood (p. 62).

Step 2 (Working Drawings of A Project): Step 2 (Make working drawings of a project): Think of "tenant", someone who dwells inside a place, to help you remember that the tenon (the peg) goes inside the mortise (the hole) (p. 62).

Step 3 (Working Drawings of A Project): Step 3 (Make working drawings of a project): For requirement 6, you might choose aproject below, take an idea from a book or website listed in the resources section, or think (p. 62).

Step 4 (Working Drawings of A Project): Step 4 (Make working drawings of a project): For optional requirement 6(e), your merit badge counselor or Scoutmaster may suggest a Good Turn that you and your buddies (p. 62).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: Before changing a blade or bit on a power saw, router, or drill press, and when feeding narrow stock past a spinning blade, what workshop safety rules must you follow?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: Before changing a blade or bit on a power saw, router, or drill press, and when feeding narrow stock past a spinning blade, what workshop safety rules must you follow?
options: A. Unplug the tool (or lock out the power switch) before touching the blade or chuck, wear safety glasses and hearing protection, inspect wood for nails or loose knots, and use a push stick to keep hands clear of the blade.
B. Leave the machine plugged in with your finger off the trigger while wrenching the arbor nut, and wear loose knit gloves to guide wood within an inch of the saw blade.
C. Remove the blade guard permanently so you can see the pencil line better, and reach behind a spinning table saw blade to pull off scrap pieces.
D. Stand directly in line with the table saw blade without eye protection so you can hold the board down if it starts to kick back.
